10041-the-rivet-in-grandfather-s-neck-a-:
James Branch Cabell, dedicating this 1915 novel to the new South, called it a comedy of limitations. Its ten parts run from propinquity and renascence through tertius, appreciation, and souvenir to byways, yoked, harvest, relics, and imprimis, tracing a life shaped by family and place.

Cabell writes about a South that values its high past as foundation for the work of each day, with irony and elegance. The rivet of the title binds a man to his grandfather's world, for better and worse. Readers get Cabell's polished, bittersweet comedy about inheritance, in his invented yet familiar Virginia.
10070-stories-of-great-americans-for-lit:
Edward Eggleston's 1895 book for little Americans aims, in his preface, to furnish young learners with reading matter that excites attention and gives pleasure. That makes lighter the hard task of learning to read. Disconnected lessons, he says, only increase the ruggedness.

Its stories, opening with a song from the suds, retell great Americans in short, vivid pieces for beginners. Eggleston, author of school histories, knew how to hold a child's ear. Young readers get American history as story, and teachers get a first reader with real content. The tales stay short enough for a beginner's patience.
10116-all-saints-day-and-other-sermons:
This volume of sermons takes its title from All Saints' Day and its epigraph from Wordsworth's Excursion, praising a priest whose zeal and sanctity would spread true religion over a joyful land. A prefatory note explains that the sermons could not be arranged in proper sequence.

Those on doctrine and the church seasons mostly come first, while practical subjects close the volume, and a few appeared earlier in Good Words. The sermons speak to faith, duty, and the Christian year. Readers get earnest, old-fashioned preaching, meant for Sundays and for quiet reading at home.
10325-the-gospel-of-the-pentateuch-a-set:
Charles Kingsley preached these parish sermons on the first five books of the Bible, known as the Pentateuch, for ordinary churchgoers. The sermons open with Genesis, taking the line that God created heaven and earth as the first truth a person must learn. Kingsley speaks as a pastor, not as a scholar in a study.

Each sermon draws a plain moral from an old text: where we are, how we got here, and how we should live. Creation, law, and human choice recur as themes, tied to daily conduct. Readers get warm, direct Victorian preaching that links the oldest Bible stories to present duty.
10326-david-five-sermons:
Charles Kingsley preached these five sermons on King David, the first four before the University of Cambridge. He presents David as an almost ideal king, trained first as a shepherd, then as captain of outlaws, and at last as ruler fighting toward a secure throne. The sermons treat character, not mere Bible story.

Kingsley shows David's weakness alongside his strength: tender to the weak, fierce against the greedy and proud. Shepherd skills become kingly care for a people. Readers get warm, plain Victorian preaching on leadership, courage, and the flaws that mark even a chosen king.
10345-domestic-manners-of-the-americans:
Fanny Trollope published this travel book in 1832, after sailing from London in November 1827 with her son and daughters to the mouth of the Mississippi. Trollope, mother of novelist Anthony Trollope, wrote sharp, often unflattering notes on American homes, churches, theaters, and talk. The book stirred anger in America and delight in Britain.

Chapters follow her from New Orleans and the Mississippi through Cincinnati and other towns, judging manners, food, and public life. Her eye is keen, her temper tart, and her detail rich. Readers get a famous, opinionated portrait of Jacksonian America, best read with its bias in mind.
10461-journals-of-australian-exploration:
Augustus Charles Gregory and Francis Thomas Gregory compiled these journals of Australian exploration, published at Brisbane in 1884. The brothers, both gold medalists of the Royal Geographical Society, explored the west, north, and center of a continent then still largely unknown. Their journals had appeared only in fragments, now out of print.

Expeditions from Swan River in 1846, from Perth in 1848, and to the Geraldine lead mine fill the early pages. The editors left old impressions unaltered, even where later knowledge corrected them. Readers get a primary record of Australian exploration, hard, detailed, and full of new country.
10479-our-churches-and-chapels-their-par:
A. Hewitson, writing as Atticus, published this critical history of every place of worship in Preston in 1869, reprinted from the Preston Chronicle. Hewitson treats parsons, priests, and congregations with genial humor, refusing to sit like a grandsire cut in alabaster. His aim is to make dry facts palatable.

Each sketch gives a church or chapel, its minister, its people, and its local flavor, with facts for the solemn and jokes for the gay. The book thus serves both as guide and as social comedy. Readers get a vivid, Victorian-era portrait of a Lancashire town at prayer.
10540-mother-carey-s-chickens:
Kate Douglas Wiggin published this family novel, opening with Nancy reading from The Water Babies about Mother Carey's chickens, small petrels hopping from wave to wave. Mother Carey herself, her children, and their broken circle form the heart of the tale. Wiggin writes with warmth, humor, and moral care.

Chapters follow the chickens, a common denominator, Nancy's idea, old beasts into new, and a knight of Beulah Castle. A flitting, a housewarming, and doors of daring carry the family toward hope. Readers get a beloved, old-fashioned story of a widowed mother and her lively children.
10593-great-possessions:
David Grayson wrote this country book on the great possessions of smell, taste, and simple living. Grayson, who lived for years in the country, says sight and hearing have seized the inheritance of the senses, while smell, like hairy Esau, comes late, hungry from the hills. His book is a fragrant autobiography of the earth.

Chapters treat the well-flavoured earth, good and evil odours, following your nose, green people, places of retirement, and a good apple. A trip to the city, an old stone mason, and an auction of antiques add variety. Readers get a gentle, sensory meditation on country life and what truly counts as wealth.
10613-the-theory-of-social-revolutions:
Brooks Adams published The Theory of Social Revolutions in 1913 after more than twenty years of study, and he insists he wrote for no party or passing cause. The book argues that capitalistic government was breaking down, and that courts in America had taken on a lawmaking role they were not meant to hold. Its first chapter had appeared in the Atlantic Monthly.

Later chapters weigh the limits of judges, the balance of social forces, and the rise of political courts. Adams writes as a historian of institutions, tracing long shifts rather than daily politics. Readers get a sober, early warning about the strain between democracy, wealth, and law in modern America.
10700-the-history-of-england-from-the-fi:
John Lingard's History of England, continued in this edition by Hilaire Belloc with an introduction by Cardinal Gibbons, runs from the Roman invasion to the reign of George V. This eighth volume of the eleven-volume 1912 edition covers the later career of Charles I. It treats Edge Hill, the treaty at Oxford, the Solemn League and Covenant, Marston Moor, and the trial and execution of Archbishop Laud.

Lingard writes Catholic history with care for documents and a steady narrative pace, and Belloc carries that approach forward. The volume suits readers following the English Civil War reign by reign. It offers a detailed, older account of king, Parliament, and army in the 1640s.
10777-probable-sons:
Amy LeFeuvre, author of Cherry and The Odd One, published Probable Sons in 1896 as a story of children and conversion. It opens with Sir Edward Wentworth groaning over an unwelcome legacy: children, and worse, a girl. Chapters titled "David and Goliath," "A Prodigal," "A Promise Kept," and "He Arose and Came to His Father" trace the change that follows.

The book takes its motto from Isaiah, "A little child shall lead them," and shows hard hearts softened by young lives. LeFeuvre writes for family readers, with a plain, earnest tone. The novel offers a Victorian tale of pride, repentance, and the power of a child's example.
10938-the-headsman-or-the-abbaye-des-vig:
James Fenimore Cooper set this 1833 tale, published here in an 1860 one-volume edition, around Lake Geneva in Switzerland. An American family travelling in Europe meets Jean Descloux, a boatman with wide knowledge, and the story moves toward the Abbaye des Vignerons, a winegrowers' festival at Vevey. Beneath the festival colour lies the secret of the local headsman, or executioner.

Cooper builds the plot around birth, shame, and inherited guilt, as a young woman's parentage and a condemned man's fate intertwine. Swiss scenery, lake travel, and festival crowds give the romance its setting. The novel shows Cooper working far from his American frontier, testing how old European customs of rank and punishment shape private lives.
11113-principal-cairns:
This volume of the Famous Scots Series tells the life of John Cairns, Scottish minister and principal, printed at Edinburgh by Morrison and Gibb. Cairns was born at Ayton Hill, in the parish of Ayton in east Berwickshire, on August 23, 1818. The farm no longer exists; only trees and nettles mark the site, perched where the valley of the Eye meets the Tweed.

Chapters follow ancestry and childhood, Dunglass, college days, the student of theology, Golden Square, the central problem, the apostle of union, Wallace Green, the professor, the principal. Cairns's hopes, the book says, were realised in theology, not philosophy, though his great book on the difficulties of Christianity was never finished. The biography gives a clear portrait of a leading Free Church divine.
11126-ten-girls-from-dickens:
Kate Dickinson Sweetser retold ten of Dickens's girl characters for young readers in this illustrated volume, following her Ten Boys from Dickens. The Marchioness, Morleena Kenwigs, Little Nell, the Infant Phenomenon, Jenny Wren, Sissy Jupe, Florence Dombey, Charley, Tilly Slowboy, and Agnes Wickfield each get a chapter, with pictures by George Alfred Williams.

The Marchioness opens the book, a small servant drudge in Sampson Brass's Bevis Marks office, discovered by Richard Swiveller on his first day as clerk. Jenny Wren later startles Fledgeby by fancying she saw him come out of his grave. Sweetser keeps Dickens's plots clear and his humour warm, giving children an entry to novels they may later read whole.
11227-ten-boys-from-dickens:
Kate Dickinson Sweetser's 1901 book retells ten of Dickens's boys for young readers: Tiny Tim, Oliver Twist, Tommy Traddles. Deputy, David Copperfield, Kit Nubbles, Jo the crossing sweeper, Paul Dombey, Pip, and the boys of Dotheboys Hall. Tiny Tim opens the set, pictured as a delicate, patient child whose smile the whole Cratchit family covets on Christmas Day. Each chapter isolates one boy's story from its novel.

Sweetser writes as an admiring guide, explaining Dickens's characters without retelling whole plots. Illustrations by George Alfred Williams accompany the text. The book works as a child's first meeting with Dickens, and as evidence of how his characters circulated separately from their novels in American homes.
1132-timon-of-athens:
Timon of Athens, a lord famed for lavish gifts, finds his friends vanish when his money runs out, and he flees to the woods to curse mankind and dig for roots. William Shakespeare's bitter tragedy, likely written with Thomas Middleton, follows Timon from bounty to misanthropy and a lonely death.

Gold, dug from the earth in his exile, only deepens his scorn, and his curses rain on flatterers, senators, and whores alike. The play is uneven and fierce, with great set speeches. It draws readers who like Shakespeare at his most savage about wealth and false friends.
11427-a-grandmother-s-recollections:
Ella Rodman's 1851 book A Grandmother's Recollections opens with a best bedchamber aired for a venerable visitor. while eight little brothers and sisters place themselves to be stumbled over by industrious damsels with brooms and dusters. Nursery maids have silenced refractory children with warnings that grandmother will make them behave, and the children almost expect an ogress in features and disposition. Their mother, eldest of two children, explains the old lady is dignified and exacts respect.

The narrator, whose inflammable temper flares at the least touch, resolves to accommodate herself to her grandmother's humors, with comic reluctance. Rodman's domestic tale follows the visit's misunderstandings and reconciliations. Readers of Victorian family fiction will find its nursery comedy and generational clash gently drawn.
11536-town-and-country-sermons:
A set of sermons for town and country readers opens in Passion Week, preached before the Queen on Philippians chapter two. Christ's obedience, his taking the form of a servant, and his death on the cross give the first sermon its key note.

Later sermons take up humility from First Peter, the loftiness of a lowly mind, and the safety of standing on God's side when the world stands against a person. The language is direct and practical, aimed at ordinary hearers rather than scholars, and each text is tied to daily conduct.
11665-collections-and-recollections:
George William Erskine Russell's Collections and Recollections, written at James Payn's suggestion, opens with a verse on Payn, the most genial of companions, who died 25 March 1898. The preface explains the book first appeared as papers by one who kept a diary.

Chapters cover links with the past, Lord Russell, and Lord Shaftesbury. Later pages turn to barons, viscounts, and the merging of the twenty-third Baron Dacre's title in a new viscountcy. Russell writes of bishops, heralds, and the historic sense, with anecdotes of men he knew. The book is a memoir of Victorian public life.
12286-flowers-and-flower-gardens-with-an:
David Lester Richardson, principal of the Hindu Metropolitan College in Calcutta, published Flowers and Flower-Gardens in 1855, with an appendix of practical instructions for the Anglo-Indian flower garden. Richardson, author of Literary Leaves, writes for gardeners in India and Britain.

The preface quotes Pope on regarding the writer end, and the book mixes flower lore with how-to advice. A mid-book tale tells of fairies who returned to tulips at dawn and took away their little ones. A good old woman kept her tulip bed as holy ground until a utilitarian gardener turned it to parsley. Richardson blends poetry, legend, and planting rules. The book shows Victorian gardening as both science and sentiment.
12326-the-story-of-my-life-recollections:
Ellen Terry, the great English actress, published The Story of My Life in 1908 with Doubleday, Page, illustrated from photographs by Albert Sterner. Terry, who dedicated the book to her daughter Edy, looks back on a stage career of sixty years.

Contents run from a child of the stage in 1848 to training with the Charles Keans, life in stock companies, and work with Rossetti, Bernhardt, and Henry Irving. A mid-book scene recalls Irving whispering get on during a trial scene while old Mead memory failed. Terry writes with warmth, humor, and theatrical gossip. The memoir is a first-hand record of Victorian theater, from provincial tours to the Lyceum at its height.
12390-a-few-practical-suggestions:
Logan Pearsall Smith wrote A Few Practical Suggestions as Tract Number Three of the Society for Pure English in 1920. The society stated its principles in a preliminary pamphlet, and this tract answers questions about applying them to special points.

Smith treats spelling, pronunciation, and word choice, arguing for forms that are English and etymologically correct. A mid-book passage notes that brave teachers of music would speak and write tamber, a form that would look peculiar for a month or two. The tract is a small, witty piece of language reform, favoring clarity over fashion. It shows the society program: purify English by reason, not by snobbery.
1242-unconscious-comedians:
Honoré de Balzac sketches Paris life through two young men from the provinces who try to make their way as writers and men about town. They meet journalists, actresses, clerks, and sharpers, each playing a comic part without knowing it, while Paris itself acts as the great stage.

Balzac writes the city in quick, vivid scenes, with his usual eye for money, clothes, and ambition. The tale is episodic and witty rather than a plotted novel. It suits readers who like Balzac's Paris in short, sharp glimpses. Balzac's Paris glimpses reward readers who enjoy witty, episodic tales.
12444-toaster-s-handbook-jokes-stories-a:
Peggy Edmund and Harold Workman Williams compiled this 1916 handbook of jokes, stories and quotations for toasters and toastmasters. Mary Katharine Reely introduces the collection. It opens on the possession of a sense of humour. Hazlitt is quoted: man alone laughs and weeps, struck by the difference between things as they are and as they ought to be.

Sections gather toasts, toastmasters and short pieces for after-dinner use, indexed for quick finding. Horace Walpole's line, that life is comedy to those who think and tragedy to those who feel, sets the tone. The book is a practical party aid, and a snapshot of Edwardian humour, ready to be lifted, quoted and retold.
12580-beneficiary-features-of-american-t:
James B. Kennedy's Johns Hopkins monograph, series twenty-six, numbers eleven and twelve, November-December 1908, studies benefit features of American trade unions. Kennedy, professor of political economy at Wells College, began the work as a graduate student, from studies of union work in the university's economic seminary since October 1902.

The study surveys benefit work of national and international unions, though it does not detail every form of mutual aid maintained. Administration, the sixth chapter in the contents, hints at the setup behind sick, death and out-of-work benefits. The monograph offers a scholarly snapshot of unions as mutual aid societies, before state welfare took their place.
12639-spanish-doubloons:
Camilla Kenyon's 1919 novel, Spanish Doubloons, illustrated by Louis Rogers, opens with an aunt errant and a letter descending like a bolt from the blue. The narrator, taking a vacation from Aunt Jane, finds life fair and smiling at that moment, before the letter changes everything.

Chapters promise Apollo and others, engaging the enemy, the isle of fortune, and a captain's legacy. A cave with two mouths, a rabbit's foot, an excursion and alarm, what Crusoe and I found, and an island queen's freight follow. A clue, secret diplomacy, dead hands, Cookie as hero and a bishop's chest close the hunt. Kenyon writes a light treasure adventure, with humour and romance. The novel offers a breezy hunt for Spanish gold, in a girl's adventurous voice.
1279-poems-and-songs-of-robert-burns:
Robert Burns, the ploughman poet of Ayrshire, sings Scotland in this gathering of his poems and songs: love lyrics, satires, drinking songs, and laments, in Scots and English alike. "Auld Lang Syne," "Tam o' Shanter," and "To a Mouse" all appear in his voice.

Burns writes with warmth, wit, and a democrat's heart, praising honest folk and mocking priests and lords. The poems range from tender to bawdy. The book gives the core of Burns in one volume, and it remains the best door into Scotland's national poet. Burns sings Scotland with warmth, wit, and a democrat's heart.
12855-elizabethan-sea-dogs-a-chronicle-o:
William Wood's 1918 chronicle celebrates Drake and his fellow Elizabethan sailors as the men who won England command of the sea. From Henry VIII's reign through Elizabeth's, English seamen pushed into Spain's New World, blazing a sea trail for colonists to follow. Life afloat in Tudor times, with its hardship and daring, fills the early chapters.

A vivid passage recalls Hawkins's overcrowded Minion, with three hundred men aboard a three-hundred-ton ship, and Drake's tiny Judith unable to give relief. Wood writes in a patriotic, storyteller's voice. The book suits readers who want sea adventure tied to the birth of Anglo-American history.
12900-poor-relations:
Honoré de Balzac's Poor Relations, in James Waring's translation with a study by George Saintsbury, centres on Cousin Betty, a poor relation whose resentments drive a great Paris novel. The dedication honours Don Michele Angelo Cajetani, learned commentator of Dante, who taught Balzac the framework of the Divine Comedy. Paris offices, salons, and lodgings form the stage.

A mid-book office scene finds Marneffe begging Baron Hulot for promotion, fearing mockery while the chief clerk holidays for a month. Balzac's web of money, desire, and revenge tightens around the Hulot family. The novel stands among his finest studies of envy and social climbing.
12925-the-world-s-best-poetry-volume-10-:
Volume ten of The World's Best Poetry, edited by Bliss Carman in 1904, gathers poetical quotations, with John R. Howard's essay After All, What Is Poetry? Howard notes that no generally accepted definition of poetry has ever been made, though all versifiers aim at it. Some definitions exclude great poets, others shut out undeniably poetic elements.

Quotations follow by theme, from Ulysses moaning round with many voices to Wordsworth's holy evening quiet as a nun, Suckling on expectation, and Shakespeare on wishing. The volume serves readers who want apt lines at hand. It closes the ten-volume series with a treasury of famous verse.
12937-out-with-gun-and-camera-or-the-boy:
Captain Ralph Bonehill's Boy Hunters volume four, Out with Gun and Camera, sends Snap, Shep, Whopper, and Giant into the mountains with rod, rifle, and camera. A circus boy's story, a cabin in the woods, rapids, deer, wildcats, bears, and a lion fill the chapters, with a collie joining the party. The preface promises adventures in field, forest, river, and lake.

Camp cooking gets its due: grouse tender and juicy earns Giant praise as a hotel chef, while partridge baked in mud is set by for later. The boys' enemies, the Spink crowd, return to stir trouble. The book offers wholesome outdoor adventure with a camera-age twist.
12976-early-israel-and-the-surrounding-n:
Rev. A. H. Sayce, professor of Assyriology at Oxford, wrote Early Israel and the Surrounding Nations in 1899. Chapters treat the Israelites, Canaan, nations of the south-east and north-east, Egypt, Babylonia and Assyria, with appendices. Israel's origin in Ur of the Chaldees, Abraham's journey, and kinship with Ishmaelites, Moab, Ammon, and Edom open the book.

Egypt's role as bondhouse, where Israel grew from family to people, anchors a later chapter, with Solomon's splendour modelled on Pharaohs' courts. Sayce blends Bible story with ancient Near Eastern history. The book suits readers of early Israelite history in its Victorian scholarly form.
1298-the-virginian-a-horseman-of-the-pla:
Owen Wister's novel gave the western its classic hero: the Virginian, a Wyoming cowboy of few words, good humor, and a fast gun. He loves Molly Wood, a schoolteacher from the East, and faces the rustler Trampas in a duel of honor. The tale moves from roundups to lynch law to a wedding.

Wister, a Harvard man who knew Wyoming well, writes the range with affection and a moral eye. The Virginian's code, his jokes, and his famous line about calling a man a name set the pattern for westerns to come. The novel remains the genre's founding book.
12986-the-card-a-story-of-adventure-in-t:
Arnold Bennett set this comic novel in Bursley, one of the pottery towns of Staffordshire, and built it around a clerk with more nerve than money. Denry Machin, born in a street of potbanks and cheap cottages, climbs by quick wit, bold bluffs, and a gift for turning mishaps to his own gain. The town itself, with its kilns, chapels, dances, and small-town pride, shapes every step he takes.

Denry's rise runs through a string of scrapes and schemes, from a furniture van sunk in a canal to gifts that win over his stern mother. He courts, dances, speculates, and talks his way past men with far more cash and standing. Bennett keeps the tone light, but the comedy rests on a sharp point: in a town that prizes respect, sheer cheek can open doors that birth and wealth keep shut.
13180-the-tracer-of-lost-persons:
R. W. Chambers's 1906 Tracer of Lost Persons opens with a thirty-three-year-old New Yorker, agreeable to look at, with rooms at the Lenox Club, a large income, and no profession. A pessimist before breakfast, he has decided he has seen all the attractive girls in the world and found them overrated. Chambers quotes Heraclitus: the harmony of the world, like a harp, is made of discords.

The hero becomes a tracer who finds lost persons, and clients crowd his office, where precedence rules like the army. A captain named Harren insists on seeing Mr. Keen at once, but is told millions of gentlemen wait ahead of him. The novel mixes romance, mystery, and New York comedy, with Chambers's usual flair for handsome heroes and tangled hearts.
13293-tales-of-the-five-towns:
Arnold Bennett's Tales of the Five Towns, first published in January 1905 and dedicated to Marcel Schwob, his literary godfather in France, gathers short stories in two parts. Part one, At Home, holds His Worship the Goosedriver, The Elixir of Youth, Mary with the High Hand, and The Dog. Part two, Abroad, holds the Hungarian Rhapsody, the Sisters Qita, and Clarice of the Autumn Concerts.

One tale opens on a deceitful December afternoon, with snow in confectioners' windows and Father Christmas smiling in Keats's Bazaar. Another turns on a will that leaves twenty guineas to a brother in forgiveness, and the rest to found a Beechinor bed at the infirmary. A third watches a sick child, Tommy, while neighbors crowd the window. Bennett's tales are sharp, local, and humane.
13294-food-for-the-lambs-or-helps-for-yo:
Charles E. Orr's Food for the Lambs, or Helps for Young Christians, reprinted 1980, is a small devotional book for new believers. Orr, author of Christian Conduct and The Gospel Day, keeps the book short on purpose, since a large book finds fewer readers. Selections from other writers cover spiritual declension, seeking first the kingdom, stirring the eagle's nest, and the little foxes, with poems at the close.

He writes that every saintly life is a sweet fragrance unto God, as a rose scents the evening air, while a sinful life is a stench in his nostrils. Later, he warns young Christians who keep company with the idle and frivolous, read books that do not foster piety, and tamper with temptation, losing a great safeguard of virtue. The book is plain, earnest, and pastoral.
1332-peter-pan-in-kensington-gardens:
Drawn from the Peter Pan chapters of The Little White Bird, this short book tells how a baby of seven days slips out of his nursery window. He flies back to Kensington Gardens. There he lives among birds and fairies, never grows older, and learns the ways of the gardens after dark.

Four linked episodes follow him to a thrush's nest and a tiny house built for a lost boy. They also show the strange hour of lock-out time, when the gates shut and the gardens belong to fairies alone. Told with gentle teasing humour, it is the first full telling of Peter before his later stage adventures.
1376-the-little-white-bird-or-adventures:
J. M. Barrie's tender, odd book tells how a lonely bachelor in London befriends a small boy named David and spins tales for him in Kensington Gardens. The narrator's fancy turns the gardens into a fairy world, and the boy David becomes the centre of games, stories, and small adventures.

Within these chapters Peter Pan first appears, as a baby who escapes to the gardens and never grows up. The book mixes whimsy with a grown man's longing for a child of his own. It is the seedbed of Peter Pan, and a strange, moving portrait of friendship between age and youth.
1402-where-the-blue-begins:
Christopher Morley's fable follows Gissing, a respectable dog bachelor living alone in the Canine Estates with his Japanese butler. Comfortable yet restless, Gissing slips his leash and sets out to find where the blue begins, the far edge of sky and freedom he has only dreamed about.

On the road he meets other dogs, human folk, and temptations to settle or turn back, and each meeting tests his resolve. The tale is gentle satire dressed as fantasy, poking fun at suburban comfort and safe lives. It ends as a small hymn to wandering, risk, and the wish to live free.
14139-new-tabernacle-sermons:
T. De Witt Talmage preached these sermons at the Brooklyn Tabernacle, collected in a first volume dated 1886. Titles run from Brawn and Muscle to the Pleiades and Orion, the Queen's Visit, and Castle Jesus. Each sermon takes a text and presses it toward daily conduct, with vivid images meant to hold a large city congregation.

Prayer receives plain, warm treatment. Talmage pictures God not as a despot on brazen lions but as a father in a bower, waiting for children to climb onto his knee. Grace comes like water drawn with a cup, or a blessing pulled down by a pulley. Later sermons warn late repenters: a sickroom infidel, brave for weeks, trembles at a teaspoon's fall and begs for a hymnbook verse. Earnest and theatrical, the volume shows Victorian pulpit power at full stretch.
14392-george-du-maurier-the-satirist-of-:
T. Martin Wood's 1913 study examines George du Maurier, the Punch cartoonist who also wrote the novel Trilby. Wood treats him as the chief visual satirist of late Victorian society.

Chapters survey du Maurier's world of drawing rooms, seaside resorts, and artistic bohemia, his technique in pen and wash, and his career as an author. Forty-one illustrations reproduce cartoons and sketches, some with the artist's own captions. The book argues that du Maurier's gentle mockery captured his age better than harsher caricature, and it remains a useful guide to his art.
14499-the-religions-of-india-handbooks-o:
Edward Washburn Hopkins, professor of Sanskrit at Bryn Mawr, wrote this 1896 handbook on the religions of India for Morris Jastrow's history of religions series. Hopkins dedicated it to William Dwight Whitney.

The volume traces Vedic religion, Brahmanism, Buddhism, Jainism, and Hinduism through texts and rites, with footnotes to the Brahmanas on gods, truth, and human conduct. Hopkins writes as a philologist, weighing scripture against practice. The handbook was a pioneering American survey, scholarly for its day, and it opened Indian religion to English-speaking students. Hopkins later taught at Yale as well as Bryn Mawr.
14714-half-portions:
Edna Ferber's 1920 short stories take their title from half measures in life: love, work and family given in part, not in full. Aunt Sophy, a stylish stout spinster of fifty in blue serge and health shoes, opens the volume as a study in independence that the world calls merely unmarried.

Later stories follow an April date kept as usual, Old Lady Mandle, a lesson in selfishness, a long-distance call, a farmer in the dell and dancing girls. Ferber writes with wit and a sharp eye for women's work, pride and compromise. Each tale is short, but its people stay whole: funny, stubborn and recognisable, even when life serves them less than they hoped.
14948-the-girl-at-the-halfway-house-a-st:
Emerson Hough's 1900 story of the plains, dedicated to Edward Kemeys, soldier, hunter and sculptor who knew and loved the West, moves from war to settlement. Book one, the day of war, gives brazen tongues, players of the game and a victory.

Book two, the day of the buffalo, brings Battersleigh of the rile Irish, the turning of the road, Edward Franklin the lawyer and a new world. A beginning, new movers, a chase, a battle and what the hand had to do follow, with pie and ethics and a first ball at Ellisville. Hough writes the plains as a place where a girl at a halfway house can shape a community.
14994-stories-from-the-greek-tragedians:
Alfred J. Church, author of Stories from Homer and Stories from Virgil, retells Greek tragedies for young readers, with twenty illustrations from designs by Flaxman and others, published by Dodd, Mead. His preface adds to the story of the seven chiefs against Thebes a single combat between Eteocles and Polynices from Euripides' Phoenissae.

Changes to the story of Ion make it more suitable for this book, and compression and omission are used freely throughout. Church asks indulgence from readers familiar with the great originals, calling his versions pale and ineffectual copies. Dedicated to his sons Alfred, Maurice, Herbert, Richard, Edward and Harald, the book opens tragedy to school readers without Greek.
15119-handy-dictionary-of-poetical-quota:
George Powers compiled this 1901 handy dictionary of poetical quotations as a ready reference to familiar lines of chief English poets, with a few Continental writers added. Less familiar modern selections appear too, in case they grow classic in time. A portrait of Longfellow fronts the book.

Powers notes that great poets have struck every chord of human feeling, often borrowing from predecessors, and that old ideas in new dress still please. Entries let a reader find a stanza for love, grief, hope, or duty without hunting through whole books. The dictionary still serves writers, speakers, and lovers of verse.
15156-balloons:
Elizabeth Bibesco's 1922 short story collection offers sixteen tales, each dedicated to a friend, from Clarence Day to Marcel Proust. Titles include Haven, Two Paris Episodes, Courtship, The Martyr, A Motor, and The Masterpiece, with Two Taxi Drives and A Touch of Spring near the end. Paris, London, and country houses set the scenes.

Bibesco writes of love, manners, and misunderstanding in polished, witty prose, with a keen eye for clothes, talk, and social nuance. Her stories are short, sharp, and modern in feeling. Readers who enjoy 1920s society fiction will find Balloons bright, clever, and full of period charm.
15266-what-peace-means:
Henry van Dyke's 1919 book treats peace in three sermons. The themes are peace in the soul, peace on earth through righteousness, and the power of an endless life. Van Dyke dedicates the book to his son in the faith and brother in the work. A text from John on Christ's peace opens the first sermon, with peace woven through both Testaments like a golden thread.

Van Dyke writes in the wake of war, when peace was the deepest desire of many hearts. Prophets, psalmists, and evangelists all point, he says, to Christ as prince of peace. Readers who like devotional prose will find the book gentle, hopeful, and suited to quiet reflection after conflict.
15338-more-toasts-jokes-stories-and-quot:
Marion Dix Mosher, librarian of the Genesee Branch in Rochester, compiled this 1922 book of more toasts, jokes, stories, and quotations, as a companion to a toaster's handbook. A note on the divine gift of humor opens the collection, calling humor a mystery pleasantly woven into daily life. The Wilson Company published it in New York.

Toasts for occasions, funny stories, and quotations for speeches fill the pages, with an index to find them fast. The book served hosts, speakers, and club members who needed a quick laugh or a apt line. Humor lovers will enjoy its period jokes, even where some now feel dated.
1536-timon-of-athens:
Timon of Athens opens with a rich lord showering gifts on flatterers, poets, and friends in Athens. When his money runs out, those friends vanish, and Timon, turned misanthrope, flees to the woods, where he digs up gold and curses mankind with magnificent, bitter poetry.

Beside him stands Apemantus, a cynic who warned him all along, and Alcibiades, a soldier wronged by the city. The play is uneven and possibly unfinished, but its rage is unforgettable. It is Shakespeare's fiercest satire on wealth, friendship, and the price of generosity without judgment.
1549-commentary-on-the-epistle-to-the-ga:
Martin Luther's Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, in Theodore Graebner's translation of the 1535 text, expounds Paul's letter verse by verse. Luther, the greatest name in the Reformation for its publisher, reads Galatians as the charter of justification by faith alone, against works, law, and human merit.

The commentary is vigorous, personal, and polemical, full of Luther's own struggles with conscience and with Rome. Its preface tells how the edition came to be at a publisher's suggestion in 1937. The book remains a classic of Protestant theology, and a window on Luther's mind at full stretch.
15573-judith-of-the-plains:
Marie Manning published this western novel in 1903 with Harper and Brothers. Twenty chapters follow Judith, postmistress of a prairie town, through encounters, trails, round-ups, and a ball. A frontispiece shows Peter's hand seeking hers, while her fear of the night's vague terrors speaks in her answering pressure.

The story opens in June, just past sunrise, in a sleeping car toiling like a snail over endless prairie, its air stale and its sleepers restless behind green-striped curtains. Later chapters bring Leander and his lady, a daughter of the desert, a horse-thief trail, a wolf hunt, and a land of red silence. Manning writes a plains romance of strong women, rough men, and wide country, with sentiment and adventure in turn.
15781-el-estudiante-de-salamanca-and-oth:
A school edition of Spanish romantic poetry by Jose de Espronceda, edited by George Tyler Northup of the University of Chicago. The title poem, El Estudiante de Salamanca, leads a set of other selections from Espronceda's work. Northup thanks fellow scholars for help, and notes that his wife Emily Cox Northup made most of the vocabulary. Ginn and Company issued the book for American students of Spanish.

Espronceda's student hero, a wild Don Juan figure, haunts Salamanca by night in search of a veiled lady. Ghosts, duels, and doomed love drive the poem's dark romance. Other pieces show Espronceda's range as Spain's leading romantic poet. Notes and a full vocabulary help readers meet the Spanish text with confidence, making the book both a poem and a classroom tool.
1583-options:
O. Henry's Options gathers stories of choice and chance, from The Rose of Dixie and The Third Ingredient to The Hiding of Black Bill and Buried Treasure. Schools and schools, supply and demand, and moments of waiting all turn on a twist, as clerks, outlaws, and lovers weigh one road against another.

The title points to the book's theme: life as a set of options, taken or missed, with a surprise waiting at the end of each. O. Henry's New York and Western voices mix here with his usual warmth. The collection is a fine late sample of his short-story art.
15932-the-literature-of-the-ancient-egyp:
A survey of Egyptian literature by E. A. Wallis Budge, Keeper of Egyptian and Assyrian Antiquities in the British Museum. J. M. Dent and Sons issued it in London in 1914. Budge, a scholar of Christ's College, Cambridge, opens with Thoth, god and author of Egyptian literature, and with writing materials. A frontispiece shows the Elysian Fields from the Papyrus of Ani.

Chapters treat hymns, tales, wisdom books, and funerary texts, with Ani reaping and ploughing in the other world. Budge translates and explains with a museum man's care. The book still guides readers through a vast, strange library: gods, kings, and scribes, speaking across three thousand years.
16064-carolina-chansons:
A book of poems by DuBose Heyward and Hervey Allen, called Carolina Chansons, legends of the Low Country. Heyward and Allen, poets of Charleston, sing the marshes, rivers, and folk of coastal Carolina. A transcriber's note leaves two spellings, Sewee and Seewee, as in the original. Poems that cross a page boundary stand as one stanza, unless structure clearly demands more.

Legends of the Low Country give the book its subtitle: Gullah voices, hunters, fishermen, and old plantations. The verse mixes dialect with lyric grace, honouring Black and white low-country life. Heyward's later Porgy grows from this soil. The book still sings as a regional classic: Carolina, in poems that smell of salt and pine.
16138-the-cromptons:
Mrs. Mary J. Holmes's popular novel The Cromptons, newly listed among her many successes, opens with a stranger at the Brock House and a palmetto clearing in the South. Part one follows Miss Dory, church services, Colonel Crompton, a child of the clearing, and Eudora. Part two turns to letters between Howard Crompton and Jack Harcourt. Eloise, an accident, Amy, and Mrs. Biggs's reminiscences also appear.

Holmes, praised for enlisting readers' sympathy and holding their attention, writes warm domestic fiction of family, love, and social standing. The Cromptons mix Southern scenery with Northern visitors and old secrets. Readers of Victorian popular novels will find a comfortable, absorbing story in her familiar style.
16342-a-treatise-on-simple-counterpoint-:
Friedrich J. Lehmann built this Oberlin textbook around forty graded lessons in simple counterpoint. Early lessons pair note against note, then two notes against one, then four, with syncopation and mixed forms to follow. Each lesson gives rules, worked examples, and exercises for the student to write.

The seventh edition keeps the method strict and step by step, aimed at music students learning to weave two or more voice lines that sound well together. No prior counterpoint skill is assumed beyond basic harmony. For students of composition, it remains a plain, workmanlike manual from the golden age of American conservatory teaching.
16381-the-summons:
A. E. W. Mason's 1920 novel opens at the Olympic Games, then follows Hillyard through Barcelona, sleeping cars, and Spanish capes on a mission tied to ships and secrets. Mario Escobar, Harry Luttrell, Stella, and Jenny Prask cross his path, and a summons at chapter ten sets the intrigue in motion. Mason dedicates the book to those who served with him abroad through four years.

The tale mixes adventure with romance, in the polished style of The Four Feathers. The pace quickens from garden scenes to chases and close calls. Readers of classic spy and adventure fiction will find a well-made yarn with a strong sense of place.
16487-the-story-of-the-living-machine-a-:
H. W. Conn, a Wesleyan biology professor, reviews modern biology's case that the living body works like a machine in this 1903 book, with fifty pictures. His preface warns that the claim is made both too strictly and too loosely, and the book aims to state what it truly means. An introduction covers the new science, energy, evolution, and cells.

Part one asks whether the body is a machine, then treats the cell, protoplasm, and the vital factor. Conn writes for general readers, with clear chapters and plain examples. The book gives a turn-of-the-century view of life as mechanism, thoughtful rather than dogmatic.
16644-the-puritan-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote and drew this Puritan Twins tale for grades six and seven, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston. It joins her twins series, which also gives Dutch, Eskimo, Filipino, Japanese, Swiss, Irish, Italian, Scotch, Mexican, Belgian, French, Cave, and Spartan twins. The Puritan pair sail, land, and learn life in early New England.

Perkins mixes story with lessons in history, work, and manners, all in short chapters with her own pictures. The twins meet captains, kin, and town folk, and they learn to work, pray, and play by Puritan rule. Young readers get a friendly first look at colonial life, told as a family tale rather than a dry lesson.
16732-familiar-quotations:
Hurst and Company of New York put out this book of well-known sayings, drawn from the first sources and set out with full lists of authors and topics. It aims to show what English owes to its writers for phrases that have grown into household words. The author list runs from Addison and Bacon through Burns, Bunyan, and Bryant, and onward.

The book works as a desk tool: find a line, find who wrote it, and find its kin by topic. Its care for true sources sets it apart from loose quote books. Readers, writers, and speakers can still use it to check a line, trace a phrase, or pick an apt quote for a speech or essay.
16746-inquiries-and-opinions:
Brander Matthews wrote this 1907 book of essays on books and the stage, issued in September 1907 and dedicated to his friend Henry Arthur Jones. Contents run from literature in the new century and supreme leaders, through Poe and the detective story, Mark Twain, Maupassant, and Ibsen, to the art of the stage manager. The first paper was read at St. Louis in 1904.

Matthews weighs new books and plays with a critic's eye for craft, praising skill and form over mere fashion. He defends technique as an art, not a trick. The book gives a clear view of American criticism in 1907, and it still rewards readers who care how novels, plays, and poems are made, not just what they say.
16787-life-of-charles-dickens:
Frank T. Marzials wrote this 1887 life of Charles Dickens for the Great Writers series, issued by Walter Scott in London. Marzials owns a heavy debt to Forster's life of Dickens and to Dickens's letters, edited by his sister-in-law and eldest daughter, plus Kitton's Dickensiana. The first chapter follows Dickens from birth on February 7, 1812, through Chatham days, family troubles, and his father's stay in the Marshalsea.

Marzials links young Charles to David Copperfield, showing how childhood pain shaped the novelist. He tracks Dickens through work, fame, and books in short, clear chapters. The life serves as a compact, readable first guide to Dickens, best for readers who want the man behind the novels without a huge biography.
16863-lives-of-the-three-mrs-judsons:
Arabella W. Stuart wrote these lives of the three Mrs. Judsons, missionaries to Burmah: Ann H. Judson, Sarah B. Judson, and Emily C. Judson, issued by Lee and Shepard in Boston in 1855. A verse at the front calls them a self-denying band who counted not life dear, so they might fulfil their ministry and save heathen souls. Portraits of Ann and Emily front the book.

Stuart tells of wives who followed the Judson mission to Burma through hardship, loss, and death, in earnest, admiring prose. Her preface praises missions as a field for the highest female character. The book gives a period portrait of missionary heroines, useful for church history, though modern readers will read its views of Burma with care.
17006-two-christmas-celebrations:
Theodore Parker, minister of the 28th Congregational Society of Boston, wrote this Christmas story for 1856, comparing two Christmas celebrations: A.D. I and 1855. It opens with Augustus Caesar ordering his realm taxed, so Joseph the carpenter and Mary of Nazareth went to Bethlehem to be registered. In a stable, with the tavern full, a boy was born and laid in a cattle crib, the first Christmas kept in a barn.

Parker sets the humble birth against a modern Christmas of wealth and show, asking what the feast truly means. His tone is earnest, democratic, and full of biblical plainness. The story gives a thoughtful, short Christmas read, useful for readers who want Parker's liberal faith in a festive, moral form.
17206-over-there-with-the-australians:
Captain R. Hugh Knyvett, an Anzac scout and intelligence officer, tells his Great War service in this 1918 memoir. It opens with a poem for Bill-Jim, the Australian soldier in Flanders mud longing for Sydney at Christmas. Parts follow the call to arms, training camps, Egypt, Gallipoli's landing and evacuation, and the Western Front from Fleurbaix to the Somme.

Knyvett writes of scouts as the army's pair of eyes, with nights in No Man's Land, spy hunting, and a Blighty wound at Bapaume. His voice is frank, slangy, and proud of his mates. Readers of Anzac history will find a vivid, firsthand tour of the war as Australian troops lived it.
17378-successful-recitations:
Alfred H. Miles edited this collection of recitations, published in London in 1901 by S. H. Bousfield and Company. Miles takes his motto from Hamlet's advice to the players: speak the speech trippingly on the tongue, and do not mouth it as many players do. His preface argues that a clear aim and a simple style stand first among the makings of a successful recitation.

The book gathers pieces chosen to be spoken aloud, with attention to voice, sense, and effect on listeners. Readers get a period anthology for parlour, school, and platform, useful for performers and teachers of elocution. It also shows what Victorians and Edwardians liked to hear recited, from verse to stirring prose.
17465-great-singers-second-series-malibr:
George T. Ferris published this second series of lives of great singers, running from Malibran to Titiens, in New York in 1891 with D. Appleton and Company, copyright dated 1881. It companions his first series, which sketched lyric artists from Faustina Bordoni to Henrietta Sontag. Ferris kept the same limits of purpose, including only those who stand incontestably in the front rank of the operatic profession, with some account of lesser lights.

Readers meet celebrated voices through anecdote and contemporary praise, in short, vivid portraits. The book suits music lovers who want the great singers of the past in compact form. As a period collection it shows whom Victorians ranked highest on the opera stage.
17862-dream-life-a-fable-of-the-seasons:
Donald G. Mitchell wrote Dream Life in the 1800s as a kind of prose poem about a life lived through the four seasons. The New York house Scribner, Armstrong put the book out, and Mitchell frames it as a fable, with boyhood, youth, and later years matched to spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

Short scenes move from a garret in the rain to school days, first love, and quiet hours at home, all told in a soft, dream-like voice. The book does not chase a plot; it lingers on moods, small joys, and the ache of time passing. Readers who like slow, fond prose about growing up will find it a gentle, easy book to dip into.
179-the-europeans:
Two charming Europeans arrive in Boston and unsettle a staid New England family. Henry James's Europeans follows Eugenia, a baroness, and her brother Felix, an artist, as they visit American cousins. The Wentworths receive them with duty, suspicion, and quiet fascination.

Felix paints, flirts, and adapts, while Eugenia schemes for a good marriage to secure her future. James contrasts Old World ease with New World conscience in light, ironic prose. The novella's comedy hides sharp judgments on both sides. It remains a graceful early James study of cultures meeting. James later called the tale a light comedy, but its judgments on marriage and money run deep.
17952-great-possessions:
Mrs. Wilfrid Ward wrote Great Possessions in 1909, printed in New York and London by G. P. Putnam's Sons. Ward, author of One Poor Scruple, sets this novel among English Catholics and county folk, where wills, pride, and faith shape lives.

Book one opens with an amazing will, a wicked woman in Florence, and Molly coming of age, while Edmund Grosse keeps meddling. Groombridge Castle and a pet vice add color to the plot. Ward writes with a sharp, moral eye for motive and manners. It is a thoughtful Edwardian novel, best for readers who like tales of conscience and class.
17965-boy-woodburn-a-story-of-the-sussex:
Alfred Ollivant wrote Boy Woodburn in 1918, issued in New York by Doubleday, Page, as a story of the Sussex Downs. Ollivant, author of Bob, Son of Battle, here gives a girl and a foal the lead, in a tale of trainers, horses, and downland life.

Part one, The Girl and the Foal, opens with Old Mat the trainer, Boy showing her mettle, a gypsy's mare, and rides across the downs. Boy, a girl of pluck, learns horse craft and heart craft together. Ollivant writes with love for horses and country folk. It is a warm, old tale of the downs, best for readers who love horses and open air.
17967-navy-boys-behind-the-big-guns:
Halsey Davidson wrote Navy Boys Behind the Big Guns, put out in New York by George Sully, as one more in the Navy Boys series. Davidson also wrote of navy boys after submarines and chasing a sea raider, and here his lads take on German U-boats.

Chapters run from a run to Elmvale and a stranger to a water wheel, a streak on the water, fog, and a chase just too late. The gunners, stripped for action, serve the big guns with pluck. Davidson writes brisk, patriotic boys' fiction of the Great War at sea. It is a rousing, old-style navy tale, full of action and loyal chums.
17972-round-about-the-carpathians:
Andrew F. Crosse wrote Round About the Carpathians in Edinburgh in 1878, a travel book on the Danube lands and the hills of the east. Crosse, a fellow of the Chemical Society, went by steamer, horse, and foot through places few English tourists then knew.

Chapters run down the Danube from Buda-Pest, through Oravicza with gypsy music and dance, into Serbia, past New Moldova, and over storm-hit mountain roads. Crosse notes rocks, peasants, inns, and local ways with a curious, friendly eye. The book still charms as a Victorian travel tale, full of color and hard roads.
18194-the-life-of-buddha-and-its-lessons:
H. S. Olcott wrote The Life of Buddha and Its Lessons as Adyar Pamphlet number fifteen, printed at Adyar, Madras, in a second edition of September 1919. Olcott, a Theosophical leader, asks how saints become gods in the eyes of men.

He notes the invariable pull to deify any man who rises past common weakness, persecuted in life and worshipped after death. The true life is then decked with omens and wonders to fit the godhead. Olcott's lesson is to seek the man's teaching, not the myth. The pamphlet is short, thoughtful, and a clear Theosophical view of the Buddha.
1890-speaking-of-operations:
Irvin S. Cobb's Speaking of Operations, dedicated to those who have already been operated on and those who have not yet been operated on, is a comic book about surgery. Cobb writes after the last belated bill has been paid and receipted, and turns his hospital stay into a series of jokes.

A surgeon telephoning for Friday at seven, or seven-fifteen, for an important tumor case at St. Germicide's Hospital, up on Umpty-umph Street, sets the tone. Cobb's humor is warm and self-mocking, and the book's charm lies in its refusal to be solemn about pain. A patient who laughs at his own operation invites the reader to laugh with him.
18931-archeological-investigations:
Gerard Fowke prepared this report as Bulletin 76 of the Smithsonian Institution's Bureau of American Ethnology, printed in Washington in 1922. It gathers fieldwork from several regions into five parts. These are cave exploration in the Ozark region of central Missouri, caves in other states, and work along the Missouri River bluffs in Kansas and Nebraska. The last two parts cover aboriginal house mounds and fieldwork in Hawaii.

The report records sites, finds, and ground plans in plain descriptive detail, with an eye to what each place shows about the people who used it. Cave deposits, mounds, and house sites are treated as evidence for older ways of living in each region. Readers get a solid survey of early American field archaeology, valuable for its firsthand site records.
18992-current-superstitions:
Fanny D. Bergen edited this 1896 volume of superstitions gathered from the oral tradition of English-speaking folk. William Wells Newell wrote notes and an introduction for the American Folk-Lore Society, which issued the book in Boston and New York. It collects beliefs passed by word of mouth, not from books alone.

Entries cover luck, omens, cures, and customs, while Newell argues that speech, songs, and tales carry ideas across peoples even in times of hate or war. Lower cultures borrow from higher ones, he claims, and new lore sinks through all ranks. Readers get a rich store of folk belief plus a theory of how such lore travels.
19043-the-terrible-twins:
Edgar Jepson's 1913 comic novel The Terrible Twins follows Violet Anastasia and Hyacinth Wolfram Dangerfield, a pair of mischievous children whose schemes keep their household and village in cheerful turmoil. The twins, known by nicknames, defend their claims with loud vehemence, run a cats' home, and turn every visit, inspection, and local dispute into an adventure.

Chapters trace their escapades with a guardian, a landed proprietor, a sacred bird, a pond, peaches, fishing, and even royalty. They build a series of set pieces around the twins' boundless energy and literal-minded logic. Their uncle, Sir Maurice Falconer, serves as a frequent foil, impressed and exhausted in turn by their enterprises. The novel is a warm, episodic comedy of childhood daring, in which two small masterminds repeatedly outwit the adult world around them.
19056-thoughts-on-educational-topics-and:
George S. Boutwell set out these essays on schools and public life in Boston in 1859. He wrote for teachers in Massachusetts, and he treats learning as a duty shared by towns, homes, and the state. The pieces move from plain school questions to wider civic ones.

Boutwell weighs what schools should teach, how teachers should be trained, and how reading, papers, and libraries lift a whole people. He argues that a free press and free libraries only thrive where minds are trained to use them. Readers get a mid-century American view of why public schooling mattered to civic life.
1916-the-great-stone-face-and-other-tale:
Nathaniel Hawthorne's Great Stone Face and Other Tales of the White Mountains gathers stories set among New Hampshire's mountains. An introduction notes that the first three numbers in the collection belong together. The title tale follows Ernest, a boy who grows up beneath a mountain profile like a human face, and who waits for the great man the face promises.

The Ambitious Guest, The Great Carbuncle, and Sketches from Memory complete the volume. One tale has a man of mighty faculties and little aims whose life, for all its high performances, stays vague and empty. Hawthorne writes the mountains as moral landscape, and the book's tales ask, in different forms, what greatness is and how it is recognized.
19198-aliens-or-americans:
Howard B. Grose wrote this 1906 mission study, Aliens or Americans. Josiah Strong wrote its introduction, for young people's mission courses. Its opening poem pictures unguarded gates. Through them a motley throng presses, from Volga, Tartar steppes, and the Hoang-Ho. They bring strange tongues and gods. The question is whether America will welcome or fear them.

Grose counts illiterates among newcomers. Italian, Polish, Hebrew, Slav, and Magyar wards form a city of ignorance as large as Jersey City. Only a handful of Scots and Scandinavians cannot read. Readers get a period missionary view of immigration, earnest yet shaped by the prejudices of its day.
1921-the-chouans:
Early in the year VIII of the Revolution, at the start of Vendémiaire, an ambush in Brittany opens a war between royalist Chouans and the Republic. The novel opens with an ambuscade in Brittany, where royalist Chouans fight the Republic, at the start of Vendémiaire in the year VIII of the Revolution.

Marie de Verneuil, a beautiful agent sent to trap the rebel leader, finds her mission tangled by love. Madame du Gua, growing prudent as she grows jealous, watches every move. Balzac writes the Breton war as romance and tragedy, and the novel's sweep — ambushes, betrayals, and a countryside at war with itself — announced a major novelist.
19395-the-new-heavens:
George Ellery Hale, director of the Mount Wilson Observatory, wrote this survey of the new astronomy, put out in New York in the early nineteen twenties with many pictures. It opens with the constellation Orion and its great nebula, then moves to giant stars and the cosmic furnaces where elements are born.

Hale explains how star diameters are measured, even when the angle is far too small for the eye, by spreading light across wide mirrors. The book brings the work of great telescopes to general readers, at a moment when the scale of the universe was growing fast.
19464-osage-traditions:
J. Owen Dorsey recorded these Osage traditions for the Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology, after a visit to the Osage in Indian Territory in early eighteen eighty-three. He learned of a secret society of seven degrees said to preserve the people's traditions, and he gathered parts of two traditions from several Osage men.

The texts that follow give the elders' accounts in order, with a symbolic chart of the Osage as a guide. Dorsey is frank that his short stay yielded only fragments, but the volume remains a key early record of Osage sacred history.
19628-the-siouan-indians:
W. J. McGee wrote this preliminary sketch of the Siouan Indians, printed in the Smithsonian's annual report for the mid eighteen nineties. It defines the Siouan stock, maps its extent, and surveys tribal names, arts, institutions, beliefs, and the growth of mythology.

Tribes from the Dakota and Assiniboin to the Mandan, Hidatsa, and Winnebago each get a section, with notes on social order and sacred rites of dance, chant, feast, and fast. The sketch remains a base source for the peoples of the Great Plains. McGee stresses that Siouan art stayed mainly symbolic, its makers still bound by fetishistic symbolism.
19739-modern-american-prose-selections:
Modern American Prose Selections, dated 1909, gathers American writing for study and reading. One piece marks the hundredth anniversary of a great American's birth. The speaker calls him one of the two greatest Americans. He ranks him among the two or three greatest men of the nineteenth century. That centenary was Abraham Lincoln's, widely celebrated in 1909.

School anthologies shaped what counted as American prose. Editors chose speeches, essays, and addresses that modeled clear writing. Lincoln pieces anchored many such collections. Students learned style by reading masters aloud. The book preserves that classroom canon in one binding. It shows which voices teachers trusted in 1909. For literary history, the table of choices matters as much as the texts.
19748-story-lives-of-great-musicians:
Francis Jameson Rowbotham wrote these story-lives of great musicians, published in New York with pictures, including Beethoven as frontispiece. Bach, Handel, Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, and Mendelssohn each get a life told as story for young readers.

The lives stress boyhood, work, and character over technical talk, making masters feel like people before they feel like names. Rowbotham, known for story-lives of authors, wrote for children who might meet great music first through a good tale. Rowbotham tells each life as a story, so young readers meet masters as people first. One anecdote has a publisher overhear a composer growl he would give his best quartet for a good razor.
19798-the-farringdons:
Ellen Thorneycroft Fowler set The Farringdons in England's Black Country. One street in the novel faces two worlds at once. West-side houses have sunny gardens and orchards sloping to meadows. Eastward stand tall chimneys, weird and terrible yet fascinating. Beyond the fields rise the Clee Hills and the Wrekin. Blue Welsh mountains close the far distance.

Fowler's novels mixed industry, faith, and family ambition. The Farringdons are a clan shaped by that divided landscape. Money from furnaces meets conscience from chapel and garden. Her Black Country detail comes from living beside it. The book preserves a region literature often skipped. It does so with affection and a sharp eye.
19977-the-blue-pavilions:
The Blue Pavilions is a historical romance by Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch, writing as Q. It opens at Harwich on 11 October 1673, at noonday. More than a hundred tall ships have newly returned from the Dutch War. The little seaport beside the Stour presents a lively appearance. Quiller-Couch builds the scene with a painter's patience. War's end fills the harbor with noise and color.

Q wrote sea-soaked Cornish and naval tales under that single letter. The Dutch wars gave him a rich, neglected century. Pavilions are campaign tents; blue ones suggest the fleet's shore world. His prose is consciously beautiful, sentence by sentence. This novel shows his romantic history at full sail. It is a connoisseur's adventure story.
20083-a-boswell-of-baghdad-with-diversio:
A Boswell of Baghdad, With Diversions, takes its name from James Boswell, the famed life writer. The narrator faces a work in four huge volumes that could fell a bookseller. That joke sets a tone of wit, books, and talk. Baghdad gives the book its far-off, storied frame.

Diversions, in the old sense, are side trips and bright asides. The book mixes tale, essay, and chat about books and men. Its charm lies in voice more than in plot alone. Readers who like learned humor will find a rich, rambling companion here.
20137-a-comparative-view-of-religions:
Francis T. Washburn wrote A Comparative View of Religions, a study of the world's faiths. He sets out each faith and weighs it against the Christian one. True religion, he argues, was prepared in Israel and fulfilled in Christ. In Christ, man knows his oneness with God, he writes.

Washburn grants that Islam holds truth and good in its teachings. Yet he holds that such truth was borrowed from older faiths. The book shows how one Christian writer of his era ranked all faiths. Readers get a clear, dated map of comparative religion from that standpoint.
20459-hours-in-a-library-volume-1-new-ed:
Hours in a Library gathers literary essays by Leslie Stephen, the critic and editor who shaped Victorian letters. This is the first volume, in a new edition with additions. Stephen writes about authors as a fellow worker among books, not as a distant judge.

The volume opens with a famous daydream about an old library. It seems, he writes, as if the souls of all the writers who left their work to the Bodleian were resting there. He feels he inhales learning while walking its shelves. The essays that follow keep that mix of deep reading and plain talk.
20468-the-delta-of-the-triple-elevens: The Delta of the Triple Elevens preserves service records of a World War outfit. It lists men one by one, with dates and postings. One clerk went on detached service on May 18, 1918, at Camp Meade. He rejoined Battery D on June 27 and sailed with it to France. Such lines trace how a unit was built and sent overseas.
20487-shakspere-personal-recollections:
Shakspere: Personal Recollections is a whimsical satire that claims an impossible narrator. The writer says it is well known among his close friends that he is no ordinary man. He claims to have lived forever, and to be ready to recall Shakespeare in person.

He says he sprang from the race of Strulbugs, who live forever on the island of Immortality. That island lies on the coast of Japan, and he began there more than a million years ago. The tall tale riffs on Swift's deathless Struldbrugs, and uses the joke to mock solemn Shakespeare worship.
20614-the-wonder-island-boys-the-mysteri:
The Mysteries of the Caverns, published in 1914, carries Roger T. Finlay's Wonder Island Boys deeper into their island's secrets. The boys and their professor friend keep building a working life from wreckage and raw materials. Each chapter reads like a lesson disguised as an adventure.

The contents move from recovering the lifeboat to deciding to row it around the point. The boys study alloys and their uses, and make stocks for their guns. They begin the hull of a new boat, learning what shape a hull should take. Their tame charge, Red Angel, even attempts to whistle.
20838-the-infra-medians:
A hot sales prospect waits, but the narrator of The Infra-Medians runs to his buddy Vic instead. Vic is Hope's brother, and the two have been pals since childhood. Sewell Peaslee Wright drops that bond into a tale of hidden beings.

Wright wrote brisk science fiction for the pulp magazines of his day. Infra-medians, creatures between worlds, give this tale its strange hook. Fast talk, sudden peril, and weird science drive the plot. Readers of early pulp tales will find Wright's pace and invention on show, with friendship, not just wonder, at the tale's core.
20980-a-survey-of-russian-literature-wit:
Vladimir, Grand Prince of Kiev, took Christianity for his whole nation in 988, this survey recounts. Baptised wholesale from Byzantium, Russia gained its Prince-Saint in that act. His grandmother Olga had paved the way with churches in Kiev before him.

Isabel Hapgood surveys Russian writing from chronicles to the great novelists of her day. Her 1902 book adds chosen pieces in her own English versions. Hapgood knew Russia deeply and turned its classics with rare care. Readers get both a map of a vast literature and a taste of its goods, in one trusted guide.
21044-the-willoughby-captains:
School parliament reports tangle speakers, teller, and heckling boys in The Willoughby Captains, Reed owns. The printed book simplifies what his tale tries to render by rule. That frank note fronts a reissue of Talbot Baines Reed's school classic.

Captains of house and games rule Willoughby's boy world in this tale. Honour, rivalry, and a disputed place drive its famed plot along. Reed helped invent the modern school story with books like this one. Willoughby's boys still feel alive: vain, brave, funny, and bound by codes they would die sooner than break in public.
21243-the-madigans:
Miriam Michelson's 1904 story collection follows the Madigan girls of San Francisco through ten linked tales. The first, Cecilia the Pharisee, opens with Sissy feeling virtuous before she has done anything at all. Other stories include A Pagan and a Puritan, The Shut-Ups, and The Ancestry of Irene.

Irene and her many supposed fathers appear in Orson Lowell's illustrations, including the frontispiece. The sisters scheme, pretend, write letters, and manage their widowed household with more wit than money. Michelson had written In the Bishop's Carriage, and she gives the Madigans the same quick talk and warm disorder. Kate: A Pretense and Old Mother Gibson close the set.
21244-by-canoe-and-dog-train-among-the-c:
Egerton Ryerson Young was a Hamilton pastor, newly married, when a letter from the Mission Rooms in Toronto reached his study in 1868. The Missionary Committee asked him to go as a missionary to the Indigenous peoples at Norway House in the Northwest. His memoir tells how he answered that summons.

Young travelled by canoe, dog train, and prairie trail toward Hudson Bay country, among the Cree and Saulteaux peoples named in his title. Chapters record frontier settlers, Sioux wars, and narrow escapes on the way. The book became a well-known record of Canadian Methodist mission life in the early Northwest, told by the man who lived it.
21315-the-king-s-sons:
King Ethelwulf of Wessex had four sons, and each in turn became king. George Manville Fenn's short tale follows the brothers, above all the youngest, Alfred, later Alfred the Great. Their tutor is Father Swythe, a monk, and only Alfred cares for what he teaches. The others prefer rougher pursuits.

Fenn pauses the story for a fine lesson in how illuminated manuscripts were made: the inks, the colours, the pens and brushes. Father Swythe later becomes Bishop Swithun of Winchester, whose feast day still carries a forty-days-of-rain legend. This quiet volume trades Fenn's usual cliffhangers for early English history told simply for young readers.
21316-the-adventures-of-don-lavington-no:
Lindon Lavington, called Don, works as a clerk in his uncle Josiah's Bristol sugar and tobacco office and hates the work. When office money goes missing, the real thief is plain to see, yet Uncle Josiah keeps accusing Don. George Manville Fenn then takes the boy's life apart in one night.

Don and Jem, a fellow worker who has also quarrelled at home, go out feeling ill-used and are seized by a press gang. They escape their ship in New Zealand, live among Maori friends, and help English settlers fight off an attack stirred by escaped convicts. In the end one villain proves to be the office thief all along.
21330-robert-burns:
Principal Shairp, professor of poetry at Oxford, wrote this life of Robert Burns. It was first published in 1879 and many times reprinted; this edition is from 1906. Eight chapters run from Burns's youth in Ayrshire through his two Edinburgh winters, his Border and Highland tours, and his farm at Ellisland. The move to Dumfries and the last years follow.

A closing chapter weighs Burns's character, poems, and songs together. Shairp notes that six biographies of Burns had already appeared before Carlyle's famous essay of 1828, and the count only grew. His own life stays compact and readable, aimed at students meeting Scotland's national poet in one volume.
21368-the-silver-canyon-a-tale-of-the-we:
Bart is a young hero out on the western plains with his uncle. In the middle of the nineteenth century, in George Manville Fenn's tale, he is seeking a new life. Antelope steaks cook over a dying fire as dangers gather: armed Native warriors skilled at creeping up unseen, rattlesnakes, and bears. The party finds a great rocky hill with a rich lode of silver in it.

The hill was mined long before, perhaps thousands of years earlier, and its summit gives grazing and a strong defensive post. They work the remaining ore commercially while attacks continue almost to the end. A railway at last reaches the mine, and a town of thousands follows the silver.
21443-vesty-of-the-basins:
Sarah P. McLean Greene sets her 1892 novel Vesty of the Basins in a small fishing village on the coast. A low, storm-beaten schoolhouse, a stranded schooner, and a fog horn mark the place. The horn was the gift of Melchias Tibbitts, a dead captain of the Basin.

Vesty's tale moves through meetings, courtship, a wedding, and village feasts. Captain Leezur's sly wooing and tall tales give the book much of its fun. Greene writes the local speech with a loving, exact ear. Her earlier Cape Cod Folks had made her name for just this kind of coastal portrait.
21459-dick-onslow-among-the-redskins:
Dick Onslow joins a party of emigrants bound for California in W. H. G. Kingston's Dick Onslow. The tale ranges in and near the Rocky Mountains, on the hard road west. Dick's friend, meanwhile, tells of cutting his way through Mexico and the settled States.

Rattlesnakes, bears, rockslides, and snow slides crowd the trail. Raids by hostile tribes bring shots, wounds, and nights spent hiding in bush and tree. Dick is shot through the leg and starves in sight of plenty. The book is not long, but Kingston packs each chapter with peril drawn from backwoods life.
21466-in-the-rocky-mountains:
Ralph and Clarice, brother and sister, lose both parents on the road west in W. H. G. Kingston's In the Rocky Mountains. Their farming family had left the middle states for a new life. Orphaned, the two young folk have no adult to lead them on.

A wagon train then comes by, and its chief proves to be their own uncle Jeff Crockett. Uncle Jeff never could abide folk crowding round his hut, and always moved on. He takes the children in and becomes dear to them. Clashes with Indigenous peoples, wolves, and bears fill the rest of this short, warm tale.
21739-hunting-the-lions:
Tom Brown, a hero with the plainest name in England, leads this Ballantyne hunting tale. Ballantyne spends his first chapter joking about the Browns of the world: grocers, butchers, milkmen, and doctors beyond counting. Then he takes his own Brown far from those safe streets.

The trail leads to lion country, where hunting tests nerve in a way no shop counter can. Ballantyne builds the tale on travel, camp life, and the charge of a lion at close range. His humor about the hero's name keeps the tone light between dangers. It is a sporting yarn of his classic kind, written for boys who dreamed of Africa from an English fireside.
21763-the-brentons:
Young Scott Brenton is led into the ministry by his widowed mother's secret prayers in this 1912 novel by Anna Chapin Ray. The prayer was never made to him, the narrator insists, but offered in silence and sincerity. Scott's path into the church gives the family of the title its center. Around him, the Brentons face the pulls of duty, love, and pride.

Ray was a practiced novelist of family life, with many titles to her name by 1912. Her touch here is quiet and close, following talk across tables and the small turns that change lives. The frontispiece shows young Catia in talk over a cup. It is a gentle book about faith tested inside a household.
21771-georgina-s-reasons:
Raymond Benyon loves a girl he cannot understand in this Henry James tale of 1885, and he knows it from the start. Georgina is tall and fair, with gorgeous auburn hair and a cold, beautiful eye. Her charm is real, yet Benyon feels a twinge of warning even in his happiness. Her parents are rude to him, and her singularity takes forms he cannot name.

James follows the love affair through its happy surface and its hidden cracks. Georgina has her reasons, and the tale's work is to bring them slowly into view. Benyon looks back in later years and calls his early unease a foreboding. It is a cool, exact study of a woman who will not be read like other people.
21903-the-californians:
Old California families collide with new American wealth in Gertrude Atherton's novel The Californians, published in 1898. Helena Belmont, sixteen and spoiled, tips her schoolbooks to the floor and demands the sun. Her dark-eyed friend Magdaléna Yorba has only her intelligence to set against Helena's beauty and money. Miss Phelps, their teacher, leaves the quarrel to Miss Yorba, as the opening scene jokes.

Atherton, a Californian herself, writes the passing of the Spanish dons' world with an insider's eye. Helena already knows the power of wealth, and sparkles with the insolence of it. Love, pride, and race run through the tale of the two girls. It is early Atherton: sharp, scenic, and set on showing California to readers who knew only its gold-rush face.
21931-sea-urchins:
Dockside boys and old sailors fill Sea Urchins, W. W. Jacobs's book of tales from 1899. The first story, Smoked Skipper, opens with a porter trotting a bran-new sea-chest toward Wapping Old Stairs. Its owner, a small ill-looking lad of fourteen, swears there is little about the sea he does not know. He orders his hellum turned with a captain's airs while the porter plays along for a cheap half-crown.

Other tales bring a grey parrot, a lost ship, pickled herring, and brother Hutchins. Jacobs writes the London river as a comedy stage where everyone is slightly at sea. The dialect is thick and the timing perfect. Sea Urchins catches his world young: urchins, skippers, and the men who carry their chests and their illusions.
21996-riviera-towns:
Hill towns above the French Riviera are walked one by one in Herbert Adams Gibbons's Riviera Towns, with Lester George Hornby's illustrations, copyrighted in 1920. From his study window at Théoule, Gibbons could almost count the windows of distant houses. Grasse on its hill was a constant temptation, and the two islands offshore kept watch. His chapters visit Cagnes, Saint-Paul, Vence, and Menton before the famous coast towns.
