Monte Carlo, Villefranche, Nice, Antibes, and Cannes each get a chapter, with Mougins, Fréjus, and Saint-Raphaël to close. Gibbons looks past the casinos to old streets, courts where stables stood downstairs, and meadows thick with violets. The book was dedicated to Helen and Margaret, who indulged author and artist both. It is travel writing with a resident's patience.
22083-myths-and-legends-of-the-great-pla:
Katharine Berry Judson gathered Myths and Legends of the Great Plains in 1913. Judson made a career of collecting Native tales for general readers. The Plains peoples here include the Kiowa, Pawnee, Osage, and their neighbours. Their stories explain the buffalo, the stars, the seasons, and the spirit world.

One plate shows a dreamer priest's vision of the land of the dead. He crosses a prairie crowded with buffalo and ponies to find his dead brothers. Creation tales, trickster stories, and war stories stand side by side. Judson aimed to keep these tales in print for readers who would never hear a tribal storyteller. The book reflects both the tales and her era.
22220-policing-the-plains:
R. G. MacBeth wrote Policing the Plains as the real-life record of the Royal North-West Mounted Police. MacBeth, author of The Romance of Western Canada, tells the Mounties' story from their founding march west in 1874. The frontispiece shows mounted police rounding up horse thieves. The force's work was exactly that: patrol, pursue, and keep order across an immense frontier.

MacBeth follows famous marches, whisky traders, Sitting Bull's arrival, and the North-West Rebellion. He writes as an admirer, and the book is a celebration. Published in the 1920s, it fixed the Mountie legend for a generation. Here was the red coat who always got his man. He ruled the plains with a handful of riders.
22362-appreciations-and-criticisms-of-th:
Appreciations and Criticisms of the Works of Charles Dickens gathers judgments on England's great novelist. After Dickens fell ill and died, a school of criticism arose. It held, oddly, that a man wrote better when he was ill.

George Gissing, an able writer, nearly argued that Little Dorrit is Dickens's best book. That claim shows the strange turns Dickens criticism took. The volume sorts praise and blame across his career. Readers can watch taste change as distance from Dickens grew. It suits anyone who wants the arguments around the novels, not only the novels themselves, preserved in period voices.
2262-timon-of-athens:
Timon, a lord of Athens famous for lavish gifts, discovers his friends vanish when his money runs out. Timon of Athens tracks his fall from open-handed host to a cave-dwelling misanthrope who digs up gold only to curse it. Shakespeare pairs the flatterers' betrayal with the cynic Apemantus, who had warned him all along.

The second half turns Timon into a prophet of contempt, hurling bitter verse at senators, thieves, and whores alike. Unfinished in places, the play still grips with its fury at wealth and false friendship. It offers a dark, uncomfortable companion to the great tragedies.
22767-pagan-passions:
Pagan Passions is a science fiction novel of 1959. In it, the gods and goddesses of Olympus return to a modern world. Their return greatly inconveniences a man named Forrester. The catalog record names no author. Its own billing gives the recipe plainly: gods, intrigue, mystery, and danger, with the supernatural made to make sense.

For science fiction it is, the blurb insists, with the supernatural made logical, and fun too, despite the sword that hangs by a thread above Forrester's head. Divine politics, played as suspense comedy, drives the plot: old gods with old grudges, armed with very modern leverage. The book belongs to the bright, cheeky school of late-1950s science fiction, when the field delighted in dressing myth in a business suit.
2279-a-waif-of-the-plains:
A boy orphaned on the California trail is taken in by rough but kind strangers in Bret Harte's frontier tale. A Waif of the Plains follows the child through camps, stage stations, and mining towns, where gamblers, schoolteachers, and reformed outlaws shape his upbringing. The plains themselves, with their dangers and sudden kindnesses, form the real school.

Harte balances sentiment and humor, letting the boy's innocence expose the better nature of his guardians. The story moves quickly and ends with a satisfying homecoming of sorts. It is a gentle example of Harte's California fiction for younger readers.
22892-the-best-made-plans:
Everett B. Cole opens The Best Made Plans with a camera's eye sweeping a future city. It centers on a large sports stadium where players dash across the turf, then swings away over city scenes. The view then crosses the palace walls and drops to the Royal Guards' parade ground.

That cool, surveying gaze suits a story about schemes inside a polished state. Plans here are made by rulers and plotters alike, and the title warns how the best of them go. Cole wrote workmanlike science fiction for the magazines, strong on setting and mechanism. Readers get a future court, a watching lens, and intrigue that unfolds at a steady clip.
2290-twenty-two-goblins:
A king must carry a corpse hung with a goblin through the night, and at each step the goblin tells a tale ending in a riddle. Twenty-Two Goblins, translated from the Sanskrit by Arthur William Ryder, preserves this classic Indian frame story, in which the king's silence or answer decides his fate. The tales mix wit, magic, and moral puzzles.

Each goblin story poses a question of conduct: whose fault was a death, who should a woman marry, which are worse, men or women. Ryder's translation keeps the stories crisp and readable. The collection delights lovers of world folklore and riddling tales.
23066-the-prairie-traveler-a-hand-book-f:
Randolph B. Marcy offers hard-won knowledge in The Prairie Traveler, his handbook for overland expeditions. The information is so varied, and drawn from so many sources, he writes, that every new expedition still adds to his practical knowledge. A sound prairie manual, Marcy is convinced, belongs in every young traveler's kit, worth more than its weight many times over.

Marcy, an army officer, wrote the West's most trusted guidebook for the wagon and saddle era. Routes between the Mississippi and the Pacific, water, grass, camps, and encounters fill its chapters. Emigrants carried it like a spare wheel. Modern readers find in it the whole logistics of westward travel, exact, unromantic, and quietly lifesaving.
23169-the-diamond-lens:
Fitz-James O'Brien buys a microscope in The Diamond Lens. The promised instrument arrives at last, a simple Field's microscope costing perhaps fifteen dollars. For teaching purposes, the narrator judges, no better apparatus could have been chosen. A small treatise on microscopy, its history and discoveries, came with it.

From that schoolboy instrument O'Brien builds his famous tale of obsession. A diamond lens, a world within a water drop, and a beauty beyond reach complete it. Written in 1858, it stands near the head of American science fiction. The fifteen-dollar microscope does real work in the telling, grounding the wonder in a boy's budget. Every later story of microscopic worlds descends from this drop.
23261-oowikapun-or-how-the-gospel-reache:
Oowikapun tells how the gospel reached the Nelson River Indians, through the life of a young Indigenous hunter. His simple, quiet, monotonous life is broken in upon in a way he cannot undo. He can never be the same again after what reaches him.

A decided awakening has come. The circle of his vision has suddenly widened, and he has become aware that he is something more than he had imagined. The tale is a missionary story told from inside that change of mind. Readers get a period account of faith arriving in a northern hunting community, and of one young man's response.
23354-vegetable-teratology-an-account-of:
Maxwell T. Masters, a doctor and fellow of the Linnean Society, wrote this eighteen sixty nine Ray Society study of plants that grow out of their usual form. Leaves, stems, roots, and flowers that split, fuse, double, or change place are grouped, named, and drawn with care.

Masters works through case after case, from odd petals to whole flower heads gone wrong, and asks what each freak shows about how a normal plant is built. The book pairs plain accounts with many plates by E. M. Williams, so a reader can see each change. Plant lovers and students of form still gain from its orderly survey, which treats odd growth as a clue rather than a joke.
23372-the-buffalo-runners-a-tale-of-the-:
R. M. Ballantyne set this long tale of the Red River plains among early settlers east of the Rockies, where the Hudson's Bay Company and its rivals vied for the fur trade. Two young heroes, one frail and weak, lead the action, with Lord Selkirk's settlement plan as the backdrop.

Hardship piles up: bad men in camp and out, Sioux, Salteaux, and Cree neighbours, swarms of grasshoppers and mice, storms that wreck nets, and wounds from mishaps. Through it all, the boys show grit, good sense, and loyalty to kin and friends. Ballantyne writes the plains with gusto, giving young readers a full blooded tale of settlement, hunting, and survival on open ground.
2346-the-adventure-of-the-bruce-partingt:
In a dense London fog, Holmes takes on the theft of the Bruce-Partington submarine plans, a case where national security hangs on a missing document. Arthur Conan Doyle opens with Holmes cross-indexing his references, then sends him and Watson into the fog to trace a body found on the Underground tracks. The solution hinges on a window, a train, and a brother's treachery.

Mycroft Holmes appears to lend the case its official weight. The story blends espionage with classic deduction. It is one of the finest of the later Holmes tales.
23465-the-story-of-the-three-goblins:
Mabel G. Taggart wrote this nineteen hundred three tale of three little goblins: Red Cap, Blue Cap, and Yellow Cap. They live in a mountain with their father, Old Black Cap, king of the mountain. Their great friend is Rowley, a green frog who visits each year with stories of the Big World where he lives.

The goblins beg to go with him. Their father always says not yet, until one day he sends them into the Big World to seek something the fairies stole from him long ago. Grant Richards printed the book in London, with pictures to match the fun. Small children will enjoy the caps, the frog, and the quest, a gentle fairy tale of three brothers setting out where they have longed to go.
23492-fast-in-the-ice-adventures-in-the-:
R. M. Ballantyne set this small Arctic tale in the early nineteenth century, when voyagers still hoped an ice free sea ringed the North Pole. A ship sails north to test that hope, only to grow fast in the ice and stay stuck, unable to move.

The crew meet Inuit folk and learn how they live: hunting walrus, catching birds, and dwelling in ice houses, or igloos, through the long cold. Polar bears, musk oxen, and two years in the ice follow, with scurvy striking men who lack fresh food, a fate the meat and fat diet of their hosts seems to spare. Ballantyne writes the Arctic with warmth and wonder, making a fine young reader's tale of ice, endurance, and respect for native skill.
23540-the-twin-cousins:
Sophie May, author of the Little Prudy and Dotty Dimple stories, wrote this eighteen eighty Flaxie Frizzle tale of twin cousins, printed in Boston in eighteen ninety three. Flaxie Frizzle's party opens the book, followed by staying out to tea, a lonesome visit, Lucy's mittens, and a homely Miss Pike.

The house that Jack built, a return to Hilltop, a crazy Christmas, Milly visiting, Blackdrop, Flaxie as a comfort, and brave Preston Gray fill the rest. Disagreeable Patty follows the twins in a frontispiece scene. May writes with warmth for young girls, mixing parties, visits, and small scrapes with kind morals. Readers who love old fashioned girls' books will enjoy the twins' doings, their friends, and the cosy world of Hilltop.
23570-stories-about-indians:
Merriam and Merrill printed this eighteen fifty four children's book of stories about Indians, from Concord, New Hampshire, with a picture of Indians hunting buffalo. The book opens by noting that Indians were once lords of the soil now occupied. They lived mainly by hunting and fishing in villages of fifty to five hundred families.

Wigwams of poles bent and joined at the top, bark covered, with small window holes and a central fire under a roof smoke hole, are described in plain detail. Other tales follow in the same simple, instructive vein, aimed at young readers learning about Native peoples. Modern readers should note the book's period view and its limits, while valuing it as a record of how mid century American children were taught about the continent's first peoples.
23661-the-book-of-dragons:
E. Nesbit, beloved author of children's fantasies, gathered eight dragon stories into this collection, illustrated by H. R. Millar. Each tale gives its dragon a distinct temper and task, and each puts ordinary children in the path of something large, scaly, and surprising.

The contents run from The Book of Beasts and Uncle James, or The Purple Stranger, through The Ice Dragon and The Island of the Nine Whirlpools. The Dragon Tamers follow, and the book closes with The Fiery Dragon, or The Heart of Stone and the Heart of Gold. Nesbit's dragons are funny, fearsome, and sometimes kind, and her morals land lightly: do as you are told, keep your heart soft, and mind what you wish for.
2381-actions-and-reactions:
Rudyard Kipling's Actions and Reactions gathers stories from his later career, including tales of soldiers, engineers, and English country life. The collection shows Kipling's range beyond India: a ghost story, a tale of the sea, and the famous portrait of a village in wartime. His craftsmanship remains sharp, his views of empire more reflective.

The volume rewards readers who know Kipling's earlier work and want his mature voice. Its stories vary in mood from grim to tender. Kipling fans will find a strong late collection. The collection includes a tale of a village preparing for a German invasion.
24104-the-aliens:
Murray Leinster wrote this science fiction novella for Astounding Science Fiction in August 1959. The survey ship Niccola crosses a stretch of space some twelve hundred light-years wide, hunting for signs of the Plumies, a rival star-faring race. Their traces are strange cairns on oxygen worlds, topped with silicon-bronze plates, some a century old and some only days old.

Leinster turns on a stark question: can one galaxy hold two races with tools, fire, and starships, or must they fight as humans and Neanderthals once did on Earth? The crew must learn where the Plumies come from before the Plumies learn more first. It is a tense, idea-driven tale of first contact and the fear of war.
24152-the-guardians:
Irving Cox Jr. wrote this science fiction story for Astounding Science Fiction in June 1955, with pictures by van Dongen. Mryna Brill plans a ride on the god-car above the rain mist, though she no longer believes in the taboos or the Earth-god. Her paradise of green forests and running brooks is called Rythar, and she no longer believes she lives on Earth at all.

Six years earlier, at fourteen, Mryna asked a simple question, what lies above the rain mist, and the god ignored it, repeating only the taboo against the Old Village and its sickness. Like other children, she had run through the burned shells of old houses with eyes shaded. Readers get a tale of a guarded world, a curious girl, and truth kept behind mist.
24285-days-off-and-other-digressions:
Henry Van Dyke wrote this book of essays and digressions, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1907. It is dedicated to his friend and neighbor Grover Cleveland, a statesman whose great working years were brightened by good days of play as a fisherman. An Emerson verse opens the book: the forest is the author's loyal friend, and what has he to do with time, for this the day was made.

Contents run from Days Off, A Holiday in a Vacation, and His Other Engagement to Books that I Loved as a Boy. Later pieces include Among the Quantock Hills, Between the Lupin and the Laurel, Little Red Tom, and Silverhorns. Notions about Novels, Some Remarks on Gulls, Leviathan, and The Art of Leaving Off close the book. Readers get a gentle book of leisure, fishing, travel, and reading.
24385-lights-and-shadows-in-confederate-:
Homer B. Sprague, brevet colonel of the 13th Connecticut Volunteers, sometime professor at Cornell and president of the University of North Dakota, wrote this personal experience of 1864 and 1865, published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in New York and London in 1915. Its frontispiece shows portraits of fellow officers in prison: Captains Cook, Burrage, and Howe, Adjutants Gardner and Putnam, Colonel Sprague, and Lieutenant Estabrooks.

Sprague dedicates the record to the alumni of Yale, Cornell, and North Dakota, where he was student, professor, and president. Thousands of pupils yet living, companions of the Loyal Legion, and comrades of the Grand Army share the dedication. So do all surviving officers and soldiers, Union or Confederate, who cherish the patriot dead and hate war. Chapters open with the first battle of Winchester, indecisive, with Sheridan's and Early's mistakes and the capture. Readers get a prisoner's war, in light and shadow.
2440-the-naturalist-on-the-river-amazons:
Henry Walter Bates, the naturalist who traveled with Alfred Russel Wallace, records eleven years on the Amazon in this classic of exploration. The Naturalist on the River Amazons describes the river's peoples, its insects, its monkeys, and its forests, with Bates's discoveries in mimicry among his great contributions to evolution. His prose is clear, curious, and full of wonder.

The book remains a landmark of natural history writing, both for its science and its adventure. Readers of travel and biology will find a rich, firsthand account. It pairs naturally with Darwin's voyage.
24428-our-fathers-have-told-us-part-i-th:
John Ruskin wrote this volume for boys and girls who had been baptised into the Christian church, as the first part of his planned history of Christendom. It takes its name from Amiens Cathedral in northern France, whose carved stonework Ruskin reads as a picture Bible, a story in sculpture for people who could not read words.

Chapters follow the rivers of France, the Frankish kings, and the life of the cathedral, with plates of its carvings and a timeline of French history. Ruskin argues that the building itself teaches faith, history, and art together. Readers get both a guided tour of Amiens and a Victorian writer's passionate case for learning from old churches.
2447-eminent-victorians:
Lytton Strachey's Eminent Victorians demolished Victorian hero worship with four sharp biographies: Cardinal Manning, Florence Nightingale, Thomas Arnold, and General Gordon. Strachey's wit, irony, and selective detail turned biography into an art of debunking, and the book changed the genre forever. Each portrait mixes admiration with a cool, amused eye.

The volume's style, polished and mischievous, made Strachey famous overnight. Modern readers still enjoy its portraits, even where scholarship has revised them. Biography lovers will find a revolutionary classic. Strachey's Nightingale portrait mixes praise for her work with irony about her legend.
24509-in-the-mist-of-the-mountains:
Ethel Turner, author of Seven Little Australians, wrote this children's story of a mountain holiday in Australia. In October, when the mountains wake from their short winter sleep, mists roll over the valleys and hide the gum trees. Children Lynn and Max walk the mountain sides as the veil lifts and falls.

Chapters follow picnics at the falls, lessons in discipline, a runaway boy, and a story at last in print. Turner writes with warmth and humour about brothers, sisters, and the wild beauty of the Blue Mountains. Young readers get a sunny Australian tale of family life, mountain walks, and small adventures.
24597-games-for-all-occasions:
Mary E. Blain compiled this book of games at Chicago in 1909, published by Brewer, Barse. It covers games for tiny tots, for parties, and for all occasions, with rules plain enough for any group to follow. Its first game, A Running Maze, lines children up behind a leader who runs, and all must do exactly as the leader does.

Later games fill the book with chasing, guessing, singing, and acting games for indoors and out. Blain writes for mothers, teachers, and party-givers who need a game at short notice. The book remains a treasure chest for anyone planning a children's party, a schoolroom hour, or a family evening.
24617-the-wild-man-of-the-west-a-tale-of:
R. M. Ballantyne wrote this tale of the Rocky Mountains, set entirely in the foothills of the range in the early nineteenth century. Its first chapter introduces a mad hero, and the action follows hunters whose hard life Ballantyne narrates with excitement and interest. All sorts of threads pull together in the last few pages.

Readers will find it hard to guess the ending before the last two chapters, so well does Ballantyne hide his design. His story gives a vivid picture of frontier hunting, hardship, and friendship. Young readers get a classic Ballantyne adventure, brisk, wholesome, and full of mountain incident.
24778-the-national-nursery-book-with-120:
The National Nursery Book, published in London by Frederick Warne and Company, gathers the best-known nursery tales with 120 pictures. Red Riding-Hood and Cinderella appear beside Puss-in-Boots, Mother Hubbard, and Tom Thumb. Cock Robin's Death, Jack and the Bean-Stalk, and The Three Bears round out the set, with Punch and Judy, pets, songs, rhymes, and jingles beside them.

Each tale is told in short, simple form for reading aloud, and the pictures carry much of the fun. Tom's escape from the pudding and his ride in the cow's mouth show the book's cheerful tone. Families will find a full shelf of classic tales in one volume, in the style of the great Victorian nursery books.
2495-susy-a-story-of-the-plains:
Bret Harte's Susy: A Story of the Plains follows a girl growing up on the frontier, where her innocence and spirit meet the rough world of miners, soldiers, and settlers. The story traces Susy's path from childhood to young womanhood, with Harte's humor and pathos in equal measure. The plains themselves, wide and dangerous, shape her fate.

The novel shows Harte's later, more reflective manner, with a heroine at its center. Readers of his California fiction will find a gentle, engaging tale. It is a fitting late work. Harte wrote Susy while living in London, looking back at California.
25077-castellinaria-and-other-sicilian-d:
Henry Festing Jones's Castellinaria and Other Sicilian Diversions, first published in 1911 and reissued in 1920, records years of friendship and travel in Sicily. Jones, best known as Samuel Butler's friend and biographer, writes about towns, festivals, and people he came to know as a second home.

Chapters move from Castellinaria to Palermo, Catania, Trapani, and Mount Eryx, lingering on marionette players, sulphur miners, weddings, Holy Week, and the code of silence around the mafia. The book's charm lies in its unhurried observation and its affection for Sicilian courtesy, hospitality, and stubborn local pride.
25079-queensland-cousins:
E. L. Haverfield's Queensland Cousins is a children's adventure novel set on a Queensland station, where three young cousins await a parcel from home in England. The story opens with excitement on the veranda, as their father rides in and the household gathers around news from the old country.

Mystery and mischief follow, with a barefoot visitor, a night of terror, a riderless horse, and a voice from the scrub, all set against bush life and encounters with Aboriginal people. Haverfield writes for young readers, mixing family warmth with suspense, though modern readers will notice the dated attitudes of its colonial setting.
25080-babylonians-and-assyrians:
Babylonians and Assyrians, by the Reverend A. H. Sayce, Oxford professor of Assyriology, surveys daily life in ancient Mesopotamia for general readers. Published around 1900 as part of a series of handbooks on Semitic peoples, it draws on cuneiform tablets and excavation reports that were still fresh discoveries.

Chapters cover the family, schooling, slavery and free labor, manners, trades, wages, banking, government, the army, law, letter writing, and religion, with an appendix on weights and measures. Sayce writes in a clear, popular style, and the book remains a readable doorway into a civilization known then mainly through the Bible and a handful of digs.
2528-the-women-of-the-french-salons:
Amelia Gere Mason wrote this study of the women who ran the famous salons of France across two centuries, drawing on memoirs, letters, and chronicles. Her subjects hosted poets, philosophers, and statesmen in their drawing rooms, and their talk shaped taste, letters, and even politics.

Mason gives close portraits of hostesses like Madame de Lambert, whose salon was famed for fine moral talk, and she measures their influence with modern eyes. The book argues that these women, working through society rather than office, wielded real power. It remains a lively guide to a world where wit at tea could move a nation.
25334-deerfoot-in-the-mountains:
Edward S. Ellis's Deerfoot in the Mountains, published in Philadelphia in 1905, is the third volume of the New Deerfoot Series. Illustrated by J. Steeple Davis, it follows George and Victor, heroes of the Log Cabin Series, with the Shawnee guide Deerfoot.

Set in the time of Lewis and Clark, the story carries a small band from the Ohio toward the Pacific. Among the Nez Perces, Deerfoot burns with indignation when Amokeat rides his horse Whirlwind without asking. Victor, impulsive as ever, agrees the horse should allow no other rider. Ellis writes frontier adventure for boys.
25338-the-idea-of-god-in-early-religions:
F. B. Jevons's Idea of God in Early Religions, published by Cambridge University Press in 1913, traces how early peoples conceived of God. Jevons, professor of philosophy at Durham, builds his lectures on mythology, worship, and prayer, closing with the idea and being of God.

He begins with the child born into a community, learning its language, ideas, and actions before forming any of his own. That social view shapes his account of gods in myth and rite. A bibliography cites Frazer's Golden Bough, Grant Allen, and other pioneers of anthropology. The book is a clear early study of comparative religion.
25494-the-young-alaskans:
Emerson Hough sends young travellers through Alaska in this 1908 Harper boys' book. Chapters follow them afloat on the Pacific, lost in fog, adrift on the ocean, and sheltering in a hut on the beach. They watch the salmon run, meet the big bear of Kodiak, and deal with a savage refugee and a troublesome prisoner. Ways of the wilderness close their education in the north.

One vivid passage explains the Aleut whale hunt. A slate harpoon-head does not kill by its wound, but poisons it, so the wound festers and the whale floats ashore days later for waiting hunters. Rob learns this only after the chief's broken English puzzles him. Harper and Brothers published the book in October 1908, illustrated from the author's northern journeys.
25513-edmund-dulac-s-fairy-book-fairy-ta:
Edmund Dulac illustrates this fairy book of tales from the Allied nations, published in New York by George H. Doran. A Russian tale, Snegorotchka, opens the book, showing the daintiest little maiden her makers had ever seen.

The Buried Moon comes from England, White Caroline and Black Caroline from Flanders, and the Seven Conquerors of the Queen of the Mississippi from Belgium. Italy, France, Russia again, and Ireland add further tales, including the Serpent Prince, the Hind of the Wood, and the Queen of the Many-Coloured Bedchamber. Each tale names its nation in its heading, so young readers learn geography beside wonder.
25623-barbarians:
Robert W. Chambers writes this war novel, published by Burt in New York by arrangement with Appleton, with a front picture by A. I. Keller. He dedicates it to Lyle and Madeleine Mahan, and opens with verse on France, daughter of light, facing the bestial wrath of Barbary.

The Hun beats his painted drum, war horns blare, and France takes her stand, magnificent and fair, with Christ's lilies in her hair. Chapters titled Fed Up and Marooned follow a dozen odd malcontents into danger, as Chambers turns the Great War into a tale of French spirit against German force.
25639-graded-memory-selections:
S. D. Waterman of Berkeley, J. W. McClymonds of Oakland, and C. C. Hughes of Alameda arrange these graded memory selections, published by the Educational Publishing Company in 1903. All three men served as superintendents of schools in California cities.

Their preface warns that education and culture are not the same, and that public school children often possess facts while lacking culture. Greek youths, they recall, learned Homer and other great poets by heart, and memory work offers modern pupils the same grace. Passages graded by difficulty fill the book for classroom recitation.
25749-a-tall-ship-on-other-naval-occasio:
Bartimeus, the pen name of Captain Lewis Ritchie, writes A Tall Ship on other naval occasions, published by Cassell in 1915 and reprinted twice that year. A Masefield epigraph asks for a tall ship and a star to steer by, a laughing yarn, and quiet sleep when the long trick ends.

Contents list crab pots, the drum, a captain's forenoon, the seven bell boat, the king's pardon, and an offshore wind. The day, the mummers, chummy ships, and the higher claim follow. Ritchie writes of disciplined minds in crisis, detached and unhurried, as naval men face war, routine, and humour at sea.
25792-the-sympathy-of-religions:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson delivers this address, The Sympathy of Religions, at Horticultural Hall, Boston, on 6 February 1870. It was reprinted from The Radical in Boston in 1871, a year after delivery. Greek words appear transliterated between plus marks.

Higginson argues true religious life begins when we find an inner light, not infallible but invaluable, lighting every man who comes into the world. That light gives something to steer by, not an anchor, since the human soul, like a noble vessel, was built to sail, not to rest. The address pleads for sympathy across faiths.
26062-thoughts-on-missions:
Rev. Sheldon Dibble, late missionary in the Sandwich Islands, writes Thoughts on Missions, printed by the American Tract Society. Taking for texts the commands to go into all the world and teach all nations. Dibble sets out the true spirit of missions, Christian stewardship, guilt in neglecting the heathen, the Savior's last command, and laymen called to the field. Chapters praise lowliness like Christ's, readiness to suffer, and love that outlasts ingratitude.

Dibble argues from early church practice that common Christians, not clergy alone, spread the gospel, citing Paul's fellow travelers and helpers named in his letters. Lay members, he says, should go forth in great numbers in ways proper to them. The book is a earnest, practical plea for mission giving, going, and prayer.
26208-three-little-cousins:
Amy E. Blanchard's 1907 children's book brings three cousins together from three different worlds. Molly Shelton waits at an eastern station for Polly, who rides in from a Colorado ranch with Uncle Dick. A third cousin, Mary, comes with exact little ways shaped by life in England, and Mrs. Shelton warns Molly that Mary will differ from free-spirited Polly.

Chapters follow the rhinestone pin, discoveries, Elton Woods, Ellis and a baby, new burdens, and the Roseberry family. A Garden of Verses performance and talk of east and west round out the fun. The book treats cousinship as a meeting of manners, with ranch freedom, eastern home life, and English polish learning to share one house.
26474-some-naval-yarns:
Mordaunt Hall's 1917 collection, with a preface by Lady Beatty, gathers yarns of the Royal Navy in the Great War. British servicemen, Hall notes, are exasperatingly modest, and names must often stay hidden, but their stories ring true. A naval airman called Q opens the book, running his seaplane out at dawn, testing engines that kick, and flying over the North Sea.

Later yarns cover sweeping the seas for mines, the Royal Naval Division, a naval school, and a run in a naval ambulance train. A trip in a submarine, life in a lighthouse, and watchers of the coast follow. Lighter tales show sailors on leave, one racing from Cairo to catch his ship by motor-bicycle and motor-boat. The tone is admiring, breezy, and firsthand.
26593-the-place-of-honeymoons:
Harold MacGrath published this romance with Bobbs-Merrill at Indianapolis in 1912, with illustrations by Arthur I. Keller. It opens at a stage door, where Courtlandt sits tense, listening to a prima donna whose voice recalls a temple at Rangoon, with golden domes, candles, and yellow-robed priests. Memory, music, and longing set the novel's key from the first page.

Later chapters move to Marseilles and Paris, where a singer loses her voice and an abduction is investigated, with Courtlandt's movements closely accounted for. A duke, a colonel, a ball at a villa, and pistols for two carry the tale toward journey's end. MacGrath mixes opera, travel, and drawing-room intrigue in a honeymoon story that is rarely quiet.
26645-two-daring-young-patriots-or-outwi:
W. P. Shervill, author of Edgar the Ready, published this schoolboy war story with Blackie and Son, illustrated by Arch. Webb. It opens with a rowing crew, Benson's eight, where Durend's stroke and Montgomery's temper set the crew's troubles before the races. School rivalries give way to cataclysm when war breaks and Liège falls, and Belgian boys face German occupation.

Max Durend at home, treachery, and a manager named Schenk drive the plot, as shells cast for Belgian guns are found to fit German guns instead. Attacks on a power-house and munition-shops, a dash through the Ardennes, cutting the line, and a great coup follow. Two lads hurl stones on German soldiery and cheer their watchers, in a patriotic adventure of its wartime day.
26688-history-manners-and-customs-of-the:
Old Humphrey, the pen name of George Mogridge, wrote this volume, revised by Thomas O. Summers and published by the Southern Methodist Publishing House at Nashville in 1859. Summers notes it is one of Mogridge's books for the London Religious Tract Society, in substance a reprint chiefly compiled from Catlin, with spirited illustrations of Indian life and scenery. Parts deemed irrelevant or not well authenticated were omitted.

A frame story follows brothers Austin, twelve and daring, Brian, about ten and fearful, and Basil, six and affectionate, all lovers of books and wonderful relations. On a wild, gusty day they walk home from an uncle four or five miles away. They reach a rocky eminence above a river nearly a hundred fathoms below, where a landslip once slid half an acre of earth and oaks. In play they become Camanchee, Sioux, and Pawnee chieftains hunting a buffalo.
26879-night-bombing-with-the-bedouins:
Robert H. Reece, lieutenant of the Royal Air Force with the Distinguished Flying Cross, published this memoir with Houghton Mifflin in 1919, as one of the squadron. It is dedicated to Lieutenant Samuel Pierce Mandell, an American Air Service pilot killed in action, called a true sportsman, loyal friend, and gallant officer. Six chapters run from Per Ardua ad Astra through the Bedouin squadron at Ochey aerodrome to a night raid and the guiding hand.

Reece opens with invention itself, from the first stone hatchet to machines that swoop like swallows, raking troops by day and bombing by night. Early war planes flew unarmed, for reconnaissance only. Then two great blind armies, stretched from Belgium's coast to Switzerland's border, learned to see through eyes in the air. Among the Bedouins, the dare-devil Mid wangles his way into the squadron and becomes its life and soul.
26900-report-of-the-lords-commissioners-:
A report printed at London in 1772 by J. Almon, from the Lords Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, on the petition of Thomas Walpole, Benjamin Franklin, John Sargent, Samuel Wharton, and their associates. The petitioners sought a grant of lands on the River Ohio in North America, large enough to erect a new government. The Treasury had already accepted their price and quit-rent in principle. The commissioners report under an order of May 25, 1770.

Their sketch shows the tract taking part of Virginia's dominion south of the Ohio and stretching west from the Appalachian ridge. A considerable part, they warn, lies beyond the treaty boundary line settled with the Six Nations and the Cherokees, to whom the crown's faith stands solemnly pledged. The report also weighs a rival claim: that the Five Nations of the Iroquois are the lawful proprietors of the Ohio country by origin or conquest.
26933-visions-and-revisions-a-book-of-li:
John Cowper Powys published this book of literary devotions with G. Arnold Shaw of New York in 1915, printed three times within the year. Its dedication runs to those who love without understanding, those who understand without loving, and those who, neither loving nor understanding, are why books get written. Seventeen essays follow, on Rabelais, Dante, Shakespeare, El Greco, Milton, Charles Lamb, Dickens, Goethe, Matthew Arnold, Shelley, Keats, Nietzsche, Hardy, Pater, Dostoievsky, Poe, and Whitman.

The Rabelais essay sets the method. Critics are like children showing wreckage and shells to explain the sea. Rabelais, sanest of great writers, gives readers courage through a spiritual drunkenness without madness. The Lamb essay turns to Witches, A Child-Angel, and Dream-children, whose sentences take a natural man's breath away. Each devotion offers modest advice to the reader rather than a system.
26998-peter-pan-in-kensington-gardens:
Charles Scribner's Sons' 1910 edition of J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens presents the Peter chapters from The Little White Bird with drawings by Arthur Rackham. The Gardens, where the King lives, hold the lady with the balloons, old Mr. Salford, and Solomon Caw, who rules the birds.

Peter's story turns on the celebrated building of the boat, when thrushes stop building nests and Solomon must send sparrows to lay eggs in old thrushes' nests. Rackham's pictures give the tale its dreamlike air, and this American edition remains a favorite way into Barrie's first Peter.
26999-peter-pan-in-kensington-gardens:
J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens, in Arthur Rackham's illustrated 1906 edition, lifts the Peter Pan chapters out of The Little White Bird. The book opens with a grand tour of the Gardens, where the King lives, and follows Peter through lock-out time, the thrush's nest, and the little house.

Peter, the boy who never grows up, bargains with Solomon the crow, quarrels with birds over how nests should be built, and keeps his goat among the flowers. Rackham's pictures and Barrie's gentle prose make this the first, dreamiest telling of Peter, before Neverland.
27071-the-third-miss-symons:
F. M. Mayor's The Third Miss Symons, first published in 1913 with a preface by John Masefield, follows Henrietta Symons, the third daughter and fifth child in her family. By the time she arrived, her parents' delight in babies had faded, and at two she lost the youngest place to a new brother.

At five, Henrietta became a very pretty, charming little girl, with an air of graciousness that captivated visitors and earned her elder sisters' grudge. Mayor traces a girlhood of petting, secrets, and family feeling with quiet irony and close attention to domestic life.
27163-suspended-judgments-essays-on-book:
John Cowper Powys's Suspended Judgments, published in New York in 1916 and dedicated to Bernard Price O'Neill, gathers essays on books and sensations. The contents open with The Art of Discrimination, then turn to Montaigne, Pascal, Voltaire, and Rousseau.

Later essays take up Balzac, Victor Hugo, Guy de Maupassant, Anatole France, Paul Verlaine, and Remy de Gourmont, closing with William Blake and Byron. Powys writes as a critic of taste and feeling, suspending judgment to weigh each writer's sensations before he judges. The volume was published by G. Arnold Shaw in New York. An essay on the art of discrimination opens the book.
2725-red-pepper-burns:
Grace S. Richmond wrote this cheerful novel of a country doctor, Red Pepper Burns, whose chapters read like a diary of deeds. He vows a vow, creates a circus, assumes a responsibility, and makes a concession, rough on a friend and prescribing for himself.

He saws wood, suffers a defeat, proves himself a host, and gets even with himself, all with bluster and a kind heart. Richmond writes with humor and warmth about small town life, illness, and love. The book charms as a portrait of a doctor who heals by energy as much as medicine.
2726-eight-cousins:
Louisa M. Alcott wrote this beloved girls' book about Rose Campbell, an orphan who comes to live with eight boy cousins. The author's preface owns her hopes for the story, and the cousins, with their uncle Alec, set out to raise Rose on fun, fresh air, and common sense.

Rose learns to ride, to romp, and to choose her own way, while each cousin teaches a different lesson. Alcott writes with warmth and moral cheer, without preaching. The book endures as a classic of family life, and a portrait of a girl growing strong among boys.
2729-a-tale-of-three-lions:
H. Rider Haggard tells this hunting tale through Allan Quatermain, who came to live in England near Sir Henry Curtis after finding King Solomon's mines. Like most old hunters, Quatermain went back to the wilderness again, on one pretext or another.

The interest on ten shillings sets the story moving, and three lions provide the danger, the comedy, and the test of nerve. Haggard writes with a hunter's detail and a storyteller's timing. The tale charms as a short, vivid African adventure, told by a man who knew the bush.
27300-the-young-adventurer-or-tom-s-trip:
Horatio Alger Jr., author of Bound to Rise and Risen from the Ranks, wrote this boys' novel of a trip across the plains, published by Hurst and Company in New York. Tom, a poor boy of Mark Nelson's family, finds a wallet, raises money, and sets out west. The chapters follow him from Pittsburg to the river steamer River Belle and on to St. Joe.

Along the way Tom faces a villain named Graham, an arrest, a night panic, a lost horse, and Indians. He even becomes an Indian for a time and gives a magical soiree before his escape. Alger's moral is his usual one: pluck and honesty carry a boy through. Young readers get a lively overland adventure in the classic Alger manner.
27343-fireside-stories-for-girls-in-thei:
Margaret W. Eggleston, an instructor in story telling at Boston University, wrote this 1921 set of stories for girls in their teens. She dedicated it to the girls of two Camp Fire groups in Cleveland and Boston. The tales were meant to be read aloud by a fireside, and each one turns on a choice a young girl must make about truth, honor, or courage.

The opening tale follows a girl sent from Philadelphia to the country for pure air, simple food, and real quiet. Later stories take up school days, a search for a real mother, and the road to womanhood. Titles such as The Winning of an Honor and The House of Truth show the plain moral aim throughout. The book still reads as a warm, old-fashioned guide to growing up straight and kind.
27378-the-story-of-the-heavens:
Sir Robert Stawell Ball, Lowndean Professor of Astronomy and Geometry at Cambridge and formerly Royal Astronomer of Ireland, wrote this popular astronomy. It came in a new and revised edition from Cassell in 1900, with twenty-four coloured plates and many illustrations. Ball explains the heavens for general readers, starting with the astronomical observatory itself.

Plates show Saturn as seen in 1872 and the Moon from drawings by Nasmyth, among other sights of the sky. Ball's clear, friendly teaching made him one of the best-known explainers of astronomy in his time. The book still offers a handsome, old-fashioned introduction to the stars, planets, and the instruments that study them.
27452-a-tour-of-the-missions-observation:
Augustus Hopkins Strong, president emeritus of the Rochester Theological Seminary and author of Systematic Theology, published this account with the Griffith and Rowland Press in March 1918. After forty years of presidency and teaching, Strong found that more than a hundred of his pupils had become missionaries in heathen lands, and they had long urged him to visit them.

When he laid down his official duties, Strong chose a tour round the world over sitting down to read the new Encyclopaedia Britannica, or so he jokes in his foreword. The book records what he observed at mission stations and what he concluded from the journey. It gives a missionary statesman's view of world missions at the end of the Great War.
27886-india-and-the-indians:
Edward F. Elwin of the Society of St. John the Evangelist, Cowley, wrote India and the Indians, published in London by John Murray in 1913 with illustrations. Elwin, author of Indian Jottings and Thirty-Four Years in Poona City, draws on long missionary residence in India.

Forty-seven chapters cover Indian hospitality, the postal service, village life, music, meals, Hindu philosophy, wrestlers, pageants, unrest, and the English in India. The book is a missionary's observant portrait of India before the First World War, sympathetic in tone and wide in curiosity, though written from a colonial standpoint.
27981-the-plant-hunters-adventures-among:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote The Plant Hunters, adventures among the Himalaya mountains, opening by explaining what a plant-hunter is. Not a truffle-hunter, the plant-hunter devotes his life to collecting rare plants and flowers, and the whole civilized world owes him its gardens.

Reid lists dahlias, peonies, camelias, kalmias, azaleas, rhododendrons, and jessamines as gifts of the plant-hunter, who made cold, cloudy England a garden brighter than Cashmere. The book follows Himalayan plant-hunting as adventure, with botany, travel, and boyish enthusiasm joined in Reid's popular manner. Reid stresses that plant-hunters are not simply botanists, but professionals who make collecting rare plants their life's work.
2804-rose-in-bloom-a-sequel-to-eight-cou:
Louisa May Alcott wrote this sequel to Eight Cousins, following Rose Campbell from girlhood into young womanhood. Rose returns from travels to find her cousins grown, her fortune waiting, and suitors circling a girl who must choose wisely.

Alcott writes with warmth about work, charity, and love, as Rose tests her ideals against society's claims. The book charms as a coming of age story, and as a portrait of a good girl becoming a good woman. It remains a beloved companion to Eight Cousins. Rose's fortune proves a heavier test than poverty.
28146-on-the-future-of-our-educational-i:
Friedrich Nietzsche's On the Future of Our Educational Institutions, translated by J. M. Kennedy, forms volume three of the first authorised English edition of his works, edited by Oscar Levy. The book, published in Edinburgh and London in 1910, collects lectures Nietzsche gave on schools and universities in Germany. Its preface asks for calm, unhurried reading.

Nietzsche argues that modern schools serve the state and the market rather than true learning, and that real education needs leisure, discipline, and reverence for great culture. The lectures are sharp, witty, and often angry. They remain a starting point for debates about what schools are for.
2824-sintram-and-his-companions:
Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué wrote Sintram and His Companions as the winter tale among his four seasonal romances, with a foreword by Charlotte Yonge in this edition. Sintram, a young knight haunted by dark visions, rides through a harsh northern world of castles, pilgrims, and strange companions. Battles break out suddenly, as when Biorn's soldiers lose courage before a wondrous onset like a torrent from Mount Hecla.

The story works as a spiritual allegory, since Sintram's outward fights mirror his struggle against temptation and despair. Fouqué draws on chivalric legend, giving the tale the stern and grave tone Yonge assigns to winter. Readers who know Undine will find a darker companion piece, concerned less with love than with endurance and repentance.
2826-the-two-captains:
Friedrich de la Motte Fouqué set The Two Captains on a mild summer evening at Malaga, where guitars sound from ships, houses, and garden villas. Soldiers waiting to embark at dawn forget their orders in the pleasant air, and two captains, Fadrique and his faithful companion Heimbert, become the center of the tale. It is the summer romance among Fouqué's four seasonal stories.

The action moves from Spanish shores to a burning palace, where Fadrique rushes up marble stairs through halls lined with rolls of parchment. Honor, friendship, and love drive the captains through danger and rescue. The story charms through its southern setting and its chivalric view of loyalty tested by fire and fortune.
28303-the-smart-set-correspondence-conve:
Clyde Fitch wrote The Smart Set: Correspondence and Conversations in 1897 as a book of society letters and talk. Fitch, dedicating the book to Mumsy, to whom he owes everything. He opens with The Makeway Ball, five letters from William Makeway, his wife, his daughter, a guest, and an uninvited visitor, on a New York party. Herbert S. Stone published the volume in Chicago and New York.

Later pieces cover a plaintiff, the summer, children, maternity, Wagner, art, sorrow, theatre, opera, and a perfect day. Fitch writes with wit and polish about smart society. The book offers a charming sample of 1890s American social comedy in letters.
28379-if-yes-and-perhaps-four-possibilit:
Edward E. Hale's If, Yes, and Perhaps, published in Boston in 1869, gathers short sketches that mix fact, fancy, ancient history, modern travel, and imagination. Hale jokes in his preface about the book's odd title, after abandoning a far longer descriptive title for the manuscript.

The sketches illustrate, in his words, the poetry of the Bible, the history of Christianity, the manners of the times, and the politics of past and present generations. Some pieces lean on real history, while others invent freely. Together they show a popular nineteenth-century American writer entertaining readers while slipping moral and historical points into lively tales.
28388-the-wreck-on-the-andamans:
Joseph Darvall wrote The Wreck on the Andamans in 1845 from authentic documents, at the request of the troop-ships' owners. On the morning of November 12, 1844, the Runnymede and Briton, both troop-ships, wrecked on an Andaman island in the Bay of Bengal. Soldiers and seamen faced storm, shore, and rescue, with cool intrepidity, Darvall says, that deserves a monument.

Darvall, with access to official papers, shapes the facts into a narrative of preservation and ultimate deliverance. Pelham Richardson published the book in London. The volume offers a vivid, primary account of a remarkable shipwreck and the discipline that saved its people.
28425-the-cave-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote The Cave Twins as the sixth book in her Twins series. It is set in a distant age before houses, farms, roads, wheels, or books existed. The twins Firetop and Firefly live by hunting, fishing, and quick thinking, since every tool and skill must be worked out from scratch.

When their parents set out to explore beyond the horizon, the twins secretly follow them. An earthquake and great wave then strand the whole family on an island later known as the Isle of Wight. Their father builds the first canoe from an idea the twins suggest, and uses it to fetch the rest of the family. The story teaches early human invention through adventure.
28426-the-italian-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins's The Italian Twins follows twelve-year-old Beppo and Beppina Grifoni, children of the Marchese Grifoni of Florence. On Easter Saturday they visit the cathedral with their nurse Teresina, lose her in the crowds, and lose their way home.

A couple traveling with a trained monkey and bear offer to take them home, but the children are kidnapped instead and travel through villages, dancing and singing to earn their keep. After many months Beppo steals a boat, and the twins reach Padua, where Teresina and their mother have come to pray to Saint Antony. The reunion closes a gentle adventure.
28431-the-irish-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins's The Irish Twins, published in 1913 as the third book in her Twins series, was intended as a Grade V reader for American children. It pictures Irish farm children in the late nineteenth century, with just enough Irish speech to carry the flavour of their talk.

The story opens with old Grannie Malone alone in her one-room cabin, knitting by a peat fire and turning over a letter from Michael that she cannot read herself. She talks to her tea-kettle, fetches water, and waits for someone learned to tell her the letter's news. Through Grannie Malone and the twins, Perkins introduces young readers to Irish home life.
2851-sixes-and-sevens:
O. Henry packed Sixes and Sevens with twenty-five short stories that show his range beyond the famous twist ending. The contents run from the last of the troubadours and a pair of sleuths to witches' loaves, a holdup of a train, and a New York seen by campfire light. Detectives, tramps, clerks, and society figures all get their turn in the spotlight.

The stories mix humor, sentiment, and surprise, with dialogue carrying much of the work. A haunted house tied to a Revolutionary captain and a church with an overshot wheel show how O. Henry grounded jokes in vivid places. The collection suits readers who want O. Henry at his most varied, funny, and humane.
28558-the-ancient-history-of-the-egyptia:
Charles Rollin's Ancient History, volume 1 of six, appeared in a new illustrated London edition in 1850, translated from the French. Rollin, late principal of the University of Paris, covers Egyptians, Carthaginians, Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes and Persians, Macedonians, and Grecians. Maps and engravings accompany the text, and a letter from Bishop Atterbury commends the work.

Book 1 describes Egypt by region, from Thebais through Middle Egypt to Lower Egypt, then treats kings, priests, soldiers, arts, and fertility. Book 2 turns to Carthage, its character and foundation, and book 3 to Assyria, Media, and Lydia. Readers get an eighteenth-century classic of ancient history in Victorian dress.
28819-the-school-queens:
L. T. Meade wrote this 1910 school story for girls, published in New York. Meade, born Elizabeth Thomasina Smith in County Cork in 1854, was a prolific English novelist whose girls' books were popular on both sides of the Atlantic. She edited the magazine Atlanta for six years and studied East London life in the British Museum, bringing that observation to her fiction.

The School Queens follows her usual pattern of schoolgirl friendship, influence, and moral growth, told with pathos, love, and humor. Meade's girls shape their elders as much as they are shaped, a trait her readers prized. The book offers a period picture of girls' school life and of the values Meade's generation wanted young readers to carry: loyalty, courage, and kindness under pressure.
28889-the-mexican-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote this 1915 children's book about the Mexican twins, illustrated by the author and published by Houghton Mifflin. Antonio Francisco Gomez and his twin sister Margarita Teresa Gomez live on the hacienda of Señor Fernandez in Mexico, and they are eight years old. Everyone calls them Tonio and Tita, to save time, and their father goes by Pancho.

The chapters follow San Ramon's day, the blessing, the party, Tonio's bad day, Judas Iscariot day, and an adventure, ending with Christmas at the hacienda. Perkins, who wrote twins books for many countries, teaches Mexican life through daily scenes and festivals. Readers get a warm, old-fashioned geography story, told through two children on a great plantation.
29085-adventures-and-recollections:
Bill o' th' Hoylus End tells his own life story in this book, transcribed from the Keighley Herald in 1893. Bill, a Yorkshire character who has been everything by turns and nothing long, looks back from later life on a youth spent in pranks, work, and wandering. He calls himself a son of mischief, art, and guile.

Chapters follow his birthplace and musical father, a mischievous boyhood, school life, work at the mill and among hand woolcombers, learning the fiddle, and trying life as an acrobat and strolling player. Readers get a vivid local memoir, told in Bill's own voice, that doubles as a picture of working life in a Yorkshire mill town.
29106-a-bride-of-the-plains:
Baroness Orczy wrote this 1915 novel, A Bride of the Plains, published by George H. Doran in New York. Orczy, author of The Scarlet Pimpernel, dedicates the book to the memory of Louis Kossuth, the Hungarian patriot. She laments that Hungary now sits tied to Austria's chariot wheel, a tool of the Teutonic race Kossuth abhorred. The Magyar peasant lad on the vast plains still dreams of national liberty.

The novel's chapters carry titles like God bless them all, money won't buy everything, you will wait for me, and love will follow. Orczy sets a romance of plain folk against Hungary's national sorrow. Readers get a passionate period novel of love and patriotism, by a writer famous for swashbuckling romance turned to a people's cause.
29140-the-mathematicians:
Arthur Feldman wrote this short science fiction story, framed as a tale a father tells his nine-year-old daughter Zoe in a garden. Drake Hawkins settles Zoe in a hammock and promises a true story. Two thousand and eleven years ago, he begins, a tribe of beings from Sirius, the Dog-star, invaded Earth.

The magazine's editors add their own joke in the introduction. They gave the story to an artist, who drew the hero. When challenged, she asked them to prove it was not the hero. Readers get a playful, family-framed invasion tale, where a bedtime story carries a cosmic joke and the art itself becomes part of the fun.
29310-the-affair-of-the-brains:
Anthony Gilmore wrote this complete novelette, published in Astounding Stories in March 1932. Hawk Carse himself sets out to meet Judd the Kite and the sinister genius Ku Sui at their rendezvous. Though Earthmen seldom hear Carse's name now, the tale says, outposts of the farthest planets still remember his magic, and outlanders yarn about him in idle hours.

Carse, a slender adventurer with gray eyes and queer bangs obscuring his forehead, won fame through steely will, a phenomenal ray-gun draw, and reckless spaceship maneuvering. That was before the patrol ships came. Readers get a pulp space yarn of a rendezvous with a villain, told as a legend from a raw, lusty period of frontier space.
29323-an-old-sailor-s-yarns:
N. Ames, author of Mariner's Sketches, published this collection of sea yarns in New York in 1835. George Dearborn issued the book, printed by William Van Norden, with dialect, spelling, and punctuation preserved as far as possible. Ames writes as an old sailor telling stories from a life at sea.

Contents include Mary Bowline, Old Cuff, Rivals, Morton, and the Pirate of Masafuero. The yarns mix love, rivalry, and piracy with the working detail of ships. Readers get an early American sea-story collection, rough in dialect and rich in salt-water incident, from a time when sailing ships still ruled the oceans.
29372-a-discourse-on-the-study-of-the-la:
Sir James Mackintosh, M.P., gave this discourse as the opening to a course of lectures on a wide and weighty science: the law of nature and nations. The second edition, printed in London in 1828, lays out why such study matters, how it should be pursued, and what it can teach the student of law and statecraft. Mackintosh speaks to beginners, urging care, order, and a wide view.

His plea is for a humane science of law, one that joins reason with history and morals. The discourse abridges the labor of the student, guides inquiry, and lightens the tedium of first steps. Readers of legal history will find a classic statement of how the law of nations was once taught and why its teachers held it so high.
29450-the-prodigal-returns:
Lilian Staveley's 1921 memoir of the soul's return was printed in London by John M. Watkins. In five parts it traces a life from first memory onward: sunshine and a garden path, a nurse's face and voice, then the pain of parting at two years old. A pond, a baby brother held fast, and a meadow of buttercups follow.

Staveley reads her own life as a parable of the prodigal: loss, longing, and at last a homecoming to God. The prose is tender, inward, and plain. Readers drawn to spiritual memoir will find a moving account of how a soul wanders, suffers, and returns.
29641-the-business-career-in-its-public-:
Albert Shaw, editor of the American Review of Reviews, wrote The Business Career in Its Public Relations. It was a Barbara Weinstock Lecture on the Morals of Trade, printed by Paul Elder and Company of San Francisco. Shaw argues that losses from fraud and dishonesty keep shrinking, and standards keep rising. An honest man's odds of success in business, he says, grow with that rise.

The lecture treats business as a public trust, judged by its relations with customers, workers, and the community. It belongs to a series on the moral law in business under a new economic order. Students of business ethics will find a hopeful, Progressive-era case for honesty as sound policy.
29693-a-waif-of-the-mountains:
Edward S. Ellis published this mountain tale in 1900, and it opens in a hard Sierra blizzard at Dead Man's Gulch. Snow has fallen for a full day, the gale howls through the gorges, and travel is near impossible for man or beast. Eleven miners' shanties stand on a shelf above the pass, safe from the spring torrents that rush through the ravine below.

Into this camp comes a waif, a lost child found among rough men, and the tale follows what the miners do for her and what perils follow. Ellis, a veteran writer of boys' tales, keeps the pace brisk and the scenes stark: deep snow, hidden hollows, and a small life at stake. The book is a plain tale of rough kindness in a hard place.
29808-the-man-who-wins:
Robert Herrick published The Man Who Wins with Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1897. It opens on a drive from the university town of Camberton to the Four Corners in Middleton. Young fellows often drove the old turnpike from the arsenal quarter, past Spring Pond's low marshes, toward Middleton's rolling hills. After dinner, a dance, or late chat over supper, they rode home at midnight, singing.

On frosty October mornings they snuggled into overcoats, lit pipes, and spun over hard roads where night frost lay like a crust of milk. Crossing the meadows toward Camberton, they faced the autumn sun head-on while heading to report at the little stucco chapel, as the tinny college bell summoned them to prayer. The Ellwells kept the old Four Corners house long after the family moved out. Herrick's novel grows from that house and town.
29815-the-declaration-of-the-rights-of-m:
Georg Jellinek, professor of law at Heidelberg, wrote this contribution to modern constitutional history, translated by Max Farrand and revised by the author. Henry Holt and Company printed it in New York in 1901. Farrand says the essay had reached only a few specialists in modern European history, though it matters most to students of early American constitutional history.

Jellinek traces the origin of bills of rights, and his thesis is bold. The French Declaration of August 26, 1789, did not come from Rousseau's Contrat Social. Its models were the bills of rights of the individual states of the North American Union, Virginia foremost among them. Chapters compare the French and American texts, set them against English practice, and treat religious liberty and the Teutonic conception of right.
30050-tales-from-catland-for-little-kitt:
An Old Tabby, signing herself Tabitha Grimalkin, wrote Tales from Catland for Little Kittens, printed in Boston in MDCCCLII by Ticknor, Reed, and Fields, with engravings from designs by Billings. Tabitha dedicates the pages very affectionately to the kittens of England, as their sincere friend and well-wisher. The Three Cats opens the book, many hundred years ago, in the good old times of the fairies.

A young princess lives in a very grand palace, its walls of purest white marble, its doors of orange-wood, its window frames of gold, and its furniture of the most costly kind. Tapestry hangs her drawing room, crimson silk curtains bear golden flowers, mirrors reach from floor to ceiling, and ebony chairs are inlaid with precious stones. The princess, the cats, and the fairy times that follow make a charming picture book for very young readers.
30088-dorothy-dainty-at-the-mountains:
Amy Brooks sends Dorothy Dainty to the mountains in one more volume of the popular series for younger readers, with pictures drawn by the author herself. Dorothy, already known from books at school, at the shore, in the city, and at home, now takes a mountain holiday. An early scene has her calling out and hearing the echo answer back. Large type, cloth binding, and Brooks's own cover designs mark the series throughout.

The volume stands among a long shelf of Dorothy books, beside the Randy books and the Prue books, all priced at one dollar in the publisher's list. Brooks writes in a warm, simple style for girls, with good manners, kind friends, and small adventures at the center. Readers who like old-fashioned series fiction will find the mountain book an easy, cheerful entry point.
30089-young-barbarians:
Ian Maclaren wrote Young Barbarians, printed in New York in 1910 by Dodd, Mead and Company, with a first edition in October 1901. The book was copyrighted in 1899 and 1900 by the Curtis Publishing Company as A Scots Grammar School, and in 1901 by Dodd, Mead. Maclaren had already written Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush. A frontispiece shows Nestie standing in the centre of the large entrance hall. Sixteen chapters follow a Scots grammar school's boys.

Speug, Bulldog, and Nestie open the roll, with a famous victory, his private capacity, and the disgrace of Mr. Byles. The Count, a tournament, Moossy, and a last resource follow, with a pleasant sin, guerilla warfare, and the fall of Goliath. The bailie's double, the triumph of the seminary, and Bulldog's recompense close the book.
3012-the-acharnians:
Aristophanes wrote The Acharnians as the first of three comedies on war and peace, produced in the sixth year of the Peloponnesian War. The introduction places it beside Peace and Lysistrata, written in the tenth and twenty-first years of the war, each pressing Athens toward an end to fighting. Dicaeopolis, a farmer weary of war, makes his own private peace with Sparta.

The comedy turns on disguise and parody, as Dicaeopolis begs Euripides for the rags of Telephus, the lame, begging, boastful, fine-speaking Mysian, rather than Bellerophon's filthy dress. Euripides's slave fetches Telephus's tatters from atop the rags of Thyestes. The play remains a brilliant antiwar farce, funny, obscene, and serious at once.
30127-tales-from-dickens:
Hallie Erminie Rives retells Charles Dickens for young readers, opening with a short life of the novelist and then giving each novel in brief chapters of its own. Little Nell wanders with her grandfather, and Oliver Twist finds his way to London. Barnaby Rudge drifts toward riot and ruin, and David Copperfield grows from a hard childhood toward a steadier adult life. Pip, Nicholas Nickleby, and the Pickwick club each get the same plain, swift treatment.

Reginald B. Birch drew the pictures for the 1905 Bobbs-Merrill volume, and the retellings keep the best-known scenes while cutting the long side plots. Florence Dombey, Sam Weller, Miss Havisham, and Mr. Micawber all appear in short form, so a reader new to Dickens can meet his chief figures and chief turns of plot without first facing a full-length novel.
30131-nye-and-riley-s-wit-and-humor-poem:
James Whitcomb Riley and Bill Nye pair their comic voices in a volume of poems and yarns, with pictures by Baron de Grimm, E. Zimmerman, Walt McDougall, and others. Riley brings homely verse and warm dialect talk, while Nye brings dry western jokes and tall tales from his days as teacher, justice of the peace, and frontier wit. Short pieces follow one another at a brisk pace, so the book reads well in small doses.

A biographical sketch opens the 1900 and 1905 Thompson and Thomas volume, tracing Nye from a Maine birth in 1850 through hard Wisconsin years to fame as a humorist. The humor itself stays plain and good natured, aimed at everyday folk, small-town pride, and the gap between grand talk and plain fact. Readers who like old American newspaper humor will find both men at their most easy and funny here.
30327-democritus-platonissans:
Henry More's Democritus Platonissans, first issued in 1646, returns in an Augustan Reprint Society volume from the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at Los Angeles in 1968. P. G. Stanwood supplies the introduction, and George Robert Guffey, Maximillian E. Novak, and Robert Vosper serve as general editors, with advisory editors from Michigan, Columbia, Virginia, and Los Angeles. Publication number 130 marks the reprint in the society's series.

A prefatory note explains the plain-text form for readers whose devices cannot use the Unicode version, with the oe ligature unpacked, Greek shown in transliteration, and Hebrew marked in turn. Spelling, punctuation, and capitalization stay as in the original, with the old distinction between vowel u and consonant v kept. The volume suits students of seventeenth-century thought who want More's text in a clean, scholarly reprint.
30336-hours-in-a-library-volume-2-new-ed:
Leslie Stephen gathers literary essays in volume 2 of Hours in a Library, in a new edition with additions from Smith, Elder in London in 1892, the second of three volumes. Dr. Johnson's writings open, followed by Crabbe, William Hazlitt, Disraeli's novels, and Massinger. Fielding's novels, Cowper and Rousseau, the first Edinburgh reviewers, Wordsworth's ethics, Landor's imaginary conversations, and Macaulay complete the set.

Stephen opens on Johnson by refusing to discuss a recent book that professed to give lazy modern readers the pith of Boswell's immortal biography. True lovers of Boswell, he says, find such a book superfluous, since gentle omissions mangle favorite passages and additions, however skilled, change the work. The essays that follow judge writers with the same firm, independent taste, in prose that rewards slow reading.
30356-the-boy-from-hollow-hut-a-story-of:
Isla May Mullins tells a Kentucky mountain story dedicated to education in the mountains, copyrighted in 1911. A stranger and a promise open the book. A package by mail follows, then travel through wild country, a halt on the road, and a double rescue that binds the boy to new friends.

Later chapters take him to the city and test him with a startling appearance. He develops a mind of his own as opportunity opens. Mullins writes for young readers, pairing mountain speech and rough travel with lessons about courage, learning, and self-reliance. The tale stays simple, warm, and hopeful about what schooling can do for a remote home.
305-the-count-s-millions:
On a stormy October Thursday evening, servants gather in a Paris porter's lodge. Émile Gaboriau's Count's Millions opens at the Hotel de Chalusse, a mansion on Rue de Courcelles, where the concierge rules with cruel authority. Rain and wind beat the great gateway.

Pascal and Marguerite, the novel's first part, follows a count's fortune, a lost heir, and a web of Paris intrigue. Part two continues in Baron Trigault's Vengeance. Gaboriau, father of the French detective novel, builds suspense from documents and disguise. The book rewards patient mystery readers. Gaboriau's serial plots set the pattern for detective fiction in France.
3072-andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-mili:
John McElroy wrote Andersonville as a private soldier's account of fifteen months as a guest of the so-called Southern Confederacy. A private in Company L of the Sixteenth Illinois Cavalry, McElroy survived Richmond, Andersonville, Savannah, Millen, Blackshear, and Florence prisons, and published his story in 1879. He dedicates it to Supreme Court Justice Noah Swayne, a counselor of Lincoln's years.

The narrative records prison violence without flinching, including a scene where captors crowd a prisoner with clubs and a man called Egypt fells a guard with a pile-driver left arm. McElroy's plain style carries the hunger, disease, and cruelty of the camps. The book remains a central firsthand source on Civil War prisons and the Andersonville tragedy.
30721-robert-burns:
Gabriel Setoun wrote this short life of Robert Burns for the Famous Scots Series, published in Edinburgh and London in June 1896. Setoun opens by saying that Burns, more than any other writer, reveals himself in his own work, and that his poems are the direct expression of his feelings at a given moment. That claim shapes the whole book, which reads Burns's life through his verse.

Nine chapters trace birth and education, Lochlea and Mossgiel, the satires, the Kilmarnock and Edinburgh editions, Burns's tours, Ellisland, and Dumfries, closing with a summary and estimate. Setoun gives a vivid, compact portrait of the poet as a man of strong feeling and sharp tongue. Readers new to Burns will find a clear first life, and fans will enjoy its stress on the poems as self-portrait.
30828-the-barbarians:
John Sentry wrote this science fiction tale of a future America split into warring regions, where history seems to repeat itself with moats, nobles, vassals, and invading hordes. Young Giulion Geoffrey fights for the Seaboard League, whose armored vehicles cut the inland invaders to flaming ribbons in a first decisive victory. With his own cannon still hot from a shell that jammed a foe's turret, Geoffrey wheels for a finishing shot.

His target is the Barbarian general himself, in a squat black tankette with a scarlet bearpaw on its skewed turret. Then, out of the corner of his eye, Geoffrey sees another swift tankette rushing up on his port side, graceful in its handcrafting and clearly one of the League's own. The tale turns on betrayal at the moment of triumph, and on war fought with tanks where feudal loyalties rule again.
30861-breakfasts-and-teas-novel-suggesti:
Paul Pierce compiled this 1907 book of novel suggestions for social occasions, published by Brewer, Barse in Chicago. Pierce edited and published What to Eat, the national food magazine, served as superintendent of food exhibits at the St. Louis World's Fair, and as honorary commissioner of foods at the Jamestown Exposition. He dedicates the book to women editors, in thanks for favorable press notices for his earlier books and magazine.

Pierce argues that a woman, once done with the schoolroom and caught in the social whirl, must learn a new course: how to entertain well. The woman's page editor, he says, teaches a class numbered by thousands and tens and hundreds of thousands. Breakfasts and Teas answers that need with fresh ideas for morning and afternoon gatherings, in a practical, early twentieth-century guide for hostesses.
30891-the-co-citizens:
Corra Harris wrote this 1915 novel for Doubleday, Page in Garden City, New York, with pictures by Hanson Booth. Harris had already written A Circuit Rider's Wife, Eve's Second Husband, and The Recording Angel, among others. The book is set in Jordantown. Its frontispiece scene has a man sending for the oldest and very ugliest and the youngest and fairest women in town to meet him at an outrageous hour of the afternoon.

Chapter one opens with the death of Sarah Hayden Mosely, who, Harris says, did something in dying, where most people simply cease and are forgotten. From there the novel follows town folk, mayors in the making, and a confession about darning socks after marriage, with humor and small-town talk. It is a warm, witty portrait of Southern community life and the ties that bind neighbors together.
31143-talkers-with-illustrations:
John Bate's 1878 book, published by Elliot Stock in London, is a gallery of bad talkers, each given a chapter and an illustration. The monopolist, the false humourist, the flatterer, the brawler, the mischief-maker, the pleonast, the self-disparager, and the common swearer all take their turn. So do the slanderer, the whisperer, the pedant, the egotist, the liar, and the dogmatist, thirty types in all.

Bate's preface warns that speech misused has brought grief on families, churches, and empires, and that even small annoyances of talk can poison a household. Part moral handbook, part social comedy, the book amuses while it scolds, and it still offers a sharp mirror for anyone who has suffered a tedious or wounding talker.
31163-are-we-ruined-by-the-germans:
Harold Cox, formerly scholar of Jesus College, Cambridge, answers the alarm of Ernest Williams's Made in Germany in this volume republished from the Daily Graphic for the Cobden Club. Its preface is dated December 1896. Cox argues, chapter by chapter, that British trade was expanding, that Germany ranked among Britain's best customers, and that much of the panic rested on picturesque exaggeration.

Williams's own letters of reply are reprinted verbatim in an appendix, so readers can judge the exchange whole. As a document of the 1890s free-trade debate, the book shows a Cobdenite case against protectionist fear, made with figures, humor, and confidence in open markets.
31230-allopathy-and-homoeopathy-before-t:
F. Hiller, a San Francisco doctor, published this 1872 pamphlet from Bruce's Job Printing House to put homeopathy's case before common sense. Dedicated to the memory of Samuel Hahnemann, discoverer of the true law of cure, born in 1775 and died in 1843, the work makes its argument. Medicine, an art of daily necessity touching mankind's dearest interests, had failed to improve as it should.

Hiller contrasts the old allopathic practice with homeopathic treatment, appealing over the profession's head to plain readers and to the friends to whom he dedicates the book. As a document, it captures the fierce nineteenth-century war between medical schools in a frontier city.
31235-natural-history-of-the-brush-mouse:
Charles A. Long's 1961 paper studies the brush mouse in Kansas and names a new subspecies, Peromyscus boylii cansensis. To map the mouse in the state, Long snap-trapped fifteen localities chosen for suitable habitat across the winters and springs of 1959, 1960, and 1961. He analyzed the contents of thirty-eight stomachs and watched captive mice from Cherokee County almost daily for over a year.

The new form rests on an adult male taken four miles east of Sedan in Chautauqua County, and the paper combines trapping data to sketch population size and fluctuation.
