Published as volume 14, number 6 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series, it is the formal record for the southern Kansas brush mouse.
31241-aliens:
William McFee's 1918 novel, published by Doubleday, Page and dedicated to Margery Allingham, opens with a mystery next door. The narrator and Bill, his companion, notice their neighbor Mrs. Carville stooping over a scaldino, a small iron grate on legs burning charcoal, an object neither English nor American, and they make a game of collecting evidence about the family.

Fifteen chapters follow letters from Wigborough, Miss Fraenkel, the stranger's arrival and his tale, diaporesis, Mr. Carville seeing three green lights, a vision from the Kills, miscellany, discussion, and conclusion. Quiet, curious, and strange, the novel turns neighborhood watching into a tale of visitors who may not belong to this world at all.
31308-orientations:
W. Somerset Maugham's Orientations gathers six early stories: The Punctiliousness of Don Sebastian, A Bad Example, De Amicitia, Faith, The Choice of Amyntas, and Daisy. The first opens in Xiormonez, called the most inaccessible place in Spain, reached by a single train, setting the collection's tone of remote places and exacting codes of honor.

The volume's French epigraph suggests that a young writer finds his own literary self through a series of trials in different genres and styles, like so many orientations. For Maugham readers, the book shows the future novelist testing his range, from Spanish punctilio to friendship, faith, and choice.
31342-the-3-little-kittens:
McLaughlin Brothers' 1890 picture book in the Pleasewell Series gives the nursery rhyme of the three little kittens in full, with illustrations of their search and their washing. Three kittens lose their mittens and cry to their mother, who scolds them and denies them pie until the mittens are found, when they become darling kittens and pie is restored.

The tale continues as the kittens soil their mittens eating pie and sigh over the scolding. They wash the mittens and hang them to dry, then feast by a running stream and dance at a ball one night in the fall. Drawn from the Baldwin Library of Historical Children's Literature, the book preserves a Victorian nursery favorite exactly as young readers first met it.
31407-delco-radio-owner-s-manual-model-6:
This volume joins two Delco manuals: the Delco Radio Owner's Manual, model 633, and the Delcotron Generator Installation manual, separated by a divider in the text. The radio is a six-tube superheterodyne set built for use with a header-type speaker, and the manual praises it as the best in automotive radio engineering. Its features include Syncro-Tuning, described as the newest and most efficient antenna circuit yet developed, and a sensitivity control.

Speaker and remote unit came in separate packages, in types and styles suited to the make and model of car. The manual gives installation and operating instructions, with a parts list headed by the receiver unit complete with tubes. For readers of automotive history, it is a practical record of car radio at a moment when the dashboard set was becoming standard equipment.
3142-plays-and-puritans:
Charles Kingsley takes up the stage in this essay from his 1890 collection Plays and Puritans and Other Historical Essays. The British Isles, he says, ring with talk of art in its German sense: high art, symbolic art, ecclesiastical art, dramatic art. Yet the common people care little for the talk, and sit content under the charge of bad taste.

Kingsley finds the stage long dead, poetry dying, and music and building content to copy the past. Painting wins first rank only with landscape and animals. Against Puritan suspicion of the playhouse, he defends drama as a fit art for a Christian people, and asks why a nation so earnest will not take its own theatre seriously.
3150-human-nature-and-other-sermons:
Joseph Butler, Bishop of Durham, preaches the sermons collected here. Born in 1692 at Wantage in Berkshire, he was the youngest of eight children of a linen draper. His father was a Presbyterian, and Joseph trained for that ministry at an academy in Gloucester. This 1887 Cassell edition presents his sermons to a new generation of readers.

Butler's theme is human nature itself: conscience, self-love, and the pulls that steer conduct. His famous claim is that conscience holds rightful rule over the other parts of our frame. The sermons reward slow reading. They offer a careful moral map, plain in language and steady in argument, from a bishop who trusted reason to serve faith.
31731-aus-meinem-ko-nigreich-tales-from-:
Carmen Sylva, Queen Elisabeth of Roumania, wrote the tales in Aus Meinem Königreich, Tales from the Carpathian Mountains, selected and edited for early reading by Dr. Wilhelm Bernhardt, and published at Boston by D. C. Heath and Company in 1900. The five stories are Piatra Arsa, Die Jipi, Die Hexenburg, Der Tschachlau, and Rîul Doamnei. Bernhardt's edition adds an introduction, notes, and vocabulary for young readers.

The introduction tells of the Roumanians of Moldavia and Wallachia, a Latin-speaking people between the Danube and the Carpathians, descended in part from Roman colonists. Sylva's tales carry mountain lore, and the edition makes them a schoolbook as well as a storybook.
31814-literary-new-york-its-landmarks-an:
Charles Hemstreet's Literary New York, published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in November 1903 with sixty-five illustrations, traces the city's writers through its landmarks and associations. Its first chapter, Writers of New Amsterdam, opens with the fashion of trimming brick house fronts with black bricks among the red. That style began when Peter Stuyvesant governed a Dutch colony of fifteen hundred people.

Hemstreet describes a tiny, picturesque town of low houses with sloping roofs and street-facing gable ends, built mostly of wood, with chimneys outside the walls. Readers get a literary guidebook to New York, from New Amsterdam to the nineteenth century, that lets a walker see the city through its authors.
31827-etna-a-history-of-the-mountain-and:
G. F. Rodwell's Etna, a history of the mountain and of its eruptions, published in London in 1878, grew from an article Rodwell prepared for the Encyclopaedia Britannica. Surprised to find no single English work devoted to the world's most famous volcano and its history, he enlarged the article into a book.

Its facts come from German, French, Italian, and English sources and from Rodwell's own observations in the summer of 1877. He had help from Frank Rutley of the Geological Survey on the lavas collected during his ascent. Readers get a Victorian scientific history of Etna, from Pindar, Aeschylus, and Virgil to modern eruptions, with maps and illustrations.
3185-those-extraordinary-twins:
Mark Twain's twins, Angelo and Luigi, arrive as one body with two minds, and the town of Dawson's Landing must cope. Chapters follow Ma Cooper getting all mixed up, Angelo turning blue, and a duel, a baptism of the better half, and a drinkless drunk. Guilt and innocence blend finely in the title's own words, and the book ends, bluntly, with Luigi hanged.

The tale began as a part of Pudd'nhead Wilson cut loose to stand alone. Its comedy is also its argument: when two wills share one frame, law, church, and custom lose their bearings. Twain uses the freak-show premise to tease justice itself, and the laughter never quite hides the question of who should pay for a shared crime.
31895-in-and-out-of-rebel-prisons:
Lieutenant A. Cooper's 1888 memoir In and Out of Rebel Prisons, published at Oswego, New York, tells his service with the 12th New York Cavalry and his prison life in the South. It is dedicated to Captain Robert B. Hock, his gallant comrade in the field, faithful friend during the dark days of prison, and daring companion in escape and a three-hundred-mile tramp through the Confederacy.

The book opens at Plymouth, North Carolina, in 1863 and 1864, a small town on the Roanoke River enclosed with earthworks, with Battery Worth on the river bank. Readers get a firsthand Civil War prison narrative, written by a man who escaped and walked home through enemy country.
31986-no-charge-for-alterations:
H. L. Gold's short story No Charge for Alterations, printed in Amazing Stories in April and May 1953 and illustrated by H. Sharp, opens with a sidenote quoting a speaker who complains that women these days are spoiled, wanting nightclub singing, millionaires, and beautiful clothes, with housework left to gadgets and maids. The magazine's own aside promptly adds that H. L. Gold said that, not us.

The story proper begins with Dr. Kalmar. He hated nothing so much as a newly arrived assistant, fresh from an Earth medical school. Such assistants always want to change things, never realizing that each planet develops techniques fitted to its own requirements. Readers get a satirical science-fiction tale of a Deneb clinic, an Ego Alter room, and the price of reshaping people.
32010-a-feast-of-demons:
William Morrison's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in March 1958, opens at a class reunion with a joke about names. Its narrator did not attend Harvard, Princeton, or Yale, or even Columbia or Chicago. He went to Oglethorpe Agricultural and Mechanical College, a school he calls Old Ugly, where his graduating class numbered fifty-eight. At the reunion feast, he finds himself seated next to El Greco.

That El Greco is not the Spanish painter, who the narrator notes is dead. He is Theobald Greco, a man the narrator's circle calls by that name. The tagline says old Maxwell should have kept his big mouth shut, or El Greco could never have put Earth in a frame. The story blends reunion talk, money, and business contacts with a sudden, fantastic twist.
32070-specimens-of-german-romance-vol-i-:
C. F. van der Velde's historical romance opens the first volume of Specimens of German Romance, a set of translations from various German authors printed in London in 1826. The tale, The Patricians, begins on May 17, 1568, old style, at Schweidnitz. There, Althea, widow of Netz of Bogendorf, sits in mourning with her four-year-old son Henry on her knee. Her uncle, Seifried von Schindel, stands by with a goblet, urging her not to let grief ruin her health.

From that opening, the romance builds a picture of sixteenth-century noble life, where widowhood, family duty, and the claims of kin shape a woman's choices. Althea weeps at every reminder of her husband, from his sword on the wall to his horse in the stable. Her uncle argues that even good grief can be carried to excess.
32240-the-boy-scouts-in-the-blue-ridge-o:
Herbert Carter's The Boy Scouts in the Blue Ridge, or Marooned Among the Moonshiners, was published in New York by A. L. Burt Company in 1913. It sends the scouts hiking through the Smoky Range. Carter, author of The Boy Scouts First Camp Fire and The Boy Scouts in the Rockies, opens with a missing knapsack. Step Hen, unluckiest fellow in the bunch, finds his things disappearing in the most remarkable way and bobbing up somewhere else.

His companions Bumpus and Giraffe deny touching the old grub sack, while an illustration shows Thad crying Good shot, Bob, and urging another stone, quick, for he is coming after you. Readers get a Blue Ridge scout adventure, where a hike meets moonshiners and the boys are marooned among them. The tone is boyish and brisk, with nicknames, camp talk, and a stone-throwing stand.
32317-the-world-with-a-thousand-moons:
Edmond Hamilton's short story, printed in Amazing Stories in December 1942, is a Mars adventure of failure and a last chance. The cover line says only grim death passed for romance on this moon-crowded world, and a picture shows its woods as a den of savage beasts. Its first chapter, Thrill Cruise, opens with Lance Kenniston feeling the realization of failure as he steps into the Martian night's sharp chill.

Kenniston stands a moment, his haggard face lit by two hurtling moons, looking across a spaceport. Syrtis is the port of Mars. Flying moons light ships docked on the tarmac: liners, freighters, and small craft. For lack of one of those ships, his hopes are ruined, until a squat figure in a space-jacket comes to his side. Readers get a Mars tale of a ruined man.
32337-belcaro-being-essays-on-sundry-aes:
Vernon Lee's Belcaro, being essays on sundry aesthetical questions, was published in London by W. Satchell and Company in Covent Garden, and dedicated to A. Mary F. Robinson. Lee, author of Studies of the Eighteenth Century in Italy, thanks the editors of the Cornhill, Fraser's Magazine, and the Contemporary Review. They gave permission to republish studies that had previously appeared in print.

Its contents run from The Book and Its Title and The Child in the Vatican through Orpheus and Eurydice, Faustus and Helena, and Chapelmaster Kreisler. They continue to Cherubino, In Umbria, Ruskinism, A Dialogue on Poetic Morality, and a Postscript or Apology. The opening essay sends a bundle of proofs and manuscript to a first and earliest reader, wishing to give the writing as completely as a painter gives a picture. Readers get Victorian aesthetic essays, on music, myth, and art.
32343-an-englishman-in-paris-notes-and-r:
An Englishman in Paris, notes and recollections, two volumes in one, was published in New York by D. Appleton and Company in 1892 as an authorized edition. Its first chapter treats the Quartier Latin in the late thirties, and the difference between then and now. It follows a caricature on the walls of Paris, whose quarter the author is anxious to be introduced to, and whose original he meets at La Childebert.

Later pages tell the story of Bouginier and his nose, and Dantan as a caricaturist. Dantan quits that art form after his statuette moves Madame Malibran to tears on seeing it. Bouginier comes to be immortalized on the facade of the Passage du Caire. An early French co-operative society and an artists' hive complete the chapter. Readers get a Paris memoir of the eighteen-thirties, artists, caricatures, and the Latin Quarter.
32503-swamp-demons:
C. A. Butz's sonnet, printed in Weird Tales in August and September 1936, pictures lights winking across a sodden moor like phosphorescent eyes. The lights beckon travellers to risk steps in a treacherous fen, where they sink in loathsome muck without leaving a spoor. Butz asks what ghosts of former days and what dread allure abide in that subterranean den, reaching out with wraith-like fingers to snare victims.

The poem answers that unseen evils linger there, while bones rot in the muck. Those bones, once clothed in flesh, now harbour deadly spite against the living, and the swamp still brews its curse in bubbling depths. In fourteen lines, Butz turns a marsh light into a meditation on old wrongs that refuse to rest, and on travellers drawn toward ruin.
32581-little-aliens:
Myra Kelly offers nine linked stories about immigrant children, their mothers, and their teachers in a New York school. The tales move between home and class, where two busy women shape the same child in very different ways.

Episodes follow games in gardens, a burned child taken in by a teacher, a magic cape, and babies left in care. One girl learns the rules of polite speech, while others test pride, fear, and hope. Kelly writes with warmth about how a small child learns to live between two worlds. The school scenes show teachers learning from pupils as much as pupils learn from them.
32590-the-old-martians:
Rog Phillips's The Old Martians, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in March 1952, opens at Martian ruins newly opened to tourists at a dollar a head. A narrator watches a film crew at work. A girl named Dotty worries over a man whose looks mark him as someone from ten thousand years ago.

The man studies broken walls and faded inscriptions with strange excitement, claiming he has found proof that he was there before, when the place was whole. Phillips turns the tourist scene into a puzzle about memory, identity, and what a surviving ancient mind might mean for a future society.
32688-the-ordeal-of-colonel-johns:
George H. Smith opens at a convention of the Patriot Daughters of America, where Clark Decker squirms through speeches by Mrs. Appleby-Simpkin and her successor Rebecca Johns-Hayes. The ladies await a display of Professor MacCulloch's Historical Reintegrator, a device that can fetch the past into the present.

Its subject is Colonel Peter Johns, a Revolutionary rifleman whose stand before Saratoga may have saved an army. Brought face to face with his great-great-great-great granddaughter, Johns must weigh duty, marriage, and history itself, and Decker must watch a hero choose anew.
32776-women-of-the-teutonic-nations:
Hermann Schoenfeld traces the status of women among the Teutonic peoples. His book is volume eight of the Woman in All Ages series, published by George Barrie and Sons. He begins with the pagan Teutons, for whom a wife was a chattel. Her husband might bequeath, sell, hire out, or kill her, and widows were burned with their dead masters.

Marriage by capture, marriage by treaty, and payment to a bride's kin slowly replaced communal use. By the age of minnesong in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, woman's legal standing had risen. She ruled the household, guarded the hearth, and became the almost exclusive subject of Germany's lyric and epic poetry.
32969-trees-and-shrubs-for-english-garde:
E. T. Cook's Trees and Shrubs for English Gardens, in a second edition of 1908 for the Country Life Library, is a gardener's guide to planting with variety and sense. Its chapters open by warning that want of variety is a blemish. They then take up ornamental planting in woodland, grouping of trees and shrubs, heathy paths, poor soils, pruning, and propagation. The chapters then turn to winter gardens, catkins, autumn color, fine fruits, and weeping trees.

Later chapters treat variegated trees, sea-coast planting, wind-swept gardens, and conifers, so a reader can match plant to place. Cook writes for owners of English gardens large and small, and his advice balances beauty with hardiness. The book remains a useful period guide to a garden style that valued structure through the year, not color for a single season alone.
33014-to-the-work-to-the-work-exhortatio:
D. L. Moody's To the Work! To the Work!, exhortations to Christians published in 1884, urges believers from talk to action. Its chapters run from take ye away the stone through love as the motive power for service, faith and courage, faith rewarded, and enthusiasm. They go on to the power of little things, she hath done what she could, who is my neighbor, and ye are the light of the world. The opening chapter takes Lazarus's tomb as its text.

Moody argues that before Lazarus could be raised, the disciples had their part to do. Christ, who could have moved the stone with a word, left that work to them. The lesson runs through the book: God works with human hands, not instead of them. Short, direct, and full of homely illustration, these exhortations show Moody's revival method at its simplest, calling ordinary Christians to ordinary service done with heart.
33015-the-overcoming-life-and-other-serm:
D. L. Moody's Overcoming Life and Other Sermons, copyrighted in 1896, gathers the evangelist's plain, direct preaching on how a Christian meets the world. The title sermons divide the Christian's warfare into internal foes and external foes. It opens from the first epistle of John: whatsoever is born of God overcomes the world, and the victory is faith itself. Moody admits his own early mistake in thinking the battle already won at conversion.

Other sermons follow on true repentance, true wisdom, humility, rest, and the seven I wills of Christ, with a sermon on Noah's household entering the ark. The tone is practical and urgent, aimed at listeners who wanted help for daily struggle rather than fine theology. As a record of Moody's revival preaching, the book shows why his simple texts and homely illustrations moved large audiences.
33142-stories-about-indians:
Stories about Indians, published at Concord, New Hampshire, in 1854 by Merriam and Merrill, is a short book for young readers on Native American life as nineteenth-century writers understood it. It opens by noting that Indians were formerly lords of the soil now occupied by settlers, living mainly by hunting and fishing in villages of fifty to five hundred families. Their wigwams, built of poles bent together and covered with tree bark, held a central fire with a smoke hole above.

An illustration shows Indians hunting buffalo, and the text goes on to describe customs, crafts, and ways of living in simple terms for children. Modern readers will recognize the book's period limits and its settler viewpoint, but it remains a document of how American children were taught about Native peoples in the 1850s. As history of education and of attitudes, it is a revealing, if dated, primer.
33192-john-marsh-s-millions:
Charles Klein and Arthur Hornblow's novel opens with the death of John Marsh, a steel magnate whose millions stir New York's inner circles. The story turns on his will, his heirs, and the claims that rise around a great fortune. Scenes in homes, offices, and an asylum test who is sane, who is greedy, and who can be trusted. Paula, a key figure, moves through this tangle as the plot tightens.

Published in 1910, the book blends society drama with a legal puzzle, told in twenty chapters that move briskly from shock to scheme. Klein and Hornblow, known for stage hits, write with a dramatist's eye for a sharp scene and a sudden turn. It is a lively novel of wealth, kin, and law, made to keep readers guessing to the last page.
332-the-burial-of-the-guns:
Thomas Nelson Page opens with a cousin Fanny who was foolish about Christmas in old Hanover. The Burial of the Guns, from the 1894 edition, gathers Virginia stories: My Cousin Fanny, the title tale, and the Gray Jacket of Number Four. Miss Dangerlie's roses and a captain's Christmas follow.

Page writes postwar Virginia with local color and reconciliation sentiment. His narrators recall vanished customs with affection. The title story buries cannon as a symbol of war's end. The collection suits readers of Southern local color. Page's Virginia tales shaped the Lost Cause image of the old South.
33235-a-defence-of-the-hessians:
Joseph G. Rosengarten's defence, reprinted from the Pennsylvania Magazine of History and Biography in July 1899, answers the old charge that Hessian soldiers were mere mercenaries sold by their prince. Rosengarten takes up a pamphlet from Melsungen that denied the fairy stories told about Frederick the Second and modern history. He argues that the Hessians who fought in America deserve a fairer hearing.

The pamphlet is short, pointed, and scholarly, aimed at readers of Revolutionary history. It weighs pay, service, and motive, and it asks whether hired men can still fight with honor. For those who study the American war, it is a useful corrective, showing how a much-maligned force looked to a defender who knew the German sources.
33253-gala-day-luncheons-a-little-book-o:
Caroline Benedict Burrell's little book of suggestions, published in 1901, plans gala-day luncheons for every season and taste. Its table runs from luncheon giving in general to a New Year's luncheon, a musical luncheon, and a Japanese luncheon for children. Burrell, with leave to reuse parts that had appeared in Harper's Bazar, writes for hostesses who want a festive table without fuss.

The book's charm lies in its practical detail: menus, table settings, and small touches that make a day feel special. Its tone is cheerful and clear, suited to cooks of any skill. For readers who enjoy old cookbooks and social history, Gala-Day Luncheons offers a delightful glimpse of how Americans once marked holidays at table.
33343-campmates-a-story-of-the-plains:
Kirk Munroe's story of the plains, Campmates, follows boys through a weary ride, a rude baptism, and a boy without a birthday. Its chapters move from a hatred of study to swimming into friendship, receiving an offer, and further camp adventures. Munroe, author of The Flamingo Feather and Wakulla, writes for young readers who love the open West, with an illustration of a live baby found on the trail.

The tale blends camp life with frontier color, as its heroes learn courage, loyalty, and the ways of the plains. Its pace is brisk, its tone wholesome, and its scenes of riding, swimming, and camp talk stay vivid. For fans of old boys' books, Campmates offers a hearty, outdoor story of friendship forged on the trail.
33407-bee-and-butterfly-a-tale-of-two-co:
Lucy Foster Madison's Bee and Butterfly, a tale of two cousins, copyrighted in 1913, follows two girls. Their lives cross in mischief and affection. Its chapters move from an impulse of mischief and the omen of a butterfly to good news and further turns. An illustration shows a girl crying to William that he has made a mistake about her daughter Adele. Madison, author of the Peggy Owen books, writes for young readers.

The tale's charm lies in its lively cousins, whose pranks and reconciliations carry the story. Its tone is warm and comic, suited to girls who love tales of kin and fun. For fans of Madison, Bee and Butterfly offers a bright, old-fashioned story of two cousins learning to live together.
33537-life-on-the-stage-my-personal-expe:
Clara Morris's Life on the Stage, copyrighted in 1901, gives her personal experiences and recollections as a great actress. Morris, author of The Silent Singer and Little Jim Crow, dedicates the book to her husband, in memory of a labor shared. Her frontispiece shows the actress herself, and her pages move from early struggles to triumphs on the American stage.

The memoir's charm lies in its vivid, first-hand theatre life, from rehearsals to audiences, told with warmth and candor. Its tone is personal and lively, suited to readers who love the stage. For students of acting history, it is a classic memoir, preserving the voice of a star who knew the theatre from inside.
336-indian-heroes-and-great-chieftains:
Charles Eastman, a Sioux writer known as Ohiyesa, profiles fifteen Native leaders in this set of short lives. The men range from Red Cloud and Crazy Horse to Sitting Bull and Chief Joseph. Eastman writes from inside Sioux life, not as a distant onlooker, and he sets each man in his own time.

Each sketch traces how a chief led, fought, or sought peace as white settlement pressed west. Eastman stresses the gap between early spokesmen with little formal power and later leaders who acted more like rulers. The book still reads as a plain plea for fair judgment of men long misread.
3362-the-kentons:
William Dean Howells sets this novel among the Kentons, a family of a pleasant county town in the Middle West. The Kentons were not rich, Howells writes, but certainly richer than the average there, where they had spent nearly their whole married life. As their circumstances grew easier, they mellowed more and more in the keeping of their comfortable home.

They hated to leave it even for the short outings their children made them take, to Niagara or beyond. That reluctance drives the novel's comedy and its feeling: a family rooted, coaxed outward, and changed by travel. Howells writes middle western life with his usual quiet precision, where the largest events are a journey taken and a home left behind.
33652-dinners-and-luncheons-novel-sugges:
Paul Pierce, editor of What To Eat, the national food magazine, compiled this 1907 guide to dinners and luncheons for American hostesses. Dedicated to the overworked, perturbed hostess, it promises to turn entertaining from a task of dread into one of delight. Dedicated to the overworked, perturbed hostess, it promises to opens a series that would also cover parties, suppers, breakfasts and teas, and weddings. Pierce had supervised food exhibits at the St. Louis World's Fair and served as honorary food commissioner at Jamestown.

Chapters treat dinner giving for busy housewives, serving wines, sending invitations, and planning menus and service for social occasions. The directions invite ingenuity and variation to suit every need. The book preserves Edwardian ideals of hospitality in practical form, and remains a charming source for food historians and for hosts seeking period inspiration.
33670-maxims-and-reflections:
Bailey Saunders translated Goethe's prose maxims in this 1906 volume, the first attempt to present the greater part of these sayings in English. In the complete collection the maxims number over a thousand, and Saunders notes that no more than about a hundred and fifty had previously reached English, in magazines or miscellaneous extracts. Some were already quoted as if they were common literary property.

Sections cover life and character, literature and art, science, and aphorisms on nature, with an index. Saunders praises the maxims' deep wisdom, wide reach, and compact genius, and wonders that they had remained largely untranslated for sixty years. The book gives English readers direct access to Goethe's tersest thinking, in sentences meant to be read slowly and returned to often.
33676-general-catholic-devotions:
The Reverend Bonaventure Hammer compiled this manual of general Catholic devotions, published by Benziger Brothers in 1909 with imprimatur from the Archbishop of New York. Its contents cover morning and evening prayers, prayers at and after Mass, prayers for confession before and after, prayers for Holy Communion, a visit to the Blessed Sacrament.

Four approved litanies follow: the Holy Name of Jesus, the Sacred Heart, Loreto in honor of the Virgin, and All Saints. Morning prayer begins on waking with the sign of the cross, rising in the name of Christ who redeemed the reader by his precious blood. The book offers a complete, traditional daily companion for Catholic prayer, in the practical format Hammer's readers knew well.
33702-the-story-of-sir-launcelot-and-his:
Howard Pyle retells the story of Sir Launcelot and his companions in this third book of his Arthurian series, first published by Scribner in 1907 and reprinted by Dover in 1991. The foreword explains that the preceding book told of Launcelot of the Lake. This volume follows him as he rescues Queen Guinevere, fights in the tournament at Astolat, and pursues further adventures with the knights of the Round Table.

Pyle writes in a rich, old-fashioned prose that suits the legends, with illustrations in the style his readers loved. Launcelot's courtesy, prowess, and troubled love for Guinevere give the book its center, while companions' quests widen the canvas. Young readers and Arthurian enthusiasts will enjoy a retelling that keeps the romance and chivalry of Malory while speaking in Pyle's clear, storyteller's voice.
3378-my-literary-passions:
William Dean Howells recalls his reading life in this 1895 volume. The bookcase at home opens it, with Goldsmith, Cervantes, and Irving following. First fiction and drama, Longfellow's Spanish Student, and Scott come next, with lighter fancies, Pope, and various preferences. Uncle Tom's Cabin, Ossian, and Shakespeare follow, with Ik Marvel, Dickens, and Wordsworth, Lowell, and Chaucer.

Macaulay, critics and reviews, and a non-literary episode close the recollection. Howells writes of books as friends met young and kept for life. Howells traces the authors who made him, from a boy's bookcase to the Atlantic Monthly's chair, book by book.
33855-provocations:
Sibyl Bristowe published this small book of verse in London in October 1918, with an introduction by G. K. Chesterton. Bristowe dedicates the poems to the memory of her father, John Syer Bristowe. The contents move from the Great War and a London garden in 1914 and 1918 to sorrow, love, Christmas, and Queen Elizabeth.

Poems on the Transvaal, Johannesburg, and the land of silences sit beside songs of May, wind, and the long ago. Bristowe writes in a lyrical, feeling voice, shaped by war and loss. The book offers a personal wartime lyric voice, tender rather than grand.
33922-true-detective-stories-from-the-ar:
Cleveland Moffett gathered these true detective stories from the Pinkerton archives, published in New York with copyrights in 1893, 1894, and 1897. Cases include the Northampton Bank robbery, the Susquehanna Express robbery, the Pollock diamond robbery, the Rock Island Express, the destruction of the Renos, and the American Exchange Bank robbery.

The Northampton case opens at midnight on January 25, 1876, when five masked men entered the home of bank cashier John Whittelsey with false keys. Moffett tells each case with the detail of a report. The book gives a vivid look at American crime and detection in the late nineteenth century.
33975-suppers-novel-suggestions-for-soci:
Paul Pierce, editor of What to Eat and food superintendent at the Saint Louis World's Fair, compiled this book of supper ideas, copyrighted in 1907. Pierce dedicates it to the society women of America; his dedication calls them the better half of the best aristocracy in the world. Suppers, he says, are their favorite social function.

The book offers novel suggestions for social occasions, with menus and plans for hosts who want more than the usual fare. Pierce writes for readers who entertain and who prize novelty with good taste. It preserves the supper customs of its age in lively detail.
33998-the-story-of-our-hymns:
Ernest Edwin Ryden, pastor of Gloria Dei Lutheran Church in Saint Paul, wrote this history of hymns, first published in December 1930 with a second edition in April 1931. Ryden dedicates the book to his son Richard, who died at ten. A foreword presents hymn lore as a field of study in the spiritual life of the church through the centuries.

Ryden traces hymns and their writers, showing how song carried faith, comfort, and memory across ages. The book serves church readers, singers, and students of sacred music alike. It remains a warm, readable guide to the hymns many still sing.
3408-the-shame-of-motley-being-the-memoi:
Rafael Sabatini tells this tale of Renaissance Italy in the form of a memoir, as if written by a man who lived through the events. The narrator begins as a court fool in motley, the patched costume that marks his low station, yet he moves close to cardinals, governors, and ambitious ladies. Chapters carry names such as the Cardinal of Valencia, Madonna Paola, and the Fall of Pesaro.

The plot turns on disguise, poison, and sudden reversals of fortune in the Italian city states. A fool can hear what great men hide, and Sabatini uses that license for intrigue and swordplay. Readers who enjoy swashbuckling stories with a historical frame will find a fast plot, vivid courts, and a hero who survives by wit.
34112-in-jail-with-charles-dickens:
Alfred Trumble, editor of The Collector, wrote this book on Dickens and prisons, published in London in 1896 by Suckling and Galloway, with pictures. Trumble notes Dickens's deep interest in prisons, which he visited whenever he could and studied in their rules, practices, and abuses. Penology, Trumble says, was one of Dickens's hobbies.

When Trumble first visited England, many Dickens landmarks stood, but of the principal prisons in his works only Newgate kept much of its integrity. The papers gathered here trace Dickens through the gaol. The book serves Dickens readers who want the prisons behind the novels.
3473-the-poems-of-emma-lazarus-volume-2-:
This second volume of Emma Lazarus's poems gathers her Jewish poems and her translations, with a biographical sketch first printed in volume one. Contents include The New Year, The Crowning of the Red Cock, In Exile, The Banner of the Jew, and The Guardian of the Red Disk. Translations from Petrarch and from Alfred de Musset sit beside original work.

Lazarus writes about exile, faith, and the hope of a homeland for Jews, themes that shaped her later fame as the poet of the Statue of Liberty. Her verse is formal and earnest, often biblical in tone. The volume suits readers interested in American Jewish literature and in a poet whose public voice grew from private devotion and study.
3496-the-japanese-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins writes a children's story about Japanese twins, part of her Twins series for young readers. The book follows a brother and sister through home, school, and festival life in Japan, teaching geography and custom by story rather than by lesson. Simple chapters and pictures in the original edition carry the tale.

Children meet Japanese houses, gardens, clothing, and holidays through the twins' daily adventures and small troubles. Perkins aimed to make foreign lands familiar and friendly to American children. The volume suits early readers and families reading aloud, offering a gentle, old fashioned introduction to Japan.
3497-the-swiss-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins writes a children's story about Swiss twins, part of her popular Twins series that follows pairs of children around the world. The book introduces young readers to Swiss life through the daily work, school, and play of a brother and sister in the mountains. Simple chapters, pictures in the original, and a gentle plot carry the lesson.

Children learn how Swiss families farm, herd goats, make cheese, and travel steep paths, all through the twins' own adventures. Perkins wrote the series to teach geography by story, and this volume gives a warm, old fashioned view of Switzerland before modern tourism. It suits early readers and families reading aloud together.
3610-the-daisy-chain-or-aspirations:
Charlotte Yonge writes a long family story about the May children. She presents it as neither a simple tale for the young nor a novel for their elders, but a mixture of both. The book began as a series of conversational sketches in a magazine and outgrew its first plan, becoming an overgrown account of a large household.

At its center stands the eldest daughter, whose aspirations give the book its subtitle: to build, to teach, and to serve her family and parish after loss. Yonge follows school lessons, church work, quarrels, and kindnesses across years. The novel suits readers who enjoy Victorian domestic fiction with a strong moral thread and a warm, crowded home.
3642-the-belgian-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins writes a children's story about Belgian twins, part of her Twins series that teaches geography by tale. The book opens late on a long summer afternoon in Belgium, where Father Van Hove still works in the harvest field though the sun hangs low and his shadow stretches far. The twins belong to a farm family whose daily work, food, and festivals shape the story.

Perkins, whose series also covers Dutch, Eskimo, Filipino, Japanese, Swiss, Irish, Italian, Scotch, and Mexican twins, keeps the tone gentle and instructive. Young readers learn Belgian farm life through the twins' chores and adventures. The volume suits early readers and families reading aloud, offering a warm view of Belgium before the wars that later scarred it.
3668-the-albert-n-yanza-great-basin-of-t:
Samuel White Baker writes an account of his discovery of Lake Albert, the great basin of the Nile he named Albert N'Yanza. Baker traveled south from Gondokoro through swamp, forest, and hostile country to reach the lake, solving part of the great puzzle of the Nile's source. His narrative follows the expedition's hardships, its porters and soldiers, and its meetings with African peoples.

Baker writes as a Victorian explorer, confident and detailed about geography, wildlife, and the slave trade he opposed. The book stands beside his earlier Nile work and his later Ismailia volume. It suits readers interested in African exploration and in the race to map the White Nile.
3705-happy-hawkins:
Robert Alexander Wason tells this western in the voice of Happy Hawkins, an Indiana farm boy who drifted west and turned cowboy. Happy swears he is no true Westerner, since a real one turns to alkali when he dies, while he expects to turn to good Indiana soil. From the Diamond Dot ranch he spins yarn after yarn, on cooks, races, lasso duels, faith cures, dress reform, and the higher education of women, each tale taller than the last.

The chapters read like campfire talk, with dialect, boasts, and sudden sentiment in equal share. A wedding, a lost mine of luck, and a final reckoning close the round. Readers who enjoy Mark Twain style humor and the old cattle country will find Happy a genial guide, even when his facts wobble and his morals wander off the trail.
3760-sybil-or-the-two-nations:
Benjamin Disraeli wrote this novel to show England split into two nations, the rich and the poor, who live side by side without knowledge of each other. Young Lord Egremont, bored with fashion and racing, stumbles into the world of miners, weavers, and Chartist agitators, and there he meets Sybil Gerard, whose faith and fire rebuke his idleness. Her father Gerard and the scholar Stephen Morley, whose shelves hold devotion, church history, and old chronicles, anchor the working class story.

Disraeli based his scenes on royal commissions and parliamentary reports, and he warns that he suppressed much truth lest readers disbelieve it. The novel mixes romance with reform, as Egremont learns that a nation cannot stand divided. Readers who like political fiction with a love story at its heart will find Sybil still sharp on class, power, and pity.
3774-the-eskimo-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote this children's book about Menie and Monnie, five year old twins living near the edge of the far north. The twins dress alike, so even their mother cannot always tell them apart at a distance, and their two little dogs, Nip and Tup, are twins as well. The village, which had never seen twin babies before, marvels at them, while old Akla, the medicine man, watches over their world.

Chapters follow the twins through coasting, fishing, a snow house, a feast, and a reindeer hunt, then on a voyage in woman boats toward summer. Perkins writes in short, clear scenes with notes for teachers at the close. Young readers get a gentle first view of Arctic family life, told as a true story of two small children and their dogs.
3829-love-among-the-chickens:
P G Wodehouse built this comic novel from a friend's real adventures on a Devonshire chicken farm, as the dedication owns. The narrator goes down to join the scheme and finds hens, hopes, and hard work in comic disorder. His friend, full of plans and short of cash, treats every setback as a trifle, while the narrator falls for the professor's daughter and must win her regard despite the farm's chaos.

A boating scene shows the method, as Mr Hawk plunges, the boat turns over, and the professor swims with energy but little skill. Wodehouse keeps the tone sunny and the dialogue brisk. Readers who like light romance with farming farce will find an early Wodehouse in full feather, before Jeeves and Wooster took the stage.
4012-the-dutch-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote this children's book about Dutch twins, a boy and a girl who live with their parents in Holland. The sampled scenes show home work done with song, as their mother churns butter and the twins drink buttermilk at dawn.

Each chapter follows a small task or holiday, from butter making to market days, with the twins learning the ways of their village. Perkins wrote the book for young readers, with simple words and homely detail. It suits children first meeting another country's daily life, and adults who enjoy a gentle, old-fashioned school story.
4086-the-scotch-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote this children's book about Scotch twins, a boy and a girl growing up in a Scottish village. A sampled scene finds the mother baking scones when three boys burst in, one dripping wet from head to heel, mud and water running in streams.

Jean throws up her hands at the mess on her clean floor, in the book's homely, humorous manner. Each chapter follows small tasks, holidays, and mishaps, teaching young readers about Scottish home life. Children who enjoyed the Dutch Twins will find the same gentle pattern here, with scones, kilts, and kind neighbors.
4091-the-french-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote this children's book about French twins, a boy and a girl living near a cathedral in wartime France. The Abbe asks Pierre to fetch two large Red Cross flags for the towers, since wounded may arrive at any moment.

The Red Cross, he says, will guard the cathedral from shell fire, for not even Germans would destroy a hospital. The twins run off with careful directions and a note for the shopkeeper. The book mixes daily French life with the Great War, in Perkins's gentle manner for young readers learning about another country.
4092-the-monikins:
J. Fenimore Cooper's satire The Monikins sends its narrator among a race of intelligent monkeys, whose society mirrors human folly. A chapter on palpable sublimity and practical ideas opens with intense feeling disturbing the narrative, as new sources of happiness break on the writer's mind.

Cooper uses the monkey world to mock politics, law, and social climbing, in the manner of Swift. The satire is odd, wordy, and often funny, with the author's earnest moral voice behind the jest. Readers who enjoy strange, old-fashioned satire will find a curious Cooper work, far from his frontier tales.
4096-verses-and-translations:
A book of verses and translations gathers light, witty poems, including lines that tease a fellow poet's quoting. The speaker notes that if he had said beginning, the line might do, but he dislikes quoting wrong, and Cowper wrote middle for beginning.

Other verses turn on abstinence from malt, on Greek minds and their injurious liquors of wine, water, and temperance drinks. The collection favors humor, craft, and classical play over grand feeling. Readers who enjoy clever verse and translation will find a pleasant, old-fashioned book of short poems.
4244-among-the-tibetans:
Isabella L. Bird, writing as Mrs. Bishop, recorded this journey from Kashmir into the high valleys of Ladakh and Tibet. The opening chapter leaves the Vale of Kashmir, a resort of tourists and traders, and moves toward Shergol and Leh, through country governed harshly and served by mission schools and hospitals.

Bird traveled with porters and guides, noting the people, monasteries, and daily life of a region few Europeans had reached. Her eye is practical as well as curious: she records roads, food, shelter, and the costs of travel, alongside the customs of a Buddhist land on the edge of British India. The book remains a vivid Victorian travel account.
4340-the-british-barbarians:
Grant Allen called this a hill-top novel, a story written from a height above the common run of fiction. In an introduction he asks readers to read it first, and he dedicates the book to all with heart, brain, and soul enough to understand it. A hill-top novel, he explains, raises a protest in favor of purity.

Allen complains that recent fiction has been flooded with stories of evil tendencies, while writers of higher aims struggle to earn bread and find publishers. His novel answers with a stranger's view of British manners, judging them as a visitor from a simpler world might. The book is a satire of 1895, earnest in its moral purpose.
4530-precipitations:
Evelyn Scott published this book of poems in 1920, drawing pieces that had first appeared in journals such as Poetry, The Dial, and The Egoist. Many poems take New York as their subject: Manhattan streets, the Brooklyn Bridge, Central Park at dusk, crowds, riots, and night lights. Others turn to home life, illness, children, and love, in short, sharp lyrics rather than long narratives.

Scott's title suits her method, since feeling falls suddenly, like weather, over city scenes and private moments. The poems are modern in image and free in form, yet they stay close to sights a reader can picture. Readers who like early modern verse will find a vivid city book, with tenderness and unrest running side by side through its pages.
465-the-mountains:
Stewart Edward White recounts a horseback trip into the California mountains in this outdoor book. Six trails lead to the main ridge, and White takes the Cold Spring Trail with friends, horses, and a tenderfoot who stands for many greenhorns he knew. Ridge trails, coast ranges, canyons, and giant forests fill the chapters.

White writes on gear, horses, camp cookery, trout, and cowboys with practical humor. The tenderfoot's blunders supply much of the fun, while the lure of the trail supplies the theme. The book charms as a classic of western camp life, best read by anyone who loves high country.
4709-brewster-s-millions:
George Barr McCutcheon, author of Graustark, opens Brewster's Millions with a birthday dinner, where the Little Sons of the Rich gather around a long table in Pettingill's studio. Nine of them sit there, and from that dinner grows the famous bargain: Monty Brewster must spend a million dollars, and spend it in a set time, to inherit far more. Chapters trace shades of Aladdin, Mrs. and Miss Gray, a second will, and a message from Jones.

Monty Cristo, a lesson in tact, the forelock of time, love and a prize-fight, and the Napoleon of finance follow. Coals of fire, Christmas despair, a friend in need, a cut direct, and the sunny south lead to a prodigal at sea, a rescue of Peggy, a mutiny, and a catastrophe. Readers get a light, clever American comedy of money, love, and reckless spending, with a race against the clock at its heart.
4731-seven-little-australians:
Ethel Turner tells Seven Little Australians, opening with a warning to readers. If you imagine model children, with one naughtily inclined child to point a moral, she says, lay the book down and take up Sandford and Merton. Not one of the seven is really good, Turner admits, and that fact sets the tone.

Chapters run from chiefly descriptive, through fowl for dinner and virtue not always rewarded. The general seeing active service and next Monday morning follow. Sweet sixteen, falling in love, a catapult and a catastrophe, and consequences follow. Bunty in the light of a hero, a truant, and uninvited guests lead to a squatter's invitation and three hundred miles in the train. Yarrahappini, cattle-drafting, a picnic, a pale-blue hair ribbon, and little Judy follow, before a last chapter at sundown. Readers get a lively Australian children's classic, full of mischief and affection.
4734-the-grim-smile-of-the-five-towns:
Arnold Bennett gathers stories of the Five Towns in The Grim Smile of the Five Towns. He dedicates the book to Joseph Dawson, a student profoundly versed in Five Towns human nature. Its contents include The Lion's Share, Baby's Bath, and The Silent Brothers. The Nineteenth Hat follows. Vera's Christmas adventures, the murder of the Mandarin, and the burglary follow, with news of an engagement, and the death of Simon Fuge.

The Lion's Share opens as a history told in the Five Towns as side-splittingly funny, one of the best jokes in a district devoted to jokes. Bennett, writing it down, finds it a pretty grim tragedy instead, and leaves readers to laugh or cry as they please. It begins in Mrs. Carpole's house at Bleakridge, on the hill between Bursley and Hanbridge. Readers get Bennett at his best: pottery towns, sharp humour, and sadness close beneath the joke.
4738-three-prayers-and-sermons:
Jonathan Swift's Three Prayers and Sermons appears here from the 1889 Routledge edition of The Tale of a Tub and Other Works. Its contents list three prayers used by the Dean for Stella in her last sickness in 1727. Sermons follow, on mutual subjection, on sleeping in church, and on the wisdom of this world. The first prayer opens with a plea for pity toward a languishing servant.

Swift asks God to teach Stella to place hope and confidence entirely in him, to sense the emptiness of earthly things, and to feel true repentance for infirmities of life past. He prays for a sound mind during visitation, kept from presumption and despair, and for grace to remember mercy if health returns. Readers get Swift as clergyman and friend, not only as satirist, in short, moving devotional prose from his Dublin years.
4755-california-and-the-californians:
David Starr Jordan, president of Stanford University, wrote California and the Californians, opening with the Californian's love for his state. The Californian loves his state because his state loves him, Jordan says, returning her love with affection that surprises strangers to California. Hence he grows impatient of outside criticism, since strangers to California cannot understand her.

In discussion the Californian may admit hard charges himself, yet he does not find them acceptable from outsiders. Jordan lists them plainly: California commercially asleep, her industries gambling ventures, and local politics in professional pickpockets' hands. Small towns, he says, are the shabbiest in Christendom, saloons control more constituents than churches, and the state is a slave to corporations, with no public opinion. Nor has she learned, critics say, to tell enterprise from highway robbery, or reform from blackmail. Readers get Jordan's sympathetic portrait of a proud state and its people.
5220-the-satyricon-volume-03-encolpius-a:
This third volume of Petronius's Satyricon, in W. C. Firebaugh's translation, carries the further adventures of Encolpius and his companions from chapter seventy-nine onward. The volume opens at midnight, with the travellers drunk, torchless, and lost in an unfamiliar district, and follows their wanderings, quarrels, and encounters through the chapters that follow.

The volume holds only this stretch of the novel, between Trimalchio's dinner and the escape by sea. Its bracket code marks forgeries and additions woven into the text, and readers following the story in order will find here its restless middle passage, full of low comedy and sharp satire.
5601-jan-of-the-windmill-a-story-of-the-:
Juliana Horatia Ewing wrote Jan of the Windmill as a story of the plains, in a fifth edition illustrated by Mrs. W. Allingham. The book is dedicated to Ewing's dear sister Margaret, and its cover picture shows even a sandy kitten neglected when a slate pencil's moving point tempts a child to play. Jan grows up around a windmill, among plain folk and country work.

The story follows a boy's childhood, friendships, and lessons on the plains, told with Ewing's warmth and attention to rural detail. Readers get a classic Victorian children's tale, gentle, observant, and full of country life.
5677-jimmie-higgins:
Upton Sinclair's novel follows Jimmie Higgins, a working man and socialist agitator, through the years when war and politics test his beliefs and his marriage. It opens at home, where his wife Lizzie asks to see the pictures. Jimmie, three and a half years married, holds back words he knows better than to say. From that small domestic scene the story widens to meetings, campaigns, and the hard choices of a propagandist with a family to feed.

Sinclair uses Jimmie to show how large causes land in a small household. Meetings compete with wages, and ideals compete with loyalty. Lizzie learns that a propagandist husband is not the worst fate a wife can meet. Readers get a vivid, partisan portrait of American labor politics, told with sympathy for ordinary people caught between conviction and daily need.
5687-the-water-of-life-and-other-sermons:
Charles Kingsley gathers sermons on faith, duty, and daily conduct in The Water of Life and Other Sermons. The volume, first issued in 1867 and reprinted through the 1870s and 1880s, draws its texts and images from Scripture, including Isaiah, and speaks to ordinary listeners rather than scholars alone. Kingsley preaches in plain, earnest English, with nature and home life close at hand.

Readers will find encouragement to live honestly, to care for neighbors, and to trust a faith that works in weekday life. The sermons avoid abstract debate and return again and again to conduct: how to bear trouble, how to treat others, and how to keep hope. For readers of Victorian religion, this is a warm, direct sample of a popular preacher at work.
5995-chapters-of-opera-being-historical-:
Henry Edward Krehbiel chronicles the lyric drama in New York from its earliest days to the present time. The Metropolitan Opera House completed twenty-five years with the season of 1907-08. From his seat, stall D-15, Krehbiel watched each season as music editor of the New York Tribune.

Krehbiel witnessed the institution's ups and downs across a quarter century and recorded its significant turns. The book mixes history with critical judgment, naming managers, singers, and fashions that shaped the house. It serves as both memoir and record of opera in America's largest city.
6458-air-service-boys-in-the-big-battle-:
Charles Amory Beach sends air service boys Tom Raymond and Jack Parmly into the big battle to silence the big guns. Bad news from the air opens it, with Tom in French aviator uniform on a cot in a tent near Paris airdromes. Jack teases him about his head and calls him cabbage, a pet name picked up from French flying comrades. Such odd, endearing terms, cucumber or rose, cabbage or cart wheel, matter less than the meaning behind them.

Chapters promise a girl's appeal, anxious waiting, transfer, resolve, Paris, the American front, a battle in the air, a falling glove, stunts, and a daring scheme. A mid passage reaches General Pershing's headquarters with the cry that the American front is here at last, though strictly no American front yet existed, troops being brigaded with French and British. Beach writes war flying adventure for boys, with chums, machines, and battle.
6581-a-treatise-on-the-six-nation-indian:
J. B. Mackenzie first gave this short work as a lecture on the Six Nation Indians, and later set it in print with a frank correction. He takes back a harsh phrase he had laid on a Native writer, Peter Jones, and admits the faults he named belong to many whites as well. That honest note opens a study meant to be fair, not flattering.

The treatise sketches the history, ways, and standing of the Six Nations in Canada, in plain, direct prose. Mackenzie writes as a man of his time, with limits his own correction hints at, yet keen to set the record right. Readers get a brief, early Canadian view of a proud confederacy and its place in a changing land.
6675-the-loss-of-the-s-s-titanic-its-sto:
Lawrence Beesley, a survivor of the Titanic and a scholar of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, wrote his account five weeks after landing in New York. At a Boston lunch, he told fellow guests how survivors left the ship and reached the Carpathia. An editor of the Boston Herald then urged him to write a correct history for the public good. That lunch gave the book its start.

Beesley tells the sinking as he lived it, with care for fact over thrill, and draws lessons from the loss. His voice is calm, clear, and first-hand. The Loss of the S. S. Titanic is a key survivor's record, still read for its sober, human detail.
6983-missionary-work-among-the-ojebway-i:
Edward Wilson, a missionary, tells his work among the Ojebway Indians in Canada, from his first call to the opening of the Shingwauk Home. His contents trace how he came to Canada, first missionary trials, arrival at Sarnia, Kettle Point, and Indian names given. Christmas on the reserve, mission work at Sarnia, the bishop's visit, and the baptism of pagan Indians follow, with a Red River expedition and changes in prospect.

Later chapters rough it through a first winter in Algoma, meet Chief Little Pine and Chief Buhkwujjenene, and carry an Indian chief to England. A trial of faith, a wedding and a death, fire and rebuilding, and the laying of a foundation stone close the arc. Wilson writes to help readers know his people, not merely to count converts.
7010-graded-lessons-in-english-an-elemen:
This elementary English grammar, built as graded lessons, teaches sentence structure with diagrams drawn in plain text. A transcriber's note explains the marks: underscores for italics, plus signs for boldface, slashes for underlining, and tildes for wavy underlines. Heavy horizontal lines for main clauses appear as equals signs, verticals as minus signs, diagonals as backslashes, and dotted lines as periods or apostrophes.

Words on broken lines or bending around a diagonal are shown with matching breaks, so a pupil can follow the diagram in type. The lessons rise step by step, from simple sentences to fuller constructions, in the graded manner of the schoolroom. The book serves teachers and learners who want grammar made visible, rule by rule.
7042-discipline-and-other-sermons:
Charles Kingsley preaches discipline and other sermons in this 1881 Macmillan collection of twenty four discourses. The contents run from Discipline, preached at the Volunteer Camp at Wimbledon on July 14, 1867, through the Temple of Wisdom, Prayer and Science, and God's Training. Good Friday, False Civilization, the Name of God, and the End of Religion follow, with the Humanity of God and God's World.

Later sermons treat the Armour of God, Paul and Felix, the Good Samaritan, and Consider the Lilies of the Field. Jewish rebellions, terror by night, the son of thunder, humility, and a Whitsun sermon lead to self help, endurance, toleration, and the kingdom of Christ. The first sermon opens on Numbers, with a lion couched and laid down.
7172-early-plays-catiline-the-warrior-s-:
Henrik Ibsen's three early plays stand together here: Catiline, The Warrior's Barrow, and Olaf Liljekrans, translated from Norwegian by Anders Orbeck. The volume belongs to the Scandinavian Classics series, which sought to bring the chief literary monuments of the North to American readers and to build sympathy between peoples through books.

These are young works, written before the great prose dramas that made Ibsen famous, and they show a poet-dramatist still testing history, legend, and heroic speech. Orbeck's translation keeps their verse and stage shape plain enough for English readers to follow. Read together, the three plays trace the first steps of a major playwright.
7415-a-shepherd-s-life-impressions-of-th:
W. H. Hudson spent years walking the South Wiltshire Downs, and this book gathers what he saw there. Salisbury Plain opens the volume, followed by Salisbury as Hudson saw it, the village of Winterbourne Bishop, and a shepherd of the downs. That shepherd is Caleb Bawcombe, whose life, memories, and talk fill the heart of the book.

Through Caleb, Hudson shows a vanishing England: sheep on chalk hills, long days in all weather, and a knowledge of land and sky learned by living outdoors. The chapters move with the seasons and with old stories told on winter evenings. It is nature writing of the best kind, built from patient watching and from friendship with one remarkable working man.
7510-keith-of-the-border-a-tale-of-the-p:
Randall Parrish, author of When Wilderness Was King, sets this tale on the plains. Its hero rides in at about thirty, slender and long of limb, with broad squared shoulders above a deep chest. He sits the saddle easily in plainsman fashion, yet with an erectness that suggests military training. That combination, soldier and plainsman, drives the story that follows.

The contents promise arrest, an old acquaintance, the one way, an escape, a sand desert, and a wilderness cabin with a girl in it. Mr. Hawley reveals himself, a fight breaks out in the dark, and the trail runs through the ford of the Arkansas toward Sheridan and a marshal. Christie Maclaire and Doctor Fairbain join a plot of conspiracy and pursuit. It is a rattling western of the old school.
755-a-lady-s-life-in-the-rocky-mountains:
Isabella Bird travelled the Rocky Mountains in the 1870s and wrote these letters home about her journey. She rode on horseback through Colorado, climbed peaks, stayed in rough cabins, and met miners, settlers, and the famous mountain man Jim Nugent. Her letters describe the land with a sharp, fearless eye.

Bird writes as a Victorian lady who refused to be dainty, enduring cold, danger, and bad roads with good humour. Her account gives a vivid, first-hand view of the frontier West and of a woman travelling alone in it. The book remains a classic of travel writing, prized for its candour, courage, and love of wild country.
7954-twenty-five-village-sermons:
Charles Kingsley, rector of Eversley in Hampshire and canon of Middleham, published these twenty-five sermons in London in 1849. Each takes a short Bible passage as its text, most often from the Psalms, and speaks directly to a village congregation. The subjects run from God's world and daily work to life and death, prayer, and how faith should show itself in ordinary conduct.

Kingsley preached in plain, earnest language, drawing his examples from fields, homes, and the changing seasons his hearers knew. The sermons were meant to be heard on Sundays, not read as theology, and they still read that way: warm, direct, and practical. They give a clear picture of Victorian parish preaching, and of a clergyman trying to connect Scripture with the working lives around him.
7961-in-and-out-of-three-normandy-inns:
Anna Bowman Dodd wrote this travel book about stays in three Norman inns, dedicating it to Edmund Clarence Stedman. Its sections visit Villerville on the coast, an old manor along a post-road, and Honfleur and Dives. With chapters on mussel beds, village life, a pagan cobbler, Norman landladies, a country priest, and Guillaume-le-Conquérant. The tone is that of a curious, observant guest.

Dodd sketches the people she meets more than the sights she ticks off: innkeepers, fishermen, farmers, and children, in their homes and markets. The book gives a warm, pre-war picture of Normandy before modern tourism changed it. Readers who like travel writing built from conversation and small detail will enjoy its unhurried, affectionate pace.
7980-the-sewerage-of-sea-coast-towns:
Henry C. Adams wrote these engineering notes for colleagues who, knowing sewerage in general, might be called on to design a system for a sea coast town. His chapters move from tides and currents, their rise and fall, to the choice of a site for an outfall sewer and the volume of sewage. They also cover gauging flow, rainfall and storm water, wind and windmills, the design of sea outfalls, the action of sea water on cement, diving, and trigonometrical and hydrographical surveying.

The book is practical throughout, aimed at engineers facing a real scheme rather than students of theory. Its period detail, from windmills to diving work, gives it charm for historians of public health. It shows how Victorian and Edwardian engineers kept crowded seaside towns healthy by carrying waste safely out to sea.
7995-the-reconciliation-of-races-and-rel:
Thomas Kelly Cheyne, Fellow of the British Academy and member of the Bahai community, wrote this short book with a twofold aim. To serve universal peace and to show that the world's religions, rightly understood, are one. Dedicated to his wife, whose poems he praises for faith, charity, and simplicity, the volume argues that races and faiths need not be rivals. Cheyne writes as a scholar-priest who calls himself a priest of the Prince of Peace.

The book is earnest and idealistic, addressed to readers troubled by division between peoples and creeds. Its case rests on sympathy across traditions rather than on doctrine alone. As an early twentieth-century plea for interfaith understanding, it captures a hopeful moment, and it still speaks to anyone seeking common ground between faiths.
7997-america-to-day-observations-and-ref:
William Archer, the Scottish critic, recorded his American travels in this 1899 volume from Charles Scribner's Sons, dividing it into observations and reflections. His chapters begin with the straits of New York, fog in the harbour, the customs house, and a literary car-conductor, then compare New York with other cities, its slums, advertisements, and architecture. Later sections weigh American universities, character, rapid transit, and the whirl of life by night.

Archer writes as a friendly but sharp-eyed visitor, admiring American energy while noting its excesses. His book preserves the United States at the turn of the century as a European man of letters saw it. For readers of travel literature, it is both entertaining and historically valuable, a snapshot of a country becoming a world power.
8025-the-bible-king-james-version-book-2:
Five poems of grief make up Lamentations, traditionally linked to Jeremiah, mourning Jerusalem after its fall to Babylon. The city that was full of people sits solitary like a widow; its gates are desolate, its children hungry, and its temple ruined. Each poem circles the same ruin from a new angle, confessing the people's sins while crying out against the scale of suffering. The middle poem still finds a note of hope: God's mercies are new every morning.

Lamentations gives Scripture its most sustained voice of sorrow, and Jewish tradition reads it on the fast day marking the temple's destruction. Its acrostic form, each verse beginning with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet, disciplines grief into art. In the King James Version, its images of a widowed city remain haunting and unforgettable.
8045-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Paul, servant of Jesus Christ, wrote to the church at Rome the most systematic letter in the New Testament. Romans argues that all people, Jew and Gentile alike, stand under sin, and that God justifies the ungodly through faith in Christ. Its chapters move from wrath and law to Abraham's faith, Adam and Christ, life in the Spirit, Israel's future, and practical counsel on love, government, and the weak in conscience.

Romans has shaped Christian theology more than any other letter, from Augustine to Luther to Wesley. Its argument is dense and demands slow reading, but its passages on grace and freedom reward the effort. In the King James Version, its long sentences carry a weight that matches its subject, and the letter remains the standard for understanding Paul's gospel.
8046-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Paul wrote to the church at Corinth, a busy port city, answering reports of division, immorality, lawsuits, and confusion over worship. His first letter moves from party spirit and the wisdom of the cross to practical counsel on marriage, food, spiritual gifts, and orderly services. Its centre is the great chapter on love, followed by a long argument for the resurrection as the ground of Christian hope.

First Corinthians is the most down-to-earth of Paul's letters, showing a real congregation with real quarrels. Its counsel on love, humility, and resurrection has shaped Christian ethics ever since. In the King James Version, the love chapter's cadences are among the most quoted lines in English, familiar even to readers who know little else of the letter.
8047-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Paul's second letter to Corinth opens with comfort: the Father of mercies comforts us in trouble so that we may comfort others. Written after a painful visit and a severe letter, it defends Paul's ministry against rivals. Celebrates the new covenant's glory over the old, and makes a moving appeal for the collection for Jerusalem's poor. Its final chapters turn sharp, as Paul answers his critics with irony and a boast of his own weaknesses.

Second Corinthians is Paul's most personal letter, revealing his anxieties, his tears, and his thorn in the flesh. Its teaching on comfort, generosity, and strength made perfect in weakness has consoled readers for centuries. In the King James Version, its shifts between tenderness and anger give it a human immediacy unmatched in his letters.
8048-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Paul's letter to the churches of Galatia is his most urgent and combative. Alarmed that his converts are turning to another gospel, one that requires circumcision and law-keeping. He defends his apostleship and insists that a person is justified by faith, not by works of the law. The letter's argument runs through Abraham, the curse of the law, freedom in Christ, and the fruit of the Spirit against the works of the flesh.

Galatians became a foundation text of the Reformation, when Luther found in it the doctrine of justification by faith. Its brevity gives it force: Paul writes as a man fighting for the gospel itself. In the King James Version, its sharp contrasts between bondage and freedom still make it the most passionate of the Pauline letters.
8049-the-bible-king-james-version-book-4:
Paul wrote to the saints at Ephesus of blessings in heavenly places in Christ, chosen before the foundation of the world for adoption as children. Ephesians rises from that vision of the church as one body, Jew and Gentile reconciled, to practical counsel: put off the old self, speak truth. Forgive, let wives and husbands love, let children and parents honour, and stand firm in the armour of God against spiritual powers.

Ephesians is the most elevated of Paul's letters, a hymn to the church's unity and calling. Its prayers for enlightened hearts and its picture of marriage as an image of Christ and the church have shaped Christian worship. In the King James Version, its long, rolling sentences suit its soaring theme, and the letter rewards slow, prayerful reading.
807-hunted-down-the-detective-stories-of:
Charles Dickens wrote these tales of detection, opening with Hunted Down, narrated by the chief manager of a life assurance office. The manager, a man used to romances in life, finds himself tracking a villain who preys on the trust of others. Other pieces in the set turn on clues, disguise, and the slow net of the law.

Dickens brings his gift for character to the detective tale, making rogues and clerks live in a few lines. The stories show the novelist trying a form that later writers would perfect. For Dickens lovers, the volume is a treat: short, sharp, and full of the London streets he knew so well.
8123-the-virginians:
William Makepeace Thackeray's novel The Virginians, inscribed to Sir Henry Madison in London on September 7, 1859, continues the story of the Esmond family into the next generation. Its heroes are the Virginian twins, George and Harry Warrington, who visit home, quarrel, see the world, and prepare for war. Chapters follow Harry to England, a Sunday at Castlewood, Gumbo's skill with old English ways, and news from the camp as the American Revolution approaches.

Thackeray mixes family comedy with history, letting his Virginians stand between old England and new America. The novel is long and leisurely, full of conversation, duels, and social observation. For readers of Henry Esmond, it is the essential sequel, and for others, a rich portrait of the eighteenth century on both sides of the Atlantic.
8127-songs-of-two-nations:
Algernon Charles Swinburne's Songs of Two Nations gathers poems for Italy and for France, opening with A Song of Italy. Inscribed with devotion and reverence to Joseph Mazzini in 1867, and an Ode on the Proclamation of the French Republic. The Dirae sequence begins with a double-faced statue, half veiled in night and bound with iron, half crowned with light, holding all men's future in its hand. Swinburne's music and fire drive every page.

The collection is political poetry at full stretch, celebrating republican hopes in two nations struggling toward freedom. Its rhetoric can seem overwrought today, but its energy is undeniable. For readers of Victorian poetry, the book shows Swinburne as prophet of liberty, singing for Italy and France with equal passion.
8171-modern-italian-poets-essays-and-ver:
William Dean Howells wrote Modern Italian Poets as essays and versions growing out of studies begun years earlier. His contents move from Arcadian shepherds through Parini, Alfieri, Monti, Foscolo, Manzoni, Pellico, Grossi, Carrer, Berchet, Niccolini, Leopardi. Giusti, Dall'Ongaro, Prati, Aleardi, Carcano, Fusinato, and Mercantini, to a conclusion, with portraits of the major poets. Each chapter pairs criticism with Howells's own translations.

Howells, the American novelist and critic, introduced Italian poetry to English readers who knew little of it beyond Dante. His versions are clear and readable, and his essays place each poet in Italy's struggle for unity. For students of Italian literature, the book remains a friendly, well-informed guide, and a landmark of cultural exchange.
8177-the-esperanto-teacher-a-simple-cour:
Helen Fryer wrote The Esperanto Teacher as a simple course for non-grammarians, published in a tenth edition by the British Esperanto Association, with profits devoted to spreading Esperanto. Her presentation argues that Esperanto serves the non-grammarian above all: for a minimum of time and money, it gives insight into grammar and the meaning of words. And after only a few months of study lets a learner communicate with fellow speakers in all parts of the world.

The course teaches the planned language step by step, without assuming Latin or school grammar. Fryer's plain method suits self-study, and the book's many editions show its success. For language learners and historians of internationalism, it preserves the hopeful moment when Esperanto promised a common tongue for ordinary people.
820-edison-his-life-and-inventions:
Frank Lewis Dyer, with Thomas Commerford Martin, wrote this life of Thomas Edison, from his boyhood at Port Huron, Michigan, to his fame as an inventor. Dyer, counsel for the Edison laboratory, and Martin, a leader of electrical engineers, had close access to the man and his work. Chapters trace the age of electricity and Edison's pedigree.

The book follows Edison through telegraphy, the phonograph, the light bulb, and the many workshops where he tried, failed, and tried again. It praises his grit and his gift for practical work, while recording his rivals and his misses. The volume remains a rich, early life of America's most famous inventor.
8252-the-world-english-bible-web-lamenta:
Lamentations, in the World English Bible, opens with a cry over Jerusalem: how the city sits solitary, that was full of people, become as a widow, great among nations, now tributary. She weeps sore in the night, her tears on her cheeks, with none to comfort her among former lovers, now enemies. Judah has gone into captivity, the ways of Zion mourn, and her gates are desolate. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the five poems grieve the fallen city.

The modern wording keeps the laments' stark images while making their grammar plain, so the shift from desolation to hope, God's mercies new every morning, stands clear. For readers mourning loss, this version gives Scripture's grief a contemporary voice. Lamentations here remains a powerful book for times of ruin.
8272-the-world-english-bible-web-romans:
Paul wrote his letter to the Christians in Rome before he had ever visited them, and it became the fullest statement of his teaching. He sets out how people stand before God, why he believes all people have failed, and how trust in Jesus Christ opens the way to mercy and new life. The letter moves from guilt to grace, then to the place of Israel and the Jews in God's plan.

Later chapters turn to daily life: how believers should treat one another, honor rulers, and live with a clear conscience. Romans has shaped Christian thought for centuries, quoted by reformers and preachers alike. In this modern English rendering, Paul's long, careful argument reads in clear, direct prose.
