8273-the-world-english-bible-web-1-corin:
Corinth was a busy, quarrelsome port city, and Paul's first surviving letter to its church tackles its troubles one by one. Factions claimed rival leaders, members sued each other, worship ran wild, and some doubted the resurrection itself. Paul answers with patience and bite, urging unity, humility, and love above showy gifts.

The letter holds two passages every reader knows: the hymn to love in chapter 13, and the long argument that Christ's resurrection guarantees the believers' own. It also gives the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper. For churches and readers alike, 1 Corinthians remains a practical guide to holding a divided community together.
8274-the-world-english-bible-web-2-corin:
Paul's second surviving letter to Corinth is his most personal writing, sent to a church that had quarreled with him and doubted his standing. He defends his work as an apostle, speaks openly of beatings, shipwrecks, and a painful thorn he could not remove, and insists that strength shows itself most clearly in weakness. The tone swings between tender pleading and sharp rebuke.

Alongside the defense runs a warm appeal to give generously for poor believers in Jerusalem, and a closing call to test themselves and make peace. Readers find here Paul the man rather than Paul the teacher: weary, proud, hurt, and stubbornly hopeful. It is the New Testament letter that feels most like a private letter.
8275-the-world-english-bible-web-galatia:
Galatians is Paul's angriest letter, written in haste to churches in Asia Minor that were turning to a stricter gospel. Teachers had told Gentile believers they must follow Jewish law, including circumcision, to belong fully. Paul answers with heat: if law could save, Christ died for nothing. Freedom, he insists, comes by trust alone.

The letter also gives a frank account of Paul's clash with Peter in Antioch, when table fellowship between Jews and Gentiles broke down. Its closing chapters list the fruit of the Spirit, love, joy, and peace, against the works of the flesh. Short and fierce, Galatians became a touchstone of the Reformation and of every later argument about grace.
8276-the-world-english-bible-web-ephesia:
Ephesus was a great port city of the Roman world, and this short letter speaks to its Christian community about who they are. Paul, or a writer in his name, describes believers as chosen, forgiven, and joined into one body, with Jews and Gentiles made one people. The letter's long opening sentence piles up blessing upon blessing, as if words could barely hold the good news.

The second half turns practical: put off old habits, speak truth, forgive quickly, and let homes and workplaces run on love and respect. Its picture of marriage, family, and the armor of God has echoed through preaching ever since. In plain modern English, the letter's soaring praise and plain advice sit side by side.
8382-canadian-crusoes-a-tale-of-the-rice:
Catharine Parr Traill wrote this tale in 1852 for the children of settlers on Ontario's Rice Lake plains, and it follows three young cousins lost in the bush. Like Robinson Crusoe, they must learn to build shelter, find food, and keep courage through a Canadian winter, with the help of an Indigenous friend and their own growing skill. Agnes Strickland edited the volume, and Harvey's illustrations picture the lake country.

Traill, herself a settler, knew the bush she described, and the book mixes adventure with practical lessons on plants, animals, and survival. It was among the first Canadian stories written for children. Readers get both a Robinsonade and a settler's-eye view of a new land, told for young listeners.
8411-forest-and-frontiers-or-adventures-:
Roualeyn Gordon-Cumming, a British officer at the Cape of Good Hope, gave up service for hunting, and this profusely illustrated volume collects his thrilling stories. The book promises his attack on four lions and other adventures. It calls him the most daring of all hunters, a reputation he built in southern Africa among lions, elephants, and frontier peoples.

Gordon-Cumming's tales belong to the Victorian hunting book, where sport and travel mix, and where Indigenous peoples appear as guides, foes, and background figures. Readers today get both adventure and a period document, best read with its colonial viewpoint in view. The illustrations and first-person brag make it vivid, if dated, frontier reading.
8522-the-puritans:
Arlo Bates wrote The Puritans as a novel. It opens with Shakespeare's line that the web of life is of mingled yarn, good and ill together, and a Persian hymn on religion and reason forsaking the speaker. Contents move from After Such a Pagan Cut through There Begins Confusion, As False as Stairs of Sand, and further chapters of social and moral entanglement.

Bates, a Boston novelist and critic, writes of New England character, where Puritan inheritance meets modern life. Readers get a novel of manners and conscience, in the Boston tradition, where old ideals strain against new desires. The book suits readers of American regional fiction, and of the Puritan theme in later literature.
857-evergreens:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this short piece on evergreens, those dull, dowdy trees in spring weather, when snowdrops and crocuses put on dainty frocks of white, mauve, and yellow. Baby buds peep from every branch, and soft leaves stretch toward the coming gladness, while the evergreens stand dark and unchanged.

Jerome turns the contrast into a meditation on constancy against show, praising the trees that keep their green through winter's worst. His prose is lyrical and lightly comic, with a moral that favours steady faith over fair-weather bloom. The piece charms readers who like nature writing with a human point tucked inside.
8671-the-pagans:
Arlo Bates dedicates The Pagans to those who would be pagans, if any such organization existed, offering a picture of a phase of life they know. The novel follows people who call themselves pagans in spirit: lovers of art, beauty, and freedom, set against conventional marriage, piety, and respectability. Chapter titles move from some speech of marriage through the heavy middle of the night, the shot of accident. The bitter past, toward bonds of air and the inly touch of love.

Bates, who also wrote The Philistines, again uses talk, art, and social comedy to test his characters' ideals. The pagans' rebellion is more pose than programme, and Bates watches, half-sympathetically, as fine phrases meet real consequences. Readers interested in Boston literary life and the aesthetic revolt of the 1890s will find a novel that treats its bohemians seriously, without sparing their self-deception.
8676-the-heavenly-twins:
Sarah Grand wrote this long Victorian novel around a pair called the Heavenly Twins, a boy and a girl whose closeness lets Grand probe marriage, morals, and the double standard. The opening dialogue plays on their nickname: not signs of the zodiac, says the Boy, but signs of the times. Grand's epigraph pictures truth born gasping and misshapen, passed from hand to hand until it slowly finds its form.

Through the twins and their circle, the novel attacks the ignorance imposed on girls, the licence allowed to men, and the damage done by venereal disease and bad marriages. Grand, author of Ideala, was a leading voice of the New Woman movement. The book's frankness shocked many readers and made it famous. It remains a key document of late Victorian feminism, long but readable, and fiercely serious beneath its melodrama.
8713-a-man-of-means:
Pelham Grenville Wodehouse and C. H. Bovill wrote these six stories for the Pictorial Review between May and October 1916, following one man of means through a string of comic enterprises. The episodes run from the landlady's daughter and a financial Napoleon to a theatrical venture, a live weekly paper, an exiled monarch, and a hired past. The first story opens with a cautious seed-merchant receiving an enormous order for clover-seed from a firm of jam-makers, joy predominating over caution.

Wodehouse's light touch is already clear: a respectable man's plans collide with rogues, romances, and his own optimism. Bovill's partnership adds pace and plot twists. Readers who know Jeeves and Blandings will recognize the same world of clubs, schemes, and cheerful scrapes, in shorter, earlier form. The collection is pure entertainment, best read for its jokes and its gallery of Edwardian confidence tricksters.
8731-five-sermons:
Henry Benjamin Whipple, bishop of Minnesota, published these five sermons and addresses in 1890, spanning the church years 1888 and 1889. The first was preached at the opening services of the General Convention in October 1889. On the text that fathers have told what God did in days of old. A second marks the centennial of George Washington's inauguration at Faribault, and a third addresses the Missionary Council in Washington.

An address in Lambeth Chapel at the first session of the Lambeth Conference in July 1888. A sermon to the Brotherhood of St Andrew in Cleveland in September 1889, complete the set. Whipple, known for his work among Native Americans and for church unity, speaks as a bishop to bishops, missionaries, and laymen. The volume preserves Episcopalian preaching at a moment of national celebration and growing missionary ambition.
8833-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul's letter to the Romans, in Weymouth's modern speech, opens with Paul, bondservant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart to proclaim God's good news. That news, promised through the prophets, concerns God's Son, descended from David in human terms and proved Son of God by resurrection. Through him, Paul says, grace and apostleship came, to win people of all nations to obedience to faith, including the Romans themselves.

Weymouth renders Paul's long argument about sin, law, faith, and grace in steady, modern sentences, keeping the letter's structure clear across its sixteen chapters. Romans has shaped Christian theology more than any other letter, and this version helps a reader follow its logic without stumbling over Tudor English. Students and general readers alike can use it as a first Romans, then turn to commentaries for its famous cruxes.
8834-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul, called apostle through God's will. Brother Sosthenes, addresses the church of God in Corinth in Weymouth's version: men and women consecrated in Christ Jesus, called to be saints. All in every place who call on the Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord as well as ours. Grace and peace are wished. Paul thanks God continually for grace bestowed on the Corinthians, who have been richly blessed with readiness of speech and fullness of knowledge.

The letter then tackles divisions, lawsuits, sexual ethics, marriage, food offered to idols, worship, spiritual gifts, and the resurrection, capped by the famous hymn to love. Weymouth's modern speech keeps Paul's pastoral argument accessible across its sixteen chapters. Readers meet the most varied of Paul's letters here, and a translation that lets its practical theology and its rhetoric come through in plain, current English.
8835-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul writes to Corinth a second time in Weymouth's version, opening with himself as apostle by God's will. Together with brother Timothy, greeting the church of God in Corinth and all God's people throughout Greece. Grace and peace are wished, before Paul turns to heartfelt thanks: God, the Father of compassion and comfort, comforts Paul in every affliction. That he can comfort others in theirs with the same comfort he received.

That theme of comfort in suffering runs through the letter, alongside Paul's defence of his ministry, his collection for Jerusalem, and his painful relations with a divided church. Weymouth's modern speech keeps Paul's emotional shifts audible: tenderness, irony, boasting, and pleading in turn. Readers meet the most personal of Paul's letters here, and a translation that lets its pastoral warmth come through without archaic distance.
8836-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul opens Galatians in Weymouth's version as an apostle sent not from men nor by any man. By Jesus Christ and by God the Father, who raised Jesus from the dead, writing with all the brethren to the churches of Galatia. Grace and peace come from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Who gave himself for sins to rescue believers from the present wicked age, according to God's will, to whom be glory for ever.

Then Paul turns, marvelling that the Galatians are so readily leaving the grace of Christ for a different good news. Defends justification by faith against law-keeping with fierce, personal argument. Galatians is Paul's shortest, angriest letter, and Weymouth's plain rendering lets its urgency hit hard. Readers get the Reformation's favourite epistle in a version that prizes clarity, and a vivid sense of Paul fighting for his gospel.
8837-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul's letter to the Ephesians, in Weymouth's modern speech, addresses God's people in Ephesus, believers in Christ Jesus. Grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Blessing follows at once: God has crowned believers with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms in Christ. Choosing them in love before the world's creation to be holy and blameless. Predestining them to adoption as sons through Jesus Christ.

From that soaring opening, the letter moves through unity of Jew and Gentile, the mystery of Christ, and practical counsel for households, work, and spiritual armour. Weymouth's plain rendering keeps the letter's long, worshipful sentences readable. Ephesians is the New Testament's most lyrical letter on the Church. This short volume gives a reader the whole of it in one sitting, in language free of Jacobean archaism.
8838-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul and Timothy, bondservants of Christ Jesus, greet all God's people at Philippi in Weymouth's letter, with the ministers and assistants of the church. Grace and peace are wished, and Paul thanks God at every remembrance of the Philippians, always praying for them all with joy. He thanks God for their cooperation in spreading the good news, from its first arrival until now, confident that he who began a good work in them will perfect it.

The letter that follows is Paul's warmest: joy in prison, the hymn of Christ's humility, warnings against rivals, and thanks for a gift. Weymouth's modern speech preserves its affectionate, personal tone, making Philippians one of the easiest Pauline letters to read whole. Readers looking for a short, encouraging epistle will find it here, complete and in plain English, with Paul's joy audible even from chains.
8839-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul and Timothy greet the people of God at Colossae in Weymouth's Colossians, wishing grace and peace from God the Father. Paul gives constant thanks, he says, because he has heard of their faith in Christ Jesus and their love toward all God's people. Rooted in hope treasured up for them in Heaven. That hope, they have already heard in the message of truth, the good news, which has reached them and remains at work.

The letter that follows warns the Colossians against hollow philosophy and empty rules. Pointing them to Christ as head of all things and to a life of thankfulness, prayer, and household duty. Weymouth's modern speech keeps Paul's argument short and direct, which suits this brief letter well. Readers get a compact, clear Colossians, useful for study or for reading straight through in one sitting.
8840-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul, Silas, and Timothy greet the church of the Thessalonians in Weymouth's first letter. A church in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, wishing grace and peace. They continually thank God for the Thessalonians, remembering them in prayer, never failing to recall their works of faith, labours of love. Persistent, unwavering hope in the Lord Jesus Christ, knowing they are beloved by God and chosen by him.

The good news, they add, came not in words only but with power. The letter that follows encourages a young church facing persecution, teaches holy living, and answers questions about those who have died and the Lord's return. Weymouth's plain version suits this earliest Pauline letter's simplicity and warmth. Readers meet Christianity's first surviving letter here, short, pastoral, and full of affection for a community Paul had to leave too soon.
8841-weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-sp:
Paul, Silas, and Timothy address the church of the Thessalonians in this second letter, wishing grace and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Unceasing thanks are due, they write, because the Thessalonians' faith grows greatly and their love for one another keeps increasing. The writers themselves boast of the church among other churches for patience and faith amid persecutions and afflictions.

The letter then steadies readers troubled about the Lord's coming, warning against idleness and disorder while urging steadfast work and discipline. Weymouth's plain version makes the short letter's pastoral purpose easy to follow: encouragement under pressure, correction without harshness. It is a brief, practical epistle, and this volume presents it whole, in the modern speech that marked Weymouth's whole New Testament.
8858-earthwork-out-of-tuscany-being-impr:
Maurice Hewlett gathers impressions and translations from Tuscany in Earthwork Out of Tuscany, opening with a verse from Maccabees: as wine mingled with water delights the taste. Speech finely framed delights the ears of readers. He dedicates the little book to his father, modestly, as all he has, not as worthy of the bays his father wears. An advertisement to the first edition addresses the polite reader who has travelled Italy, promising something beyond the usual tour.

Hewlett's sketches mix Tuscan landscape, peasant life, medieval story, and his own translations from Italian sources, in prose that aims for beauty as much as information. The book belongs to the aesthetic travel writing of the 1890s, when Italy was a place of art and feeling rather than mere sightseeing. Readers who love Italy, and Hewlett's later romances, will enjoy a short, fragrant volume that reads like a notebook kept in sunshine.
8867-the-magnificent-ambersons:
Booth Tarkington opens The Magnificent Ambersons with Major Amberson, who made a fortune in 1873, when other people were losing fortunes. The magnificence of the Ambersons began then. The novel follows the family through thirty-five chapters, from its Gilded Age height in an Indiana town to its slow decline as automobiles, new money. New manners remake the streets it once ruled.

George Amberson Minafer, spoiled heir of the clan, must learn humility as the family's power fades. His mother, his aunt, and the inventor Eugene Morgan embody older and newer Americas. Tarkington won the Pulitzer Prize for this portrait of change, and Orson Welles later filmed it. Readers get a rich, ironic novel about wealth, pride, and a town growing up around a family that cannot.
887-intentions:
Oscar Wilde gathered his critical essays in Intentions, first published in 1891. The set includes The Decay of Lying, Pen, Pencil and Poison, The Critic as Artist, and The Truth of Masks. Each essay argues, with wit and paradox, that art should not copy life, but improve on it.

Wilde defends lying as an art, praise for the critic as a maker, and masks as truer than faces. His prose is brilliant, epigrammatic, and deliberately perverse, yet it holds a serious creed: form and beauty matter more than fact. The book is essential Wilde, and a landmark of aesthetic criticism.
9656-alarms-and-discursions:
G. K. Chesterton wrote Alarms and Discursions, a book of essays on sights, streets, and daily wonders. Contents run from gargoyles and telegraph poles to cheese, roses, and the glory of grey. A drama of dolls, a criminal head, and five hundred and fifty-five join the list. Chesterton opens among the wasting walls of a disused abbey, alone with gargoyles.

Essays turn common things into arguments: sight-seeing, luxury, donkeys, long bows, and modern Scrooges all earn praise or blame. Chesterton writes with paradox, humor, and a craftsman's eye. A reader gets a sparkling set of Edwardian essays, where a walk past a pole can open a philosophy.
97-flatland-a-romance-of-many-dimensions:
A Square who lives in a two-dimensional world tries to explain his home to readers in three. Flatland, published in 1884 and written by Edwin Abbott, describes a land of lines, triangles, and polygons ranked by sides. Women are lines, workers are triangles, and priests are circles.

The Square meets a sphere from Spaceland and glimpses a third dimension, then dreams of higher ones. His society punishes such talk, and his story satirizes rank, sex roles, and closed minds. The novella became a classic tool for teaching dimensions. Its wit still charms maths and fiction readers alike.
9804-stones-of-venice-introductions:
John Ruskin's Stones of Venice: Introductory Chapters and Local Indices, printed separately for travellers in Venice and Verona, gathers his teaching in serviceable form. Ruskin planned the series to place his best early work in one consistent body, with plates in numbered parts. His preface spares readers apologetic matter and promises a clear publisher's prospectus.

The volume guides a traveller through Venice's stones, arches, and history, with local indices for walks. Ruskin writes as art's great teacher, moral and exact. A reader gets Ruskin's Venice in pocket form, rich in stone, story, and seeing.
9863-the-letters-of-robert-burns:
This selection gathers the letters of Robert Burns, Scotland's national poet, arranged by J. Logie Robertson with an introduction. Burns wrote to friends, patrons, and lovers about everything that crossed his mind, from farming and money to poetry and politics.

His own rule, quoted in the book, was to write whatever came first: what he saw, read, heard, admired, or disliked. The letters show the man behind the songs, witty, warm, and often in trouble. They are the best companion to his poems, and a vivid record of Scottish life in his time.
9954-the-story-of-the-invention-of-steel:
Henry Bore's 1890 London book tells how the steel pen was invented and how it is made. In an age of public schools and popular education, he notes, almost everyone used steel pens. Yet few knew that presses and tools for making them appeared only in the first quarter of the century.

Bore describes the manufacturing process step by step, from raw steel to the finished nib, and traces the early makers and patents. His account is short, clear, and practical. Readers interested in everyday technology get the biography of a humble object that changed handwriting, schooling, and office work.
9966-the-spartan-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins's 1918 children's book introduces twin brothers growing up on a Spartan farm in ancient Greece. Company arrives at the farm, a stranger tells his story, and the boys work as shepherds, sow and reap, and learn the discipline of their city.

The high point comes when the twins travel to Athens for the festival of Athena, seeing a rival city very different from their own, before coming home again. Perkins, known for her Twins books, teaches history through daily life. Young readers get ancient Greece as a place of farms, festivals, and family.
9991-ancient-man-the-beginning-of-civili:
Hendrik Willem van Loon wrote Ancient Man in 1922 as a special history for his two young sons, Hansje and Willem, aged twelve and eight. He believed the best compass for life was a thorough understanding of how the human race grew, and he set out to give it to them.

Chapters move from prehistoric man and the end of the Stone Age through Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the story of Moses to Jerusalem, city of the law. Van Loon writes in a friendly, storytelling voice, with pictures and plain explanations. Young readers get the deep past as an adventure, not a list of dates.
a-few-practical-suggestions: The Society for Pure English offers a few practical suggestions on the use of English. Its report to Easter 1920 answers questions about applying the society's principles to special points. The society does not dictate to members, but puts forward suggestions worthy of serious thought. The pamphlet guides readers who care for clear and pure English usage.
a-grandmother-s-recollections: Ella Rodman Church recalls a grandmother's house through a child's eyes. The best bedchamber, hung with crimson moreen, opens and airs while eight little brothers and sisters get underfoot. Nursery maids silence refractory children with warnings about grandmother. Church writes a fond memoir of family life and childhood mischief. The fond tone makes the old house and its folk feel close at hand.
a-lady-s-life-in-the-rocky-mountains:
Isabella L. Bird wrote these letters to her sister during a long ride through the Colorado Rockies, when the region was still rough frontier. She travels by train and on horseback past Lake Tahoe and Utah mining towns, then into mountain boarding houses and lonely log camps. An introduction by Ann Ronald opens this edition.

Letter by letter she records grizzly bears, snow, bad roads, rough settlers, and grand peaks, along with climbs and long solo rides. She notices both hardship and beauty, and she writes with humor about her own dress and manners. The letters remain a lively record of the mountain West seen by a bold English traveler.
a-man-of-means: Pelham Grenville Wodehouse tells of a man of means in six episodes. The first episode follows a cautious seed merchant who receives a huge order for clover seed from jam manufacturers. Later episodes treat a financial Napoleon, a theatrical venture, a live weekly, and an exiled monarch. Wodehouse writes comic stories of money, ambition, and mishap.
a-rogue-s-life-by-wilkie-collins:
A Rogue's Life, published in 1856, is a short novel by Wilkie Collins, the early master of mystery and suspense who later wrote The Woman in White and The Moonstone. Collins tells the tale as a picaresque, following the fortunes of an endearing young man named Frank Softly. It is a story of thwarted ambition and forbidden love, told with a wink.

Frank's ever-hopeful father pushes him into society and tries him in one profession after another, hoping something will stick. Frank's own take on each attempt keeps the narrative comic and quick. Early Collins is on display here: entertaining, loosely plotted around scrapes and romance, and already skilled at holding a reader through a rogue's confession.
a-shepherd-s-life-impressions-of-the-sou:
W. H. Hudson wrote A Shepherd's Life from time spent on the South Wiltshire Downs, and a note records that one chapter began as articles in Longman's Magazine in 1902. The country is Salisbury Plain and the Wylye valley, and the people are the shepherds, villagers, poachers, and sheep-dogs of a chalk-down farming world already passing away when he wrote.

At the center stands shepherd Isaac Bawcombe, whose talk, Bible reading, fox lore, and early memories fill many chapters. Around him Hudson sets bird life on the downs, deer-stealers, sheep-bells, old Wiltshire days, and the hard economics of a shepherd's family. The book is part memoir, part oral history, and part naturalist's notebook, all in Hudson's plain, lingering style.
a-tale-of-three-lions:
H. Rider Haggard opens with Allan Quatermain back in the wilderness, unable to bear civilization's crowds for long, as old hunters seldom can. The first chapter, The Interest on Ten Shillings, sets up a debt owed and a story owed with it. Quatermain pays in the coin he has: a hunting tale.

Three chapters carry the party after lions, to what was found in the pool, and to Jim-Jim's revenge. Haggard writes the hunts with a sportsman's exactness about rifles, ground, and lion behavior, learned in his own African years. The tale is short, told in camp style, and it shows Quatermain's world before the great romances made him famous.
a-treatise-on-simple-counterpoint-in-for: Friedrich Johann Lehmann, instructor of theory at Oberlin Conservatory, teaches simple counterpoint in forty lessons in this seventh edition. The lessons begin with definitions and illustrations, then work through first species note against note and second species two notes against one. Third species four notes against one, and fourth species syncopated against one, complete the course. Examples and exercises accompany each stage, building a student's command of two-part writing.
a-treatise-on-the-six-nation-indians:
J. B. Mackenzie presents his treatise as a lecture preserved without change, as his preface says, on the Six-Nation Indians, the Iroquois league of Canada and New York. A prefatory note corrects his own earlier wording about the Indian writer Peter Jones, an attempt at fairness that sets the book's tone. The league's members were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, and Tuscarora.

Mackenzie describes the confederacy's councils, sachems, clan system, wampum records, and laws, and its long history of war and diplomacy with French, English, and Americans. He writes as a Canadian observer of his own century. The treatise is a compact period account of one of the strongest Indigenous political unions in North America.
a-waif-of-the-plains:
Bret Harte sees the Great Plains first through the eyes of two children in a hooded emigrant wagon in the summer of 1852. Dust, heat, the smell of cattle, and a low dark line that never changes shape: that is the world of Clarence and Susy, traveling west with a wagon train. When trouble strikes the train, the children are left to the plains.

Eleven chapters carry the waifs through hunger, rescue, and new homes among soldiers and settlers. Harte writes the crossing with a child's-eye plainness that makes the dangers sharper. The tale is one of his tenderest Western stories, balancing the cruelty of abandonment against the kindness of strangers.
actions-and-reactions:
Actions and Reactions, published in 1909, is a collection of short stories by Rudyard Kipling. Kipling, author of The Jungle Book and Kim, gathered here a set of tales from the later part of his career. The best known of them, With the Night Mail, imagines a future world of airships carrying the mail across the night sky.

Around that vision stand stories of England, empire, and ordinary work, each in Kipling's manner answered by a companion poem. The collection's title states its physics: every act in these tales draws a consequence after it. It shows Kipling in his mature short form, mixing invention, craft, and moral pressure in compact stories.
air-service-boys-in-the-big-battle-or-si:
Charles Amory Beach opens near the airdromes outside Paris. Sergeant Tom Raymond lies on a cot in his tent there. His chum Jack Parmly teases him in the slang the boys picked up from French comrades. Bad news from the air starts the tale. The contents promise a girl's appeal, anxious waiting, and transfer to the American front.

Twenty-five chapters follow Tom and Jack through a battle in the air. Stunts, flights over the lines, a perfect shot, and a daring scheme follow. A crash comes before the mission of the subtitle: silencing the big guns. Beach wrote boys' aviation adventure while the Great War still raged, and his heroes fly for the new American air service.
alarms-and-discursions: Gilbert Keith Chesterton gathers short essays that range from gargoyles and Cockney jokes to telegraph poles, dolls, and the fallacy of success. Each piece starts from a small, everyday sight and spins it into a paradox, a joke, or a moral point. The collection shows Chesterton's gift for finding wonder in the commonplace and argument in the trivial.
aliens-or-americans: Howard Benjamin Grose asks whether newcomers to America will remain aliens or become Americans, in a mission study course for young people. Opening with unguarded gates, the book treats immigration as both a national question and a Christian duty of welcome. Published under the Young People's Missionary Movement, it reflects early twentieth-century hopes and anxieties about the nation's newest arrivals.
all-saints-day-and-other-sermons: Charles Kingsley preaches on All Saints' Day and other themes, from preparation for Advent and the purifying hope to the Lord coming to his temple. The sermons speak of God's secret counsels and the saints' example with Kingsley's earnest, muscular Christianity. Together they form a devotional volume for the church year, plain in language and direct in appeal.
america-to-day-observations-and-reflecti: William Archer records observations and reflections on America to-day, in two parts that move from what he saw to what he thought it meant. The Scottish critic and traveller weighs American manners, institutions, and character with a visitor's candour. The book remains a lively outsider's portrait of the United States at the turn of the century.
among-the-tibetans:
Isabella Bird's Among the Tibetans records her ride into Ladakh, the high desert the maps called Little Tibet. She travels from Kashmir over the passes to Leh, the Indus valley capital, in 1889. Her pages fill with what the road offered: Buddhist monasteries on cliffs, lamas at their prayers, prayer wheels, and villages farmed at altitudes where barley barely ripens. Bird, the indefatigable Victorian traveler of Persia and the Rockies, rides with her servant and her notebook through country few Europeans had described.

The book is short and dense: customs, funerals, polyandry, and the great monastery of Hemis pass in quick, exact sketches. She admires the Tibetans' cheerfulness in a climate that kills gardens. Readers get Bird in miniature here: an empire of observation in one summer's ride. It is a portrait of Ladakhi life before the roads came.
ancient-man-the-beginning-of-civilizatio: Hendrik Willem Van Loon writes Ancient Man, the beginning of civilizations, as a volume of pictures that will not even be a regular history. The book tells how early humans learned to live together, farm, build, and write, in Van Loon's friendly, storyteller style. Its pictures and plain talk made the deep past open to young readers.
andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-military-:
John McElroy, late of Company L, 16th Illinois Cavalry, tells what he lived through as a Union prisoner. His title page of 1879 names the prisons. They are Richmond, Andersonville, Savannah, Millen, Blackshear, and Florence. Fifteen months a guest of the so-called Southern Confederacy, he calls it, with bitter humor. The book is dedicated to Justice Noah Swayne of the Supreme Court.

Eighty-two chapters follow capture, the stockade at Andersonville, hunger, disease, the dead line, exchange, and release. McElroy writes as a private soldier, naming comrades and guards alike. His account became the most widely read Northern prison memoir, and its anger and detail still make it hard, necessary reading about the Civil War.
archeological-investigations: Gerard Fowke reports Smithsonian field work in caves of the Ozarks and other states, along Missouri River bluffs in Kansas and Nebraska, and in Hawaii. He describes house mounds, cave deposits, and stone work, and he ties finds to the peoples who made them. The survey is plain and factual, with care for where each object lay and what it shows about daily life. Readers get a broad early record of North American and Pacific sites before modern dig methods.
b09-luther-hymns:
Martin Luther wrote hymns as well as tracts, and the songs may have carried his cause furthest of all. The hymns here, Deutsche Geistliche Lieder, begin in 1524, when his first songbooks appeared. Among them stands A Mighty Fortress Is Our God, still sung around the world.

German texts stand with English versions, and the tunes are printed with the words. Leonard Woolsey Bacon edited the set in 1884 for singers and scholars alike. Luther held that music drives out sorrow and teaches faith to the young. These pages show the Reformation as people actually sang it, in church, school, and home.
balloons:
Elizabeth Bibesco published this set of society sketches with George H. Doran of New York in 1922. Each piece carries a dedication to a brilliant friend: Two Paris Episodes for Anthony Asquith, The Martyr for H. G. Wells, Misunderstood for John Maynard Keynes, and Villeggiatura for Marcel Proust. Haven, Courtship, Tea Time, and A Touch of Spring name the slight occasions.

Talk is the action. A suitor tests whether Estelle would laugh or cry at a declaration. He demands mixed effects, a little hidden tear in the voice. Meanwhile Grace and Edgar dance past, radiantly fair and colossal. Bibesco, a diplomat's daughter who moved in Asquith and Proust circles, writes dialogue like fencing: every compliment parried, every feeling priced, in rooms where wit is the only currency.
bandelier-hemenway-contributions:
Bandelier wrote his Contributions for the Hemenway Expedition, and they appeared in 1890. The Swiss-American scholar rebuilt the Southwest's written past from the archives. Pueblo and Spanish colonial history had never been traced with such care.

Dusty records in Mexico yield towns, missions, and peoples long lost. Bandelier sorts true reports from myth and mere boast by hard proof. His pages trace how Spain entered the region and what it found. Later digs and studies across the Southwest rest on this base. The book remains bedrock for the region's early history in print. Its notes still guide researchers through the archives today.
beneficiary-features-of-american-trade-u:
James B. Kennedy wrote this monograph for the Johns Hopkins University Studies in Historical and Political Science, issued in November and December 1908. Kennedy, then a graduate student and later professor at Wells College, grew the study from the Economic Seminary's long inquiry into trade-union activity. His subject is the beneficiary side of unionism: the sick, death, and out-of-work benefits paid by national and international unions.

Tables sort unions by benefit — cigar makers, compressed air workers, lace curtain operatives, freight handlers, painters, paving cutters, photo-engravers, cotton mule spinners, and tailors all appear. American Federation of Labor convention proceedings supply much of the data. One note credits the Deutsch-Amerikanischen Typographia with taking the initiative in adopting a benefit. Kennedy writes Progressive-era labour economics from constitutions and treasurers' reports, before any welfare state existed.
boy-woodburn-a-story-of-the-sussex-downs:
Alfred Ollivant wrote Boy Woodburn, a story of the Sussex Downs, issued by Doubleday, Page in 1918. Ollivant centers the tale on Boy, a girl trainer at Putnam's, and the foal she raises under Old Mat's eye. Four-Pound-the-Second, the thinking horse, heads the cast of beasts.

Stable folk fill the downs world: Jim Silver, Monkey Brand, Ikey, and the Fat Man. A trial, a fire at dusk, and a war departure darken the middle books. Silver Mug and Cannibal carry the racing hopes of the yard. Courtship and a charge of crime cross the horse plot near the end. Ollivant writes the stable talk thick and fond. Horse lovers get a full racing novel, girl, groom, and gallop alike.
brewster-s-millions:
George Barr McCutcheon's Brewster's Millions begins at a birthday dinner of the Little Sons of the Rich. Monty Brewster, a clean-looking young bank clerk, is the company favourite. His grandfather, Edwin Peter Brewster, was many times a millionaire. Monty expects a comfortable inheritance and little else.

A first will leaves him a million dollars outright. A second will, from a forgotten uncle, offers seven millions more on one condition. Monty must spend the first million within a year, show nothing for it, and keep the secret. Chapters follow his splendid waste through yachts, operas, and a rescued heroine named Peggy. The promise of thrift ends the game at the last hour. McCutcheon wrote the perfect spending fantasy, later beloved on stage and screen.
britannica-1911-abecedarians: Abecedarians is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word as a nickname for certain extreme Anabaptists. These believers held the teaching of the Holy Spirit to be all that anyone needs. On that ground they scorned all human learning, the entry states. They scorned even the power of reading the written word itself. Name, sect, and one sharp doctrine fill the whole notice, which sends the reader to the Anabaptists article for the wider story.
britannica-1911-achaeans:
Achaeans were one of the four chief divisions of the ancient Greek peoples, descended in legend from Achaeus, son of Xuthus. In Homer's poems they are the master race in Greece, arriving, by tradition, about three generations before the Trojan war. They found the land held by the Pelasgians, an older people who remained the main element in the population and in places a serf class.

Contrasts structure the entry. The Achaeans are described as tall, fair-haired, and grey-eyed, worshipping Zeus, burning their dead, carrying round shields, and bringing iron long swords. The Pelasgians were shorter and darker, buried their dead, and had raised the great Bronze Age centres at Cnossus, Mycenae, and Tiryns. Their culture matches the early Iron Age finds of the Danube.
britannica-1911-acidalius-valens:
Valens Acidalius (1567-1595) was a German scholar and critic born at Wittstock in Brandenburg. He studied at Rostock, Greifswald, and Helmstedt, spent about three years in Italy, then settled at Breslau, where he is reported to have embraced the Roman Catholic religion. An invitation took him to Neisse early in 1595, and there he died of brain fever on the 25th of May, aged only twenty-eight.

Overwork and controversy shortened his life. Excessive application to study wore him down, and attacks over a pamphlet he was reputed to have written pressed him further. His writings were notes on classical authors: Velleius Paterculus, Curtius, the panegyrists, Tacitus, and Plautus, several published only after his death.
britannica-1911-algae-alternation-of-gen:
Alternation of Generations, a section of the Algae article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, asks how far algae show the life pattern of higher plants. In the great archegoniate series, plants alternate between a sexual generation and a spore-bearing generation. The section compares algae against that pattern, starting with the red algae, the Rhodophyceae, for their high place and uniform reproduction.

Among the red algae, the product of the sexual act never grows directly into a plant bearing sexual organs. Instead the fertilised cell gives rise to a filamentous structure living on the parent plant, which in time produces carpospores. That arrangement parallels the mosses, where the sporophyte stays small and attached to the gametophyte. Hard cases follow, such as red algae where spores of another kind are absent, and the question of whether a separate spore generation exists at all.
britannica-1911-algidus-mons:
Algidus Mons owes its fame to a gap in a ridge. The ridge forms part of the lip of the great crater of the Alban volcano, on its east side most of all. A tight cut through it, now called the Cava d'Aglio, let the Via Latina pass. Armies on the move to Rome or away from it had to reckon with that pass, and so the hill crops up again and again in tales of Rome's first wars.

Did a town of its own ever stand on the hill? An old writer hints at one, but the notice doubts it: a walled post is the likelier truth. The big castle on the rise south of the Via Latina, the Maschio d'Ariano, is of the middle ages through and through. Some map men missed that late date, the account warns, and read the castle as proof of the ancient place.
britannica-1911-anglo-saxons:
England before the Norman Conquest — its history, language, and writing — goes under the name Anglo-Saxon. Alfred stands behind the term: he often styled himself king of the Angles and Saxons. The title likely grew from his union of the kingdoms in 886, though its exact start stays unclear.

Bede sorted the peoples neatly. Angli held the northern kingdoms of East Anglia, Mercia, and Northumbria. Saxons stood behind Essex, Sussex, and Wessex. Jutes held Kent and southern Hampshire. Later writers blur those lines. Language and custom barely separate Angles from Saxons, yet Kentish custom stands out sharply. Oddest of all, West Saxon writers counted their own nation within the Angelcyn and called their tongue Englisc.
britannica-1911-araucanians:
Araucanians, or Auca, are South American Indians of southern Chile. Physically they are a fine race. Their hardiness and bravery were famous. They resisted the Incas successfully. That resistance came in the fifteenth century. Four toquis, or princes, governed them. Each toqui was independent of the others. They confederated only against foreign enemies. Each tetrarchy divided into five provinces.

Five chiefs called apo-ulmen ruled each province. Nine districts subdivided each province. District chiefs bore the title ulmen. All chiefs formed the country aristocracy. Hereditary descent in the male line governed succession. A great council held supreme power. It assembled annually on a large plain. Its resolutions needed popular assent. Chiefs were little more than war leaders. Private revenge limited their judicial authority. They received no taxes at all. War declarations used blood-dipped arrows as messengers.
britannica-1911-bipont-editions:
Bipont Editions is the name of a famous series of Greek and Latin classics. The series ran to 50 volumes in all. It took its name from Bipontium, the Latin name of Zweibrücken, also called Deux-Ponts. That Bavarian town was where the editions were first issued, in 1779. The place of publication later moved to Strassburg. The 1911 Britannica entry is a short note of a few lines on this publishing landmark.

The entry gives the series' size, its twin town names, and its 1779 start date. It points readers to Butters's 1877 study of the Editiones Bipontinae for detail. No editors, printers, or single volumes are named in the text. The fame of the series is stated rather than explained in the brief note. What a reader gets is the name's origin, the move to Strassburg, and the one scholarly reference. The classics themselves must be met in the volumes.
britannica-1911-brodie-sir-benjamin-coll:
Sir Benjamin Collins Brodie (1783–1862) was an English physiologist and surgeon born at Winterslow, Wiltshire, in 1783. Taught first by his father, he chose medicine, went to London in 1801 for John Abernethy's lectures. In 1803 became a pupil of Sir Everard Home at St George's hospital. In 1808 he joined that hospital's staff and served on it over thirty years.

Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1810, he sent it several papers of original physiological research in the next few years while building a large, lucrative practice. His most important work is named as Pathological and Surgical Observations on the Diseases of the Joints. Which traces how disease begins in each tissue of a joint and fixes the exact value of pain as a sign of organic disease. That book pushed surgeons toward conservative measures in treating diseased joints, the reform the entry stresses.
britannica-1911-browne-isaac-hawkins:
Isaac Hawkins Browne (1705–1760) was an English poet born on 21 January 1705 at Burton-upon-Trent, where his father was vicar. He was educated at Lichfield, Westminster school and Trinity College, Cambridge, took his master's degree, moved to Lincoln's Inn and was called to the bar, though he never practised law. Verse and talk, not courts, fill his story.

He wrote Design and Beauty, a poem to his friend the painter Joseph Highmore. His Pipe of Tobacco parodied Cibber, Ambrose Philips, Thomson, Young, Pope and Swift while all still lived. He was returned to Parliament by private interest for Wenlock in 1744 and 1747. He published his chief work in 1754, De Animi Immortalitate, a Latin poem on the soul's immortality much admired by scholars of his time.
britannica-1911-capitulations:
Capitulations were treaties that gave foreigners special rights abroad. A state granted them to the subjects of another state. The grant covered extra-territorial jurisdiction within its borders. This 1911 Britannica article traces the practice from early times. The name comes from capitulum, since the acts were set down in chapters. A Greek equivalent, cephaleosis, also appears in old works.

The article gives early examples in a line. In the 9th century Harun-al-Rashid promised guarantees to Frankish visitors. Later, Italian city states won similar charters in the East. Antioch granted one to Genoa in 1098. Jerusalem gave the like to Venice in 1123 and Marseilles in 1136. Saladin granted a charter to Pisa in 1173. Byzantine emperors followed the same pattern. The article explains the root of the practice. Old law tied rights to a state's own subjects alone. A foreigner stood outside them, close to an outlaw.
britannica-1911-capuchins:
The Capuchins are an order of friars in the Roman Catholic Church. They are the one lasting offshoot of the Franciscans. This long 1911 Britannica article tells their story. The order arose about the year 1520. Matteo di Bassi, an Observant Franciscan, began it. He held that the Franciscan habit had changed from St Francis' own. He made himself a pointed hood and grew his beard.

Pope Clement VII sanctioned the new path in 1528. Matteo could live as a hermit and preach to the poor. Others who joined him shared the same leave. The name Capuchin came from their hood, the capuche. In 1529 they held their first general chapter. Their rules fixed a life of extreme austerity and poverty. Friars were to beg for everything, and touch no money. By 1619 they were an independent order with 1500 houses. They became a chief Counter-Reformation force.
britannica-1911-carolingians:
Carolingians is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the family, named for Charlemagne, that took the throne of France in A.D. 751. The entry traces the line to Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and Pippin the Old, two Austrasian nobles who backed Clotaire II against Brunhilda in 613. It dismisses the grand genealogies written under Louis the Pious as worthless inventions. Arnulf's son married Pippin's daughter, and from that union came Pippin II.

Pippin II won sole mastery of the Frankish kingdom by his victory at Tertry in 687 and ruled it until his death in 714. He placed his sons and grandsons as mayors of the palace in Neustria and Austrasia, building the family's grip step by step. The entry follows this slow rise from court office to kingship across the generations that followed. Readers get the dynastic groundwork that made Charlemagne's empire possible, told from the family's first clear appearance in 613.
britannica-1911-carthusians:
Carthusians is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an order of monks founded by St Bruno. In 1084 Bruno and six companions told the bishop of Grenoble that they wished to live an ascetic life in a lonely place. He pointed them to Chartreuse, a desolate mountain spot near Grenoble, snow covered for much of the year. There they built three huts and an oratory and gave themselves to prayer, silence, and hard austerity.

Pope Urban II called Bruno to Rome about 1090 as an adviser. Bruno soon won leave to withdraw and founded further houses in the forests of Calabria, where he died in 1101. The order took settled shape under the successor he left at Chartreuse. The entry quotes Peter the Venerable, writing some forty years later, on the early monks' plain dress and guarded way of life. It presents an order built from the start against pride and display.
britannica-1911-cascade-mountains:
Cascade Mountains is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a range that carries the Sierra Nevada northward for some 500 miles across Oregon and Washington into British Columbia. In American territory the range lies 100 to 150 miles from the coast. Deep valleys near Mount Shasta split it from the Sierras in the south. In the north it nears the northern Rockies below the 49th parallel.

The entry stresses how the Cascades differ from the Sierras in rock and in form. The range is a broad, fairly low mass topped by volcanic cones with snow fields and glaciers, Shasta rising to 14,380 feet. The wetter western slopes carry thick conifer forests, where the Douglas fir often reaches 250 feet. In 1910 ten national forest reserves covered nearly 16,000,000 acres of the range. Deer, bears, mountain sheep, and panthers still abounded, and two great railways crossed the range through long tunnels.
britannica-1911-chilblains:
Chilblains, or kibe, in medical Latin Erythema pernio, are a mild form of frostbite affecting the fingers, toes and other parts. They cause a painful swelling with redness and itching in the affected part, the entry explains. Two points in their cause stand out in the account given here. The sores appear at the far ends of the circulation, and rapid change from heat to cold, or cold to heat, usually starts them.

Treatment is both general and local, and the entry gives doses and dressings in detail. Calcium salts help most cases, fifteen grains three times a day, and nitrites help where fingers go dead and white. Washing should be in soft tepid water, with extremes of heat and cold avoided. Ichthyol and formalin serve in the early stage, worn on linen at night, and a named paste is given for the stage where the skin has ulcerated.
britannica-1911-confolens:
Confolens is a town of south-west France, capital of an arrondissement in the department of Charente. It stands 44 miles north-east of Angoulême by rail. Its people numbered 2,546 in 1906. The town sits on the banks of the Vienne where that river meets the Goire. Great age marks its streets and homes.

Steep, narrow streets run between old houses. Two bridges from the 1400s cross the streams. Ruins of a castle from the 1100s still stand. Two churches serve the town, one from the 1000s and one from the 1300s and 1400s. The town holds a subprefecture, a court of first instance and a communal college. Flour, leather, laces and paper form its chief goods. Trade in timber and cattle adds to its work. The entry stays within those facts and gives no siege or event from the town's past.
britannica-1911-cowpens:
Cowpens is a town of Spartanburg county, South Carolina, in the north of the state. Its people rose from 692 in 1900 to 1,101 in 1910. The Southern railway serves the town. Its name comes from colonial days on that ground. Cattle were rounded up and branded there in those times, and the name stuck.

Seven miles north of the town lies a famed field of war. The battle of Cowpens was fought there on 17 January 1781, in the War of American Independence. Americans under General Daniel Morgan met British troops under General Banastre Tarleton on that ground. The British were beaten in the fight. A monument rose on the field in 1859 to mark the win. The Civil War left that stone much defaced in time. The town itself dates from 1876 and gained incorporation in 1880.
britannica-1911-cumberland-mountains:
The Cumberland Mountains, more rightly the Cumberland Plateau, form the westernmost of the three great divisions of the Appalachian uplift in the United States. Many small ranges make up the plateau, which runs from Pennsylvania to Alabama. It reaches its greatest height, about 4,000 feet, in Virginia. Its east face drops steeply into the great Appalachian Valley, while the west slope breaks roughly down. Coal in many places and fine marbles lead its mineral wealth.

Cumberland Mountain parts the waters of the Cumberland and Tennessee rivers. Cumberland Gap, where Kentucky, Virginia, and Tennessee meet, became a main path for settlers crossing into Kentucky and Tennessee. In the Civil War both sides fought to hold that gate into Tennessee. The entry praises the scenery of forest valleys and rugged gorges as among the finest of the range. It closes with the mountain people and the schools founded for them.
britannica-1911-foster-stephen-collins:
Stephen Collins Foster (1826-1864), American song and ballad writer, was born near Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, on 4 July 1826. He was the youngest child of a merchant of Irish descent who sat in the state legislature. Stephen showed early talent for music, playing the flageolet, guitar and banjo, and he picked up French and German. At thirteen he wrote a first song, and at sixteen Open thy Lattice, Love. At seventeen he entered his brother's firm in Cincinnati, composing all the while.

In Cincinnati Foster wrote Old Uncle Ned and O Susannah, then took up song-writing as a profession. His chief successes were songs for the Christy minstrels: Old Kentucky Home and Old Folks at Home among them. Old Folks at Home is said to have brought him 15,000 dollars. He wrote words and music for most of his songs. Old Black Joe appeared in 1861.
britannica-1911-foundations:
Foundations, in building, are the works that spread a structure's weight equally over the ground. A building's loads gather at set points on piers and columns. The foundations must spread those loads out, bringing the pressure down to an average the soil can bear. Care is needed to stop the soil escaping sideways, or a bed sliding on sloping ground. The work must also guard against damage from the weather, frost and damp acting on the buried masonry.

The soils of ordinary practice, rock, gravel, chalk, clay and sand, differ widely in the weight they can carry. No English building act fixes the load allowed on each, though the New York building code does. The long technical article treats kinds of foundations, depths and footings in many soils. The hosted file opens with the end of the Fould article before reaching this subject.
britannica-1911-gallaudet-thomas-hopkins:
Gallaudet, Thomas Hopkins (1787–1851), an American educator of the deaf, was born in Philadelphia on the 10th of December 1787, of French Huguenot ancestry. He graduated at Yale in 1805 and studied theology at Andover, licensed to preach in 1814. Resolved instead to teach deaf mutes, he spent 1815 and 1816 in Europe studying the methods of Sicard at Paris and of Braidwood and Watson in Britain. With Laurent Clerc he opened a school for deaf mutes at Hartford in 1816, backed by a congressional land grant.

The Hartford school was the first of its kind in the United States and a model for those that followed, and Gallaudet led it until ill-health forced his retirement in 1830. He died at Hartford on the 5th of September 1851. His son Edward Miner built the Columbia Institution at Washington into the first college for deaf mutes, with power to grant degrees from 1864.
britannica-1911-gislebert-of-mons:
Gislebert of Mons (about 1150-1225) was a Flemish chronicler. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him a clerk who held church posts at Mons and Namur, and served Baldwin V, count of Hainaut, as chaplain, chancellor or notary. The count employed him on important business.

After 1200 Gislebert wrote the Chronicon Hanoniense, a history of Hainaut and the lands around it from about 1050 to 1195. The entry calls it specially valuable for the later 12th century and for the life and times of Baldwin V. It then lists the chronicle's editions, in the Monumenta Germaniae historica and in later Belgian and French printings. Studies of the chronicle's worth as a source for constitutional history are named at the close.
california-and-the-californians:
David Starr Jordan, president of Stanford University, wrote California and the Californians as a short essay of interpretation. The Californian, he begins, loves a state that loves him back. Outside criticism, however aimed, flies wide of the mark. Yet Californians may say hard things about themselves that strangers may not.

Jordan lists the charges cheerfully: sleepy commerce, gambling industries, shabbiness, and saloon politics. Then he answers them from the land itself. Scenery, climate, and freedom of life are the three sources of California's charm. From Siskiyou to San Diego he surveys missions, sierras, valleys, and surf. The essay is brief, fifty pages of prose, and reads as a founding president's defence of his adopted state against Eastern condescension.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-leri:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Lérins describes an island monastery off Provence, on Saint-Honorat island, a league off Provence's coast. St. Honoratus founded it early in the fifth century, living first as a hermit before followers gathered from Roman Gaul and Brittany alike.

Through the fifth, sixth and seventh centuries Lérins exerted considerable influence, until Saracen raids made monkish life unworkable or shaky for two hundred years. Restored in the eleventh century, the abbey gained estates, churches and privileges from popes, counts of Provence and kings of France. Its monks also defended the coast against Moorish incursions from Algeria through the Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on St. Albans describes a Hertfordshire abbey. Offa, King of the Mercians, founded it about 793. Bede, writing early in the eighth century, already speaks of a church of wonderful workmanship, fine enough for the martyrdom it honoured. Offa's monastery grew beside that church, which he repaired with papal approval.

Willegod, the king's kinsman, became abbot, and by 1000 the old church again stood dilapidated. Abbots Ealdred and Eadmer gathered materials from Roman Verulam's ruins, and Abbot Paul of Caen began the new church in 1077, completing the whole in eleven years. Adrian the Fourth later freed St. Albans from bishops' control and ranked it first among English abbeys.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abecedarians:
The Abecedarians were a sect of Anabaptists who scorned all human learning, holding that God enlightens his chosen people inwardly and gives them needed truth through visions and ecstasies. They rejected every other path to knowledge and claimed that salvation required ignorance even of the first letters of the alphabet, which gave the group its name. Study of theology struck them as a kind of idolatry, and they treated learned preachers as men who falsified God's word.

In 1522 Nicholas Storch and Zwickau's prophets began preaching this teaching at Wittenberg, mixed with other errors. Carlstadt was drawn to it and put it into practice so fully that he surrendered his doctoral title to work as a street porter. For a while he preached the new teaching to Wittenberg's people and students.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abraham-janss:
Abraham Janssens was a Flemish painter born at Antwerp about 1573 who probably died there about 1631. Also known as Janssens van Nuyssen, he likely took that name from his mother's family to set himself apart from other artists named Janssens. He was a pupil of Jan Snellinck and entered the Guild of St. Luke as a teaching master in 1601. He married the next year and raised a family, and his daughter Anna married Jan Breughel the younger.

Houbraken started a story that Janssens bitterly opposed Rubens, but his work is the only authority for that legend. The entry judges Houbraken hostile to Janssens. In fact Janssens was a respected contemporary of Rubens, spoken of warmly by fellow artists in Antwerp. In colour's splendour and composition's vigour, only Rubens surpassed him in his day, and many of his pictures were engraved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acclamation-i:
Acclamation is one of three valid forms of papal election, alongside scrutiny and compromise. The method rests on the constitutions of Gregory XV, confirmed by Urban VIII. Acclamation, also called quasi-inspiration, consists in all cardinals present unanimously proclaiming one candidate Supreme Pontiff without casting votes. Since it must happen without prior consultation or negotiation, it is viewed as proceeding from the Holy Ghost.

Recent examples anchor the account. Clement X, formerly Cardinal Altieri, was elected in 1670 after the crowd outside the conclave cried Altieri Papa, a cry the cardinals confirmed. Innocent XI, elected in 1676, was surrounded in the conclave chapel and, despite his resistance, had every cardinal kiss his hand and proclaim him pope. The entry cites Ferraris, Wernz, De Montor, and Keller.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acts-of-roman:
Acts of Roman Congregations is the term for documents, also called decrees, issued by the Roman Congregations under powers conferred by the pope. The entry treats the subject under six heads: kinds, authority, use, manner of preservation, accessibility, and collections. In kinds, these bodies grant privileges and dispensations, issue ordinances, give true readings of law, and decide cases between contending parties, though not every body holds all these powers.

Decrees are for single cases or church-wide, by whether they address individuals or the whole church, and most deal with discipline, explaining, enforcing, or dispensing from positive church laws. Some deal with doctrine, declaring a doctrine untenable or an act unlawful against divine law. In authority, these decrees are supreme in a sense, coming from the highest church tribunals, but not wholly supreme, since the Congregations are distinct in law from the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-advocates-of-:
Advocates of Roman Congregations, ecclesiastical or lay, know canon and civil law and plead causes before Rome's ecclesiastical tribunals. The learning required is exceptional and profound. Beyond thorough jurisprudence, canonical and civil, they must know theology and history, sacred and profane. Frequent references to councils, canons, and papal decrees demand deep and varied learning covering languages ancient and modern.

A Roman advocate differs from an ordinary legal pleader in several ways. He does not establish facts in a case, since that is the procurator's business. He assumes the facts given him to be true and builds his legal argument on them, freed from tempting distortions of testimony. He pleads always before learned judges, not a jury, so his language must be sober, refined, clear, and precise. His fee is fixed, win or lose, and consistorial advocates must defend the poor free of charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aeons:
Aeons is the term Gnostic heresiarchs used for spiritual powers arising by progressive emanation from the eternal Being. Together they form the Pleroma, the unseen spiritual world, as distinct from the Kenoma, the visible material world. The word aeon, aion, means age, the ever-existing, or eternity, and came to denote the divine eternal power and its personified attributes.

From there it extended to successive emanations from divinity, seen as needed links between spiritual and material worlds. The concept traces to a philosophy holding divinity incapable of contact with matter or evil. The wish was to square that view with Christian belief in God's direct action in creation and redemption. Jewish angelology and Hellenic systems of go-betweens suggested a series of lesser heavenly powers, each less perfect the further from the supreme deity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-agents-of-rom:
Agents of Roman Congregations look after their patrons' affairs at the Roman Curia. The name comes from Latin Agens in Rebus, matching Greek Apocrisiarius. Such agents first appear not at Rome but at Constantinople's imperial palace. There bishops, given church and state's close tie and the lack of canons on mixed matters, needed men to watch their interests at court.

Until the French Revolution, French prelates kept like agents at St. Denis's royal court. Today bishops or private persons employ agents in the pontifical courts, temporarily or permanently. Their chief business is pressing patrons' cases forward. For favours such as dispensations they prepare supplications and call repeatedly on officials until an answer comes. They rank next before the notaries, and their pay rests wholly on employers' will.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexian-nuns: The Alexian nuns, or black sisters, began early in the fifteenth century as religious women affiliated to the Alexian Brotherhood. They adopted the Rule of St. Augustine and took up the Brothers' bodily works of mercy. Their dress is black: a mantle of matching colour and a white cap gave them their common name. The black, or Cellitine, sisters now have their mother-house at Cologne, and they have no houses in the United States and Canada.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alexians:
The Alexians, also called Cellites, are a religious congregation that began at Mechlin in Brabant in the fifteenth century, during the ravages of the Black Death. Certain laymen joined under a man named Tobias to help the plague-stricken, without taking vows or adopting a rule at first. The institute took its name from St. Alexius, and its brothers devoted themselves to burying the dead and nursing the sick.

The Alexian Brothers run four hospitals in the United States. The first, built at Chicago in 1866, burned in the great fire of October 1871 and was rebuilt the next year, and the second, raised at St. Louis in 1869, covers an acre with wards for the insane, nervous diseases, and inebriety. Bishop Vaughan of Salford invited the brothers to England in June 1875, and the Bishop of Middlesborough brought them to his diocese in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-algonquins:
The Algonquins were probably once the largest North American tribes, roaming between Kentucky and Hudson Bay, and between the Atlantic and the Mississippi, perhaps further still. Shifting homes, marriages, alliances, captive-taking, and desertion blur tribal limits. Micmacs, Chippewas, Sacs, Illinois, Pequods, and Lenapes count among them, sharing language and build.

Eliot and Mather thought them utterly savage, while early French missionaries praised their minds, poetry, oratory, nobility, and even hand skill. Drake largely shares that view for Lake Superior Algonquins. Algonquin seems a general name, not a compact, permanent league like the Iroquois.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-horns:
Altar horns were four projections, one at each corner, on the Jewish altar. The projections gave the ancient altar its horned corners, a feature the Christian altar did not keep. Christian altars lack them, but cornu, Latin for horn, still names the altar's sides and corners. Cornu epistolae and cornu evangelii mean the epistle and gospel sides.

Cornu anterius and cornu posterius evangelii, or dexterum anterius and dexterum posterius, name the front or back corner on the gospel side. The old temple terms thus survive as a precise shorthand for positions around the Christian altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-lantern:
Altar lanterns shield altar candles and lamp from draughts, made of perforated metalwork or set with crystals. A lantern's closed sides still let the flame show while breaking the wind. They also accompany the Blessed Sacrament carried between altars, or as Viaticum to the sick. For processions within the church they top high staves; for Viaticum a ring tops them, carried in a cleric's or assistant's hand.

These modest guards keep the light alive where draughts would kill an open flame, in church and on the road to the sick.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-linens:
The altar linens are the corporal, pall, purificator, and finger towels. The Blessed Sacrament and its vase must always rest on a corporal of linen or hemp, without embellishment or embroidery. Fine lace edges and a cross near the front edge are allowed, none in the centre. Muslin and cotton corporals are forbidden.

The pall began as part of the oversized corporal itself, only later becoming distinct. The purificator, pure white linen or hemp, cleanses the chalice, its size unprescribed. Finger towels, used at the Lavabo and after Communion, may be any material, preferably linen or hemp.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amalricians:
The Amalricians were a heretical sect founded late in the twelfth century by Amaury de Bène of Chartres, cleric and Paris professor who died between 1204 and 1207. They professed a species of pantheism: God and the universe are one, God is everything and everything is God. That principle led them to deny Transubstantiation, confound good and evil as equally of God, and reject morality's laws, with peculiar views on the Trinity besides.

Many priests and clerics spread the errors undetected for a time, until principals and proselytes were arrested. A Paris council of bishops and doctors in 1210 pardoned ignorant converts. It imprisoned four principals for life, and burned ten obstinate priests and clerics after public degradation. The sect's end thus came by council, prison, and fire, its founder dead years before yet condemned with his disciples.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-berna:
Ambrose Bernard O'Higgins, born in County Meath in 1720, died at Lima on 18 March 1810. Schooled at Cadiz through a priest uncle, he went to South America. He peddled at Lima, contracted roads, then joined the Spanish army's engineers. Rapid promotion brought nobility as Count of Bellenar, then Marquis of Orsorno with Chile's governorship in 1788, and in 1796 Peru's viceroyalty, ending with his death.

His only son Bernard, born at Chillán on 20 August 1776, died at Lima on 14 October 1842. Schooled in England from fifteen, he returned to Chile, joined the revolution as militia colonel, and mainly won Chacabuco on 12 February 1817, breaking Spain's power in Chile. Proclaimed Dictator after the capital's capture, he ruled ably for six years until a fickle populace deposed him in February 1823.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosians:
St. Ambrose founded no religious order, though he watched monastic beginnings in his diocese and provided for monks outside the episcopal city under one of his priests, as Augustine's Confessions tell. The first Ambrosian order began in woodland near Milan. Alexander Grivelli, Antonio Petrasancta, and Albert Besuzzi, three noble Milanese, sought retreat there. Other solitaries and priests joined them, with Gregory XI giving Augustine's Rule and special rules.

St. Charles Borromeo, reforming Milan under Trent, founded the Oblates of St. Ambrose in August 1578, endowing them with diocesan livings and part of the dissolved Humiliati's goods. In the nineteenth century, Poitiers's Bishop Pie and Paderborn's Bishop Martin followed Charles's example with priestly societies on Milanese Oblate lines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-american-indi:
The American Indians entry surveys the native peoples: race type, origin, languages, houses, food, animals, industries, games, war, social order, religion, and burial. Physically the type shows brown skin, dark brown eyes, high cheek bones, straight black hair, and scant beard, colour varying from very light to almost black, not red as supposed. Origins assigned include Europe via Greenland or Atlantis, but Asia via Bering Straits has more advocates and reasons.

Religiously the Indian was an animist, every animal, plant, and object holding a spirit to propitiate or fear, sun, buffalo, and eagle among the most powerful. Burial varied by tribe and place, inhumation most widespread, Hurons and Iroquois letting bodies decay on scaffolds before gathering bones to a common place. Population collapse marks the later record. The Pawnee fell from 10,000 in 1838 to 650, the Kansas from 1,500 to 200.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amiens:
Amiens, ancient Ambianum, covers the Somme department, suffragan of Reims under the old regime, of Paris from 1802 to 1822, and of Reims again since 1822. Duchesne denies value to the two-St.-Firmin legend, an eighth-century tissue of incoherences. He holds Eulogius, defender of Christ's divinity in mid-fourth-century councils, the first bishop known to history. Later bishops include Charlemagne's Jessé, deposed under Louis the Pious, and William of Mâcon, Paris University's greatest jurist. Jean de Lagrange, the Amiens Cardinal of the Great Schism, François Faure, converter of Montausier and James II, and Bombelles, bishop from 1819 to 1822, follow.

The thirteenth-century cathedral is an admirable Gothic monument, studied carefully by Ruskin in his Bible of Amiens. Its nave is considered the ideal Gothic type.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ammonian-sect:
The Ammonian sections are marginal divisions of the four Gospels in nearly all Greek and Latin manuscripts, about 1,165 in number. Matthew takes 355, Mark 235, Luke 343, and John 232, varying slightly by manuscript. Until recently they were commonly believed devised by Ammonius of Alexandria about 220, with a now-lost Gospel Harmony. He was said to divide the Gospels into small numbered sections, similar where narratives run parallel. The last three Gospels' sections, or their numbers with evangelists' names, stood in parallel columns opposite Matthew's.

Eusebius's letter to Carpianus, however, restricts Ammonius's work to placing the last three Gospels' parallels alongside Matthew's text. The sections once once credited to Ammonius, now ascribed to Eusebius, who lived 265 to 340. The Harmony of Ammonius thus suggested the system, but Eusebius owns the sections as now known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-order:
The Ancient Order of Hibernians grew up slowly among the Catholics of Ireland, under hardship and persecution, and no exact founding date in Ireland can be given. Some trace the impulse to an edict of the Earl of Sussex, Lord-Lieutenant in 1562, barring monks and priests from eating or sleeping in Dublin and fining families who skipped Protestant services.

Rory O'Moore then took up the defence of religion, priesthood, and dominion. Priests said Mass on mountains, in valleys, and in glens. The Defenders stood sentinel against danger. In America the bodies united, and the order took its name at Trenton, New Jersey, in 1898. Its 1908 constitution names friendship, unity, and Christian charity as its aims, with a fund for aged, sick, blind, and infirm members, funeral benefits, and Irish nationality. Membership reached about 56,000 in the United States and Canada, and its ladies endowed a scholarship at Trinity College, Washington.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ansegisus-arc:
Death came to Ansegisus, Archbishop of Sens, on 25 November 879, or 883. Before that he had been a Benedictine monk and Abbot of Saint Michael's at Beauvais, becoming Archbishop of Sens in 871. After Pope John VIII crowned Charles the Bald as emperor, Charles asked the pope to make Ansegisus papal legate and primate over Gaul and Germany. A legate of French nationality, friendly to the emperor, would help Charles extend imperial influence over those countries, or so Charles thought.

The pope gave in to Charles's wish. At the Synod of Ponthion, bishops asked to acknowledge Ansegisus's primacy protested, led by Hincmar, Archbishop of Reims, against what they saw as an infringement on their rights. Ansegisus kept the title, yet it is doubtful whether he ever used the powers of Primate of France and Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antediluvians:
Antediluvians, from Latin for before the Flood, lived before the Flood. From Adam to Noah come ten patriarchs. Genesis 5 gives their genealogical table. Their names, lifetimes, and begetting ages are stated. Modern theory assigns this chapter to the Priestly Code. Critics say the patriarch table followed chapter i's Hexahemeron.
