The Creation account began with: These are the generations of the heavens and the earth.

The Septuagint chiefly adds 100 years to six patriarchs' ages at their successors' birth. The Samaritan deducts 100 years for three. No clue has yet decided which computation is original, though presumption favours the Hebrew as oldest. The Samaritan advantage: Jared, Methuselah, and Lamech's lifetimes shorten, giving a gradual decrease from Adam to Noah. The ten Babylonian kings' reigns use sares; Berosus counts 120. When primordial innocence was lost, man's lifespan shortened, so patriarchal longevity fits the primeval golden age, a fabulous period of innocence and happiness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostle-spoon:
Apostle spoons are a set of thirteen spoons, usually silver, whose handles carry figures of Christ, the Master spoon, and the twelve apostles. Long ago godparents gave them as baptism gifts, the rich giving full sets, others fewer, and a poor person a single spoon. Each apostle bears his emblem. Peter holds a key or fish, Andrew a saltire cross, and James Major a pilgrim staff and gourd. John holds a chalice, Philip a long staff topped with a cross, and Thomas a spear.

Bartholomew holds a butcher's knife, Matthew a wallet or axe, Matthias a halberd, Jude a carpenter's square, and Simon a saw. In some sets Paul replaces Matthias, sword in hand. Doubtful before 1500, they first appear as a bequest in 1516, when Amy Brent left thirteen silver spoons of Jesus and the twelve apostles. The entry traces a homely gift that doubled as a lesson in saints.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-can:
The Apostolic Canons are a collection of ancient church decrees, eighty-five in the Eastern church and fifty in the Western, on government and discipline, joined to the Apostolic Constitutions. They deal with the office and duties of a bishop, the qualifications and conduct of clergy, and the religious life of the flock. They also cover outward administration in excommunication, synods, and relations with pagans and Jews, and the sacraments of baptism, Eucharist, and marriage. They sum up early church law.

The last decree holds an important list, or canon, of Holy Scripture. In the Greek text the canons claim to be the apostles' own legislation, promulgated by their disciple Clement. Yet the article calls that claim false and untenable, though the collection remains a venerable mirror of ancient Christian life, blameless in doctrine. Readers get both the content of early church law and a warning about its invented pedigree.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-con:
The Apostolic Constitutions form a fourth-century collection in eight books, falsely claiming apostolic authorship, of treatises on Christian discipline, worship, and doctrine, meant as a manual for clergy. Its tone is more exhortation than strict precept, since injunctions often arrive as little treatises backed by scriptural texts and examples, loosely combined without great regard for order. It purports to gather instructions of the apostles, singly and as a body, handed down by its pretended compiler, Clement of Rome, whose name lent fictitious weight to such works.

The church never treated it as of undoubted apostolic authority, and the Trullan Council in 692 rejected it for heretical interpolations, or inserted passages. Only its portion called the Apostolic Canons was received. The entry thus presents a grand manual that failed its own claim, yet preserves a rich picture of fourth-century worship, morals, and church order for modern readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aquarians:
Aquarians, Greek Hydroparastatai and Latin Aquarii, is a name given to various sects in the early church. The Ebionites, Epiphanius says, showed an idolatrous veneration for water, which they took as the source of life. Manichaean sects rejected wine as evil. The name, however, was given chiefly to followers of Tatian, who after his master Justin Martyr's death set up as a heresy teacher, rejecting marriage, animal food, and wine.

Theodoret calls Tatian the father of the Aquarians and Encratites. Aquarians are named because they use water instead of wine in the Eucharist, the Lord's Supper. Encratites are named because they drink no wine and eat no animal food, abstaining as from evil things. Irenaeus and Clement of Alexandria mention them, and Augustine's catalogue of heresies says Aquarians are so called because in the sacramental cup they offer water, not wine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-araucanians:
The Araucanians, also called Araucans, Moluches, or Mapuches, were a numerous and warlike people of southern Chile. In the early sixteenth century they ranged from about 36 to 42 degrees south latitude, from the Andes to near the coast. By the article's day they were confined to areas likened to North American reservations in the same region. They numbered, it says, 73,000 in 1898, a figure probably exaggerated. Yet they still ranked among the most numerous native peoples surviving as such in America.

When Spaniards first met them in the mid-sixteenth century, they formed a league of some forty clans, or aillaragues, spread over four districts called Butalmapu. Government was rudimentary: chiefs called ulmenes held little authority, but in grave danger a general council chose a war chief, or toqui. The entry then follows their resistance, missions, and survival in the south.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assideans:
Assideans, Hebrew chasidim, saints, or in Greek Asidaioi, men endowed with grace, were defenders of the Mosaic Law against Greek customs spreading. When the Maccabees struggled against Antiochus IV Epiphanes, they naturally joined their cause, as 1 Maccabees 2:42-43 records. Not all Maccabee followers belonged to the party, however.

According to 1 Maccabees 7:13, scribes and Assideans sought peace with the Syrians, while other Maccabee followers suspected deceit. That suspicion the article calls well founded: Alcimus, made high priest by Demetrius I, slew sixty Assideans in one day. In 2 Maccabees 14:3 the same Alcimus, who had defiled himself on purpose, testified before Demetrius that the party, captained by Judas Maccabeus, stirs up wars and revolts. The entry follows a pious party caught between law, revolt, and treachery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basilians:
Basilians are the Priests of the Community of St Basil, born from a school founded in 1800. During the Revolution, Vienne's Archbishop D'Aviau watched persecution shrink his clergy to about a third, with no recruits. Unable to keep a college or seminary, he opened a school at remote St Symphorien de Mahun under Father Lapierre. Despite humble beginnings and danger, the school prospered, moving in 1802 to a former Franciscan monastery at Annonay.

In 1822 its professors won leave to found a religious community, with Annonay's college as mother-house. The community spread to Texas, founding St Basil's College at Waco in 1889 and St Thomas's College at Houston in 1900. St Mary's Seminary at La Porte opened in 1901 to train priests under Galveston's bishop. Final vows wait until the subdiaconate, with temporal vows renewed if a scholastic is not ready after three years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blackfoot-ind:
Blackfoot Indians, an important tribe of the Northern Plains, receive a full entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. They form the westernmost branch of the great Algonquian language family, but they are not one compact people under a head chief. Instead they are a confederacy of three sub-tribes speaking one tongue: the Siksika proper, the Kaina or Blood, and the Pikuni or Piegan.

Some fifty bands divide the three, with the Grosventres and a Beaver band as close allies. Wars with Cree, Sioux, Crow, and others, smallpox in 1780, 1837, 1845, and 1869, and starvation in 1883 to 1884 cut their numbers hard. The entry joins ethnology, history, and mission work in one tribal portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blood-indians:
The Blood Indians, or Kæna, form part of the Blackfeet tribe, in the western branch of the great Algonquin family. Their language, Blackfoot, shares only a few words with other Algonquin tongues. The true meaning of Kæna is lost, though it is sometimes rendered Already-chief.

Clans include the Standing-buffaloes, Black-elks, Many-scabbed-mouths, and Buffalo-coats. In sign language, Kæna is made by passing the right hand, palm down, before the mouth. Numbering about 1,800 in 1882, they had fallen to no more than 1,200 when the entry was written. Once roaming from the Missouri basin to Alberta's Red Deer River, they have lived since the 1877 treaty on the Blood Reserve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bureau-of-cat:
The Bureau of Catholic Indian Missions, founded in 1874 by Archbishop Bailey of Baltimore, guards Catholic Indian interests before the United States government. Washington holds the Indians as wards and supervises all their relations, so missionaries, traders, and philanthropists must work through government channels under Indian officials. With missions scattered across many states and dioceses, the Church set its bureau at the seat of government to deal with the Indian Office.

Its director speaks for hierarchy and missionaries in official Indian affairs, and the bureau watches missions and mission schools with limited oversight. Bishops and missionaries look to it for school support and material aid, which it raises by alms from Catholics, Indian and white, across the country. Its board joins Cardinals Gibbons and Archbishops Ryan and Farley with director Ketcham, treasurer Dyer, secretary Lusk, legal adviser Bonaparte, and field lecturer Currier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buskins: Buskins are ceremonial silk stockings, at times woven with gold thread and richly embroidered, worn by the celebrant at a pontifical Mass. Priests once wore them, but from about the eighth century they were kept for bishops alone, a privilege lately widened to lesser prelates. In color they match the chasuble, yet they are never worn with black.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caddo-indians:
The Caddo were a group of closely linked tribes holding land in western Louisiana and eastern Texas along the Red, Sabine, and Neches rivers. Spaniards first called them Tejas, the source of the state's name, and the French called them Cenis or Assinais. Some twenty small tribes made up the group, led by the Natchitoches, Yatasi, and Adai in Louisiana and the Caddo proper, Hasinai, Nacogdoches, Anadarko, and others in Texas.

They farmed corn, beans, and pumpkins and lived in large grass-thatched communal houses, with women skilled as potters and mat weavers. Descent ran through the female line across ten clans, nearly all named for animals that no clan member dared to kill. Their rites could be bloody: La Harpe, a French officer staying in their villages in 1712, saw war captives bound, tormented, and put to death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-california-mi:
California's missions began with failure: Franciscans landing with Cortés at Santa Cruz Bay in 1535 gave up after a year of hunger, and a second venture in 1596 died the same year. Jesuits under Kino tried again in 1683, but want of supplies forced withdrawal in 1685. In 1697 the viceroy charged the Society of Jesus with settling California at no cost to the crown, and Jesuit missions took root on the peninsula.

Franciscans under Junípero Serra took over the peninsula missions in 1768 and opened a larger field in Upper California, where the Indians near San Diego resisted even by arms. Dominicans added missions from San Fernando de Velicatá toward San Diego from 1774 to 1797. Mexico secularized the missions in 1834, taking land and stock from the missionaries and handing them to hired managers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-adm:
A canonical admonition is a preliminary step the Church takes toward a suspected person, to prevent harm or remedy evil. Under Leo XIII's 1880 Instruction to Italy's bishops, admonitions rank among preservative measures, with spiritual retreats and injunctions. They may be paternal and private, even by letter or intermediary, or in legal form, but always so that proof of them stays on record.

Admonitions rest on suspicion stirred by public rumor, after an inquiry by due authority gives the suspicion a reasonable base. On slender grounds a superior should not admonish at all, unless the suspect has given serious cause before. A paternal admonition tells the suspect what is said of him, without naming the source or threatening, and urges amendment. If denial fails to clear doubt, the prelate presses him by persuasion to shun occasions of wrong and repair harm or scandal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-miss:
The history of Catholic missions, taken in full, would run from the missionary labors of Christ through much of church history. This article limits itself to a general survey of missionary activity in its own day, leaving the fuller stories to entries on countries, dioceses, orders, and individual missionaries. It is organized under four heads. These are the organization of missions, their receipts and expenditure, the use and object of mission statistics, and the statistics themselves.

Direction of the missions rests chiefly with the Sacred Congregation of Propaganda. It fixes each mission's rank and appoints its superior. Seminaries train the missionaries, foremost the Urban College. The survey then gives figures for Christians, personnel, establishments, and administration across Europe, Japan, Further India, and the East Indies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-paro:
Parochial missions are special efforts of the Church's pastoral work, carried on mostly among Catholics. They teach the faith more fully, convert sinners, stir the indifferent, and lift the good to higher spiritual effort. In English-speaking countries they are called parochial missions, to set them apart from missions among pagans and heretics. A mission usually means a planned course of preaching and instruction over a set number of days, given by authorized missionaries.

Making converts is not the primary object. In the United States, though, where Catholics and non-Catholics live side by side, it became a normal result. An organized movement for converting non-Catholics grew from the 1890s. The article treats the need and value of popular missions. It also covers their origin and history, and their method, with sources from England, Ireland, and America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chaldean-chri:
The Chaldean Christians descend from Nestorians who have since rejoined the Roman Church. Ethnically they fall into two groups that must be treated apart: the Turco-Persian Chaldeans and the Indian St. Thomas Christians, of the Syro-Malabar Church. Strictly the name Chaldeans no longer fits. Very few adherents remain in Chaldea proper apart from Baghdad. Most live around Kerkuk, Arbil, and Mosul, in the Tigris and Zab valleys and the Kurdistan mountains.

The flourishing Catholic Chaldean communities cluster in the former ecclesiastical province of Ator, or Assyria. The people call themselves Atoraya-Kaldaya, Assyro-Chaldeans. Their land once belonged to the Sassanid Persian Empire, then to the Omayyad and Abbasid caliphs, before Turkish and Mongol invasions shattered its political unity. The article follows the Chaldeans in Turkey and Persia, their present status, and the Malabar Christians, whose link to the Chaldean patriarchs remained a live question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-de-bo:
Charles de Bouvens was a French pulpit orator born at Bourg in 1750 and dead in 1830. He served as vicar general to his fellow-townsman, Archbishop de Conzié of Tours. When revolution broke out, he refused the required oaths, then went with his archbishop to Germany. After the archbishop died near Frankfort, he went to London. There the Bishop of Arras, the archbishop's brother, was minister to the Comte d'Artois.

In London he preached funeral orations before Louis XVIII and the Comte d'Artois. Best known among them honoured the wife of Louis XVIII, the Duc d'Enghien, and the Abbé Edgeworth de Firmont, confessor of Louis XVI. Printed separately in 1814, they were gathered in one volume in 1824. At the Restoration he returned to France as the king's chaplain. He resigned in 1828 through infirmity, keeping the honorary title until the Revolution of 1830 drove him from Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cherokee-indi:
An entry on the Cherokee Indians, the leading tribe of Iroquoian stock in the southern United States. They once held the southern Allegheny mountains across the Carolinas, Georgia, and Tennessee. They call themselves Yunwiya, meaning real people. Their history opens with De Soto passing through their land in 1540, and their first Carolina treaty with the English dates to 1684.

In 1821 Sequoya, a Cherokee of mixed parentage, created a syllabic alphabet for the language, which became a great force in the tribe's progress. They adopted a government modelled on that of the United States in 1827, but Georgia claimed their land, and a treaty forced on them in 1835 bound them to move west. The removal of 1839 took most of them to Oklahoma, where the Cherokee Nation lasted until it was dissolved for American citizenship in 1906, while about 1,300 stayed behind in North Carolina.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chippewa-indi:
An entry on the Chippewa Indians, also called Ojibwa, the largest tribe north of Mexico, numbering some 30,000 souls split between the United States and Canada. They call themselves Anishinabag, original men, and the French knew them as Saulteurs from their home at the Lake Superior outlet, Sault Sainte Marie. Of Algonquian stock and kin to the Ottawa and Cree, they came from the east and first appear in the Jesuit Relation of 1640.

Armed with guns from French traders, they drove the Sioux from the upper Mississippi and forced the Foxes south to join the Sauk. By 1800 they held nearly all of Michigan, northern Wisconsin, and Minnesota. Unlike many tribes they were never removed, but treaty sales confined them to reservations in their homeland. Mission work runs through the Jesuits to Bishop Baraga, whose grammar and dictionary remain the standard for the Ojibwa tongue.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-choctaw-india:
An entry on the Choctaw Indians, a Muskogean people who once held most of southern Alabama and Mississippi with parts of Louisiana, and now live in eastern Oklahoma. By their own tradition they crossed the Mississippi from the west with the Chickasaw. In 1540 their giant chief Tuscalusa, the Black Warrior, opposed De Soto in one of the eastern United States' fiercest Indian battles. Their connected history begins with the French at Biloxi in 1699.

Friendlier to the French than to the English, the Choctaw made a first treaty with the United States in 1786 and never again warred with the government. Their last lands east of the river were sold in 1820, with agreement to move to Oklahoma., a removal finished about twenty years later, though a band stayed behind in Mississippi. As the Choctaw Nation they governed themselves until 1906, when they took American citizenship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-ath:
An entry on Christian Athens, from Saint Paul's visit about the year 53 to the later centuries of the city's Christian life. Paul came from Beroea, waited for Silas and Timothy, spoke in the synagogue and the market place, and preached at the Areopagus, the hill of judgement, as recorded in Acts chapter 17. Few believed, among them Dionysius of the Areopagite court and Damaris.

A community soon formed, led by tradition under Dionysius or Hierotheus, then by Narkissos, Publius, and Quadratus, whose apology to Hadrian defended the faith. Later apologists included Aristeides and Athenagoras. The entry follows Athens through its bishops, writers, and churches across the centuries, drawing on Greek and Western histories of the medieval city and its monuments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercians:
The Cistercians, religious of the Order of Citeaux, were a Benedictine reform founded at Citeaux in 1098 by Saint Robert, Abbot of Molesme. Robert sought to restore the literal observance of the Rule of Saint Benedict after Cluniac laxity defeated his reforms at Molesme and elsewhere. With twenty-one companions he retired to the solitude of Citeaux, ceded by Raynald, Viscount of Beaune, and on 21 March 1098 they began the New Monastery.

The order's history falls into four periods: formation from 1098 to 1134, golden age to 1342, decline to 1790, and restoration after 1790. Robert was recalled to Molesme at Pope Urban the Second's bidding, and his companions Alberic and Stephen carried the work forward. From this austere beginning, shaped by Bernard's arrival in 1113, grew an order that would transform monastic life across Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coeur-d-alene:
James Mooney's entry describes the Coeur d'Alene, a small Salishan people of northern Idaho. They once ranged along the lake and river of that name. Now they live on a reservation set up in 1873. They call themselves Skitswish. Their common name, said to mean awl heart, may have begun as a French traders' nickname for a chief famed for stinginess. Lewis and Clark first noticed them in 1805, living in mat-covered communal houses on fish and wild roots.

Peaceful, brave, and honest in character, they took up Christian prayer forms through French and Iroquois workers of the Hudson Bay Company. Jesuit Nicholas Point, a companion of De Smet, founded the Sacred Heart mission among them in 1841. Within ten years the whole tribe had become Christian, settled, and self-supporting. By 1906 the tribe numbered 492 souls, still guided by the mission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-collections:
Herbert Thurston's entry follows money collections in the Church, apart from the fuller treatment under Offertory and Mass. It starts with Saint Paul's order to the Galatians and Corinthians. Each believer was to set aside money on the first day of the week, so no collection need be made when Paul arrived. Sunday giving thus appears very early. Later rules split the offerings, with a third for clergy and two-thirds for the poor in the capitularies of Louis the Pious.

These gifts long stood apart from the liturgy itself. The offering stayed voluntary, with each person bringing what he had to the altar rail. In the Middle Ages the many mendicant orders strained lay charity hard. Thurston traces the methods, the abuses, and the preaching that went with the quest, down to the modern collection plate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-collections-o:
Jules Besson's long survey traces how the Church's laws were gathered into collections. Church government was fixed from the start, but church law grew slowly. Early written rules were local or provincial statutes, not universal laws. Wider force came later, through express or tacit approval by lawful authority. That growth made collecting, or codifying, the laws a real need.

Besson first sorts the collections by their authority and method. By history they are genuine, like the Versio Hispanica, or apocryphal, built on forged or misattributed papers such as Pseudo-Isidore. By law they are official or private. By method they run chronological or systematic. His survey then moves from the earliest Christian times to the Decretum of Gratian, in two great periods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Bartholomew Randolph's entry follows the Congregation of the Mission, secular priests with vows founded by Saint Vincent de Paul. Members add C.M. to their names. In France and most countries they are Lazarists, after Paris's Priory of Saint Lazare, where Vincent set his principal works. The Irish province, covering nearly all English-speaking countries except America, calls them Vincentians, gradually replacing Lazarists there. Spanish lands call them Paules, again from the founder's name.

Mission work stands first among their objects, hence the title. Origin traces to early 1617 at Folleville's Picardy château, where Vincent preached with the Gondis. Paris's archbishop approved the foundation contract on 24 April 1626, formal establishment that September. Canonically secular clergymen, it frames rule and simple government: a general assembly every six years, with general officers and one delegate per province. Establishments spread through France, Poland, and Italy during Vincent's life, then worldwide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coptic-persec:
Eugène Hyvernat's entry recounts Coptic persecutions according to Greek and Latin sources. During the first two centuries Alexandria's Church seems freer from Roman persecution than Rome's and Antioch's. Jews in Egypt held privileged status, and the Government found Christians hard to distinguish from them. Roman citizenship never extended to Egyptians except in a few cases, leaving inhabitants free from the state religion's obligations and thus removing any reason for persecution.

The first two centuries' only cause was Christian faith's incompatibility with the state religion, which every Roman citizen except Jews had to practise. Later persecutions follow in sequence: Severus from 200 to 211, Decius from 249 to 251, and Valerian from 257 to 261, even more severe than Decius. Then came Diocletian from 303 to 305 and Maximinus. A six-month lull ended when Maximinus resumed persecution at petitioning cities' request.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-l: A short reference entry on the councils of Lyons explains its own limits. One scholar counts no fewer than twenty-eight synods at Lyons or nearby Anse before 1313. Yet this entry treats only the two general councils of 1245 and 1275. It dismisses a supposed 499 meeting between Catholic and Arian bishops of Burgundy as apocryphal. A bibliography of council collections and registers closes the piece for further study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-o:
A detailed reference entry follows six national councils held at Orleans during the Merovingian period, beginning with the assembly convoked by Clovis in 511. It shows how these meetings functioned as joint business between Frankish kings and bishops, settling church discipline, sanctuary, ordination, and care for the sick and poor.

The first council's thirty-one decrees, approved by Clovis, are presented as an early pact linking the Frankish state with the Church, granting equal treatment to Franks and Romans. Later councils under Childebert and others banned marriages between Christians and Jews, regulated divorce, and defended church property. A fruitless 1478 assembly on crusade and church reform closes the long story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-s:
A reference entry traces the councils held at Sens in France from about 600 into the twelfth century, ranging from local discipline to a famous condemnation. It notes early meetings against simony, the buying and selling of church offices, and a long run of councils concerned with the privileges of the Abbey of St. Pierre-le-Vif.

Its centrepiece is the council of 1140, attended by St. Bernard, which condemned the teaching of Abelard after he appealed to Rome, prompting bishops of Sens and Reims to press Innocent II to confirm the sentence. The entry also defends the 1140 date against a rival dating of 1141, and closes with a 1198 council against the Manichaean sect of the Poplicani in the Nivernais.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crescens:
A scriptural entry examines Crescens, a companion of St. Paul named only once in the New Testament, when Paul writes that Crescens has gone into Galatia. Commentators rank him with Titus, on a missionary journey, rather than with Demas, who deserted. The puzzle is what Galatia means here: Gaul, or the Roman province in Asia Minor where Paul had laboured.

The entry argues for the province, since other regions named in the same passage lie east of Rome, and Paul had reason to send a disciple to his old Galatian churches. Earliest tradition makes Crescens bishop of the Galatian churches, while later claims place him at Vienne in Gaul or Mainz. Those later claims, it warns, rest on mistaken identification and a desire for apostolic origins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crown-of-thor:
This relic entry traces the Crown of Thorns from Gospel mention to its later history as a venerated relic. Though three Evangelists mention it and early Fathers allude to it, few writers of the first six centuries speak of it as a relic still in existence. Jerome, writing at length on the Cross and Nails found by Helena, says nothing of the Crown.

Exceptions appear: Paulinus of Nola after 409 names the thorns among relics honoured with the Cross, and Cassiodorus about 570 places the Crown among Jerusalem's glories. Gregory of Tours claimed its thorns stayed green, renewed daily by miracle. Sixth-century pilgrim accounts state plainly that the Crown was then shown at Jerusalem. The entry leans on De Mely's authoritative study of the subject.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deacons:
A long entry defines the deacon, from the Greek diakonos, minister or servant. It traces the office from Scripture to modern practice. Paul addresses bishops and deacons at Philippi about AD 63. His Pastoral Epistles set their qualities: chaste, not double-tongued, not given to wine, not greedy, holding faith in a pure conscience. They must first be proved, and be husbands of one wife.

Catholic tradition sees the first institution in Acts chapter 6. There apostles appointed seven men to serve Hellenistic widows neglected in daily ministrations, Stephen foremost among them. Sections cover origin and early history, duties as stewards of funds and alms, dress and number, and the sacramental character affirmed at Trent. A final section covers deacons outside the Catholic Church, above all in Anglican and Episcopal communions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-delaware-indi:
An ethnological entry describes the Delaware Indians, an important Algonquian confederacy first holding the Delaware River basin, eastern Pennsylvania, and most of New Jersey. They called themselves Lenape, or Leni-Lenape, real men. English named them Delawares for the river, French called them Loups, wolves, and Algonquian neighbours called them Wapanaki, easterners.

As parent body of cognate tribes holding ancestral land, they held precedence in intertribal councils under the respectful title grandfather. The Lenape proper formed three tribes, Munsee, Unami, and Unalachtgo, under Wolf, Turtle, and Turkey totems. Sedentary farmers of corn, beans, squash, and tobacco, they lived in bark or mat houses of wagon-top shape holding several families, with clans reckoning descent through women.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demons:
A word-history entry tracing demon from a Greek term for a divine being to its Christian sense of a fallen angel. Early Greek writers used it for kindly spirits between gods and men, much like angels in later thought. Scripture and Catholic teaching then narrow it to evil spirits, with the devil as their chief.

Latin usage keeps the split clear: diabolus names Satan himself, while daemones name his lesser angels. Yet Satan still counts among the demons in passages from James and Luke, so the gap is one of rank, not of nature. Even Iranian speech flips the same root, turning the good deva of India into the hateful daeva of the Avesta.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-distributions:
Distributions, called daily distributions in canon law, are shares of a church's income paid to canons present at divine service. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes many rules on them in the body of canon law. The latest law comes from Trent, whose decrees allowed bishops to turn one-third of cathedral and collegiate dignitaries' income into such shares. That third became distributions for those who met their duty of daily personal presence.

Canons retired for age keep their right, as do those who have received coadjutors and extra canons. To earn the share, a canon must chant the office in common as his church customs demand. Mere bodily presence, without heed to the service, earns nothing in conscience, the entry warns, tying pay to prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dositheans:
The Dositheans were followers of Dositheus, a Samaritan who founded a Gnostic-Jewish sect before Simon Magus. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that his name is often paired with Simon's as first of all heretics, yet we know very little of him. Justin and Irenaeus never mention him. He first appears in a Latin version of Hippolytus's lost Syntagma, about the year 220.

There the author skips past Dositheus, who first dared to deny that the prophets spoke in the Holy Spirit. He also passes over the Sadducees, sprung from this root, who denied even the resurrection of the flesh. Should the Sadducees descend from Dositheus, his teaching must date very early, a puzzle the entry weighs with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-early-christi:
Early Christian inscriptions, as non-literary remains, are a rich source for the growth of Christian thought and life. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sorts them into three classes, tomb inscriptions, epigraphic records, and inscriptions of private life. The matter matches heathen practice, stone above all, native or imported, with metal less common. A text cut into stone is called a titulus or marble, one scratched is a graffito, one painted a dipinto.

Mosaic inscriptions abound in North Africa, Spain, and the East. The entry guides readers through collections from the epitaphs of the first six centuries to handbooks of Christian archaeology. For students of the early Church, these stones speak where books fall silent, naming the dead and their hopes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Ecclesiastical abbreviations are the shortened forms most used for names, titles, and words of constant occurrence. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry starts with Roman republican and early imperial lists, such as Egbert's Latin Inscriptions, and notes that Jewish scribes and Talmud scholars also shortened freely. Between the seventh and ninth centuries the Roman system gave way to a harder one grown in monasteries and chanceries.

Merovingian, Lombard, and Anglo-Saxon scripts each made their own marks, besides the Irish hand and its books. The entry then gives tables for apostolic rescripts, general church use, and catacomb inscriptions. It points readers to Reusens, Carini, Thompson, and Steffens for the full science of reading shortened Latin.

Ecclesiastical canons are rules of conduct or belief laid down by the Church. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry derives the name from the Greek kanon, the straightedge of builders and craftsmen. Some writers hold that the Church favored canon over law, since law sounded harsh to the faithful in days of persecution. Early fathers used canon for the rule of faith or for a formula binding Christians.

Bickell argued that for three hundred years canon seldom meant a single decree, but rather the rule of faith as a whole, since the plural is rare in the earliest writers. The entry follows the word from that broad sense to the canons of councils and popes. It cites Ferraris, Smith, and Wernz, and it warns that corruption of morals often follows contempt for canons.

Ecclesiastical commissions are bodies of clergy set up by law and charged with set tasks. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sorts them into pontifical, Roman prelatial, and diocesan kinds. Pontifical commissions are small groups named by the pope for one purpose, such as reading Scripture aright, studying history, or codifying canon law.

Other pontifical commissions watch the service books, restore church music, seek reunion with separated churches, or preserve monuments. Roman and diocesan commissions serve lesser spheres with like care. The entry cites Battandier, Baumgarten, and Taunton, giving readers the map of the Church's standing groups at Rome and at home.

A constitution, in general, is the make-up of a body, whether physical or moral. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains the singular sense for civil or religious societies: the basic law that fixes their governing, legislative, and executive shape. In the plural it means the enactments and laws issued by the supreme power to advance the society's aim.

In legal speech, constitutiones means only church ordinances, while civil ordinances are called laws. Church ordinances share with civil laws the binding force drawn from their makers, but they differ as Church differs from civil society, in origin, object, and sanction. The entry closes with the constitutions of the Baltimore councils, which fitted the Church's ancient laws to America.

Ecclesiastical prisons show the Church's claim, as a perfect and visible society, to guard its members by jailing offenders. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that decrees in the body of canon law prove the claim and its exercise. Among Hebrews and Romans, prisons at first served only to hold an accused person, real or pretended, until trial. The church idea adds more, making confinement both a punishment and a chance for reform and reflection.

The method reached even clerics in old times. Boniface the Eighth decreed that, though prisons were made for custody and not for punishment, no fault would be found with those who used them to punish. The entry cites Reiffenstuel, Pirhing, and Piatus on a discipline that sought amendment behind bars.

Basins were widely used in Jewish ritual and came early into Christian churches for washings and to catch lamp drippings. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that the Missal orders a basin at the Lavabo of the Mass. The Ceremonial of Bishops provides one for bearing the cruets and for bishops' preparatory washings. Such basins are ordinarily made of ornamented metal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edmond-reusen:
Edmond Reusens was a Belgian priest, archaeologist, and historian, born at Wijneghem in 1831 and dead at Louvain in 1903. Ordained in 1854, he soon became head librarian of Louvain University, a post he held from 1859 to 1896. With his rector he founded a review of Belgian church history in 1864 and ran it until his death.

He taught Christian archaeology from 1864 to 1900 and gave Belgium its first course in old handwriting and charters, from 1881 to 1903. His handbooks on Christian archaeology and on old handwriting were widely used, and he spent his last years on the records of Louvain University. Readers get a clear sketch of a librarian-teacher who built two fields of study in Belgium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elizabeth-ass:
Elizabeth Associations were German women's charities that served the sick poor and neglected children for love of Christ. On 10 December 1842 eight ladies of Munich, led by Princess Leopoldine von Lowenstein, formed a society to visit and aid the sick poor at home. In 1851 it became a religious congregation, and in 1870 the first local branch, or conference, was founded to organise visiting better.

Members fell into two classes: associates, who gave yearly money, and active members, who also visited the sick and ran the work under a president. Branches stayed tied to the main society but ran their own affairs. Munich alone counted one hundred and fifty-seven active and over three thousand six hundred associate members in 1907, helping more than four thousand poor people that year. The model spread to Barmen, Trier, Cologne, and across Bavaria and the Rhineland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-episcopal-and:
Episcopal and pontifical capitulations were bargains struck at elections, by which voters imposed conditions on a bishop or pope to be kept after his election. Episcopal capitulations arose because, from the eleventh and twelfth centuries, real elections of bishops lay with cathedral canons. The canons sought to trim the bishop's powers or income and to secure privileges or larger revenues.

From the early thirteenth century the canons of Mainz agreed not to elect a bishop unless he promised in advance to levy no financial contributions on the clergy. Such capitulations spread through Germany, where chapters kept elections in their hands. A diet at Nuremberg in 1522 condemned chapters for extorting such concessions. Popes from Nicholas III to Benedict XIV declared capitulations that curbed authority invalid, even when sworn. Penalties were suspension, interdict, and excommunication, yet in Germany they endured, partly because church states were built upon them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistle-to-th:
The Epistle to the Colossians is one of four Captivity Epistles written by Paul during his first imprisonment at Rome, the others being Ephesians, Philemon, and Philippians. That they were written in prison is stated in the letters themselves: Paul mentions his chain and bonds, names fellow prisoners, and calls himself a prisoner. They belong to Rome, not Caesarea, where some once placed them.

Paul, having appealed to the emperor, awaited trial in the custody of the Praetorian prefect, probably Burrhus. He lived in military custody, his right wrist chained to a soldier's left arm. In such straits the letters were written, some time between the years 61 and 63. Colossians, Ephesians, and Philemon were written and sent at one time, with Tychicus as messenger, joined in Colossians by Onesimus, in whose favour Philemon was written.

The Epistle to the Ephesians is treated under analysis, object, addressees, and date and place. The letter falls into two parts, split by a doxology, and its address names Paul alone. A long sentence like a hymn praises God for blessings given to all the faithful. That plan is that all things should be united under one head, Christ, a plan once secret, now revealed.

The readers share those blessings, and Paul, hearing of their conversion and faith, thanks heaven and prays for them. The rest of the doctrinal part explains that prayer: that readers may know the hope of their calling, the riches of their inheritance, and God's great power. That power raised Christ from the dead, exalted him above all creatures, and made him head of the Church. Next it rescued the readers from sin and raised them with Christ.

The Epistle to the Galatians opens with a survey of Galatia itself, and this entry follows those Gauls. Gallic tribes akin to those who sacked Rome wandered east through Illyricum and Pannonia, then through Macedonia in 279 before Christ. Under Brennus they aimed at Greece and Delphi, but the leaders quarrelled. One part marched south, the other, under Leonorius and Luterius, turned east and overran Thrace and the land round Byzantium.

In 278 before Christ, twenty thousand Gauls crossed to Asia Minor in two divisions. They helped Nicomedes I of Bithynia beat his younger brother. As reward they received a large tract in Asia Minor, henceforth called Galatia. The Galatians formed three tribes: Tolistoboii in the west with Pessinus, Tectosages in the centre with Ancyra, and Trocmi in the east round Tavium. Each tribal land was split into four cantons, each with a tetrarch, a judge, and a general.

The Epistle to the Philippians is a letter of joy and gratitude, and this entry sets out its occasion. The Philippians, dear to Paul, had sent him help on former occasions. Learning of his imprisonment at Rome, they sent Epaphroditus, one of their own, to carry alms and tend his needs. Paul received him gladly, rejoicing in their affection and in their church's sound state.

Epaphroditus fell dangerously ill at Rome and nearly died, and on recovery he longed to return home. Paul hastened to send him back with a letter to the faithful and their leaders, probably written by Timothy at Paul's dictation. Joy and gratitude form its keynote, an outpouring of spontaneous, paternal intimacy. Familiar thanks mingle with doctrine and moral exhortation, with no strict order. Paul also warns against pride and vainglory, naming Evodia and Syntyche.

The Epistle to the Romans is treated under seven heads, from the Roman church to its teaching on faith and works. Among Paul's letters it stands first in the manuscripts that survive, though the order was probably different early on. It introduces a community Paul did not found but long wished to visit, whose faith was already known everywhere.

The Roman church was no recent plant, but a firm, old institution Paul regarded with reverence, almost awe. On its foundation the letter gives no information, and the entry warns against reading that silence as proof against Peter's founding role. It cannot be fixed with certainty when Peter first reached Rome, and Christians may have been in the capital before any apostle set foot there. Yet the entry holds it inconceivable that so firm a faith arose without a leading authority laying its foundation and directing its growth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epistles-to-t:
The Epistles to the Corinthians open with Paul founding the church at Corinth, and this entry follows his first visit to Europe as Luke describes it. On his second missionary journey, with Timothy and Silvanus, Paul reached Troas and met Luke, probably for the first time. At Troas he had a vision of a man of Macedonia pleading, pass over into Macedonia and help us.

In response he went to Philippi, where he made many converts but was beaten with rods. He then travelled south to Thessalonica, where some Jews and many Gentiles believed. Unbelieving Jews stirred up the city, so the brethren sent Paul and Silas away by night to Beroea. From there Paul was brought to Athens, where he preached in the Areopagus, converted only a few, and left disappointed, never to visit again.

The Epistles to the Thessalonians are two canonical epistles of Paul, treated here through the church of Thessalonica, authenticity, canonicity, time and place, occasion, and contents. After leaving Philippi on his second missionary journey, Paul and Silas proceeded to Thessalonica, the modern Saloniki, perhaps because the city had a synagogue of the Jews. Thessalonica was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a free city ruled by a popular assembly and magistrates.

Paul at once preached the Gospel to Jews and proselytes. For three successive sabbaths he explained the Scriptures in the synagogue. He led his hearers to the truth that the Christ must die and rise again, and that Jesus whom Paul preached was this Christ. The entry argues Paul stayed longer than three weeks, since Philippi sent alms to Paul at Thessalonica twice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-our-:
Our Lady, Help of Christians, is honoured by the Church each year on 24 May. The title Auxilium Christianorum entered the Loreto litany in the sixteenth century. Warriors from Lepanto may first have saluted Mary by that name. Pius V is also said to have inserted it after the victory.

Pius VII instituted the feast after his release from long Napoleonic captivity. Freed in 1814, he entered Rome on 24 May to great public rejoicing. The feast, set for 24 May, recalls his return and thanksgiving. Don Bosco later made it famous through his great Turin mother church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Crown of Thorns feast honours the relic brought to Paris in 1239. St Louis carried the crown thither, and it now rests in the Royal Chapel. The first feast, on 11 August, spread through northern France. A second festival on 4 May arose in Spain, Germany, and the north in the next century.

Dominicans keep the feast on 24 April, and Spanish dioceses still observe it. Rome adopted it in 1831 for the Friday after Ash Wednesday. Its Office draws on the rich seventeenth-century Gallican Breviary of Paris. The hymns were composed by Habert for that Office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferns:
Ferns is an Irish diocese in Leinster, suffragan of the see of Dublin. St Aedan founded it in 598 and ruled with quasi-supremacy over Leinster's bishops. Its abbey held cells and a cathedral built in the Irish style. Scandinavian raiders burned the town repeatedly in the ninth and tenth centuries.

Dermot MacMurrough burned Ferns in 1166 and three years later brought Welshmen over. Henry II landed in Ireland in 1171, the year Dermot died. Later bishops rebuilt cathedrals and founded friaries, enduring the penal laws. The diocese still bears St Aedan's name in its wells, townlands, and churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-first-council:
The First Council of Lyons opened on 28 June 1245, summoned by Innocent IV at Lyons. The pope, threatened by Emperor Frederick II, had fled to Lyons in December 1244. Innocent preached on the five wounds of the Church, naming Frederick's persecution last among them. Frederick's envoy Thaddeus of Suessa pleaded for delay, but the emperor never came.

On 17 July Innocent pronounced Frederick deposed, and 150 bishops signed the sentence. Dominicans and Franciscans were charged with publishing the deposition everywhere. The council also ordered cardinals to wear the red hat and set the octave of the Nativity. Its thirty-eight constitutions taxed benefices for the Holy Land and the Latin Empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flathead-indi:
The Flathead Indians of western Montana are the Salish people, easternmost of the Salishan stock. Their name is a puzzle: they never flattened skulls, but neighbours' pointed skulls made theirs look flat. Hunters and root-gatherers, they lived in skin tipis and kept peace with all save the Blackfeet. They won a name for bravery, honesty, and friendly dealing with white newcomers.

Learning of Catholicism from Iroquois traders, they sent delegations to St. Louis asking for missionaries. In 1840 Pierre De Smet answered, founding St. Mary's mission, later moved to St. Ignatius. An 1855 treaty kept them a reservation south of Flathead Lake, where they farmed and raised stock. They numbered about 620, within a confederated body of 2,200, and were still growing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flavius-valen:
Flavius Valens ruled the East from 364 until his death near Adrianople in 378. Raised to the throne by his brother Valentinian, he dealt cruelly with Procopius the usurper. Baptized an Arian in 367, he harried Eastern Catholics from about 369 to his death. Eighty clergy who pleaded for freedom of worship were burned alive aboard a ship in 370.

A visit to Basil at Caesarea failed to bend the bishop, though exile was meant for him. On the Danube frontier he fought Goths, Isaurians, and Persians through a troubled reign. In 376 Goths settled south of the Danube, then rose when imperial officers plundered them. Defeated near Adrianople, he burned to death in a country house, unwittingly avenging the eighty clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florens-radew:
Florens Radewyns helped found the Brethren of the Common Life and died at Deventer in 1400. Born near Utrecht about 1350, he took his M.A. at Prague and became a canon of St. Peter's. Converted by a sermon of Gerard Groote, he gave up his canonry for a poor benefice. At his urging, the first Brethren community formed in his own house.

Six men from his house founded Windesheim in 1386. Thomas à Kempis lived under his care from thirteen to twenty-one and wrote his life. Thomas praised him as learned, devout, humble, zealous, and charitable. His austerities wore down his health and may have cut his life short.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-wichm:
Francis Wichmans, in religion Augustine, was born at Antwerp in 1596 and died in 1661, a Norbertine abbot who kept the Catholic faith alive in Tilburg under persecution. After classical studies he took the white habit at Tongerloo Abbey in 1612 and was ordained in 1620. He studied theology at Louvain and served as master of novices and circator, the monk who oversees discipline. In 1630 he became parish priest of Mierlo and rural dean of Helmond, conferring almost daily with the exiled Bishop Ophovius at Geldorp.

Transferred to Tilburg in 1632, he faced the Retorsion laws of 1634, which expelled Catholic priests and handed their churches to Protestant preachers. From Alphen, six miles outside the town, he administered his parish at risk of liberty and life, and through his fearless zeal not one Catholic of Tilburg apostatised. Elected coadjutor in 1642, he became abbot of Tongerloo in 1644 and promoted education in his abbey lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-jacob-c:
Franz Jacob Clemens, born at Coblenz on 4 October 1815 and dead at Rome on 24 February 1862, was a German Catholic philosopher and lay defender of the Church. After an institution at Metz he entered the Jesuit college of Fribourg at sixteen and attended Coblenz gymnasium, then Bonn University. In 1835 he matriculated at Berlin, studying philosophy and taking his doctorate in 1839. After a literary tour of Germany and Italy he became instructor in philosophy at Bonn in 1843, teaching with high success until 1856.

In 1848 he sat in the Frankfort Parliament and attended the first general congress of German Catholics at Mainz, where he proposed founding the St. Vincent de Paul Society in Germany. Appointed professor of philosophy at Munster Academy in 1856, he was so popular at Bonn that some seventy students followed him. His Westphalian lectures drew extraordinarily large audiences, though his health soon failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerard-manley:
Gerard Manley Hopkins, a Jesuit and poet born near London in 1844, wrote verse of daring music that his age left uncollected. Schooled at Highgate, he felt the Oxford Movement and the mid-century Anglican conversions, and was received into the Church in October 1866. After Balliol, prepared by Walter Pater, he spent time with Newman at the Birmingham Oratory and entered the Society of Jesus in 1868.

Ordained, Hopkins worked among Liverpool's slum poor, preached in London, and served Saint Aloysius's, Oxford, where the Paravicinis raised his memorial. In 1884 he became a fellow of Ireland's Royal University and classical examiner at Dublin, where a contagious fever killed him in 1889. As a novice he destroyed his school poems, saving one fragment, and wrote nothing for nearly ten years. His later poems, Crashaw-like in exuberance and daring metaphor, reached print only in anthologies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grey-nuns:
Montreal's Grey Nuns, formally the Sisters of Charity of the Hôpital Général, began in 1738. Marie-Marguerite d'Youville and Father Louis Normand du Faradon gathered four women in a rented house to shelter a handful of poor people. Royal sanction followed in 1753, a rule took shape in 1754. Leo XIII approved their constitutions in 1880.

Beyond the three vows, the sisters pledged their lives to suffering people, running orphanages, homes for the aged and infirm, hospitals, and schools. By 1906 the entry counts 1,893 professed sisters, 135 establishments, nearly 7,000 poor inmates housed, and close to 26,000 children taught. Their work reached from Montreal and the American northeast to missions in Manitoba and the far north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guaicuri-indi:
Lower California's Guaicuri peoples, small tribes sharing related dialects, ranged between about the 24th and 26th parallels north, south of the Cochimi and north of the Pericue. They may once have numbered some 7,000. The entry leans on the Jesuit Baegert, who worked among them for seventeen years, for its picture of open-air living, hunting, and a diet drawn from whatever the desert offered.

Baegert's harsh verdict was that missionary effort found little ground to build on. Yet Jesuits still gave years to the peninsula, starting with Salvatierra's Loreto mission of 1697 and a chain of fourteen missions. After the Jesuits left in 1768, Franciscans and then Dominicans carried the work on, until secularization in 1833 and population collapse left only a handful of Guaicuri by 1908.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guarani-india:
South America's Guarani, who called themselves Abá, meaning men, belonged to the great Tupí-Guaraní stock spread from the Paraná toward the Amazon. Their home lay mainly between the Uruguay River and the lower Paraguay. Sedentary farmers living in palisaded villages of large communal houses, they grew manioc and corn, worked as potters and woodcarvers, and numbered at least 400,000 when first known.

Their fame rests on the Jesuit missions of Paraguay, begun after 1585 and authorized in 1608 to shield them from enslavement. It rests also on the slave hunters of São Paulo, who over 130 years killed or carried off an estimated two million Indians. The entry follows that struggle from first Spanish contacts through the mission towns to the later Paraguayan resistance against three neighbours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hare-indians:
Canada's Hare Indians, a Déné people living south of the Eskimos from Fort Norman on the Mackenzie around Great Bear Lake toward the Arctic coast. They number no more than 600 in this account. Five bands divide them, named for moss, hares, big hares, Great Bear Lake, and the end of the world. Their name itself is traced to the Arctic hares of their country rather than to timidity.

Gentle and fearful, long exploited by bolder neighbours, they kept customs of abandoning the old in famine long after other Déné gave them up. Evangelization came late: a first baptism in 1839 far to the south, Father Grollier's arrival at Fort Norman in 1859. Petitot's visit to Great Bear Lake in 1866, after which the Hares became almost all Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-robert-:
Henry Robert Stephens, a Belgian theologian born of English parents at Liège in 1665, entered the Society of Jesus in 1683. He spent over twenty years at Liège's episcopal seminary, first teaching dogmatic theology and then serving as superior. His published works all arose from Jansenist attacks in Belgium. There Jansenists assailed the Jesuits and resisted papal decrees condemning Jansenism.

When a libellous Jansenist work charged the Liège Jesuits with corrupting faith and morals through their teaching, Stephens answered with theological theses publicly defended by a pupil in 1702. He followed with a defence of the Church's authority in 1707 and a fresh confutation of the Epistola Leodiensis in 1709. Two further works in 1710 treated the condemnation of the Jansenist book and peace among disputants. In all of them his name appears in Latin form as Stephani.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hopi-indians:
The Hopi, from Hopita or peaceful ones, their own name, are a Pueblo people of Shoshonean stock, also often called Moki or Moqui. Seven communal pueblo towns on a high mesa are their home, inside a reservation in north-east Arizona. Hano, one pueblo, holds Tewa immigrants from New Mexico with their own distinct tongue.

Like every Pueblo people, they farm settled land. Though desert sand surrounds them, small streams from the mesa base water crops of corn, beans, squashes, tobacco, and peaches, the last inherited from former missionaries. They also make fine pottery and basket-work, excel in wood-carving and cotton weaving, and work metal skilfully. Their square, flat-roofed stone or adobe houses rise several stories and hold stores enough for a year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-humbert-of-ro:
Humbert of Romans was the fifth master general of the Dominican order, born at Romans in the diocese of Vienne about 1194 and dead at Valence in 1277 or 1274. A student at Paris in 1215, he joined the Dominicans in 1224, taught theology at Lyons in 1226, and served as prior there from 1236 to 1239. He became provincial of the Roman province in 1240 and of the French province in 1244.

After ten years as French provincial, he was elected master general at Budapest in 1254. During his generalate the Dominican liturgy took its permanent form. He resigned voluntarily at London in 1263 and retired to Valence, refusing the patriarchate of Jerusalem offered after his resignation. His ascetical treatises were later collected, and one work sharply criticizes clerical faults for the Council of Lyons in 1274.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-huron-indians:
This vast article treats the Huron Indians before and after their dispersion. Before dispersion it covers their place in the Huron-Iroquois family, their name, country, population, government, religion, history, and the Jesuit mission stations of Huronia. After dispersion it follows the extinction of the Neutral Hurons and the migration of the Hurons proper to Quebec.

At some unknown date all Iroquois and Huron tribes formed one single people. Father Lallemant noted that fact over two hundred and fifty years ago, and every modern philologist since has accepted it. Language stands as the fair criterion of that kinship. The article then traces Quebec stations from the Island of Orleans through Beauport and Lorette, with lists of missionaries and grand chiefs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hypsistarians:
The Hypsistarians, worshippers of the Hypsistos or Most High God, were a distinct Jewish-pagan sect. They flourished from about 200 BC to about AD 400, mostly in Asia Minor and on the Black Sea's southern Russian coasts. Their names first appear in Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa around AD 374, but votive tablets, inscriptions, and oracles prove the cult widespread near the Bosphorus.

The sect likely arose when the native Cappadocian cult of Zeus Sabazios merged with the worship of Jahve Sabaoth practised by numerous, intellectually leading Jewish colonies. Associations of strict monotheists formed, fraternizing with Jews yet counting themselves free from Mosaic law. The entry traces their exalted ideas, their associations, and their place between Judaism and paganism in the ancient world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-illinois-indi:
The Illinois were a major Algonquian confederacy that once held most of today's Illinois plus nearby Wisconsin, Iowa, and Missouri. French writers took their name from Illini-wek, or men, the people's own word for themselves. Of all Algonquian tongues theirs may have sounded softest, and it differed from Miami speech, their eastern neighbours' and usual allies' tongue, only in dialect.

At first they may have counted eight to ten thousand people across five main sub-tribes: Cahokia, Kaskaskia, Michigamea, Peoria, and Tamarosa. Old reports call them tall, sturdy, and good-looking, yet short on courage and steady purpose. Hunting mattered more to them than farming, and villages rarely stayed put long. Families lived in long shared cabins, each with four or five fires down the middle passage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-infralapsaria:
In the seventeenth century, a group of Dutch Calvinists tried to soften Calvin's stark teaching on predestination. They take center stage here. Calvin's system, as the entry presents it, was supralapsarian. Every event flows from God's eternal decrees. The Fall itself seems not merely foreseen and allowed. It seems positively decreed as a means to display divine power in damnation and mercy in rescue. That corollary troubled many, and the Arminian disputes sharpened the fight.

Infralapsarians, from the Latin for “after the Fall,” placed God's decree of election after the Fall in logical order, easing the harshest edge of the doctrine. The entry sets their case against both Calvin's stricter followers and their outside critics. It shows why they could argue with some advantage in a controversy that split Dutch churches and spilled far beyond them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-burns:
Publisher and author James Burns was born near Montrose, Scotland, in 1808. He died in London on 11 April 1871. In the later nineteenth century his work for Catholic literature and church music greatly advanced the Church in Britain. It also aided many conversions of that period. His father, a Presbyterian minister, sent him to a Glasgow college to follow the same calling. Feeling no inclination for it, Burns left school in 1832 and went to London. There he joined a publishing firm.

He mastered the trade and then set up modestly for himself. He soon succeeded, and Established Church ministers adopted him as an active helper in their tract and polemic campaign. He then became a Puseyite, or high churchman. From his press came many tracts and Catholic works after his own conversion. The entry follows a Presbyterian minister's son turned Catholic publisher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-gamans:
Jean Gamans, a German Jesuit born in 1606 at Ahrweiler and dead at Aschaffenburg in 1684, entered the Society at Trier in 1623 after study at Cologne. He taught humanities for five years at Würzburg, studied theology at Mainz and Douai, and was ordained in 1633.

War with Sweden had closed his province's houses, so Gamans served as chaplain to troops in Belgium and Germany, professed his four vows at Antwerp in 1641. He joined the Bollandists, the Jesuit editors of saints' lives. His patient work on early documents helped lay the ground for that great collection, though his own name stays less known than the project he served.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jibaro-indian:
The Jíbaro Indians, whose name means forest man, form a major tribal group of Ecuador, many small subtribes sharing one tongue with dialect variants and one distinct language stock. They hold broad forests between the Santiago and Pastaza rivers south to the Amazon, and are often confused with their eastern Zaparo neighbours.

More than any upper Amazon people, the Jíbaro resisted conquest and conversion with success, keeping old manners after three centuries of Spanish contact. They live without villages, in scattered communal houses fifty to eighty feet long near streams, with separate doors for men and women. A great hollow-log drum, the tunduli, heard ten miles off, carries coded messages through the forest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-dobree-d:
John Dobree Dalgairns, known in religion as Father Bernard, was an Oratorian scholar and preacher of the Oxford Movement generation. Born at Guernsey in 1818, he entered Exeter College, Oxford, in 1836 and followed Newman ardently. In 1842 he joined Newman at Littlemore, writing saints' lives for Newman's series. They won praise even from the Protestant Dean Milman for their grasp of medieval history.

Received into the Catholic Church by Father Dominic in September 1845, he was ordained at Langres in 1846. He joined Newman in Rome in 1847 and entered the English Oratory. He served at Maryvale, Birmingham, and South Kensington, where he became superior on Faber's death in 1863. As a preacher he ranked second to Faber alone, and as a confessor his languages drew penitents including Queen Marie-Amelie. He defended Catholicism against scientific agnosticism until his death in 1876.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-gibbons:
John Gibbons was an English Jesuit theologian whose Concertatio became the groundwork of England's martyrology. Born near Wells in 1544, he entered Lincoln College, Oxford, in 1561, studied seven years at the German College in Rome, and took doctorates in philosophy and theology in 1576. Given a Bonn canonry by Gregory XIII, he resigned it to enter the Society of Jesus at Trier in 1578.

At Trier he served as confessor, professor of theology and Scripture, prefect of studies, and rector, and won fame in contests with German Lutherans. He declined the English mission as beyond his spiritual strength but aided it with his pen. His Concertatio of 1583, republished larger by Bridgewater in 1588 and 1594, gathered the sufferings of English Catholics, and his posthumous Confutatio answered a Heidelberg professor who called the pope Antichrist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jonas-of-orle:
Jonas of Orleans was a Carolingian bishop and writer on Christian life for laymen and princes. Born in Aquitaine, he succeeded Theodulf as Bishop of Orleans in 818 and played a leading part in Frankish church affairs until his death in 843 or 844. He attended the Paris councils of 825 on images and 829 on reform, carrying the first council's acts to Pope Eugene II.

His writings include On the Instruction of Laymen, made almost entirely of Scripture and Fathers and addressed to Count Matfrid of Orleans. They also include On the Instruction of Kings, a companion addressed to Pepin of Aquitaine. Their contents largely match the 829 council's acts. That match raises a debated question of priority, now usually resolved in favor of the acts borrowing from neither but sharing Jonas's authorship. He also wrote on the veneration of images against Claudius of Turin, without having read Claudius, and restored St. Mesmin's monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joris-karl-hu:
Joris Karl Huysmans was a French novelist whose conversion turned his realism from the sordid to the sacred. Born in Paris in 1848, he studied at the Lycee Saint-Louis and entered the Ministry of the Interior at twenty. He stayed there until 1897 except for service in the Franco-Prussian War, winning the Legion of Honour and helping found the Goncourt Academy, which he presided over from 1900.

His early books belonged to the most realistic school, showing humanity at its most base and vile. A week spent at the Trappist monastery of Issigny in 1895 changed his life, as En Route that year shows. Openly professing Catholicism, he retired to Liguge near the Benedictines and returned to Paris after the monks' expulsion. He spent his last twelve years fighting for his faith in works on cathedrals, Lourdes, and Saint Lydwine, with a colorist's eye worthy of Rembrandt and Rubens.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kalispel-indi:
The Kalispel Indians, popularly Pend d'Oreilles, French for ear pendants, were a Salishan lake-and-river people. They lived about Pend d'Oreille Lake and River in northern Idaho and northeastern Washington, now gathering chiefly on the Flathead Reservation in Montana and the Colville Reservation in Washington. Upper Kalispel lived on the lake, Lower Kalispel on the river. Lewis and Clark met them in 1805, when they crossed the mountains each year to hunt buffalo on the Missouri.

Jesuit Father Adrian Hoecken began their Christianization in 1844 with St. Ignatius Mission on Clark's Fork. Governor Isaac Stevens praised the mission in 1853 as a beautiful example of successful missionary labor. Treaties of 1855 settled the Upper band with the Flatheads on the Flathead Reservation, while part of the Lower band reached Colville in 1872. Lewis and Clark had reckoned the tribe at 1,600 souls; by 1908 the reservations counted about 1,000, still served by Jesuits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-ernst-fr:
Karl Ernst von Moy de Sons was a jurist born at Munich in 1799 and dead at Innsbruck in 1867. His Picardy noble family fled France in 1789 for Munich. He became an auditor in the war office, a privatdocent in 1827, and an attorney from 1830 to 1833. He was extraordinary professor at Würzburg in 1833 and ordinary professor at Munich in 1837.

A senate address to King Ludwig II about the dancer Lola Montez cost him his Munich chair. On leave in 1848 he went to Innsbruck and took its chair of German law and imperial history in 1851. He later led the General Assembly of German Catholics and defended the Concordat. His best work treated Christian marriage law to Charlemagne's time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kaskaskia-ind:
The Kaskaskia once led the Illinois confederacy, a group of related peoples in what is now the American Midwest. Their name may come from a word for a hide scraper. This entry traces the tribe from its first meetings with French missionaries in the 1660s through its missions, moves, and sharp decline in numbers over the next century.

Jesuit priests reached the tribe at Chequamegon in 1667, and Jacques Marquette founded the Mission of the Immaculate Conception among them in April 1675, the first Illinois mission. Father Gravier later wrote the first grammar of their language and helped settle them near present-day Kaskaskia, Illinois, around 1700. War with northern tribes and drink brought in by French garrisons cut them from perhaps 2,000 people to 600 by 1764 and 210 by 1778.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kickapoo-indi:
The Kickapoo, whose name seems to come from a word meaning 'roamers', are an Algonquian people first met in south-central Wisconsin. This entry follows them south to the lower Wabash in Illinois and Indiana, then west to Missouri and Kansas after land cessions between 1809 and 1819.

They farmed from bark houses in summer and mat lodges in winter. They hunted buffalo and raided horses across the Mississippi. They kept eleven clans traced through fathers, with personal names marking clan membership. Their story is one of frequent war. They fought the French with the Foxes, stood with Pontiac against the English in 1764, and sided with the English in the Revolution and the War of 1812. Around 1852 a prophet named Kanakuka preached temperance, peace, and a return to old ways, and a large party broke off from the Kansas body.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kiowa-indians:
The Kiowa, pronounced Kai-o-wa, are a Plains people forming their own language stock, now in western Oklahoma but once living near the Missouri headwaters in Montana, allied with the Crows. Driven from the Black Hills by the Sioux about 1800, they settled on the upper Arkansas.

Peace with the Comanche about 1790 bound the two peoples in raids deep into Texas and Mexico, as far as Zacatecas, until they were confined to a reservation in 1869. A small Athapascan band, the Kiowa-Apache, lived as part of the tribe in all but speech. Treaties followed in 1837 and at Medicine Lodge in 1867, kept only after Custer's Washita battle in 1868. Noted chiefs were Satank, Satanta, and Lone Wolf.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kutenai-india:
The Kutenai are a major tribe of south-eastern British Columbia and nearby Montana and Idaho, living mainly in Kootenai County between the Rockies and the Selkirk Range, down to Lake Pend d'Oreille. They form their own language stock, Kitunahan, from their own name Kitanqa.

Neighbours called them Skalzi, lake or water people, and the French called them Flatbows. Tradition puts their old home on the plains east of the Rockies, whence the Blackfeet drove them. They still made yearly buffalo hunts with Flatheads, Kalispel, and Nez Perces. Tall and well built, traders and missionaries praised them for honesty and steadiness. They lived in skin or mat tipis, hunted, fished, and gathered camas roots. They wove baskets so tight they could boil food in them with heated stones.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lake-indians:
The Lake Indians, called Senijextee by themselves, were a small Salishan tribe along the Columbia River in north-east Washington. They ranged from Kettle Falls to the British line and were perhaps the Lahanna of Lewis and Clark in 1805. Fort Colville's Hudson Bay post rose in their country in 1820, yet they changed little until Christianized.

Jesuit Father Adrian Hoecken brought that change in 1846 with the summer mission of St. Paul at the Falls. By 1870 officials described them as living wholly by hunting and fishing, selling their furs, well fed and clothed, peaceable, friendly, and independent Catholics, numbering 239. Gathered onto Colville Reservation in 1872 with kindred tribes, they counted 283 by 1908 under the mission of St. John Francis Regis at Ward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-le-mans:
Le Mans is a French diocese covering the whole Sarthe department, once 636 parishes before the Revolution and among France's largest sees. At the 1801 Concordat it lost parishes in Vendomois and Normandy and gained some in Anjou. It held 665 communes until Mayenne split off as Laval in 1855.

Its origins spark scholarly dispute over the Gesta of Aldric and the Acts of Le Mans bishops, both compiled under Aldric from 832 to 857. The Acts make St. Julian one of Christ's seventy-two disciples and stretch Pavatius across two centuries. These absurdities lead Duchesne to date the first certain bishop as Victurius, at Angers and Tours councils in 453 and 461. Turibius followed Victurius from 490 to 496, and later saint bishops include Principius, Domnolus, and Bertram, founder of La Couture abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lillooet-indi:
The Lillooet Indians are a Salishan tribe in British Columbia. They formerly held a territory 100 miles long, including its river and lake of the same name. Their bands fall into Upper and Lower divisions, marked by slight dialect differences.

Their settlements are Fountain, Bridge River, Pemberton, and Skookumchuck. From 4,000 souls they have fallen to 1,230, through disease after the whites came. Lillooet, meaning wild onion, is properly one of their former settlements, and the lower division's name. They have no self-name, but neighbours call them Stlatlimuq. Though nearby tribes had gained Catholic knowledge by 1810 through North-West Fur Company men, Christianity in the tribe begins with Father Modeste Demers, from Quebec in 1837 with Father Norbert Blanchet. After years in the Columbia region, Demers in 1842 went up the Fraser to Stuart Lake. In 1847 the Oblates reached Fort Walla Walla, and in 1861 Father Charles Grandidier preached to the Lillooet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-loyola-univer:
Loyola University New Orleans, in 1912 the only Catholic university in the Old South, grew from a small Jesuit arts and sciences college founded in 1904. Plans were already afoot to build every arm of a modern university.

Marquette Hall's cornerstone was laid on 13 November 1910 by Archbishop Blenk with fourteen bishops beside him, while ground broke the same day for Louise C. Thomas Hall. The Marquette Association for Higher Education, formed in 1906 under President Biever, raised the funds, and Thomas gave 50,000 dollars toward her hall. Both Tudor Gothic blocks, joined by a cloister, face St. Charles Avenue by Audubon Park.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lule-indians:
The Lule Indians are a name that has bred much confusion in Argentine ethnology. It was given at different times to two quite different peoples, neither now bearing it, and the earlier tribe's word list is lost. Lule means inhabitants, a tag Mataco invaders laid on peoples they found in place.

Earlier Lule, better called Cacana or mountaineers, held the upper Salado hills in Catamarca and Tucuman, kin to the Calchaqui and touched by Quichua culture. Barcena gathered them into mission in 1589, and a 1692 quake wrecked Esteco and scattered them into the Chaco, losing their grammar. Later Lule, a Chaco group of cognate tribes, form the Lulean stock the entry sorts out next.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lummi-indians:
The Lummi Indians, from Nuglummi, meaning people, are the chief of more than twenty small Salishan tribes that once held Puget Sound's lower shores, islands, and eastern hinterland. By the Treaty of Point Elliott in 1855 they were gathered onto five reservations in the same country under Tulalip Agency.

Lummi villages stood about the mouth of the Lummi River in Whatcom County, and their tongue matches, with dialect shifts, the speech of Samish, Klallam, Semiahmoo, Songish, and Sooke neighbours. Oblate missionaries under Casimir Chirouse, working from about 1850, Christianized them wholly. By 1909 the reservation, with smaller bands, counted 435 souls, half the number of forty years before.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lyons:
Lyons is an archdiocese covering the Rhone and Loire departments, with a history reaching to the second century, when, by Duchesne's proof, its church alone was organized in Gaul. At the Rhone-Saone confluence, where sixty tribes raised an altar to Rome and Augustus, Christianity spread outward across the land.

Under Marcus Aurelius a persecution killed forty-eight at Lyons, half Greek, half Gallo-Roman, including St. Blandina and St. Pothinus, first bishop, sent by Polycarp.
