The Concordat of 1801 fixed the archdiocese and joined to it the titles of Vienne and Embrun. It gave it suffragans from Mende to Grenoble, later trimmed when Ain left in 1822 to form Belley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-magdalens:
Magdalens were women in religious houses who had left a life of wrongdoing for penance. In time, women of spotless reputation joined too. Some houses at last held only those women. They still kept the name Magdalens, or White Ladies for their white dress. Their first house is uncertain, and the usual Metz date of 1005 remains disputed.

Germany links its Magdalens by tradition to Rudolph of Worms. Houses rose at Naumburg in 1217 and Speyer in 1226. Popes backed them, and most took the Rule of St Augustine. France, Belgium, Italy, Spain, and Portugal soon had houses as well. Marseilles dates from about 1272, and Rome from 1520. A separate Paris group, the Madelonnettes, began in 1618. It split into three ranks with separate houses and rules, and it no longer exists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maina-indians:
Maina Indians were tribes on the north bank of the Maranon, forming their own language stock, the Mainan. Their older home lay on the upper Morona and Pastaza in Ecuador. Scholars differ on their divisions. Brinton counts six tribes or dialects. Hervas counts two languages in six dialects.

They matter because they were the first peoples of the upper Amazon to be evangelised. Their name passed to the whole mission region of Mainas. That region covered much of present Ecuador and northern Peru east of the Andes. From 1638 to the Jesuit expulsion in 1767, some 157 Jesuits from Quito founded 152 missions there. Eight died as martyrs. Work began at San Francisco de Borja in 1638. It faded under Brazilian slave raids. Today the people are largely extinct or absorbed, with a few wild bands still roaming the forests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maipure-india:
Maipure Indians were once an important group of tribes on the Upper Orinoco. Their range ran from above the Meta to the mouth of the Cassiquiare. It lay in Venezuela and Colombia. They spoke related dialects of one stock. Mission work among them faced fierce local warfare.

When the Guipunave stopped raiding the missions, a neighbouring cannibal people took up the attacks. The Manitivitano kept up the destruction for the rewards offered. Then the Jesuit expulsion from Spanish America in 1767 wrecked most Orinoco missions. In daily life the Maipure went almost naked apart from a scant breech cloth. They painted their whole bodies, usually bright red from plant dyes. Gilii, Gumilla, Humboldt, Hervas, and Brinton supply the sources for their missions, customs, and decline.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maliseet-indi:
Maliseet Indians, also called Malecite and officially Amalecite in Canada, were an Algonquian people of the lower St John River, the St Croix, and Passamaquoddy Bay. Their land lay in western New Brunswick and north-eastern Maine. They were close kin, in speech and story, to the Abnaki of Maine. Their chief town was Medoctec, ten miles below present Woodstock.

French fleets may have met them before Cartier's 1535 voyage. Champlain first names them as Etchemin in 1604, welcomed with feasts and dances. They traded for European goods and guns and fought beside the French in later colonial wars. Jesuit Pierre Biard visited in 1611 and 1612 and put them at about 2,500 souls. Missions at Riviere du Loup and Medoctec, revived by Joseph Aubery in 1701, at last made them wholly Catholic. By the 1909 report they numbered 843, chiefly on small New Brunswick reserves, above all Tobique.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mandan-indian:
Mandan Indians were a once important, now reduced, tribe sharing the Fort Berthold reservation with the Hidatsa and Arikara. Their land lay on both banks of the Missouri near the Knife River in North Dakota. The Mandan call themselves Numankaki, meaning people, while Mandan itself is said to come from Cree through Sioux form.

Their origin myth says they first lived underground beside a hidden lake. Some climbed to the surface by a grapevine and found earth covered with buffalo and fruit. Mission work came late, apart from priests with La Verendrye. Father Francis Craft, famed for Sioux work, began the Sacred Heart mission at Elbowoods with Sioux sisters. It now counts over 500 communicants across the three tribes. The Mandan were horsemen, living about equally by hunting and farming, and a Benedictine mission house was planned before the close of 1910.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcosians:
Marcosians were a sect of Valentinian Gnostics founded by Marcus and answered at length by Irenaeus. They lived on around Lyons, in the Rhone Valley, and in Spain well into the fourth century. They held their system not only as theory but as practice, forming Gnostic groups with their own rites.

In their meetings prophecy ran habitually, with men and women alike bidden by leaders or lot to stand and prophesy. Women also spoke the Eucharistic words over the bread and wine, and wine poured into a larger cup was made to grow by a chemical trick. Irenaeus scorns the sect as an affair of foolish women, ruining soul and body, and tells of penitents who confessed their shame on returning to the Church. Its system kept Valentinus's thirty Aeons, renamed Greatnesses, and fitted them to Pythagorean number lore, with the fall of Sophia recast as a divine deficiency.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mascoutens-in:
Mascoutens Indians were a Wisconsin tribe of Algonquian stock, important to seventeenth-century missions but long extinct. Their tongue was a dialect shared with Sauk, Fox, and Kickapoo, with whom, and the Miami, they allied closely, while warring hereditarily with Iroquois and Sioux. Their Algonquian name means People of the little prairie.

Early French records call them the Fire Nation, Gens de Feu, from Huron Asistazeronon, people of the fireplace, properly a Potawatomi tribal name. The error came from the tribes' closeness and the likeness of Algonquian roots for fire, ishkote, and prairie, mashkote. In 1669 Jesuit explorer Claude Allouez founded St Francois-Xavier mission at Fox River rapids near present De Pere. In 1672 he set up regular mission St Jacques with a chapel cabin and two great crosses. In 1712 the Mascoutens joined Kickapoo and Sauk with Foxes in war against the French, dragging on desultorily for years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mataco-indian:
Mataco Indians, or Mataguayo, were a group of wide tribes of very low culture across much of the Chaco. They lived about the Vermejo and Pilcomayo headwaters in Argentina's Salta province and Bolivia's Tarija province. Jesuit and Franciscan missionaries laboured for them in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The group held about a dozen tribes speaking one language with slight dialect differences, forming the distinct Matacoan stock.

Late in the eighteenth century Tarija Franciscans restored Chaco missions, founding Selenas for Mataguayo and Chiriguani and Centa, now Oran, for Mataguayo and Vejoz. In 1799 the two missions held nearly nine hundred Indians with 7,300 cattle. Marriage was simple and at the young people's will, wives usually joining husbands' kin, divorce easy, and fathers observing the couvade. Medicine men drove disease off with singing and rattles, and souls after death were thought to enter animals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matins:
Matins takes its name from Latin Matutinum, from Matuta, the Latin name for Greek Leucothea, goddess of morning or dawn. Its primitive meaning was sunrise, and it first denoted Lauds, said at dawn. Vigils, the Night Office, comes from Roman soldiers' nocturnal watches: night from six evening to six morning split into four three-hour vigils.

Yet night prayer elements recur across authors: psalms chanted responsorially, Old and New Testament readings, later Fathers and doctors, litanies, and prayers for members. In modern Roman liturgy Matins ranks as the day's most important office for length, place, and matter, opening with Psalm 94, the Invitatory, in ancient responsorial form. Its psalms run Psalm 1 to 108 without break, except feasts choosing within that series, the rest reserved for Vespers and other hours. Its lessons, unique among offices, replace the short Capitulum elsewhere.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maya-indians:
The Maya peoples, the most advanced native cultures of North America, once held about 60,000 square miles. Their lands covered Yucatan, southern Mexico, and northern Guatemala, and they still form the main population there outside the big cities. Their language, now displacing Spanish in places, is spoken by some 300,000 people, two-thirds of them pure Maya. The Mayan stock counts some twenty tribes in closely linked dialects, from Tabasco and Chiapas to Guatemala, Honduras, and Salvador.

The builders of ruined Palenque and Copan came from this stock, and after the Maya proper the chief nations were the Quiche and Cakchiquel of Guatemala. In all they number about two million souls. The entry's history section traces the Maya proper entering Yucatan from the west, while its second part covers institutions, arts, and literature. Readers meet a civilization the entry calls the most advanced, and likely the most ancient, in aboriginal North America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mayo-indians:
The Mayo Indians, a tribe of fifteen towns on the Mayo and Fuerte rivers in Sonora and Sinaloa, speak Cahita. With dialect shifts, it matches the tongue of their neighbours the Tehueco and Yaqui. It belongs to the Piman branch of the Shoshonean stock. Ribas says Mayo is properly the name of their chief river and means boundary. Their known history opens in 1532 with Diego Hurtado de Mendoza's naval foray, in which he died with his companions.

In 1609-10 the Mayo aided the Spaniards against their hereditary foes the Yaqui, and peace between the tribes became a settlement term. In 1613, at their own request, Jesuit Pedro Mendez opened the first mission among them. He baptized over 3,000 people within fifteen days. Seven mission churches soon rose in seven towns, launching mission work in Sonora. In 1740 the friendly tribe joined a revolt, a turn the entry traces with the missions' later fate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mayoruna-indi:
The Mayoruna Indians, a noted and fierce tribe of Panoan stock, range the forests between the Ucayali, Yavari, and Maranon rivers in north-east Peru and nearby Brazil. Some are light-skinned and bearded, which bred a legend of descent from Spanish soldiers of Ursua's 1569 expedition. The entry judges later mixing with captives the likelier cause, noting the tribe is full-blooded and typically Indian. The name may come from confusion with Maranones, Ursua's and Aguirre's followers.

Markham reads the name as Men of Muyu, pointing to an old home near Moyobamba farther west. Subtribes include the Barbudo, or Bearded, plus Itacule, Musimo, and Urarina. The Mayoruna were gathered into the Mainas missions of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, at San Joaquin, Nuestra Senora del Carmen, and San Xavier. Portuguese slave raids from 1680 to 1710 and mission revolts in 1695 and 1767 drove them back to forest refuge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mazatec-india:
The Mazatec Indians, a Mexican tribe of Zapotecan stock, live in the mountains of north-east Oaxaca, chiefly around Cuicatlan and Teotitlan. They number some 18,000 to 20,000 souls, and their chief town, Huantla, with its villages, holds about 7,000. The Aztec name Mazateca is said to mean Lords of the Deer; the people call themselves A-a, with a nasal sound.

Kin to the cultured Zapotec and Mixtec, the Mazatec kept a rougher mountain habit and held their freedom against the Aztec empire in near-constant defensive war. Cortes brought Oaxaca under Spain in 1521, and in 1535 it became a diocese. Dominican missionaries won the people over despite their fierce love of old rites, even hiding sacred images beneath altars. Jesuits joined the work in 1575, and the Mazatec still keep outward church ways today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mbaya-indians:
The Mbaya Indians, also called Guaycuru, were a raiding horse tribe of the Paraguay River country, on Paraguay's north and north-west frontier and into Brazil's Matto Grosso. They belong to the Guaycuran stock, a group of mounted warlike tribes that once roamed northern Paraguay and the upper Chaco. Kin groups include the Abipon, famed through Dobrizhoffer, the Macobi, and the still powerful Toba.

The Guarani name Mbaya meant terrible, bad, or savage, while Guaycuru is said to mean runner. Spaniards called them Caballeros for their fine horsemanship. They preyed on settled Guarani villages with swift raids and quicker retreats into tangled forest and treacherous swamp. The entry follows them from Cabeza de Vaca's passage in 1542 through mission contacts and later wars, mapping their divisions and their stubborn resistance to conquest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-megarians:
The Megarians, or Megarian School, rank among the imperfectly Socratic schools, so called because they pushed Socrates' doctrines one-sidedly. Their chief lights, Euclid the founder and Stilpo, flourished at Athens early in the fourth century B.C. Borrowing from the Eleatics, above all Parmenides, they held that the world has no change or multiplicity. They wedded this to Socrates' teaching that knowledge through concepts is the only true knowledge.

From this union follows their creed: the only reality is the changeless essential nature, sense experience is illusion, and nothing is possible except what actually exists. Their bodiless forms, the changeless natures of things, mark their chief gift to speculative thought, with clear kinship to Plato's ideas. In conduct they stressed the supremacy of goodness. Knowledge is the only virtue and one with moral excellence, so the highest good and the highest reality are one and the same.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchisedechi:
The Melchisedechians were a branch of the Monarchians founded by Theodotus the banker, and the name also covers a quite distinct party refuted by Marcus Eremita, a disciple of St. John Chrysostom. His book Against the Melchisedekites says these new teachers made Melchisedech an incarnation of the Logos. Bishops anathematized them, yet they kept preaching, though otherwise orthodox.

St. Jerome refutes an anonymous work that identified Melchisedech with the Holy Ghost. About 600, Timotheus, priest of Constantinople, lists the Melchisedechians, now called Athingani, or Intangibles, among heretics needing rebaptism. They lived in Phrygia and were neither Hebrews nor Gentiles. They kept the Sabbath but were not circumcised. They would touch no man: food offered to them had to be set on the ground before they took it, and they gave to others with the same care. Nothing more is known of this curious sect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-menominee-ind:
The Menominee Indians, an Algonquian tribe, once ranged north-eastern Wisconsin west of the Menominee River and Green Bay, and now hold a reservation in Shawano and Oconto counties in the same land. Their common name, rendered Folles Avoines by the French, comes from their word for wild rice, menomin, which grows thickly in small lakes and feeds the region's tribes. Before white contact they may have numbered about 3,000 souls; in 1909 officials counted 1,487.

The first known explorer among them was Champlain's interpreter Jean Nicolet, who visited the Green Bay tribes about 1634, likely the first white man in present Wisconsin. In 1640 Le Jeune named them Maroumine, a tribe still without missionaries. The Relation of 1657-58 calls them Malouminek, allied with the Noukek and Winnebago, reaping unsown wild rye held better than corn. In May 1670 the Jesuit Claude Allouez visited them near the river mouth and founded the small mission of St. Michel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mercedarians:
The Mercedarians, the Order of Our Lady of Mercy, are a congregation of men founded in 1218 by St. Peter Nolasco, born in 1189 at Mas-des-Saintes-Puelles in Aude, France. Joining Simon de Montfort's army against the Albigenses, he became tutor to the young King James of Aragon, who took the throne after his father Pedro II fell at Muret. 

From 1192 certain Barcelona noblemen had formed a brotherhood to tend the sick in hospitals and rescue Christian captives from the Moors. The Blessed Virgin, in a vision, asked Nolasco to found an order wholly devoted to ransoming captives. His confessor, St. Raymond of Pennafort, canon of Barcelona, encouraged and aided him, and King James lent protection. Those noblemen became the order's first monks, based at St. Eulalie's convent in Barcelona, raised in 1232. They followed a rule drawn by St. Raymond, approved by Honorius III and Gregory IX.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-messalians:
The Messalians, or Praying Folk, take their name from the Aramaic participle for to pray. This heretical sect arose in Mesopotamia about 360 and lasted in the East until the ninth century. They are also called Euchites, from the Greek for to pray, Adelphians from their first leader, and Lampetians from Lampetius, their first priest, ordained about 458. Enthusiasts they were called from their tenet of the Holy Ghost dwelling within, by whom they thought themselves inspired or possessed.

The non-Christian Euphemites were also called Messalians, and Epiphanius, our sole informant on them, treats them as forerunners of the Christian sect. Those pagans admitted many gods but worshipped only one. The Christian Messalians were a kind of Eastern Circumcellions, or vagrant Quietists. They held sacraments useless though harmless, trusting prayer alone to drive out the evil spirit baptism had not expelled and to reach union with God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-miami-indians:
The Miami Indians, an important Algonquian tribe, once claimed prior rule over all of present Indiana and western Ohio, including lands drained by the Wabash, St. Joseph, Maumee, and Miami rivers. They were closely tied, in tongue and politics, to their western neighbours the Illinois, both groups speaking dialects of one language. The Miami, however, were more independent and warlike. Their tribal name, rightly said as in Latin, Me-ah-me, whence Maumee, and in full plural Ou-miami-wek, is of uncertain sense and root.

Early English writers called them Twightwee, a corruption of their Iroquois name, meant to echo a crane's cry. About 1685 the French counted six bands, later merged into three: Atchatchakangouen, crane people, or Miami proper; Ouiatanon, whirlpool people, or Wea; and Pianguichia, separators, or Piankishaw. The United States government treated these as three distinct tribes. Altogether they may first have numbered over 4,000 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michelians:
The Michelians, a German Protestant sect named for Michel, the popular name of its founder Johann Michael Hahn, were born of his preaching. Hahn, of peasant stock, was born at Altdorf near Stuttgart on 2 February 1758 and died at Sindlingen near Herrenberg in Wurttemberg on 20 January 1819. Deeply religious by nature, he claimed a three-hour vision at seventeen. 

His oddities drew his father's energetic disapproval, even physical violence, but driving the son from home changed nothing, so opposition was soon dropped as useless. After a seven-week vision, alleged in 1780, Hahn began proclaiming his beliefs by speech and writing. Large crowds flocked to his preaching, and church and civil authorities moved against him. He sought quiet abroad, notably in Switzerland, where he met Lavater. From 1794 until death he gave himself, undisturbed, to religious propaganda, living on Duchess Frances's Sindlingen estate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mixe-indians:
The Mixe Indians, also called Mije, are a mountain tribe of southern Mexico, noted for extreme conservatism. With the neighbouring Zoque they form a distinct linguistic stock, the Zoquean. The Mixe occupy towns and villages in Yautepec, Villa Alta, and Tehuantepec in southern Oaxaca, numbering about 25,000 in all.

They kept their independence against both the Aztec Empire and the powerful Zapotec, with whom they remain at enmity. Even yet they can hardly be said to have been subdued by the Spaniards. Holding themselves aloof from the whites, they keep their own language almost to the exclusion of Spanish, and preserve old customs and dress. Missionary work among them has made slow headway against this proud isolation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mixteca-india:
The Mixteca Indians, also called Misteca, rank among southern Mexico's leading civilized peoples, holding broad lands in western and northern Oaxaca, with ground reaching into Guerrero and Puebla. Their count runs near 250,000 souls, a little above all the Indians of the United States put together. To their east and south live the rough Mixe and the refined, strong Zapotec.

With the Zapotec they form a distinct linguistic stock, the Zapotecan. Their ancient culture and governmental forms were practically the same as the Zapotec's. They are now industrious farmers and craftsmen, famed for pottery, weaving, and metalwork, and most are Catholics, evangelized by Dominicans in the colonial period.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mocovi-indian:
The Mocovi Indians, also written Macobio, Mbocobi, or Mocobio, are a warlike and predatory tribe of the Guaycuran stock. They are closely related in language to the Toba, Mbaya, and Abipon, their usual allies. They settled chiefly along the middle and upper Vermejo River in the Chaco region of northern Argentina. Their forays once reached as far south as Santa Fe and even to the gates of Buenos Aires.

In habits of life and general character they resembled the tribes just named. But they were distinguished even beyond them, as Dobrizhoffer says, in atrocity and steady hatred of the Spaniards. Jesuit missions among the Mocovi in the eighteenth century won some converts, but the tribe's raiding life long resisted settled Christian communities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-modern-dioces:
The Modern Diocese of Athens faces a peculiar situation, since Greeks have long regarded their religion as a national affair. The notion is so deep-rooted that they cannot understand how a citizen can be a true Greek while giving allegiance to any religion but that of the Greek Church. At present most Catholics within the diocese are therefore foreigners or of foreign descent.

Of the foreign Catholics, the greater part are Italian. Most of those of foreign descent have come into Athens and other parts of the diocese from the Aegean and Ionian islands, whose Catholics are largely of Venetian or Genoese stock. After some years' lapse, an archbishopric was established at Athens in 1876, its holders including Marangos, Zaffino, De Angelis, and Delendas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monarchians:
Monarchians were second- and third-century Christians who stressed God's oneness so fiercely that they denied or blurred the Trinity. This entry untangles the two very different groups lumped under the nickname. Tertullian coined the label for the Patripassians. They held that the Father himself suffered on the cross.

Alongside them stood the Adoptionists, or Dynamists. Their founder was the Byzantine leather-seller Theodotus. He taught that Jesus was a man upon whom the Christ descended at baptism. Jesus became God only after the resurrection, in his teaching. The entry weighs both schools against early orthodox writers. It explains why the protest appealed to ordinary believers. It shows how it forced clearer teaching on the Trinity and the person of Christ.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montagnais-in:
Montagnais, as applied to the Chippewayans, is a name given in error. It came from a fancied likeness to the Montagnais of Quebec. The Chippewayans are truly a Dene people. Their name draws from Cree words for pointed skin or blanket, recalling the shape of their chief garment.

They live around Cold, Ile-a-la-Crosse, Heart and Caribou lakes and near Methy Portage and the English River. Athabascan kin live around Lake Athabasca and the Slave River basin. The two divisions total some 4,000 people, mostly nomadic hunters, though some now farm potatoes. They welcomed the first Catholic missionaries in 1845 and remain practically all Catholic. The thriving mission at Ile-a-la-Crosse shows their attachment to the faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moulins:
Moulins is a French diocese, suffragan of Sens, covering the whole department of Allier. Under the old regime it did not even hold a parish of its own. Its churches served as chapels of neighbouring country parishes at Yzeure and Saint-Bonnet. A see created there in 1788 lapsed when the Revolution broke out before its bishop was preconised.

Re-established by the Concordat of 1817 with titulars from 1822, the diocese was pieced together from Autun, Bourges and Clermont-Ferrand. Its deaneries uniquely bear saints' names rather than place names. Joan of Arc passed through in November 1429 writing for aid. Henry IV authorised a Jesuit college in 1604. Devotion to the Sacred Heart began at its Visitation convent in 1676, and Saint Jane Frances de Chantal died there in 1641.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moxos-indians:
The Moxos, also called Moyos, are a group of tribes famous in South American mission annals. They once ranged the forests and prairies of the upper Mamore between the Guapore and Beni rivers, centred in the present Mojos province of Beni, Bolivia. They numbered at least 50,000 souls in perhaps a hundred small tribes speaking at least thirteen distinct languages.

Moxo proper, Baure and others belong to the widespread Arawakan stock. Movima, Cayubaba, Itonama, Canichana and Rocotona each form a distinct stock, and the rest remain unclassified. Jesuit missionaries gathered them into reductions, with immigrant Chiquito, Siriono and Chiriguano joining from southern missions. The entry follows their primitive life, shaped by floods and forest, and their mission history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mozetena-indi: The Mozetena are a group of some half dozen tribes forming a distinct linguistic stock on the headwaters of the Beni River in northwestern Bolivia. Among their peculiar customs is the couvade, the ritual observance by a father at his child's birth. In the early eighteenth century Jesuit efforts Christianised part of them. They now live in three mission towns on the Beni near the Mapisi confluence: Muchanes, founded in 1725, Santa Ana and Magdalena.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nasoraeans:
The Nasoraeans, also known as Mandaeans, Sabians, or Christians of Saint John, were pagan Gnostics whose sect took shape just before Christianity appeared. Mesopotamia and Babylonia were its early ground, and in the first years of Mohammedanism it stood among the leading faiths of Western Asia. Roughly 2,000 families belonged to it in the seventeenth century. Today only about 1,500 followers remain, settled along the Shat-el-Arab near the Persian Gulf.

No other Gnostic sect endures, and no other keeps sacred writings still in being; the Christian Gnostics' writings have vanished apart from a few scraps. Mandaean comes from Babylonian-Aramaic and marks people skilled in knowing, since their worship turns on knowledge of life. Sabian means baptist, a label Muslims recognize from the Koran, which names Christians, Sabians, and Jews side by side. Baptism runs through their discipline, which helps explain the Sabian label.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-navajo-indian:
Navajo Indians, numbering about 20,000, form the largest group of the Athapaskan, or Dene, stock. Kindred groups include the Apaches, Lipanes, Hupas of California, and Dene tribes of British Columbia and Alaska. That kinship points to a migration centuries ago from the far north. The Navajo themselves tell of other Navajos living far away, and their myths bring them from lower worlds in the San Juan Mountains of southwest Colorado.

They now hold an extensive reservation in northeast Arizona and northwest New Mexico, with many living beyond its borders southward. First mentioned in 1626 as Apaches de Nabaju, they were called great farmers by Benavides in 1630, who glossed Navajo as great planted fields. The word may come from Spanish nava, plain or field, while they call themselves Dine, the people. The entry follows their life, crafts, religion and missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-orleans:
The Archdiocese of New Orleans was erected on 25 April 1793 as the Diocese of Saint Louis of New Orleans, and raised to its present rank on 19 July 1850. Its original territory covered the ancient Louisiana Purchase and East and West Florida. It stretched from the Canadian line in the north to the Rocky Mountains and Rio Perdido in the west, Baltimore in the east, and Linares and Durango in the south. Its present bounds cover Louisiana between 29 and 31 degrees north, 23,208 square miles.

Louisiana's history divides into four periods. Discoverers De Soto, Iberville, La Salle and Bienville travelled with missionaries, and the Cross blazed the way through feeble military-post settlements. From the start Louisiana stood under Quebec's bishop, and in 1696 Quebec's seminary sought authority for western missions. The entry follows French, Spanish and American rule, its bishops, parishes, schools and institutions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaites-or:
The Nicolaites, a group named in the Book of Revelation at Ephesus, Pergamum, and other cities of Asia Minor, remain shadowy in this entry. Early writers add little beyond Revelation itself, though Irenaeus charges them with loose living and Hippolytus links them to the deacon Nicholas.

Clement of Alexandria defends Nicholas, blaming a twisted reading of harmless words for the group's teaching on shared partners. The entry judges the sect short-lived and leaves open whether Revelation uses the name as a coded jab at the followers of Balaam. No later writer adds firm evidence beyond Irenaeus, and the sect soon disappears from view.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nocturns:
Nocturns, the night divisions of the Office of Matins, began as one long vigil rather than three separate services. Early writers speak of night prayer in general, and the entry warns against reading the present threefold split back into the early church as three risings.

Some authors describe three night watches: evening prayer, midnight vigil, and dawn prayer matching Lauds. In practice the vigil formed a single office of psalms and readings, later divided for convenience into three nocturns, each with its own psalms, lessons, and responses. Durandus of Mende and his followers claimed early Christians rose thrice nightly to pray.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notre-dame-de:
Notre-Dame de Saint-Lieu Sept-Fons, a French abbey in the diocese of Moulins, was founded in 1132 by Guichard and Guillaume de Bourbon. Their generosity, with the monks' energy, soon raised a church to the Virgin and the full monastic buildings, earning the house its royal name.

Neglect by founders left the monks so poor they sold land to live, and never more than fifteen religious dwelt there before the 1663 reform. Saint Bernard visited in 1138, popes protected the abbey, and wars after the fifteenth century repeatedly drove the monks out and stripped their goods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nuns:
Nuns and sisters, women who embrace religious life in orders devoted to perfection, date from the church's first ages. Paul praises widows set apart for church work and virgins devoted to the Lord, and early writers hail their chastity and poverty as a contrast to pagan corruption.

At first virgins lived at home under a veil, then gathered in communities under rules from Pachomius, Basil, and Benedict to later orders of teaching, nursing, and contemplation. The entry follows that growth through vows, enclosure, and the many congregations active in the modern church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-o-antiphons:
The O Antiphons are the seven great antiphons sung to the Magnificat in the seven days before Christmas Eve. Each opens with the cry O and addresses Christ by a scriptural title: Wisdom, Adonai, Root of Jesse, Key of David, Dayspring, King of Nations, and Emmanuel.

Each antiphon ends with a plea to the coming Lord, such as teaching prudence, redeeming by an outstretched arm, or freeing captives from darkness. Medieval breviaries added further O antiphons, and the entry traces their texts, music, and Advent place. Medieval breviaries added O Virgo Virginum and O Gabriel to the seven Roman antiphons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-obregonians:
The Obregonians, also called Poor Infirmarians, were a small congregation of men who nursed the sick under the Third Order of Saint Francis. Bernardino Obregón, a Spanish army officer born in 1540, retired to serve Madrid's hospitals, and companions joined him until the nuncio approved the congregation in 1567.

Adding a vow of free hospitality to the three usual vows, the brothers served existing hospitals rather than founding their own, spreading through Spain, Belgium, and the Indies. Paul V let them wear a black cross in 1609, and they vanished after the French Revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-olivetans:
The Olivetans, a branch of the white Benedictine monks founded in 1319, began with a Sienese professor's vow of thanks for restored sight. Giovanni Tolomei left home in 1313 for the wilderness with two Sienese senators, Ambrogio Piccolomini and Patricio Patrici, settling on his own mountaintop land.

Accused of heresy six years later for their severe ways, the disciples won John XXII's goodwill at Avignon and were sent to the bishop of Arezzo for an approved rule. The bishop gave them Benedict's rule, and the congregation, named for the Mount of Olives, spread from its hermit roots.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orans:
The Orans, a female figure with arms outstretched in prayer, fills Roman catacomb art more than almost any other image. Jews and pagans alike prayed with raised arms, and classical models shaped the type, yet Christian meaning differs from its prototypes.

Biblical figures like Noah, Abraham, Daniel, and the Three Children appear as Orans pleading for the tomb's owner, as God once delivered them. Besides these, 153 ideal figures, mostly female even on men's tombs, symbolize the soul in heaven praying for friends on earth. Wilpert counts 153 ideal figures in the ancient attitude of prayer in the catacombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-order-of-trin:
The Trinitarians, or Order of the Holy Trinity for the Redemption of Captives, ransomed Christians from Muslim hands. Crusade centuries saw orders for that mercy, from short-lived Montjoie to Peter Nolasco's Mercedarians, but John of Matha's order, founded with Felix of Valois at Cerfroid, endures.

A Paris doctor inspired by a hermit's vision, John won Innocent III's approval and built his chief house at Cerfroid. There brothers collected alms, bargained with captors, and at times offered themselves in exchange. The entry follows the order's houses, rule, and redemptions to modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orleans:
Orléans, a French diocese covering the Loiret and suffragan to Paris since 1622, was remade by Revolution and Concordat. Re-established in 1802 with Loiret and Loir-et-Cher, it lost the latter to Blois in 1822, with Romorantin and Janville going elsewhere, while gaining Montargis, Gien, and Châtillon-sur-Loire.

Legend sends Savinianus, Potentianus, and Altinus from Peter to Sens and Orléans, but no trace of that mission appears before the fifteenth century. Diclopitus, who ratified Athanasius's absolution about 344, stands as first authentic bishop, and the entry follows his successors, Joan of Arc's city, and its schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pakawa-indian:
The Pakawa Indians were one group of the Pakawan, once called Coahuiltecan, peoples of southern Texas. They ranged the upper San Antonio and Nueces rivers and reached beyond the Rio Grande. The stock held at least fifty small tribes, few over two or three hundred souls, chief among them the Pakawa, Payaya, Sanipao, Tilijae, Pamaque, and Xarame.

They are famed for their tie to the San Antonio missions and for Father Garcia's record of their tongue, used widely for talk between tribes. Almost nothing is known of their ethnology. They were of low culture, without farming or fixed homes, roaming for game and wild mesquite, pecan, and cactus fruits, and living in brushwood shelters. Unlike their Tonkawa neighbours, they seem to have been unwarlike and friendly, and Cabeza de Vaca met them in his Texas wanderings of 1529 to 1536.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pano-indians:
The Pano Indians were a leading mission tribe of the middle Ucayali River in Peru, head of a group of twenty or more kindred tribes forming the Panoan stock. They held most of the Huallaga, Ucayali, and Javari lands in north-eastern Peru, with outliers on the Jurua, Purus, Beni, and upper Madeira in Brazil and Bolivia. Kin tribes included the Cahibo, Conibo, Mayoruna, Remo, Sensi, Setibo, and Shipibo.

Most were once tied to the Jesuit missions of Mainas, centred first at San Francisco de Borja and later at the Pano town of Laguna. Their culture sat between the Quichua of Peru and the wandering Amazon peoples. They farmed and lived in villages by the water, in great oval communal houses over 120 feet long, thatched with palm, with clay pots, chicha troughs, and fishing gear. Only the Cashibo stayed cannibal savages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papago-indian:
The Papago Indians, a Shoshonean people speaking a Pima dialect, shared the culture of the Pima in all essentials. Their land, shared with the kindred Sobaipuri, covered the San Pedro and Santa Cruz valleys in south-eastern Arizona and most of the Altar River in Sonora, Mexico. Their common name comes from Papah-ootam, bean people, as given by their missionary Father Kino, whence Spanish Frijoleros.

It has no link to baptized, as sometimes claimed. The Papago were semi-settled farmers in scattered villages of dome-shaped, grass-thatched houses, watering corn, beans, and cotton, and gathering mesquite beans and saguaro fruit. They traded lagoon salt, and their women wove fine baskets, though their pottery ranked lower. Men once went nearly naked, women in short skirts, and their myths and rites nearly match the Pima pattern.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-constit:
Papal constitutions are ordinances issued by Roman pontiffs, binding all the faithful or special classes or persons. From the earliest times Christians worldwide asked popes for rulings on faith, morals, and discipline. The first known case is Corinth's appeal to Clement I in the first century, during Saint John's lifetime, and answers from Rome were honoured as from Christ's chief apostle and vicar.

Council decrees were anciently sent to the pope for revision or confirmation, which prompted many constitutions. After Constantine, contact with Rome grew freer and more frequent, and Jerome, as secretary to Damasus, witnessed the flood of responses sought from East and West alike. Later pages sort constitutions by form and force, and trace how papal replies hardened into a body of church law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-electio:
Papal elections have taken many forms across church history, and this entry traces how the choice of a pope changed with the ages. Early lore credits Saint Peter with a senate of twenty-four priests and deacons to counsel Rome's bishop and choose his heirs. Historians and canonists more often hold that Rome's bishop was chosen like other bishops, by neighbouring bishops with Rome's clergy and faithful.

Some argue the choice lay with Roman clergy alone until Sylvester I, with the people admitted later. After Constantine, Christian emperors meddled often and heavily, and disputed elections gave them their opening. Later pages follow the shift to cardinal electors, conclave rules, and the long struggle to free the election from emperors, kings, and Roman factions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-passions:
Passions, in this entry's sense, are movements of the sensitive appetite toward some real or apparent good, or away from some evil. The stronger the desire or loathing, the fiercer the passion. Paul writes that when we were in the flesh, sinful passions worked in our members toward death. They earn the name passion because they shift the body's normal state, often visibly.

Man also holds a rational appetite, the will, whose love, joy, and sorrow count as passions only by likeness. Thomas and the Schoolmen sort the sensitive appetite in two: concupiscible, aiming at suitable good, and irascible, aiming at good hedged by difficulty. Eleven chief passions follow: six concupiscible, joy, sadness, desire, aversion, love, hatred, and five irascible, hope, despair, courage, fear, and anger.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-quentin-:
Paul Quentin Desains was a French physicist born at Saint-Quentin on 12 July 1817 and dead at Paris on 3 May 1885. He studied letters at his home town's College des Bons-Enfants, then entered Paris's Lycee Louis-le-Grand, where he took first prize in physics. In 1835 he joined the science section of the Ecole Normale, where La Provostaye, then a monitor, became his lifelong friend and research partner.

After his course he taught at Caen in 1839, then at Paris's Lycees Saint-Louis and Condorcet, succeeding La Provostaye on his retirement for ill health. Growing fame won him the Sorbonne physics chair in 1853, held thirty-two years, where his lectures shone for clarity and precision. From 1858 to 1861 he observed terrestrial magnetism, but his chief work, with La Provostaye, proved radiant heat travels like light, as transverse waves through ether.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulicians:
The Paulicians were a dualist heretical sect sprung from Manichaeism, whose name's origin is murky. Gibbon reads it as Disciples of Saint Paul, since they revered the Apostle and renamed leaders after his disciples. The form Paulikianoi, not Paulianoi, is odd, and foes alone used the name, holding them followers of Paul of Samosata, though no doctrine links them. Photius tells of a Manichee woman Kallinike sending sons Paul and John to Armenia, whence Pauloioannoi, but such persons are now generally denied.

Ter-Mkrttschian calls the name an Armenian diminutive for followers of little Paul, without saying who little Paul was. It first appears in the Armenian Synod of Duin's acts of 719, barring nights in the wicked heretics' houses. Their cardinal doctrine splits the God who made and rules matter from the God of heaven who made souls. Later pages trace their churches, persecutions, migrations, and influence on later sects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peba-indians:
The Peba Indians, or Peva, were chief of a group of tribes, Peba proper, Caumari, Cauhuachi, Pacaya, and Yagua, forming the Peba linguistic stock. They held country around the Javari's meeting with the Amazon, in Peruvian territory partly claimed by Ecuador and Colombia. At first they resembled neighbouring Jivaro and Pano, though less fierce. They kept friendship with the Amagua of Colombia, and in the eighteenth century formed a major part of the Jesuit Mainas missions on the Amazon.

In 1735 or 1736 Jesuit Father Singler of the Omagua mission reached the Caumari mission and later the Peba. They welcomed him and gave jars of curari poison for blowgun arrows. They let him raise a cross in the village and heard his teaching. Some of both tribes followed him to San Joaquin, but failing health brought them back to San Ignacio de Pebas, under Father Adan Vidman.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-penelakut-ind:
The Penelakut were a small Salishan people living at the south end of Vancouver Island. They spoke a Cowichan dialect and held reservations on Kuper, Tent, and Galiano Islands and at the mouth of the Chemainus River. Disease from coastal traders, white settlement after 1858, and the smallpox year of 1862 cut them from about 1,000 a century earlier to roughly 250, with 140 at the Penelakut village.

They lived from the sea, and their customs and ceremonies resembled their Songish and Squamish kin. Mission contact may have begun with Father Demers and the Jesuits in 1841, but steady work dates from Father Bolduc's arrival in 1843 and the Oblates under Father Durieu from 1854. By the entry's time they were entirely Catholic, fishing, boat-building, farming, and labouring, with a Catholic boarding school on Kuper Island.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-penitential-c:
Penitential canons were the rules councils and bishops laid down for penances owed for particular sins. Gathered, adapted, and completed with directions, they formed the core of the old Penitential Books. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry treats them as history: the ancient discipline has passed, though indulgences still reckon by its periods of years, days, and quarantines. It sorts the canons into Eastern, Roman, and Anglo-Saxon families.

Eastern practice stands at the centre of the account. Penitents moved through graded classes, from hearers kept from the altar to the prostrate, prayed over by the bishop, and finally to those who attended the whole service without receiving communion. Periods ran from three to fifteen years by the gravity of the sin. The discipline softened fast and had faded by the close of the fourth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-penitential-r:
Penitential redemptions let a sinner swap one imposed penance for a lighter or shorter exercise, often an alms-deed. This Catholic Encyclopedia entry places the practice in the history of indulgences, since both shorten or soften owed atonement. Among Anglo-Saxons and Irish, the guiding idea was repayment in proportion to the number and gravity of sins, almost a blood-price paid to God and the Church.

Confessors set penances of prayers, fasts, scourgings, and alms over long periods, and penitents naturally sought to compress them. Scales grew up for the exchange: fifty psalms might stand for a fast, and an alms of twenty solidi for seven weeks of fasting. A year's penance could be packed into days by piling up psalters, genuflexions, and breast-beatings. Paying others to perform penance was tried, then firmly condemned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-penobscot-ind:
The Penobscot were the leading tribe of Maine's Abnaki confederacy, and the only one to keep its name, land, and tribal identity. Small Algonquian tribes across Maine, linked to the Pennacook south and the Maliseet north, formed the confederacy. As French allies in the colonial wars they shrank from perhaps 3,000 souls in 1600 to about 785 in 1910, with 425 Penobscot among them.

Jesuits Biard and Massé began mission work in 1611, and later priests built chapels on the Kennebec despite English raids and the murder of Father Rasles. After the wars the tribe appealed to Bishop Carroll, and the Oldtown mission reopened in 1785 under Father Ciquard. The entry closes with village life at Oldtown on the Penobscot River, its St. Anne church, and a people living by lumbering, boating, hunting, and farming.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peoria-indian:
The Peoria were a leading tribe of the Illinois confederacy, living in the seventeenth century along the Illinois River and lake near the modern city of their name. Jesuit Claude Allouez first met Illinois visitors at La Pointe in 1667, Marquette passed through their country six years later, and La Salle built Fort Crèvecoeur on Peoria Lake in 1680. A regular mission began under Allouez in 1684.

His successor, Father Gravier, compiled a great dictionary of the Peoria language, now at Harvard, the chief literary relic of the extinct Illinois tongue. Attacked at medicine men's urging in 1705, he died of his wounds in 1708. The tribe still resisted conversion as late as 1721, then shared the Illinois decline. In 1832 the remnant sold its Illinois claims and moved to Kansas, then in 1868 to north-east Oklahoma.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pericui-india:
The Pericú were a fierce tribe of unknown language at the far south of California's peninsula. With their Cora allies they once numbered about 4,000 souls. They resembled the Guaicuri in habits but surpassed them in hostility, fighting Spaniards and neighbouring tribes alike. Jesuits Bravo and Ugarte founded the La Paz mission among them in 1720, with more houses following within a few years.

In 1734, under two chiefs of African origin, the tribes rose against mission rules on polygamy and morals, killing Fathers Carranco and Tamaral and burning four missions. Order returned, but smallpox from 1742 to 1748 cut them to a sixth of their number, and a further plague in 1769 left under 400 by 1772. Franciscans and Dominicans kept the last missions going, but the tribe is long extinct.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-dens:
Peter Dens was a Belgian theologian and seminary builder, born at Boom near Antwerp in 1690. Formed by the Mechlin Oratorians, he became a Louvain master of arts in 1711. He taught theology to Afflighem monks, then held Mechlin's seminary chair, its metropolitan pastorate, and its presidency from 1735 until his death in 1775. Simplicity, solid piety, love of the poor, and zeal for clerical training marked him throughout.

His lasting work was institutional: competitive examinations for parishes and a reform of theological teaching in the Mechlin diocese owe much to him, and he enlarged the seminary itself. He did not write the famous Theologia published under his name in 1777, though Mechlin professors still issue it revised. His own books treat penance and the virtue of religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-paul-ru:
Peter Paul Rubens was the great Flemish painter of the Baroque, born at Siegen in 1577. His father, a Protestant lawyer exiled from Antwerp, died after prison and scandal, and his Catholic mother brought the boy home to a Jesuit schooling. After a page's service and training under Verhaecht, van Noort, and van Veen, he entered Antwerp's painters' guild in 1598 and sailed for Italy in 1600.

Court painter to the Infanta Isabella, he worked as diplomatist as well as artist. Charles I knighted him at London in 1630, and he painted the twenty-two Marie de' Medici canvases now in the Louvre. His Antwerp studio poured out huge pictures, tapestries, and pageants, pupils roughing out designs he finished with his own glazes. Broken in health, he died at Antwerp in 1640, leaving works in nearly every great gallery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-petrobrusians:
The Petrobrusians were twelfth-century heretics named for Peter of Bruys, a deposed priest of south-eastern France. Our knowledge comes from Peter the Venerable's treatise against them and a passage in Abelard. Between about 1117 and 1120 Peter began preaching in the dioceses of Embrun, Die, and Gap, and twenty years later the crowd at St. Gilles burned him for burning crosses.

His teaching kept only the Gospels in their literal sense, setting the epistles lower and rejecting the Old Testament, the Fathers, and the Church. Baptism counted only with personal faith, so infant baptism was void, and Mass and Eucharist were refused, since Christ gave his flesh but once. Violence against priests and monks followed. Henry of Lausanne carried the teaching on, softened, after Peter's death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piatus-of-mon:
Piatus of Mons, born Jean-Joseph Loiseaux in 1815, was a Belgian canonist who ended life as a Capuchin. As a seminarian he shone in moral theology and canon law, was ordained for Tournai in 1838, and studied canon law at Louvain and Rome. In 1847 he took Louvain's chair of canon law and church history, holding it for decades.

With Abbé Felise he founded the quarterly Mélanges théologiques in 1847, then the Revue théologique and the Nouvelle revue théologique, which he edited until 1895, when Redemptorists took it over. He twice refused the bishopric of Tournai. In 1871 he entered the Capuchin Friars Minor. His chief works treat regular law, Bonaventure on penance, and the jubilee, with many review articles beside. He died at Bruges in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-lamber:
Pierre-Lambert Goossens was the Belgian cardinal-archbishop of Mechlin who rebuilt Catholic schooling and parish life across his diocese. He was born at Perck in 1827 and taught at Mechlin. He served as cathedral curate and archbishop's secretary, became bishop of Namur in 1883, and succeeded as archbishop of Mechlin the next year. He received the red hat in 1889.

Across twenty-two years he created eighty-six parishes. He founded 840 primary schools attended by 120,000 children. He opened high schools, teacher-training colleges, and ten colleges for the humanities. He also organised congresses on the social question for working people and left five volumes of pastoral letters noted for clear thought and polished French.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pima-indians:
The Pima are a Native people of southern Arizona centred along the middle Gila River and its Salt River branch. Their language belongs to the Piman branch of the Shoshonean stock, shared with the Pápago and the extinct Sobaipuri. Their own name for themselves is simply Aàtam, meaning people, while Pima comes from a native word for no, mistaken by missionaries for a tribal name.

Their recorded history begins with the Jesuit explorer Eusebio Kino, who from 1687 worked the whole Pimería. He said Mass at Casa Grande in 1694 and mapped the Gila in 1701. The entry describes their farming, their villages, and their long peaceable stance toward whites. It notes that the great ruined pueblos of their country were built by an earlier people, not by them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pious-associa:
Pious associations are church groups approved by church authority and founded, mostly in recent times, to advance works of prayer and charity. Other names for the same thing are pious union, pious work, league, and society. Well-known examples include the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul, the Society for the Propagation of the Faith, and the Apostleship of Prayer.

They differ from plain groups of church members by their plainly religious aim, their indulgences and spiritual benefits, and their church approval. They differ from confraternities by simpler rules, no fixed probation, no elaborate ritual or special dress, and no duty to meet for shared devotions. Only the lack of canonical erection, formal church establishment, seems essential to the distinction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piro-indians:
The Piro are a Native people of northeastern Peru living some three hundred miles along the upper Ucayali River and its Apurímac and Urubamba branches. They are known to Quechua speakers as Chantaquiro, nearly black teeth, from their old custom of staining teeth and gums with dye from the black-wood palm. They belong to the great Arawakan language stock.

They are described as jovial, quick-witted, and gifted with languages, many speaking Quechua and Spanish besides their own. They are splendid, daring boatmen much in demand on the rivers. Semi-farmers living on plantain and manioc, they brew the intoxicating masato, build light palm-thatched houses, and once used bow, lance, and blowgun with poisoned arrows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piscataway-in:
The Piscataway were an Algonquian people of lower Maryland, the first tribe whose conversion was attempted under English auspices. They occupied the peninsula between the Potomac and Chesapeake Bay, north to the Patapsco and including the site of Washington. They had about thirty settlements and a population near 2,500, all recognising the chief of Piscataway as emperor.

Captain John Smith visited their towns in 1608, and in March 1634 Lord Baltimore's Catholic colony landed with the Jesuits Andrew White and John Altham. The newcomers set up the first altar in an Indian wigwam. The entry follows the Jesuits' study of the language, the tribe's later removal north under the name Conoy, and the pressures that scattered them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontifical-de:
Pontifical Decorations are titles of nobility, orders of knighthood, and other marks of honour. The papal court confers them on men of unblemished character who have served society, the Church, and the Holy See. Titles run from prince to baron, the ordinary grant being count, personal or hereditary in the male line by primogeniture.

The papal orders, ranked by dignity, are six. They are the Supreme Order of Christ, the Order of Pius IX, and the Order of Saint Gregory the Great. They are also the Order of Saint Sylvester, the Order of the Golden Militia, and the Order of the Holy Sepulchre. Pius X ruled in 1905 that Christ and the Golden Militia should have one grade and the other four three grades. The entry traces the orders from the Crusades, when kings founded chivalric orders that popes later approved or restored.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-popular-devot:
Popular devotions are the outward practices of piety by which ordinary devotion finds life and voice. Devotion itself means an ardour of affection for the things of God. The practices work through four sources. They pull on human feeling, come in simple forms open to all, gain from joining many others, and copy holy people's example.

Most familiar devotions began by imitating a practice of religious orders or a privileged class, so the fourth source explains most of their vogue. The Rosary began as Our Lady's Psalter, when reciting all one hundred and fifty Psalms was urged on religious orders and privileged persons. Other devotions attach to months: October for the Guardian Angels, though the Rosary's papal praise has dimmed it; March for St Joseph; September for the Seven Dolours; July for the Precious Blood. Local devotions like the Little Offices have largely faded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-potawatomi-in:
The Potawatomi are an Algonquin tribe, close kin in speech to the Ojibwa and Ottawa. The French first knew them about 1640, on islands at the mouth of Green Bay on Lake Michigan, lately driven from the lower peninsula by Iroquoian foes. Until their removal west about 1835 to 1840, they held both shores of Lake Michigan. Their land ran from Manitowoc round to Grand River, and south to the Wabash, with some fifty villages.

Lore makes them one folk at first with the Ojibwa and Ottawa. Potewatmik means people of the fire place, or fire makers, from their move south to kindle a new fire. Treaties shrank their land, and bands went west to Iowa and Kansas against their will. Ere 1836 ended, more than sixteen hundred had gone. In September 1838, eight hundred in Indiana were ringed by troops at church and marched west on foot, Father Benjamin Petit walking with them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-premonstraten:
St Norbert founded the Premonstratensian Canons at Prémontré, near Laon, France, in 1120. At first no fixed rule bound them: charity was their bond, and their founder's example served as their guide. After a while Norbert laid out the rules they should take. Then St Augustine appeared to him, giving him his rule.

All agreed on a canonical institute, and Norbert framed a form of profession, which they spoke on Christmas Feast 1121. The first two centuries shone with spiritual fire, and George Lienhardt's Hagiologia names hundreds whose holy lives crown the Order of St Norbert. Later fire cooled: with manual work, mind work, and set observances fading, growth stalled and a kind of stagnation set in. Wealth fed the chill, since cleared forests and gifts had swelled revenues, and with wealth came a worldly spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prisons:
Many count imprisonment among Hebrew law's penalties, but the point is open to doubt. When the Chaldeans came under Nebuchadnezzar, at least three prisons stood at Jerusalem, and their names spoke of the regime within. Beth ha-keli meant house of detention; Beth haasourim, house of those in chains; Beth ha-mah-pecheth, and Bor, cistern or underground pit. At Athens one prison stood under the Eleven, and prisoners could be visited by friends and kin.

At Rome the old Mamertine prison still stands at the Capitol's foot, with an upper part and a dungeon. Prisoners sat in the upper part, and the doomed were cast into the dungeon through a hole in its roof. In later ages, the Auburn regime rules prisons such as Chatham, Dover, and Plymouth: separation at night, work in common by day. Culprits split into four classes by work and conduct, under a marks system.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-private-revel:
Revelations come in two kinds. Universal revelations stand in the Bible or in the deposit of Apostolic tradition. They ended with the Apostles' preaching and bind all belief. Particular, or private, revelations keep occurring among Christians. When the Church approves private revelations, she says but that nothing in them clashes with faith or good morals. No duty to believe them is thereby laid on the faithful.

Benedict XIV says of approved revelations, such as Hildegard's, Bridget's, and Catherine of Siena's, that they claim not Catholic faith's assent, nor is it even possible. They claim only human faith's assent, as prudence commends them as likely and worthy of pious belief. Visions of past scenes are oft but roughly true, and may mislead if trusted as absolute history. A revelation must agree with Church teaching and with known history or natural science. It must teach nothing against good morals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-processions:
Processions, a part of all ceremonial, appear in near each form of religious worship. The Ark processions of the Old Testament and the Saviour's triumphant entry into Jerusalem in the New likely shaped later ritual. Ere Constantine's age, Christian funeral processions already ran with some solemnity, and Tertullian's use of the word may point to a formal march of the faithful churchward.

About St Gregory the Great's time, and perhaps earlier, two processions loomed large in papal ceremonial. One was the march to the Station, the other the celebrant's solemn entry from the sacristy, or secretarium, to the altar. The St Amand Ordo paints the stational march: pontiff, clergy, and folk met in the set church, where clergy vested and the office began. The hospital's poor went first with a painted wooden cross. Seven stationary crosses, each with three candles and a retinue, followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-protectorate-:
This long encyclopedia article explains the protectorate of missions. It is the standing right of a Christian state to shield missionaries and their houses in a non-Christian land. The right rested not on goodwill but on treaty or long custom. Sometimes it was freely granted, sometimes imposed. It could cover only the protecting state's own subjects. It could also cover missionaries of every nation, and even their native converts.

Two histories carry the argument, one for the Levant and one for the Far East. France, Portugal and other powers feature in turn, with the Chinese story taking the most space. After the murder of the missionary Chapdelaine in 1856, Britain and France went to war with China. The Tientsin treaties of 1860 won freedom for missionaries to preach and for Chinese subjects to embrace Christianity. A closing section weighs the Portuguese patronage in Asia and Africa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pueblo-indian:
Pueblo Indians takes its name from the Spanish word for village or town. This long encyclopedia entry uses it for the sedentary farming peoples of central New Mexico and north-eastern Arizona, who lived in permanent communal houses of stone or adobe. The name marks a way of life, not a language or a tribe, setting these villagers apart from roving neighbours of ruder culture.

Ruins show the ancient Pueblo country stretching from the Arkansas and Grand rivers in Colorado and Utah far south into Mexico, and from central Arizona almost across the Texas Panhandle. Later pages trace the missions, whose friars served almost as parish priests under their provincial, paid by the king. Famine, pestilence and smallpox ravaged the pueblos: smallpox alone carried off 5,000 mission Indians, and in 1782 the governor cut eight missions despite the friars' protests. Bancroft and Bureau of Ethnology reports anchor the account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-puritans:
Puritanism resists a tidy definition, and this encyclopedia entry begins with that difficulty. The varied and sometimes clashing beliefs grouped under the name share a common root. In its first sense the word meant those who sought worship purified from every taint of popery, in Maitland's phrase. Trevelyan adds two marks of the type: an aversion from gaiety, and a passionate love of civic freedom.

English Puritanism first shows itself in the Vestiarian Controversy of 1563. Opponents there rejected the clergy's cap and gown in daily life and the surplice in church. Scotland built its own church order alongside. The First Book of Discipline, drawn up at Edinburgh in 1560, ordered the congregation itself. The Second Book of Discipline of 1578 tied congregations to higher courts, abolished superintendents, and put authority in four bodies, starting with the Kirk Session.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-puyallup-indi:
The Puyallup, an important tribe of Salishan stock, once held the land along their river near the head of Puget Sound, Washington. They now live on an allotted reservation near Tacoma, in Pierce County, together with several kindred tribes. The neighbouring Nisqually speak a dialect of the same tongue. The tribal name is said to mean shadow, pointing to the dense forest shade, and it first named the country around the stream's mouth.

Catholic contact reaches back to the Spanish explorers of 1774 to 1795. Franciscans travelling with them gave rosaries and crucifixes, which the people still treasured sixty years later. French Canadians in the service of Mackenzie, Fraser and the Hudson's Bay Company kept that Catholic memory alive. Sources from the Bureau of American Ethnology to the Bureau of Catholic Indian Missions close a compact tribal portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quamichan-ind:
The Quamichan are the largest of the small bands under the Cowichan agency, at the south-east end of Vancouver Island, British Columbia. They are of Salishan stock and speak Cowichan, a language shared by neighbouring bands and by peoples across the mainland strait. Their chief settlement lies in Cowichan valley, about forty miles north of Victoria. In their old condition they lived by fishing, hunting, and gathering wild berries and roots.

Their customs, beliefs and ceremonies closely matched those of their neighbours, the Songish and Sechelt. Fathers Bolduc and Demers visited them as early as 1847, but the Oblate Fathers, who reached Victoria in 1857, did most of the converting work. From perhaps 1,000 souls sixty years earlier, smallpox and other diseases cut them to 300 in 1901 and 260 in 1909. Of those, all but about 60 were Catholics, the rest Methodists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quapaw-indian:
The Quapaw, now nearly extinct, once ranked among the most important tribes of the lower Mississippi. This encyclopedia entry places their villages about the mouth of the Arkansas, chiefly on the west bank. At times one or two stood on the east bank. The tribe claimed the whole Arkansas River country up to Osage territory in the north-west. They are of Siouan stock, speaking a language shared, with dialect differences, by the Osage, Kansa, Omaha and Ponca.

Their true name, Ugakhpa, means down-stream people, set against Omaha, up-stream people. To Illinois and other Algonquian tribes they were the Akansea, whence the French Akensas and Akansas. Later pages follow their removals and the 1834 treaty that moved them to the north-east corner of Oklahoma. Saracen, their last chief before removal, was a Catholic and a friend of the Lazarist missionaries who arrived in 1818.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quichua-india:
The Quichua Indians, once the dominant people of the Peruvian Empire, still form the largest homogeneous body of Indians in existence. This long encyclopedia entry counts them as the bulk of the rural population of Peru and Ecuador. Their name, also written Quechua or Kechua, most likely means those who speak correctly. The Quichuan tribes held a territory nearly matching the empire at its widest, south to Coquimbo in Chile.

The Inca seem to have started between Paucartambo and Cuzco, and the Quichua proper, living south of Cuzco, fell among their earliest conquests. Military service bound every man. Conquered peoples were moved into older districts, and older inhabitants into new lands. The Sun religion became obligatory empire-wide, as did, as far as possible, the Quichua tongue. The entry argues the ancient Peruvians had reached the idea of one god, the Sun, ancestor of the Incas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-dis:
Religious discussions are oral duels, formal contests between champions of opposing beliefs, set apart from polemical writing. Most famous examples were staged at the urging of civil rulers, since the Church seldom favoured airing revealed truth this way. A champion of orthodoxy with every gift of a public debater is hard to find. It seems improper to let opponents assail mysteries and institutions due reverent speech. The Catholic side nearly always fights on the defensive.

The survey runs through great Reformation conferences. At Hagenau the Protestant champions Brenz, Blaurer, and Urbanus Rhegius faced Bishop Faber of Vienna and Doctor Eck. John Calvin, exiled from Geneva, intrigued as the French king's agent to keep discord alive in his rival's lands. After a month of fruitless wrangling, King Ferdinand adjourned the meeting to Worms, and the emperor pressed on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reordinations:
Reordinations is the name Jean Morin, an Oratorian of the 1600s, and Cardinal Hergenröther gave to ordinations done again. They were ordinations judged null for reasons other than bad form or intention. By that definition any such reordination was wrong, since only form or intention can void Holy Orders. Yet history admitted other causes at times, above all sacraments given or received outside the Church, extra ecclesiam, which were treated as null and repeated.

The survey follows the dispute through its famous cases. Pope Formosus's ordinations were declared null and repeated. After the eleventh century the simony debates sharpened the quarrel, with Cardinal Humbert and the Synod of Girona in 1078 calling simoniacal ordinations void. German emperors and popes in the eleventh and twelfth centuries likewise denied schismatic bishops' power to ordain, and the thirteenth century set new terms for the dispute.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-gibbo:
Richard Gibbons, a Jesuit scholar born at Winchester around 1550, spent his long life teaching, editing, and translating learned works across Europe. After early study in England, philosophy at Louvain, and time at the German College in Rome, he joined the Society of Jesus in 1572. Ordination led to years teaching mathematics, philosophy, Hebrew, and Scripture in Italy, France, Portugal, Spain, and Belgium.

His later years at Douai were given to the printing press. There he edited old manuscripts and brought out editions and translations. These covered the stigmata, the prophets, English church history, and the meditations of Luis de la Puente. He also issued devotional books in English. The entry lists these publications in detail. Together they picture a quiet, industrious scholar whose books served Catholic readers in an age when such printing often had to happen abroad.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-person:
Robert Persons was a Jesuit leader of the English Catholic mission whose energy shaped recusant resistance. Born at Nether Stowey in 1546 to yeoman parents, he was sent by the local parson to St Mary's Hall, Oxford, in 1562. After distinction there and a fellowship at Balliol, he was forced to resign in 1574, partly for Catholic leanings and partly through college quarrels. Abroad he was reconciled and became a Jesuit at Rome in 1575.

At Rome he proposed the English mission and the oath of the missions, and served briefly as rector of the English College. His year on the English mission, from June 1580 to August 1581, was his most useful period. Ever at the post of danger yet never seized, he preached, heard confessions, planned missionary tours, and set up a secret press that printed Campion's Decem Rationes. Later he worked from the continent until his death at Rome in 1610.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rosicrucians:
Rosicrucians is the name given to alleged members of an occult brotherhood, described in the pamphlet Fama Fraternitatis R.C. Circulated in manuscript as early as 1610, it was printed at Cassel in 1614. Boccalini's Ragguagli di Parnasso was prefixed to the first two editions, and the Confessio joined the Fama from 1615. According to these writings, Christian Rosenkreuz, a German nobleman and former monk, founded the brotherhood in 1408 after learning Arabian lore in Damascus, Jerusalem, and Fez.

The brothers counted gold-making unimportant and studied nature's hidden forces in secrecy, sharing discoveries for humanity's needs. They met yearly at the Edifice of the Holy Spirit, healed the sick free of charge, and each procured a successor. Unknown for two hundred years, the brotherhood became known about 1604, when the Fama invited Europe's scholars and rulers to seek admission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rosminians:
The Rosminians, officially the Institute of Charity, are a religious congregation founded by Antonio Rosmini, first organized in 1828 and formally approved by the Holy See in 1838. It draws its name from charity, the fullness of Christian virtue. In English-speaking lands members are commonly called Fathers of Charity; in Italy, Rosminians.

Rosmini alone strictly founded the society, yet his age supplied the bent of his thought and the chance to embody it. Born in the wake of the French Revolution, he weighed Christendom's intellectual and moral inheritance whole. He did so neither in blind protest nor mere reaction, but weighing new ideas with old. He saw the Church's enemies attack with fresh vigour. Within the Church he saw a growing danger: denial or belittling of the supernatural, ill-regulated activity, impatience of tradition, and by reaction an ill-timed passiveness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ruthenians:
Ruthenians are Slavs dwelling in north-eastern Hungary and Austria's Bukowina, as well as Galicia and southern Russia. In Russian they are also called Malorossiani, Little Russians, and in their own Hungarian dialect, Russniaks. In Russia they occupy Lublin, Volhynia, Podolia, Kieff, Tchernigoff, Kharkoff, and Poltava, numbering about 18,000,000. In Austria they occupy Eastern Galicia and Bukowina, and in Hungary the northern counties, amounting to about 4,500,000 more.

Along the old Polish borderland they are also called Ukrainians, from the Ukraine, the vast steppes of southern Russia. In the Austro-Hungarian Empire the Carpathians divide them between Galicia and Hungary. Ruthenians in Russia and Bukowina belong to the Greek Orthodox Church, while those of Galicia and Hungary are Greek Catholics in unity with the Holy See. Hence Ruthenian generally means the Catholic part of the race, and Little Russian the Orthodox part, though the terms are usually interchangeable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saba-and-sabe:
This Saba, or Sheba, must not be confused with Saba in Ethiopia. It lies in the southern Arabian Jof, about 200 miles northwest of Aden. Sabeans appear in the Bible as a distant people, famous traders exporting gold, precious stones, perfumes, and incense. Genesis genealogies connect them with Dadan and with Asarmoth. These details suggest two Sabas: a southern one and a northern one. Which was the original home cannot yet be decided.

Hommel places the original home in the north, near Idumean Dedan, identifying it with Aribi-Yareb. Thence, Glaser holds, Sabeans moved south and built their kingdom on Minaean ruins. This theory is plausible, but identifying Saba with Aribi-Yareb is arbitrary. Sargon refuses the king title to Ithamara, and inscriptions show long rule by Mukarribs, priest-kings. Their capital was Cirwah.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sahaptin-indi:
Sahaptin Indians were a prominent tribe formerly holding considerable territory in western Idaho and adjacent Oregon and Washington. It included the lower Snake River with the Salmon, Clearwater, and Grande Ronde. It ran from about 45 degrees down nearly to the Palouse, and from Oregon's Blue Mountains west to the Bitter-root divide east.

They belong to the Shahaptian stock, with Palouse, Umatilla, Tenino, and Yakima westward, keeping close friendly relations. They call themselves Numipu, meaning simply people. The name Sahaptin comes through Salishan tribes. Lewis and Clark in 1805 called them Chopunnish. Their popular name Nez Perces, Pierced Noses, from French trappers, refers to wearing a dentalium shell through the nose's septum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-daniel-:
Daniel and companions were Friars Minor and martyrs, died 10 October 1227. The martyrdom of Berard and companions in 1219 had inflamed many Friars Minor with desire to preach in heathen lands. In 1227, the year after St Francis's death, six Tuscans petitioned Elias of Cortona to preach to Morocco's infidels.

The six went first to Spain, where Daniel of Calabria joined them as superior. Sailing from Spain, they reached Africa's coast on 20 September. Very early on Sunday they entered the city, preaching the Gospel and denouncing Mahomet's religion. Soon apprehended before the sultan, who thought them mad, they were cast into prison. The next Sunday the sultan vainly tried to make them deny Christianity. Condemned to death, each asked Daniel's blessing. All were beheaded, and Daniel and companions were canonized by Leo X in 1516.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saliva-indian:
The Saliva, principal people of a small language family called Salivan, lived in the eighteenth century near the junction of the Meta and Orinoco rivers in Venezuela. They had come from farther up the Orinoco near the Guaviare. Kindly and sociable, and fond of music, they still killed the aged and feeble, as was common among neighbouring peoples. Their entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia records customs and missions together.

A year after death they dug up the bones, burned them, and mixed the ashes in drinking water, and their rites used the batuto, a great clay trumpet of the region. Jesuit Father Anisson wrote a grammar of their tongue. Monteverde and Castan founded the first mission in 1669 but died within the year, scattering the people, until new missions at Carichana, Sinameo, and San Lorenzo followed in 1671.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samuco-indian:
The Samuco, also called Zamuco, are a group of tribes in south-western Bolivia speaking dialects of one language, the distinct Samucan stock, which also covers the Guaranoca, Morotoco, Poturero, and others. Their homeland lay along the northern Chaco, between about 18 and 21 degrees south and 58 and 62 degrees west, bordering the Toba wanderers and the mission peoples of Chiquito and Chiriguano. Their entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sketches a semi-settled people.

They farmed corn, manioc, and a kind of plum, then the men returned to the woods after planting to hunt and dry meat. Women wove mats and hammocks from native cotton thread and made pottery, while the men, famed for warlike spirit, went naked and the women wore only a small cloth.
