The entry records their crafts, dress, and country before turning to mission contact.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sandemanians:
Sandemanians are the English form of the Scottish Glassites, followers of John Glas, born in 1695 and dead in 1773. Deposed from the Presbyterian ministry in 1728, Glas taught that the Church must answer to no league or covenant, but only to apostolic teaching. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a small sect through his son-in-law's name.

Robert Sandeman, born in 1718 and dead in 1771, long an elder among the Glassites, moved to London in 1760 and gathered a congregation at Glovers' Hall, Barbican. Mostly faithful to Glas, he went further in holding faith to be simple assent to divine testimony, no different from belief in ordinary human evidence. In 1764 he sailed to America and founded congregations there, so Glassites in both countries bear his name, though England holds under a dozen meeting-places.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanetch-india:
The Sanetch, a sub-tribe of the Songish Indians, speak a Cowichan dialect of the Salishan language family and hold small reserves around the Saanich Peninsula at Vancouver Island's south-west tip. Counted at 600 in 1858, they had fallen to about 250 by the early twentieth century. Their short entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia records a people wholly won to the Church.

In old customs and beliefs they resembled the Songish. Father John Bolduc began Christian work among them in 1843, and Oblate Fathers finished it. Now entirely civilised and Catholic, they farm, fish, and take paid work of many kinds. Their government agent praised them as industrious and law-abiding, fairly temperate, and moral, and the entry leaves that verdict as the tribe's modern portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schwenckfeldi:
Schwenckfeldians are the followers of Caspar von Schwenckfeld, a Silesian nobleman born at Ossig in 1489 or 1490 who died at Ulm on 10 December 1561. After studies at Cologne and Frankfurt-on-the-Oder, he served several Silesian dukes' courts. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a reformer too radical for Luther.

In 1521 Schwenckfeld publicly joined the new teaching of the reformers and spread it through Silesia. But his views clashed irreconcilably with Luther's, and in 1529 he left Silesia for Strasbourg. Banished from Strasbourg in 1533, he began a life of forced moves, hounded mainly by Lutheran preachers who condemned his writings at Schmalkalden. His followers, never numerous, organised only after his death and lived secretly under persecution until toleration came.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sechelt-india:
The Sechelt, properly Siciatl, are a small tribe speaking a distinct Salishan language. They once held lands around the Jervis and Sechelt inlets, Nelson Island, and south Texada Island. Now they gather on a reserve on the Sechelt Peninsula in south-western British Columbia under the Fraser River agency. Their entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia describes a potlatch society.

In old times the Sechelt formed four divisions in separate settlements, with three castes: chiefs, nobles or respectables, and a lower class. Chiefs usually owed hereditary rank to some ancestor's lavish generosity at a great gift-feast, or potlatch, common to all north-west coast tribes. Nobles, the wealthy and those of undoubted respectable birth, could reach chiefship through the potlatch. The lowest class held the thriftless and slaves, prisoners of war or their descendants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-second-counci:
The Second Council of Lyons, one of the most largely attended councils ever, gathered five hundred bishops, sixty abbots, and over a thousand other prelates and their agents. Gregory X presided; he had earlier served as a canon of Lyons. Peter of Tarentaise, assisting as cardinal-bishop of Ostia, had been its archbishop. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens on 7 May 1274 in St John's church.

Five further sessions followed on 18 May, 7 June, 6 July, 16 July, and 17 July. At the second session Gregory, faced with excessive numbers, rejected proxies of chapters, abbots, and unmitred priors except those summoned by name. James I of Aragon attended, with ambassadors from France, England, Emperor Michael Palaeologus with Greek clergy, and the Tatar Khan. Gregory had called the council for two aims: winning back the Holy Land and reuniting the Churches.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seleucians:
A Gnostic group said to have flourished in Galatia, the Seleucians took their name from Seleucus. He taught the errors the entry sets out, along with a certain Hermias. Their system rested on a crude dualism. God was bodiless, yet matter was eternal beside him. They went beyond other dualists by laying the blame for evil on God as well as on matter. Human souls, they said, were not made by God but shaped from fire and air by angels.

Christ, they argued from a psalm verse about a tent in the sun, had left his body in the sun rather than sitting at the Father's right hand. They refused baptism and read hell as this present world. They treated resurrection as begetting that conquers death. Disciples called Prolinianites carried the errors further, denying resurrection and judgment outright.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seneca-indian:
The Seneca were the westernmost and largest of the five tribes of the Iroquois Confederacy in central and western New York. They nearly equaled the other four tribes together in population, largely through wholesale adoption of captives. Yet in the ancient council they held only eight of fifty chiefs. They called themselves People of the Great Mountain, and the English name Seneca came, by corruption, from an Algonquian term for the place of the stone.

Holding the western door of the confederacy between Seneca Lake and the Genesee River, they grew by conquering the Neutrals in 1651 and the Erie in 1656. They took a leading part in tribal and colonial wars, kept some thirty villages a century later, and later split between New York and Oklahoma. A few in Oklahoma joined the Catholic mission of Saint Mary's at Quapaw, while most kept to pagan ways.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sens:
The archdiocese of Sens, covering the French department of the Yonne, is traced here through a stormy institutional history. It was suppressed by the Concordat of 1802, which folded Sens and Auxerre into Troyes and left the archbishop of Paris with only an honorary Sens title. The Concordat of 1817 restored it, but the settlement of 1821 suppressed Auxerre instead and gave Sens the whole Yonne department, with Troyes, Nevers, and Moulins as suffragans.

Religious beginnings reach back to Saints Savinian and Potentian, though Gregory of Tours stays silent about them. The entry then runs a long roll of bishops, from Henri Sanglier, who condemned Abelard's propositions in 1140, to cardinals, royal ministers, and a bishop who died in a Revolutionary prison. It also covers the diocese of Auxerre, famed for its multitude of sainted bishops, and Sens's shrines, schools, and monasteries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-setebo-indian:
The Setebo, a considerable tribe of Panoan stock, once centered where the Manoa meets the Ucayali in northeastern Peru. They now work as boatmen and rubber gatherers along the Ucayali down toward its junction with the Marañon. They speak the same language as their neighbors the Pano, Conibo, and Sipibo, and share their customs and beliefs. Gold hunters from Peru entered the upper Ucayali early in the 1600s, and their harsh treatment made the tribes bitterly hostile to Spaniards.

In 1657 Franciscan Alonzo Caballero reached the Setebo with two priests and three lay brothers, passing through cannibal Cashibo country. After a year of patient work they gathered part of the tribe into two mission villages. The Sipibo, hereditary enemies, attacked and destroyed them, killing the five religious and many converts. A second attempt in 1661 met the same fate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seven-deacons:
The seven deacons were the seven men elected by the whole Jerusalem community and ordained by the Apostles, chiefly to care for the poor and the common love feast. Believers in Jerusalem had grown fast, and complaints arose that poor widows of Hellenistic Jews were neglected. The Apostles, unwilling to leave preaching for material cares, proposed that suitable men take over those duties. The Seven were appointed, as Acts chapter 6 records.

This was the first separation of a hierarchical office from the Apostolate itself. The seven were full of the Holy Spirit and could partly stand for the Apostles in spiritual matters, as Stephen showed at Jerusalem and Philip in Samaria. Philip, called the Evangelist, baptized the Ethiopian eunuch and later lived at Caesarea. Of Nicanor, Timon, and Parmenas, nothing further is known.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shuswap-india:
The Shuswap, properly Su-khapmuh, were the most important Salishan tribe of British Columbia, holding a large territory on the middle and upper Thompson River, with Shuswap, Adams, and Quesnel Lakes inside it. From perhaps 5,000 souls a century before, smallpox cut them to about 2,200.

Early history records little beyond tribal wars and dealings with the Hudson Bay Company, which built Fort Thompson at Kamloops by 1810. Christian work began in the winter of 1842 and 1843, when Father Modeste Demers traveled with the annual company caravan and preached among the Shuswap at Williams Lake in a temporary chapel. The people now gather on small reservations under the Kamloops-Okanagan and Williams Lake agencies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siletz-indian:
Siletz is the collective name for the dwindling remnant of some thirty small tribes of five language stocks. They once held Oregon's whole coast from near the Columbia to the California border. Several tribes are now wholly extinct. The rest gather on the Siletz Reservation in Lincoln County, except perhaps seventy on Grande Ronde nearby.

From perhaps 15,000 souls before the troubles, smallpox in 1782 and 1783 cut the people by more than a third, and traders' diseases and dissipation hastened decline. The 3,240 assigned to the reservation in 1857 had shrunk to 430 by 1910. Father Croquette of Grande Ronde served both reservations for nearly forty years. Fish, acorns, and game fed them. Cedar-board houses sheltered them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simonians:
The Simonians were a Gnostic, antinomian sect of the second century that took Simon Magus as founder and traced its doctrines to him. Hegesippus mentions them, and their doctrines are quoted and opposed by Irenaeus, the Philosophumena, and later Epiphanius. In the Philosophumena, Simon's teaching follows his reputed Great Declaration, showing the sect's doctrines as they had grown by the second century.

At the base stood a perfect, eternal, ungenerated being, pictured as fire, holding a hidden and a manifest element, like Plato's intelligible and sensible. From the hidden being six roots or powers flowed in pairs, matching heaven and earth, sun and moon, air and water, and holding all power potentially. A seventh power, the Standing One, matching the seventh day after creation's six, existed before the world as the Spirit of God moving over the waters. The entry follows the system's unfolding from there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sioux-indians:
The Sioux, largest and most important Indian tribe north of Mexico except the Ojibwa, are virtually all within the United States. They long kept close ties among their bands. Their name comes from a French spelling of an Algonquian enemies' term meaning little snakes, while they call themselves Dakota, Nakota, or Lakota by dialect, meaning allies. Linguistically they belong to the great Siouan stock they named, forming nearly three fourths of it.

Christian Indians stood loyally by the government in the Minnesota outbreak of 1862. Little Crow's forces massacred settlers, attacked Fort Ridgely and New Ulm, and were beaten at Birch Coulee and Wood Lake. Thirty-eight prisoners were hanged at Mankato that December, after Lincoln cut the condemned list from three hundred. Later chapters carry the story through the western wars and reservations at Crow Creek and Santee.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sipibo-indian:
The Sipibo, a numerous Panoan tribe, once centered on the Pisqui and Aguaitia tributaries of the upper Ucayali in northeastern Peru, now work as boatmen or laborers along the whole river. They speak the same language as the Conibo, Pano, and Setebo, sharing their habits and ceremonies. Known from the early 1600s, they long resisted gold hunters and missionaries, frustrating Ucayali evangelization by raids on mission settlements.

Smallpox wasted them in 1670. In 1736 they broke Setebo power in battle, but in 1764 Franciscan Juan de Frezneda entered their country and made peace between the two tribes. The next year he founded the first Sipibo mission, Santo Domingo de Pisqui, soon followed by Santa Barbara de Archani and Santa Cruz de Aguaitia, with work resumed among the Conibo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-henry-haw:
Henry Hawkins, raised to the peerage as Lord Brampton, was an eminent English lawyer and judge, born at Hitchin on 14 September 1817 and dead in London on 12 October 1907. Eldest son of a Hitchin solicitor, he was schooled at Bedford, articled to an uncle. Hating an attorney's drudgery, he moved to London, trained at the Middle Temple, and was called to the Bar in May 1843. Without money or influence, he rose by sheer hard work and became Queen's Counsel in 1858.

He fought many famous lawsuits, above all the Tichborne case, where his cross-examination exposed the false claimant and he then led the prosecution. Made a judge of Queen's Bench and knighted in November 1875, he married a Catholic lady the next year. Stern where duty required, he was kindly to mere human weakness, opposed long or vindictive sentences and vivisection, loved animals, and took his recreation at the races.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-slaves-dene-i:
The Slaves are a tribe of the great Dene family of American Indians, named, it seems, because the Crees drove them back to their northern haunts. They live in the forests west of Great Slave Lake, from Hay River inclusive. Five main bands make up the tribe: Fort Norman, Horn Mountain, Trout Lake, Hay River, and the forks of the Mackenzie. Their total population is about 1,100.

Their morals were formerly poor, the entry says, but improved considerably after Catholic missionaries arrived, and many exchanged old teepees for more comfortable log houses. Religious feeling runs less strong among them than among most northern Dene, and they were slower to welcome Catholic missionaries. Today about one-twelfth of the tribe is Protestant and the rest Catholic, served from missions at Saint Joseph on Great Slave Lake, Sainte Anne, Hay River, and Providence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sobaipura-ind:
Once an important tribe of the Piman branch of the Shoshonean stock, the Sobaipura lived along the Santa Cruz and San Pedro Rivers in southeastern Arizona and adjacent Sonora, Mexico. In dialect and custom they closely resembled the Pápago, by whom and by the cognate Pima most were finally absorbed. Their chief centre was Bac, later San Xavier del Bac, nine miles south of present Tucson.

Jesuit explorer Eusebio Kino visited Bac in 1692 and began its church in 1699. Suamca and San Miguel de Guevavi, founded in 1732 near present Nogales, served the same tribe along the Santa Cruz. The missions survived the Jesuit expulsion of 1767 by only a few years. Before the century ended the tribe itself had disappeared, and tradition says Apache attacks about 1790 destroyed it, carrying off some and forcing others into Pápago and Pima communities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-soissons:
The Diocese of Soissons covers nearly the whole Department of Aisne. Re-established by the concordat of 1802 as suffragan of Paris, it became suffragan of Reims in 1821. It joins the ancient Diocese of Soissons with all of Laon, part of Vermandois from Noyon, and parishes from Cambrai, Meaux, Troyes, and Reims. Its bishops also bear the titles of Laon, from 1828, and Saint-Quentin, from 1901.

Soissons played a great political part under the Merovingians, serving as capital of one of four Frankish kingdoms after Clovis died in 511. The kingdom vanished in 558, returned in 561, and disappeared finally in 613. The see dates from about 300, with patrons Crepinus and Crepinianus, martyred about 288. The Abbey of Saint-Médard, founded in 557 by Clotaire I, ranked as France's chief Benedictine abbey, holding over 220 fiefs, and Louis the Pious suffered public penance there in 833.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-songish-india:
The Songish, whose proper name is Lkungen, were a Salishan people of the south coast of Vancouver Island, near the present city of Victoria. And this entry records their territory, language, and decline Once holding the coast around Victoria, they gathered by the early twentieth century on small reservations at Songhees, Beecher Island, Discovery Island. And Esquimalt, speaking the same tongue as the Sanetch, Sooke, and Lummi.

From about a thousand souls, disease and dissipation after the whites arrived cut them to 215 in 1895 and 171 by 1910. And the entry grimly expects them to vanish within a generation. Their first regular contact with whites came with Fort Camosum, built by the Hudson's Bay Company in 1843. And the account stands as a stark record of a people in rapid retreat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spokan-indian:
The Spokan were an important Salishan tribe of the Spokane River country in eastern Washington and nearby Idaho, kin to the Colville, Coeur d'Alene, Kalispel, and Flathead peoples. This entry first notes them under the name Lartielo in the journals of Lewis and Clark in 1805, then follows their dealings with Hudson's Bay and American Fur Company traders.

A Presbyterian mission opened among the Lower Spokan at Chemakane in 1839 and ran until 1849, when it closed after the Whitman massacre among the Cayuse. Though Chief Garry shielded its people until danger passed A Spokan primer printed by the missionaries in 1842 ranked among the earliest books on the Pacific coast. And the entry closes with the Upper Spokan coming under Catholic influence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-squamish-indi:
The Squamish were a considerable Salishan tribe of the Squamish River and Howe Sound country in south-western British Columbia, speaking a language of their own. This entry traces a people who may have numbered two thousand a century before the encyclopedia. They were cut by the smallpox visitation of 1862 and earlier dissipation to 690 in 1890 and 396 in 1910, living on six small reservations under the Fraser River agency.

Vancouver met and traded with them in 1792. Regular white contact followed the Hudson's Bay posts in 1810 to 1820, and missionary work began with Father Modeste Demers in 1841 before becoming systematic in 1857. The entry stands as a sober census of a shrinking people and the missions among them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-aedan-of-f:
St. Aedan of Ferns, also called Aedh-og or Mo-Aedh-og, was bishop and patron of Ferns in Ireland, born near Templeport in County Cavan about 550 and dead at Ferns on 31 January 632. This entry follows a youth held hostage by High-King Aedh Ainmire, educated at Kilmuine in Wales by St. David, then came back to Ireland in 580, reaching the Wexford coast.

After the victory of Dunbolg in 598, where King Aedh fell. Bran Dubh, King of Leinster, called a synod that made Ferns an episcopal see with Aedan as first bishop, granting him the title of chief bishop over Leinster. Popularly known as Mogue, my dear Aedh, he founded thirty churches, and the entry gives a full Irish episcopal career in miniature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-columba-of:
St. Columba of Sens suffered towards the end of the third century, probably under the Emperor Aurelian. This entry follows a woman said to have been beheaded near a fountain called d'Azon. Tradition holds that her murderers left her body on the ground, until Aubertus buried it in thanksgiving for sight restored on invoking her.

A chapel later rose over her relics, and then the Abbey of Sens, which pilgrims once visited in her honour. Chevilly's parish church in the Diocese of Paris also claims her as patroness, but her whole history is somewhat legendary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-berch:
John Berchmans, Jesuit scholastic who died at twenty-two, was loved for a bright, joyful holiness. Born at Diest in Brabant on 13 March 1599, he was naturally kind, gentle, and affectionate to his parents, a favourite with playmates, brave, open, attractive, and joyful. Yet by nature he was impetuous and fickle. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Rome to 13 August 1621.

At seven his parish priest Emmerick already saw the Lord would work wonders in the child. At nine his mother fell into long, serious illness, and John spent hours daily at her bedside, consoling her with affectionate, serious words. Living with other boys at Emmerick's house, he took more than his share of housework, choosing harder tasks by preference. Loved by comrades, he repaid affection with kindness. The entry preserves a boy saint in household detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-joseph-s-s:
St. Joseph's Society for Colored Missions began in 1871 with four Mill Hill priests at a Black parish in Baltimore. He took charge of St. Francis Xavier's church, whose congregation of Black Catholics was large, the young priests soon opened further Black missions across the South, at Louisville, Charleston, Washington, Richmond, and Norfolk. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 traces a society growing fast enough to stand alone.

In 1892 it became independent of Mill Hill and set headquarters at Baltimore. It soon counted almost fifty priests running thirty-five missions through the South. Its schools included St. Joseph's Seminary in Baltimore for missionary training and Epiphany Apostolic College at Walbrook as its preparatory school. A catechetical college near Montgomery, Alabama, trained young Black catechists and teachers, and an industrial and trade school at Clayton, Delaware, served Black youth.

St. Joseph's Society for Foreign Missions, the Mill Hill Missionaries, trained priests for peoples beyond Europe. Cardinal Vaughan, while still a priest, founded St. Joseph's Missionary College in 1866 in a villa near Mill Hill, ten miles north of London. Its purpose was to train missionaries for unevangelized races beyond Europe, above all African and American Black peoples. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates the college's move to Mill Hill's larger building to 1 March 1871.

In 1884 St. Peter's School rose at Freshfield near Liverpool as the college's preparatory school. Two branch colleges followed: St. Joseph's Missiehuis at Rozendaal in Holland, built in 1890, and St. Josef's Missionshaus at Brixen in Tyrol, built in 1891. Under Superior General Francis Henry, the society counted about two hundred priests and ten lay brothers. A society of priests and laymen, it laboured, in the entry's phrase, for the conversion of heathens abroad.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-nazarius-a:
Nazarius and companions, four Roman martyrs named for 12 June, survive more as names in old lists than as known lives. The Roman Martyrology and Bede's list name Basilides, Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius as sufferers under Diocletian. Their names trace to the Hieronymian Martyrology, whose Berne manuscript mixes genuine entries with African names and a place-name misread as a person.

Neither the date nor the circumstances of their deaths are known. A mortuary chapel of Basilides stood on the Via Aurelia. The trio of Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius, later joined by Basilides, won a special invocation in the Gelasian Sacramentary's Canon of the Mass. Bishop Chrodegang of Metz later moved the bones of Nazarius and Nabor to his diocese. The entry is a lesson in martyrology detective work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thomas-chr:
The Thomas Christians, an ancient body of Christians on India's Malabar and Coromandel coasts, claim descent from the apostle Thomas. Their history, treated here under seventeen heads, rests for its earliest period on tradition alone, embodied in a manuscript Statement of 1604. They revere Thomas's tomb at Mylapur, upheld by the Edessan Church.

Syrian merchant Thomas Cana's arrival in Malabar, two church-building brothers, ancient stone crosses, and early prelates fill the early narrative. The entry then weighs Nestorian influence before 1599, medieval travellers, the Synod of Diamper under Archbishop Menezes, Jesuit and Carmelite periods, and division into three vicariates under native bishops. It offers a full reference history of a community between East and West.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ursula-and:
Ursula and the Eleven Thousand Virgins of Cologne rest, the entry warns, on ten lines open to question. The legend, in countless versions and ever more fanciful growth, would take over a hundred pages to tell. Medieval writers already suspected parts of it, and since Baronius its apocryphal character has been recognised by degrees.

For solid reconstruction only two sources remain: the inscription of Clematius, carved on stone in the choir of St Ursula's church at Cologne, and meagre details from ancient liturgical books. The inscription, partly obscure, tells how Clematius restored a basilica on the site for virgin martyrs from the East. Everything beyond it, including the eleven thousand, belongs to legend's growth. The entry is a masterclass in stripping a famous tale to its stones.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vincent-of:
Vincent of Lérins, a fifth-century writer of southern Gaul, is known almost wholly through one book. His work is far better known than his life, and nearly all information comes from Gennadius's Lives of Illustrious Men. Entering the monastery of Lérins, today Isle St Honorat, he wrote his Commonitorium in 434 under the pseudonym Peregrinus.

He died before 450, probably shortly after 434. Eucherius of Lyons praises him as a holy man of striking eloquence and learning. No reliable authority identifies him with Marius Mercator, though Prosper may have aimed his Responses at him. A Semipelagian, he opposed Augustine's doctrine, arguing that what all men have always and everywhere believed must count as true. His rule of antiquity, universality, and consent still frames Catholic theology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-statistics-of:
Statistics of religions counts religious bodies, their members, and their spread across countries. In a wider sense it also covers the numerical account of outward religious life, though recent usage assigns that group to ecclesiastical statistics, treated separately. The field has only lately been thoroughly worked, and language still lacks a sharp distinction between the terms.

Practical reasons favour keeping the distinction, and the article retains it. Historical development begins with Jesuit and Franciscan missionaries of the 1500s and 1600s, who counted Christians but not adherents of native religions. From the eighteenth century, accounts of various systems multiplied, and modern censuses, yearbooks, and church returns made comparison possible. The entry surveys methods, sources, and pitfalls of counting faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-eustachiu:
Eustachius and his family were martyred under Hadrian in 118. They are honoured through a legend the entry frankly calls fabulous. Placidus, a Roman general under Trajan, saw a stag bearing a crucifix between its horns while hunting. He heard a voice warning of suffering for Christ, and was baptized with his wife and two sons.

Scattered by misfortune and reunited, the family refused to sacrifice after a victory. They died in a heated bronze bull. Their Acts date from the seventh century, yet devotion runs far older in Greek and Latin churches alike. Eustachius counts among the Holy Helpers, patron of Madrid and of hunters, and his Roman church already stood by 827.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-peter-bap:
Peter Baptist and twenty-five companions died crucified at Nagasaki on 5 February 1597. This entry follows the road to that scaffold. In 1593 the governor of the Philippines sent Peter Baptist with other Franciscans as envoys to the Japanese emperor, and they built convents, schools, and hospitals while winning converts.

Disaster struck when a Spanish warship, the San Felipe, wrecked off Tosa in 1596. Its captain boasted that missionaries paved the way for conquest, and the furious emperor jailed the friars. On the February morning, six Franciscans, three Japanese Jesuits, and seventeen native tertiaries were crucified together. Urban VIII beatified them in 1627, and Pius IX canonized them in 1862.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-swedenborgian:
Swedenborgians believe the doctrines taught by Emanuel Swedenborg, though as a body they prefer the name Church of the New Jerusalem, or New Church. The older label suggests a human origin for their faith, while they claim divine authorship working through a human instrument. Swedenborg himself, born at Stockholm in 1688 and dead in London in 1772, was the son of Jesper Swedberg, later Lutheran bishop of Skara.

His life splits in two. To 1745 he shone in mathematics and physical science. He served Charles XII on the Board of Mines from 1716, and once hauled boats fourteen miles overland at the siege of Fredrikshald. Ennobled in 1719, his family name changed from Swedberg to Swedenborg. After 1745 he wrote only theology, and later sections treat those writings, the New Church bodies, and Catholic assessments of his doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-swinomish-ind: The Swinomish are a tribe of Salishan stock, closely tied to the Skagit, who once held land around the mouth of the Skagit River and part of Whidbey Island. They now live on a reservation in the same territory, near Mount Vernon in Skagit County, northwestern Washington. Missionaries reached them about 1850, through Father Casimir Chirouse and the Oblates, and by 1910 the whole tribe, 267 people, was Catholic. They fall under the Tulalip agency.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tacana-indian:
The Tacana are a group of tribes forming the Tacanan linguistic stock. They live in the upper Beni and Madre de Dios valleys, on the Andes' eastern slope in Bolivia's Beni department. Tacana proper, Isiamo, Cavina, and Aten or Leco were missionized by Franciscans of Ocopa College in Peru near the end of the eighteenth century. Toromona, Araume, and the distant Sapibocona stayed wild.

In 1832 five Tacana missions held 5,304 Christian Indians, with perhaps a thousand wild Toromona besides. By 1883 the Cavina had shrunk from a thousand to seventy souls. Tall, light-skinned, and fine-featured, the Tacana speak a guttural, jerky tongue, farm, hunt, and fish, and weave well, though only for immediate needs. Civilized members wear a sleeveless shirt, bareheaded and barefoot, and some tribes were reputed cannibals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-taensa-indian:
The Taensa were a Muskhogean tribe of superior culture. They lived on the Mississippi's west bank, in today's Tensas parish, Louisiana. Perhaps 1,200 souls lived in several villages. In language, religion, and custom they nearly matched the Natchez across the river. They were sedentary farmers and expert canoe men. Their large houses used logs plastered with clay and roofs of cane mats.

Their chiefs ruled despotically and drew great reverence. Attendants swept the road before a chief visiting La Salle. Friendly to the French from the first, they were praised as dignified and humane. Yet they practised bloody rites. A domed temple bore eagles on top and skulls on its palisade. An altar held scalp locks, and wives and attendants died at a chief's funeral. Father Montigny once stopped a sacrifice in person.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tait-indians:
The Tait, or Te-it, those up river, are Cowichan people of Salishan stock. They live on the Lower Fraser between Nicomen and Yale in British Columbia. Their chief reserves sit under the Fraser River agency. Chehalis holds 116 people, Cheam 95, Hope 79, and Yale 76. From perhaps 3,000 souls a century ago, they fell to 932 in 1890. By 1910 they numbered only 578.

Oblates began preaching with Father Grandidier in 1869. Drunkenness and violence had then sunk the whole Cowichan tribe low. Within two years the Tait were reclaimed, sober, law-abiding, and nearly all Catholic. Protestant testimony credited one unpaid priest fed by the Indians. St Mary's Mission, founded in 1861, remains their chief school. A smaller school stands at Yale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tamanac-india:
The Tamanac were a formerly important Cariban tribe on the Cuchivero River. That river feeds the lower Orinoco in Venezuela. In 1749 part of them joined part of the Saliva at San Luis del Encaramada. The Jesuit historian Father Gilii founded that mission on the Orinoco above the Apure. Gilii lived with them eighteen years, until the Jesuits' expulsion handed the missions to Franciscans.

New rulers, revolutionary disorder, neglect, fevers, and war then ruined the missions. By 1840 the Tamanac were virtually extinct except for scattered individuals. Like the Maipure in culture, they told a deluge myth. A man and woman survived atop Mount Tamanaca and refounded humanity from a palm fruit. Their hero Amalivaca came by boat from the east. He left sacred carvings on inaccessible cliffs before returning the same way.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-acacians:
The Acacians, also called Homoeans, were an Arian sect that emerged before the Synods of Ariminum and Seleucia in 359. The sect owed its name and importance to Acacius, Bishop of Caesarea, whose scriptural phraseology theory it adopted, summed up in catchwords like homoios and homoios kata panta. To grasp Acacianism's significance in Arianism's progress, recall that Nicaea's homoousion definition of 325, far from ending debate, sharpened it. It confused formulations on the Lord's relation to His Father.

After Constantius gained sole power on his brother's death in 350, crisis ripened. The new Augustus, vacillating and fond of theological debate, became a puppet of the Eusebian faction. Three parties stood in the Church: the Orthodox or Nicaean party, backing Athanasius; the Eusebian or Court party with Semi-Arian followers; and last, the Anomoean party of Aetius. In 357 Ursacius and Valens, astute advocates of the Anomoeans, pushed their line.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-ass-in-ca:
An ugly ancient slur gives this entry its subject: the charge that Christians worshipped an ass, known as onolatry. Tacitus and other writers first laid it on the Jews, and hatred later passed it to Christians. Tertullian, writing about 197, tells of an apostate Jew parading through Carthage with a toga-clad figure bearing ass's ears and hoofs, labelled as the God of the Christians.

Minucius Felix repeats the insult. The entry then turns to its pictured form: a caricature of the Crucifixion scratched on a Palatine wall, found in 1857. It shows a boy before a crucified figure with an ass's head and the words Alexamenos worshipping his God. Readers learn how mockery, graffiti, and pagan gossip combined into one of antiquity's most persistent libels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-florians:
A free-standing order often misread as a Cistercian branch is set right here. Abbot Joachim of Flora founded the Florians in 1189 and wrote their rules, keeping many Cistercian ways while adding sharper hardships. Barefoot, in white garb of very coarse cloth, they prayed from a Breviary set out unlike that of Cîteaux.

Celestine III blessed the rules in 1196, and the order spread swiftly to some thirty-five houses, all within Italy. Paid abbots named from outside, starting in 1470, sped its decline, and houses passed to Cîteaux, the Grande Chartreuse, or the Dominicans. By 1570 no free Florian house remained.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-pious-soc:
Vincent Mary Pallotti founded this missionary society in 1835, and its members, generally called Pallottini Fathers, carry its work here. Its object joins two tasks: keeping faith among Catholics, above all emigrants facing grave dangers, and spreading faith among non-Catholics and unbelievers. Three classes make up the society's membership.

Priests, clerics, and lay brothers form the first class. Sisters, following the Rule of Saint Francis, teach, catechise, and tend the temporal needs of churches and houses, working among emigrants in America and unbelievers in Africa and Australia. Affiliated clergy and laity, the third class, aid the missions by prayer, work, and money.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-roman-con:
Departments that help the Holy See run the universal Church are the subject here, above all the Roman Congregations, Sacred Congregations of Cardinals. Their members, cardinals as chief collaborators of the sovereign pontiff, give them weight beyond any other curial body. Yet cardinals have not always shared in administration the same way across history.

Necessity birthed them: questions submitted for papal decision needed study, legal sifting, and facts established before judgment. Origins, growth, and the great congregations themselves, from Holy Office to Propaganda, follow in turn. Readers learn how Rome's machinery of government took shape and still turns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-fitz-s:
Thomas Fitz-Simons, an American merchant born in Ireland in 1741, helped frame the United States and sat in its first Congress. In Philadelphia by 1758, he married into the Meade family and traded in partnership with George Meade until 1784. He was among the deputies at Carpenter's Hall whose conference grew into the Continental Congress. His 1774 election as a provincial deputy was the first time a Catholic held public office in Pennsylvania.

He raised a militia company for the Trenton campaign and served in the Congress of the Confederation from 1782. In 1787 he helped frame the Constitution, where he voted to limit suffrage to freeholders. Under the new Constitution he entered the first Congress and sat on the Committee on Ways and Means.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-stephe:
Thomas Stephens, also known in India as Padre Estevao, was the first Englishman in India, born about 1549 at Bulstan, Wiltshire, and dying at Goa in 1619. His father was an influential London merchant. Careful searches find no trace of him at Oxford, despite older claims, though he likely knew Campion and other Catholic Oxford men whose example may have shaped his conversion.

Joining Thomas Pounde in a wish for the Indian missions, he entered the Jesuits at Rome and reached Goa, where he spent the rest of his life. His Christian Puranna is a Marathi-Konkani poem in over ten thousand stanzas on the Old and New Testaments. His grammar of Konkani was the first grammar of an Indian tongue by a European, and the two works made him a pioneer of Indian Christian literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thompson-rive:
The Thompson River Indians, also called Thompson Indians or Knife Indians, are a Salishan people of British Columbia. Their proper name is Ntlakyapamuk, and they lived around the meeting of the Thompson and Fraser rivers, from Yale toward Lillooet and Ashcroft. They counted five subtribes among themselves and lived by hunting, fishing and gathering roots and berries.

Simon Fraser passed through their country in 1808, and Hudson's Bay posts soon followed. Jesuit missionaries reached them from 1845. Their numbers, perhaps near four thousand at first, fell to 1,782 by 1910 through smallpox and other ills that came with white settlement. They now live on small reserves under the Kamloops-Okanagan agency, chief among them Lytton, Lower Nicola and Cooks Ferry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ticuna-indian:
The Ticuna are an Indigenous people of the upper Amazon, forming a distinct language group. They lived in river settlements and forest camps along the north bank of the river, from Loreto in Peru to below Tabatinga in Brazil. About 2,500 in number, they were split almost evenly between Peru and Brazil, with about a third Christianized in missions.

They lived by hunting and fishing, and by gathering wax, rubber, gum and sarsaparilla for trade. They were famed as makers of curare poison for blowgun arrows, a secret craft using Strychnos and Cocculus plants. The poison, kept in cane tubes or clay pots, was their chief trade good across the upper Amazon. Mission visitors also record their singing, dress and village order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-timucua-india:
The Timucua were a principal group of ancient Florida, later destroyed by the English of Carolina and their Indigenous allies. Their name, also spelled Atimuca and Timucua, likely comes from atimoqua, meaning lord or chief, a title early Spaniards mistook for a tribal name. Cognate tribes held all of north Florida, from Cape Canaveral and Tampa Bay to beyond the St. Mary's River.

The Timucua proper centred on the St. John's River, where the chief Outina ruled some forty villages near present Welaka. They lived in settled, partly farming villages, eating game, fish, wild fruit and bread from the koonti root. Spanish missions among them flourished for a time after St. Augustine's founding in 1565, before the English of Carolina and their allies utterly destroyed them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-toba-indians:
The Toba are a people of the Gran Chaco in South America, of Guaycuran language stock, kin to the Abipon and Mocovi. Their range covered forest and marsh west of the Paraguay River, near the lower Pilcomayo and Vermejo, across Paraguay and north-east Argentina, with raids westward to Oran and Tarija. Their name comes from the Guarani tobai, meaning opposite, for those across the river from the Guarani.

Perhaps two thousand in number, they lived by hunting and fishing, went nearly naked, wore their hair long, and tattooed face and body with vegetable dye. They were tall and well built, hardened by going barefoot over thorns and sharp rock. Their language, customs and way of life closely match the Abipon, among whom the Jesuit Dobrizhoffer worked a century and a half earlier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tonica-indian:
The Tonica, also called Tunica, are a small Indigenous people of the lower Mississippi, forming a distinct language group. When the French first knew them they lived in small villages on the lower Yazoo River, allied with the Yazoo and Ofogula, numbering perhaps seven hundred. Their name means the people, and they may be the Tanico met by De Soto's expedition in 1540.

Their recorded history opens in the summer of 1698, when Quebec missionaries Montigny, Davion and La Source visited them just after smallpox had ravaged the region. Davion founded a mission among them the next year, learning their language and serving allied tribes. The Tonica stayed loyal friends of the French, a loyalty the entry links to their lack of kinship with surrounding peoples. They kept a temple with a sacred fire and honoured nine chief gods.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tonkawa-india:
The Tonkawa are a tribal group of eastern Texas, forming a distinct language group, now reduced to a remnant of about forty people. They may once have numbered two thousand, counting the Tonkawa proper with the Yojuane, Mayeye, Ervipiame and others. They call themselves Titskan-watich, meaning natives, and the origin of the name Tonkawa is unknown.

They roamed the middle Trinity and Colorado rivers, planting nothing and living on buffalo, game, mesquite fruit, cactus fruit and wild roots. They dwelt in buffalo-skin tipis or brush shelters, rode well, and carried bow, spear and shield. Neighbouring peoples hated them for their practice of eating human flesh, which gave them the name Man Eaters and led to their outlawry. They also led the ritual use of peyote, a cactus eaten to bring waking visions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-totonac-india:
The Totonac were one of the smaller cultured peoples of ancient Mexico, holding the coast province of Totonicapan at the Spanish conquest. Their land covered most of modern Vera Cruz state with the Zacatlan district of Puebla, holding some fifty towns and perhaps a quarter of a million people. Their capital, Cempoala, five miles inland from Vera Cruz, held about 25,000.

They were the first people Cortes met on landing in 1519. By their own tradition they had come from the northwest some eight centuries earlier and ruled an independent kingdom until the Aztecs subdued them about twenty-five years before the Spaniards came. Ground down by tribute and seizure for sacrifice, their king Chicomacatt welcomed Cortes, offered fifty thousand warriors against Montezuma, and helped found Vera Cruz. About 100,000 Totonac still survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ubiquitarians:
The Ubiquitarians, also called Ubiquists, were a Lutheran party that taught the ubiquity of Christ's body. Ubiquity means bodily presence everywhere. The doctrine took shape at the Lutheran synod of Stuttgart on 19 December 1559, under John Brenz of Swabia. It built on the Württemberg Confession sent to the Council of Trent in 1552. It grew from the fierce dispute over Christ's presence in the Eucharist, the tenth article of the Augsburg Confession of 1530, which Melanchthon had drafted for Charles V.

Brenz and his allies argued that Christ's human nature shares in the divine attributes after the union of natures. His body must therefore be present wherever his divinity is, and so in the sacrament. Other Lutherans rejected the claim, splitting German Protestantism for a generation. The entry lays out the doctrine, its grounds, and its slow fading, giving background to a controversy now largely forgotten outside church history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-unitarians:
Unitarians are a liberal Protestant body whose distinctive tenet is belief in a one-person God rather than a tri-personal Trinity. The name in a broad sense covers all deniers of the Trinity, Christian or not. In its specific use it marks the organized form of Christianity that stresses the unity of God's personality. The term seems to have arisen about 1570, appears in a decree of the Transylvanian Diet at Lecsfalva in 1600, and gained official church sanction in 1638.

It replaced older labels such as anti-Trinitarian, Arian, Racovian, and Socinian. The name first appears in England in 1682 and grew frequent in the United States from 1815, though some anti-Trinitarians received it coldly. The entry traces the body through Poland, Transylvania, England, and America, setting out its doctrine, worship, and leading minds, and noting how far its liberal temper carried it from older Christian creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valentinus-an:
Valentinus was the best known and most influential of the Gnostic heretics, born, by Epiphanius's account, on Egypt's coast. Trained in Hellenistic learning at Alexandria, he went to Rome, perhaps to spread his views, arriving under Pope Hyginus and staying until the pontificate of Anicetus. For perhaps fifteen years he first allied himself with Rome's orthodox community, then tried to set up his heretical system.

His errors brought excommunication, after which he moved to Cyprus, resumed teaching, and died probably about 160 or 161. Valentinus claimed his ideas came from Theodas, a disciple of St Paul, but his system wove Aeons, a fall, and redemption into an elaborate myth. The entry sets out his doctrine, his school's divisions, and the church's answer, a compact guide to second-century Gnosticism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-corn:
John Cornelius, also called Mohun, was born of Irish parents at Bodmin in Cornwall on the Arundell estate of Lanherne in 1557, and martyred at Dorchester on 4 July 1594. Sir John Arundell took interest in the talented boy and sent him to Oxford. Dissatisfied with the new religion taught there, Cornelius went to the great seminary of martyrs at Reims, and on 1 April 1580 entered the English College at Rome for theology.

After ordination he was sent as a missionary to England and laboured there nearly ten years, practising mortification, devoted to meditation, and zealous in ministry. While chaplain to Lady Arundell, Dorset's sheriff arrested him on 24 April 1594 at Chideock Castle. With his three companions, Thomas Bosgrave, John Carey, and Patrick Salmon, he was condemned at Dorchester on 2 July 1594 and suffered for his priesthood, the entry recounting their joint witness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-verbum-supern:
Verbum supernum prodiens is the opening line shared by two Latin hymns, one for the Nativity of Christ and one for the institution of the Eucharist. The hymnologist Daniel noted the apt parallel: the Word made flesh at Bethlehem remains present through the ages in the Eucharist, justifying the two hymns' similar forms.

The Nativity hymn, sometimes ascribed to Ambrose or Gregory the Great but of unknown authorship. Was the usual Matins hymn from the tenth century, rhymed throughout in couplets until Urban VIII's revisers altered every stanza for classical metre. Its Eucharistic twin, beginning Nec Patris linquens dexteram, escaped those revisers untouched, keeping its accentual rhythm and alternating rhyme.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-visions-and-a:
Visions and apparitions are treated here as supernatural, not natural, sights, due to direct intervention by a power above man. Cardinal Bona distinguishes them: an apparition occurs when we do not know whether the figure seen relates to a real being. A vision when we connect it with a real being, though most mystics use the terms interchangeably.

Following Augustine, mystical writers divide visions into three kinds. Corporeal vision shows an object supernaturally to the body's eyes. It may come by a figure truly present striking the retina, or by a higher agent directly modifying the visual organ to produce an equivalent sensation. The first is the usual manner, as with Bernadette at Lourdes. Imaginative vision works through the imagination, and intellectual vision through the intellect itself. By ideas acquired naturally but applied or illumined by God, or, beyond reason's range, by miraculous infusion of new ideas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wakash-indian:
The Wakash are a linguistic family of North America's Pacific coast, inhabiting British Columbia's western shore from 50°30' to Garden Channel. Western and northwestern Vancouver Island, and a small region around Cape Flattery, Washington. They comprise several tribes speaking separate dialects, the three most important being Hailtzuk, Kwakiutl, and Nootka. The name Wakash, meaning good, was given by an early explorer who mistook it for a tribal name.

In culture they closely resemble their Salishan neighbours to the south and Tsimshian to the north, and physically and linguistically they are akin to the Salishan. In 1803 Nootka killed almost all the crew of the American ship Boston. The Hudson's Bay post at Victoria in 1843 brought constant contact. With white immorality and smallpox their numbers fell from about 5,200 in 1903 to 4,584 in 1909, including 2,070 Kwakiutl and 2,494 Nootka.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walla-walla-i:
The Walla Walla are a Shahaptian tribe living on the Walla Walla, or rushing water, River and the Columbia in Washington and Oregon, from the Snake River to the Umatilla. Their language is akin to Nez Percé but forms a distinct dialect, and by the treaty of 1855 they were placed on Oregon's Umatilla reservation.

They still remain, numbering only 461 and mixed with Nez Percé and Cayuse. Family organization was loose and the clan system unobserved, while scanty food, mainly roots, berries, and salmon, forced frequent migrations and prevented any lasting village system. Today most of the tribe farm and breed stock. Visited by Lewis and Clark in 1804, they were evangelized by Jesuit pioneers of the Northwest about forty years later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-welsh-monasti:
Welsh monastic foundations begin from a striking scarcity: few saints of the early British Church before the Saxon invasion are known to history, Alban, Julius. Aaron seeming the only martyrs of Diocletian's time whose names survive. Once the British Church was driven into Wales in the fifth century, saints and scholars appear in abundance. Wales became a home for saints, with no fewer than 479 villages and towns named for local saints.

Llandewi marks where David, Bishop of Caerleon then Menevia, is said to have finally refuted Pelagius, Llangybi recalls Cybi, Llanbadarn Padern, Beddgelert Celert, Llangattock Cadoc, and Llandudno Tudno. Bangor on the Dee, its name said to derive from blessed choir, held, in Bede's words, learned men at Augustine's coming, though its founder and chronicles are lost.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wichita-india:
The Wichita are a confederacy of Caddoan stock, formerly dwelling between the Arkansas River in Kansas and the Brazos River in Texas, now located in Oklahoma within the former Wichita reservation. They call themselves Kitikitisch and sometimes Tawehash, meanings unknown, and claim common stock with the Pawnee. Nine former tribal names survive, but only three divisions remain: Tawakoni, Waco, and Wichita proper. Before Texas's annexation the Wichita proper lived north of the Red River around the Wichita Mountains.

First met about 1541 in Quivira during Coronado's expedition, they were evangelized by Fray Juan de Padilla, who stayed behind with companions and won martyrdom three years later. Visited by the French soldier La Harpe in 1719, who found them given to cannibalism, they were later driven southwest by Osage and Chickasaw. They destroyed the Spanish San Sabá missions in 1758, suffered smallpox severely in 1801, and made their first peace treaty in 1835.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-wilhelmus-nuy:
Wilhelmus Nuyens was a Dutch doctor who became a leading Catholic historian of the Netherlands. Born at Avenhorn in 1823, he died at Westwoud in 1894. He studied medicine at Utrecht, took his doctorate in 1848, and practised at Westwoud while giving spare hours to verse and history. An early poem volume on medieval themes came out in 1856, the same year as his two-volume study of Catholicism and European culture.

His masterwork traced the Dutch revolt of 1559 to 1598 in eight parts, weighing facts with care and fairness rather than unearthing new sources. It showed Dutch Catholics what rights they could claim in the state. He followed it with histories of church and political strife to 1625, a twenty-part general history of the Dutch people, and a history from 1815 onward. A school history that reached twenty-five editions followed. A fund in his name still aided Dutch Catholic historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-se:
William of Sens was a twelfth-century French architect who rebuilt the choir of Canterbury Cathedral after fire. Supposed born at Sens, he is first named in September 1174 as the master charged with raising the choir first built by Prior Conrad and burned that year. A monk's account of the blaze records the commission. Viollet-le-Duc argued from the close likeness between Canterbury's twelfth-century work and Sens Cathedral's work of the same years that the link was sound.

In 1178 or 1179 a fall forced William to quit the job and return to France, where he died within a few years. Another William, called the Englishman, finished the church's eastern arm in 1184. Beyond Canterbury histories and Viollet-le-Duc's French architecture study and Sens monograph, little more is known of him, yet his choir stands as a landmark of early Gothic building in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-stark:
William Starke Rosecrans was an American general, diplomat, and congressman, and a convert to Catholicism. Born at Kingston, Ohio, in 1819, he died near Redondo, California, in 1898. Of Dutch stock settled through Pennsylvania into Ohio, he graduated from West Point in July 1842, served in engineers, then taught at the academy until 1847, becoming a Catholic in those years. He quit the army in 1854.

Civil war recalled him as a volunteer colonel, then brigadier-general in June 1861. He commanded in West Virginia, Mississippi, and Tennessee with steady success until Bragg beat him at Chickamauga on 19 and 20 September 1863, after which Missouri service ended his field career. He then served as minister to Mexico in 1868, pursued railroads there until 1881, sat in Congress in 1880 and 1882, and ran the United States Treasury register from 1885 to 1893.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-winnebago-ind:
The Winnebago Indians are a Siouan people of Green Bay, kin to the Iowa, Missouri, and Oto. Their name, from Chippewa winipeg, means filthy water, first given to their lake; they called themselves Horogi, fish-eaters, or Hochungarra, trout nation. Nicollet found them at Green Bay in 1634 among Sauk, Fox, and Menominee neighbours, and Jesuits Allouez and Dablon wintered with them in 1669 and 1670.

Tradition places them earlier at Red Banks on Lake Michigan, and the 1671 Jesuit relation says Illinois captors once held then freed them. Friendly to the French in trade and slow to join the English, they later proved loyal in the Revolution and the War of 1812. Treaties in 1825 and 1832, removal to Minnesota in 1846 and Blue Earth in 1856, and Omaha lands in Nebraska followed the Sioux war. They numbered 2152 in 1886 and 2333 in 1910, living on fish, rice, game, and maple sugar, honouring Manuna with medicine and winter war dances.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-yakima-indian:
The Yakima Indians are a Shahaptian people of Washington, named for the Yakima River, meaning runaway. They called themselves Waptailmim or Pakintlema, from their Union Gap village. Lewis and Clark met them as Cutsahnim. By the treaty of 1855 they joined thirteen other tribes in giving up land from the Cascades to the Snake and Palus Rivers and from Lake Chelan to the Columbia. They formed one body on the reservation under Chief Kamaiakan.

War broke out and the plan waited until 1859, and some Palus never reached it. Since then Yakima has named all treaty peoples. In 1909 about 1900 Indians lived on the reservation, few true Yakima. The Yakima followed Shahaptian ways: salmon, roots, and berries, and trade between the Cascades' west and the eastern Rockies. Their life held buffalo hunts over the mountains, skin tipis, mat houses, and now farming and stock-breeding. Almost all are Catholic through Jesuit missioners.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-yamasee-india:
The Yamasee Indians were a Muskhogean people of the Savannah River country and Florida, now vanished as a separate tribe. Spanish missionaries under Fray Antonio Sedeño began work among them about 1570 with little trouble, until Spanish officials tried to ship some Yamasee to the West Indies as labourers and provoked rebellion. Many fled to English South Carolina and settled there.

In 1715 English traders' extortion and cruelty drove the Yamasee to arms and a general massacre of white settlers. Governor Craven beat them at Salkiehatchen and drove them back to Florida, where they allied with Spain. In 1727 the English destroyed their village near Saint Augustine and massacred most of them. Survivors merged with the Seminole and Hitchiti, though a small band still kept the name in 1812. Domingo Báez compiled their grammar and catechism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-yaqui-indians:
The Yaqui Indians are a Cahita people of the Rio Yaqui country, now scattered through Sonora in Mexico. They stand out as the only Indian tribe in constant contact with whites never fully subdued. Guzmán first mentions them in his 1531 expedition account. In 1610 they made peace with Spain, and Catholic missions opened at once among a people already skilled at farming and cotton weaving.

In 1740 the Yaqui attacked Spain after settlers meddled with their missionaries, and risings recurred, the latest in 1901. In 1907 Mexico tried to break hostile strength by deporting several thousand Yaqui to Yucatán and Tehuantepec. The tribe now numbers about 23,000. Old homes of adobe and reeds with grass-and-clay flat roofs still serve some, while others work Sonora mines or make palm hats, mats, and reed baskets. Most Yaqui today are Catholic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-yazoo-indians:
The Yazoo Indians were a small Mississippi tribe of the lower Yazoo River, close allies of the Tonica. Their tongue seems akin to Tonica speech. In 1699 Father Davion founded a Tonica mission and tended allied tribes too. Under Carolina English traders' sway, the Yazoo helped the Koroa murder Father Foucault and three Frenchmen asleep in 1702, and Davion withdrew for a time.

France built Fort Saint Pierre near their village in 1718, and young Jesuit Jean Rouel took the Yazoo mission in 1722. When Natchez war broke out in 1729, Yazoo and Koroa sided with the Natchez. On 11 December they waylaid and killed Rouel near his cabin with his Black servant, then stormed the neighbouring post and slew its garrison. A captive Frenchwoman had Rouel buried, and Quapaw hands later returned his bell and books. Survivors fled to the Chickasaw and were absorbed by the Choctaw.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-yuracare-indi:
The Yuracare Indians are a Bolivian people between Santa Cruz de la Sierra and Cochabamba, on the Andes' eastern wooded slopes near the Beni and Mamoré rivers. Tall, with oval faces and very dark eyes, the women are called very handsome. They hunt superbly and fight well, roaming freely until Paraguayan Reduction Jesuits founded a mission among them that thrived until the Society's suppression.

Yuracare morals stood low by the entry's account. Marriage dissolved readily, though polygamy went unpractised, families lived without government, sexes ate apart without subordination, and parents were treated almost as slaves by children. Deeply superstitious yet worshipping neither nature nor a higher being, they believed the soul immortal without future reward or punishment. They buried the dead with bows and arrows for a delightful under-earth hunting ground. They live wholly by hunting, duel by public rules, and never advise their children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zapoteca-indi:
The Zapoteca Indians are a powerful Mexican tribe, chiefly in Oaxaca and Guerrero, forming the Zapotecan stock with the Mixteca and Mazateca. At the conquest they stood independent of the Aztec, whom they resembled in customs, and yielded to Spain only after campaigns between 1522 and 1527, submitting finally in 1551. Sedentary and well advanced, they lived in large stone-and-mortar towns, recorded history in hieroglyphics, and fought in cotton armour.

The ruins of Mitla, claimed as their ancestors' tombs, are attributed to them. Modern Zapotecas, nearly 300,000 strong or 750,000 with kinsmen, are intelligent, hard-working citizens, good soldiers and political leaders; Benito Juárez, President of Mexico, was a full-blooded Zapoteca. Now Catholics, they keep some old beliefs, such as burying money with the dead. Their first missionaries were Mercedarian Bartolomé de Olmeda and secular priest Juan Díaz, martyred at Quechula for overthrowing idols.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zoque-indians: Andrew MacErlean's Catholic Encyclopedia entry describes the Zoque, a Mexican tribe dwelling in western Chiapas north of the Sierra Madre and in parts of Tabasco and Oaxaca. Their capital was Ohcahnay, called Tecpantlan in Mexican, the place of the palaces. When Spaniards first met them they practised cannibalism. Most Zoque are now Christianized yet keep traditional beliefs and customs. They speak a language akin to Mixe and live chiefly by maize, tobacco and oranges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zuni-indians:
The Zuni Indians are a Pueblo tribe living at Zuñi on the Rio Zuñi near New Mexico's boundary, with adjoining villages Nutria, Ojo Caliente, and Pescado. Fray Marcos de Niza, a Franciscan, discovered them in 1539.

After storming Hawikuh, Coronado found Civola's rich cities were only seven ordinary pueblos, none over 500 houses. The first permanent mission began at Hawikuh in 1629 under the Franciscans; Fray Francisco Letrado was martyred on 22 February 1632 and Fray Martin de Arvide five days later. In 1680 the Zuñi joined the Pueblo rising, killed their missionary, and fled to their fortress of Taaiyalone. The mission lasted until the nineteenth century, when it decayed for want of priests and resources. Now about 1640 souls, the Zuñi are becoming civilized under United States care, learning English, with Catholic missionaries again at work.
chapters-of-opera-being-historical-and-c:
Chapters of Opera, by Henry Edward Krehbiel, records the lyric drama in New York from its earliest days to the author's present. Krehbiel, musical editor of the New York Tribune, explains in his preface that the season of 1907-08 completed the Metropolitan Opera House's first twenty five years. Through that whole period he occupied the same reviewer's stall, D-15 on the ground floor, and this book is built from what he heard there.

Thirteen chapters of observations mix history, criticism, and personal record: companies, singers, conductors, and the long fight to give New York a permanent opera house. Krehbiel dedicates the volume to his wife Marie and daughter Helen, who shared many of the experiences described. Readers of his earlier Book of Operas get the companion piece here, less about plots than about performances, and about one critic's quarter century in the same seat.
charles-dickens: Charles Dickens, G, k, chesterton's great biography, the inimitable's life. This book preserves that classic. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
commentary-on-the-epistle-to-the-galatia:
Martin Luther's Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, from his 1535 lectures, appears here in Theodore Graebner's translation for a 1937 American edition. Graebner's preface recounts publisher Zondervan's condition: he would streamline Luther into American speech, since Luther remains the greatest name in Protestantism, or not publish at all. The lectures expound Paul's letter verse by verse.

Luther's theme is justification by faith against the law's proper uses: the law serves a civil purpose and drives transgressors to grace, but must not step out of character into Christ's place. The commentary's warmth and combat made it Luther's own favorite of his works. Readers meet the reformer teaching students, not debating popes, in these pages.
discipline-and-other-sermons:
Charles Kingsley's Discipline and Other Sermons gathers twenty-four sermons, opening with Discipline, preached at the Volunteer Camp at Wimbledon in July 1867. Kingsley takes his text from Numbers, on the lion couching down, asking who dare rouse him up.

Later sermons include The Temple of Wisdom, Prayer and Science, God's Training, Good Friday, False Civilization, The Name of God, The Humanity of God, and The Armour of God. Kingsley preaches as a Broad Church clergyman and social reformer, joining moral earnestness to scientific curiosity. Readers of Victorian preaching will find these sermons muscular, humane and characteristic of their author.

The pathways were warming. The data were energy. The 2C were 1.5C. The trajectories were context. The warming were pathways.
doe-osti-3369034-equivalent-equilibrium-: Ion beams — streams of charged atoms — drive everything from chip etching to fusion research. Thomas Patrick Hughes works out when different ion distributions inside a source or beam behave the same way. Knowing which setups are equivalent lets physicists swap models without losing accuracy.
doe-osti-3374722-bioaerosol-profiling-wi: BIOPOP got bioaerosol-profiled, and this DOE report covers open path sensors. The pages detail the field findings. The climate folks get their data. The campaign was profiling. The data were climate. The sensors were path. The BIOPOP were field.

The practices were best. The data were grid. The grid were folks. The communications were practices. The grid were folks.

The physicists get their data. The effects were studies. The data were physicist. The GENIE were imbalance. The kinematic were transverse. The physicists were data.
doe-osti-3684110-cultivation-ready-impro: CRIAS got algae-improved, and this DOE text covers cultivation-ready carbon strains. The pages detail the cultivation findings. The biologists get their data. The efficiency was utilization. The data were biologist. The CRIAS were strains. The carbon were utilization.
doe-osti-3895873-from-design-to-ocean-de: SURF-WEC got Hawaii-deployed, and this DOE lessons cover ocean wave energy projects. The pages detail the from findings. The energy folks get their data. The deployment was ocean. The data were energy. The SURF-WEC were Hawaii. The wave were energy.
early-plays-catiline-the-warrior-s-barro:
Henrik Ibsen's Early Plays gathers Catiline, The Warrior's Barrow and Olaf Liljekrans, translated from Norwegian by Anders Orbeck. The volume belongs to the Scandinavian Classics series, founded in the belief that familiarity with northern literature would help Americans understand Scandinavians.

Ibsen himself insisted that his dramas were not isolated accidents, and the introduction stresses the orderly development of his genius from these early works onward. Catiline shows the young Ibsen already wrestling with rebellion and fate, while the other plays display his romantic, national phase. Readers tracing Ibsen toward Peer Gynt and the later masterpieces should start here.
edison-his-life-and-inventions:
Frank Lewis Dyer, general counsel for the Edison laboratory, and Thomas Commerford Martin, past president of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote this authorized life of Thomas Edison. The contents run from the age of electricity and Edison's pedigree through his Port Huron boyhood and telegraph years. Boston, the stock ticker, and quadruplex telegraphy follow.

Later chapters cover the phonograph, the long hunt for lamp filament, Menlo Park memories, and the building of a complete lighting system. The authors had Edison's papers and cooperation, so technical claims come with inside detail. Their account of ore-concentrating work shows his optimism under staggering requirements. The biography remains a primary source on Edison's methods, if an admiring one.
eight-cousins:
Louisa May Alcott sent a delicate orphan to be raised by science and cousins in Eight Cousins. Rose Campbell, lately bereaved and brought up on salons and sickrooms, arrives at the Aunt Hill in Boston to live under her guardian, Uncle Alec, a sea-surgeon with theories. His prescription scandalizes the aunts: fresh air, plain food, loose dresses, work, and the company of her seven boy cousins, from steady Archie to baby Jamie.

Rose blooms under the regimen, and the cousins' scrapes and festivals fill the year. Alcott writes reform into a family story: health, dress, and girls' education argued through affection rather than lectures. Eight Cousins followed Little Women and shares its faith that love, properly administered, is a kind of medicine. Rose's progress from invalid to manager delights still.
eminent-victorians: Eminent Victorians, Lytton Strachey's famous biographical quartet. The debunking classic. This book preserves that biography. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. Kept for readers. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
evergreens:
Jerome K Jerome begins Evergreens by pitying the shrubs of his title, so dull beside snowdrops, crocuses, and summer roses. Evergreens stand cold and hard while everything else puts on gladness, he writes, and seem dowdier as the garden brightens. The image becomes a way into memory, youth, and the people who stay faithful out of season.

The sketches drift from garden meditation to remembered scrapes, including two proud young men trapped in an undignified position and unwilling to call the family down for help. Jerome mixes the joke with genuine sentiment about spring and lost years. Readers who like his gentle, wandering essays will find the evergreen a fitting emblem for his tone.
familiar-quotations:
Bartlett's Familiar Quotations collects phrases that became household words in English. John Bartlett first made the collection without thought of publication. His preface explains its object in plain terms. It shows what our language owes to many authors for familiar phrases.

An English work on a like plan supplied many additions, Bartlett notes. Quotations were taken from the original sources for accuracy, he claims. Complete indices of authors and subjects serve the reader. The author index runs from Addison and Akenside through Bacon, Bunyan, and Bryant. This copy is a New York issue from Hurst and Company. Bartlett hopes favor will earn a worthier future edition. The book became the standard American quotation treasury.
fast-in-the-ice-adventures-in-the-polar-:
Ballantyne's Fast in the Ice tells of a brig trapped in the Polar Seas. R. M. Ballantyne wrote the adventure, and the record dates it to 1863. Chapter One opens many years after the brig sailed from a British port. That brig never came back, the narrator states at once.

Cheers, wishes, and waved handkerchiefs marked her leaving Old England. Storms battered her, frost stiffened her rigging, and ice rasped her hull. She was forced onto a shore where winter reigns nearly all year. There she lay frozen in for two long years. Her starving crew forsook her on that coast. Ballantyne frames the tale as a wreck that may still lie unvisited.
five-sermons:
Whipple speaks to his church in Five Sermons, printed in 1890. Henry Benjamin Whipple was Bishop of Minnesota. The five pieces come from set days. They mark the opening of the General Convention in October 1889, and the Faribault celebration of the centennial of Washington's inauguration. A third was given at the Missionary Council at Washington the year before.

An address at Lambeth Chapel, at the first session of the Lambeth Conference on July 3, 1888, stands among them. The sampled pages dwell on the African bishops in that company. One had gone from Africa to a university, taken honors, and gone back as a bishop. Whipple thought of the man who carried the cross up the hill to Calvary. Bishop Smythies, off on foot into the interior, drew his tears. The sermons show a missionary bishop's wide heart and plain speech.
flatland-a-romance-of-many-dimensions:
Edwin Abbott Abbott, an English schoolmaster and church scholar, wrote Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions in 1884. He published it under the name of its hero, A Square. The hero lives in Flatland, a world of two dimensions. There men are shapes with many sides, and women are straight lines. Rank follows geometry in a strict social ladder.

A Square dreams of one-dimensional Lineland. Then a Sphere from three-dimensional Spaceland visits him. The Sphere lifts him out of his world to see it from above. Back home, no one will believe him. He is jailed for preaching a third dimension. Abbott mixes math with satire of Victorian class and sex roles. The tale also puzzles over how hard it is to picture what lies past our own senses.
flowers-and-flower-gardens-with-an-appen:
Richardson gossips about gardens in Flowers and Flower-Gardens, printed at Calcutta in 1855. David Lester Richardson was principal of the Hindu Metropolitan College. He warns the reader in his preface that the book is no scientific treatise. It is, he says, mere gossip in print on a pleasant subject, though he hopes it will not be useless.

He wrote for India, and says a good deal on the mythology and language of flowers for that reason. An appendix adds practical instructions for the Anglo-Indian flower-garden. The sampled pages sing the daisy. Richardson quotes Chaucer's praise of the flower that softens all his sorrow at dawn. Then he gives Burns his place, with the poem to a mountain daisy turned up by the plough. The book mixes verse, lore, and garden craft.
food-for-the-lambs-or-helps-for-young-ch:
Orr wrote this small devotional book for new converts, whom he calls Christ's lambs. Its chapters take up mortality, fruit-bearing, dress, and the little foxes that spoil a young faith. Some pieces are borrowed from other writers, among them essays on spiritual decline and seeking first the kingdom of God. Poems close several sections, including one that remembers a little boy taken to heaven on a winter evening.

Charles Ebert Orr signed his preface at Federalsburg, Maryland, in September 1904. He kept the book short on purpose, judging that a small volume gets read more readily than a large one. His hope, stated plainly, is that its sayings lift readers toward a higher and holier life.
forest-and-frontiers-or-adventures-among:
Gordon-Cumming's hunting adventures open with an attack on four patriarchal lions. The scene lies in the African interior, near the junction of the Mariqua and Limpopo rivers. He had resigned his army commission at the Cape of Good Hope to hunt full time. Five years of exploring and shooting wild beasts fill the account.

The compiled pages range far beyond Africa. One passage, drawn from Humboldt, watches jaguars emptying river turtles from their shells with supple paws. Alligators, herons, and vultures join the list of the turtles' enemies. Roualeyn Gordon-Cumming was billed on his title page as the most daring hunter of his day.
george-du-maurier-the-satirist-of-the-vi:
T. Martin Wood surveys the art and character of George du Maurier in this 1913 book, with forty-one illustrations. Du Maurier drew the famous Punch cartoons that mocked Victorian fashion, art talk, and smart society. Late in life he also wrote novels, among them Trilby. Wood divides the study into the artist's world, his art, his work as an author, and his life.

Plates show his work from early magazine drawings to his illustrations for Wives and Daughters. Wood shows how du Maurier's weak eyesight and French training shaped his fine line. The book captures a man who watched his age with a kind, amused eye. Art lovers get both a life story and a gallery of the drawings that made his name.
ghazali-confessions:
Al-Ghazali, the great Muslim thinker of Baghdad, wrote his Deliverance from Error near the end of his life, around 1100. Claude Field's version appeared under the title The Confessions of Al-Ghazzali. Ghazali had been the most famous teacher in Baghdad.

He tells how doubt about all knowledge drove him to quit his post and wander. Years of Sufi practice, he says, gave him the certainty that books could not. The short work reshaped Islamic theology and is still read as a classic of spiritual searching. Many call it the finest autobiography in medieval Islam.
govdocs-archive_org-fer-latin-american-l:
Knights of Lucifer gathers Latin American luciferian and Hyperborean writings by several hands, including L. Wotan, Ignacio Ondargain, Piedra Iberica, Orlando Croy Romero, and Geburah Michel Lycanon. The compilation comes from the esoteric underground of the Spanish-speaking world.

The pieces treat Lucifer as a bringer of light and a rebel against the Christian order, mixed with Hyperborean myth about a lost northern homeland. Such texts circulate in small esoteric circles rather than through bookshops. The collection is held as an archive item, without endorsement, as a sample of that Latin American fringe literature.
