govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AssassinationsR: nsia-AssassinationsRacist Assassinations De Gaulle CIA: the made public government document on killing plots against de Gaulle and the CIA's role. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIACubans_CIA_C: Myra MacPherson, an Associated Press writer, titled her piece on the Bay of Pigs' long aftermath The Last Casualty of the Bay of Pigs. The failed 1961 invasion of Cuba by CIA-trained exiles left prisoners and widows. It left a wound in Cuban-American politics that lasted decades, and MacPherson's article returns to that aftermath. It is preserved as a single article among the archive's CIA and Cuba clippings, from the years when the invasion's story was still being settled.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FensterwaldBern:
Joseph Berger wrote about a new book on the Kennedy assassination by Bernard Fensterwald, titled Coincidence or Conspiracy. Fensterwald built his book around three people. Each of the three had intriguing encounters with both Lee Harvey Oswald and Jack Ruby, the two men at the center of the Dallas story.

A book built on such crossings invites readers to judge the pattern for themselves. Coincidence or planned connection is the question the title poses. Berger's article presents the book and its three figures to readers weighing that question, part of the large literature the assassination produced.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Mexican-America:
Peter Nabokov reported for the Washington Post on December 16, 1968, that Reies Lopez Tijerina had been acquitted. Tijerina led a land-grant movement in New Mexico. The charges grew out of a 1967 raid on a courthouse, in which his followers went looking for a district attorney they meant to arrest.

The raid made Tijerina a national figure in the Chicano movement. His acquittal, on the charges Nabokov covers, was a courtroom victory after a trial that drew wide attention. The article records the verdict and the reaction of officials, who were stunned by it. It preserves a turning point in a movement that tied modern protest to old Spanish land grants.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NewOrleansExcha:
Chris Shearouse wrote about Exchange Alley in New Orleans, in an article titled 'Change in Exchange: Dilemma in an Alley.' The alley was born in 1831 as Exchange Passage. Shearouse covers the debate over its future: what to keep, what to change, and who decides.

Old alleys in the French Quarter carry two centuries of commerce in a few yards of brick. Articles like this one appear when a landmark's fate is argued in public. Shearouse gives the alley's history and the present dispute together. The piece is local journalism about preservation, filed in these papers because the alley also belongs to the Oswald story's New Orleans geography.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Translations_Tr: Called 'Translations,' this declassified US government document rests in the Internet Archive's govdocs collection. Translated from what, by whom, and when - the catalog is mute. No public text located. A task-word for a title, awaiting its papers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba_CDC:
Starting in Havana, American diplomats began reporting strange illnesses with no clear cause. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention spent two years on an epidemiologic investigation of those incidents. Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, posted in February 2021, on the CDC report.

The report left the medical mystery unresolved, as the posting's title says. That non-answer is itself the news: a long, formal study could not settle what hurt the diplomats. Readers interested in the Havana Syndrome debate get the government's own investigative record rather than rumor or press summary.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig:
The National Security Act of 1947 built the machinery of modern American power. Rachel Santarsiero compiled this briefing book, number 799, published in July 2022 for the law's seventy-fifth anniversary. The statute established the CIA and the National Security Council.

It also laid the foundations of the Department of Defense. The posting calls the law's effect a complete overhaul of the executive branch. It transformed how foreign policy was made and powered America's global engagement through the Cold War and beyond. Anyone reading declassified records works inside institutions this single act created, which makes its anniversary set a useful map of the whole system.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_COU:
A new documentary film, COUP 53, examines the 1953 overthrow of Iran's Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddeq. Malcolm Byrne edited this briefing book, posted in August 2020, around a startling item the film features. It is a recently recovered interview with a former MI6 operative.

In that interview, Britain's Secret Intelligence Service is tied to the 1953 kidnapping of Tehran's chief of police. A kidnapping of the capital's police chief was no side detail in a coup; it removed a man who could have resisted. The posting links film research with the declassified record, each strengthening the other.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_iran_Doc:
Relations between Iran and the United States from 1978 to 2015 fill this National Security Archive collection. Those years run from the last period of the Shah's rule, through the revolution and hostage crisis, to the nuclear deal era. A documentary set spanning that whole arc is rare.

Most accounts treat those decades as separate stories: revolution, war, sanctions, talks. A single collection lets readers trace the same two governments across all of them. The value is continuity. Claims made in one decade can be checked against the paper of the next, which is exactly what a relations archive should allow.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: Preoccupations with West Germany's Nuclear Weapons Potential: the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated entry, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
When Bill Clinton took office in January 1993, Boris Yeltsin's Russia was the new partner the United States had to learn to work with. The National Security Archive's electronic briefing book covers the first six months of that relationship. It is built on declassified records of the summits the two presidents held at Vancouver and in Tokyo that year.

The records show joint diplomatic work and a strikingly personal element: Clinton backed Yeltsin directly in his fight with the Russian parliament. That support helped set the tone for years of American policy toward Moscow. For readers, the papers capture a brief season when Washington treated Russia's shaky new democracy as a project worth personal risk from an American president.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_chile-cold-war-he:
Henry Kissinger shaped American foreign policy in the 1970s, and few figures of that era draw stronger praise or sharper blame. Under the heading Power by Any Means Necessary, the National Security Archive assembled a declassified dossier on his record. It is drawn from the secret files of the governments he dealt with, and of the one he served.

A dossier built from declassified papers lets readers test the legend against the memos. Kissinger, often shortened to HAK in the files of the time, left an unusually full paper trail across wars, coups, and secret diplomacy. The collection's value is that it argues with documents rather than opinion, giving critics and defenders alike the same evidence to work from.
graded-lessons-in-english-an-elementary-:
Alonzo Reed and Brainerd Kellogg's Graded Lessons in English is an elementary English grammar, famous for its sentence diagrams. The book teaches pupils to analyse sentences by placing words on a heavy horizontal line for the main clause, with vertical, diagonal and dotted lines for modifiers and subordinate parts.

Lessons proceed step by step, so that a child learns parts of speech, sentence structure and correct usage together, rather than by rote rules alone. Generations of American schoolchildren learned grammar from Reed and Kellogg, and their diagrams became a classroom institution. Teachers and historians of education will find this volume the classic statement of the diagramming method.
great-possessions:
David Grayson, the pen name of Ray Stannard Baker, writes of his country life in Great Possessions. The chapters open with The Well-Flavoured Earth, and turn on smells, green growing things, and places of retirement. One head reads Follow Your Nose! Another warns No Trespass. A good apple gets its own chapter, and so does a trip to the city.

Grayson finds his wealth in soil, seasons, neighbors, and work done by hand. An old stone mason, an auction of antiques, and a man named Bill Richards, styled His Majesty, fill the later pages. The close treats living in the country as a chosen art. The book's quiet claim is in its title: the great possessions are not bought. It is a gentle classic of American back-to-the-land writing.
great-singers-second-series-malibran-to-:
Ferris made this second series of Great Singers in 1881 as a companion to the first, which ran from Bordoni to Sontag. The same limits guide him, he says: only singers who stand without dispute in the front rank get sketches, with lesser lights brought in where a great life needs them. He also gives notice, in several pieces, to a few of the greatest men singers. The series opens with Malibran.

Maria Malibran died young after a fall from a horse, and her blaze of fame sets the tone. The sketches run on through the age of Jenny Lind's rivals to Theresa Titiens, the great dramatic soprano of London. Ferris quotes those who heard them, since no record of their voices could exist. The pair of volumes together gives a full gallery of opera's early stars.
half-portions:
Edna Ferber published Half Portions in 1920, a book of nine short stories. The first, The Maternal Feminine, opens on Aunt Sophy Decker, whom the world files as a spinster. She is unmarried and fifty, stylish stout in blue serge. Broad-toed health shoes and a small, astute hat complete the portrait. Ferber says you would have to coin a term to describe her, or fall back on the dictionary. The tale turns that dry label inside out.

Old Lady Mandle, a long-distance call, and a story in dialect stand among the rest. Ferber writes of working women, mothers, and the Jewish and German folk of her native Midwest, with warmth and a sharp comic ear. The title hints at lives served less than their due. These stories show the craft that would soon make her one of America's best-loved novelists.
handy-dictionary-of-poetical-quotations:
George W. Powers compiled his Handy Dictionary of Poetical Quotations at New York in 1901. His preface states the aim. The book is a ready reference to the most familiar stanzas and lines of the chief English poets. A few selections come from Continental writers. Some less familiar modern pieces are added, which may in time become classic. A portrait of Longfellow leads the book.

The entries run by theme, so that a speaker hunting a line on love, death, or spring can find it fast. Powers notes that the few great poets of the language have struck nearly every chord of human sentiment that verse can show. Such dictionaries stood on every parlor shelf in the age of elocution. This one is a fair specimen, handy in size and catholic in taste.
happy-hawkins:
Robert Alexander Wason put a cowboy at the center of Happy Hawkins and let him tell the tale in dialect. Happy, born in Indiana, ran west as a boy hunting Indians and found hunger instead. Lunch counters, silent ranch bosses, and open ranges school him. His nickname fits: humor carries him through work, fights, and love alike.

The Diamond Dot ranch gives the story its home ground across thirty chapters. Happy convinces a cook, rides under fire, sets a broken leg, and drifts off whenever restlessness calls. A lasso duel, a winter at Slocum's Luck, and questions over Chinese labor mark the middle episodes. Barbie, the ranch girl, slowly turns the comedy toward courtship, discovery, and a wedding day. A final reckoning and an afterglow chapter close the wanderer's account. Western readers who like talk, ranch routine, and a soft heart under the slang will enjoy Happy's company.
human-nature-and-other-sermons:
Joseph Butler, Bishop of Durham, preached the sermons gathered in this Cassell volume of 1887, and the introduction gives his life from his birth at Wantage in 1692. Butler argued his way from a Presbyterian upbringing into the Church of England, took his Oxford degree, and in 1718 became preacher at the Rolls Chapel in London. The sermons on human nature that open the book were preached there.

Butler's argument in those sermons is moral anatomy. Human nature is a system of appetites, affections, self-love, benevolence, and, ruling over all, conscience. Self-love and benevolence are not enemies; each passion has its proper object and place. The later sermons take up charity, resentment, and the love of God. Few English sermons have been argued over so long by philosophers.
hunted-down-the-detective-stories-of-cha:
Charles Dickens opens Hunted Down, his 1860 detective tale, through a retired life assurance manager who claims to have seen more romances in thirty years of business than most men. A smooth client named Slinkton wins his trust, then suspicion, as a young lady's death and an insurance policy come together. The manager sets himself to hunt the man down.

A drunken associate named Beckwith, brandy saucepan in hand, becomes an unlikely instrument of exposure. Dickens builds the short novel from office observation rather than police procedure, making the detective an amateur of character. This edition, from Hard Times and Reprinted Pieces, collects Dickens's contributions to crime writing, a field his Inspector Bucket had already transformed.
in-and-out-of-three-normandy-inns:
Anna Bowman Dodd wrote this travel book on three inns in Normandy, in northern France. Chapters move through Villerville, along an old post road, and to Dives and Honfleur. Landladies, a village, a mussel bed, and a Norman household get close attention. Dodd frames the folk she meets as wholly their own.

Later parts stage two banquets at Dives, with talk after dinner. A duchess praises an old friend's youth at Les Rochers as twilight falls. Seventeenth-century scenes are revived beside nineteenth-century ones. Readers get a warm, detailed stay with Norman hosts and guests.
indian-heroes-and-great-chieftains:
Charles A. Eastman, a Dakota Sioux doctor and writer known also as Ohiyesa, wrote Indian Heroes and Great Chieftains, published in 1919. Eastman profiles the Native leaders he most admired, telling their lives from inside the world that produced them. His pages carry Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse of the Sioux, Red Cloud, Spotted Tail, and Little Crow.

He crosses the continent for others: Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce, Geronimo of the Apache, and the Shawnee and Sac and Fox leaders of older wars. Eastman writes as a bridge figure, educated in white schools yet loyal to his people's honor. The book set out to give young readers, Native and white alike, heroes told truly, and it still reads with quiet force.
inquiries-and-opinions:
Brander Matthews published Inquiries and Opinions in September 1907, dedicating it to Henry Arthur Jones. Essays open with literature in the new century, read first at St. Louis in 1904. An apology for technic and a piece on invention and imagination follow. Poe and the detective story get their own inquiry.

Mark Twain's prose is praised for a huge vocabulary with few dead words. Matthews says Twain speaks only when he has something to say, and says it sharply. Maupassant, Ibsen, and the modern novel and play close the set. The book is a working critic's views on craft.
intentions:
Oscar Wilde gathered his four great critical dialogues and essays as Intentions, first published in 1891 and reprinted by Methuen in 1913. The Decay of Lying opens the book in a Nottinghamshire library, where Vivian argues that art should not copy life because life copies art. Cyril plays the straight man and loses beautifully.

Pen, Pencil, and Poison studies the forger Wainewright as an artist in crime. The Critic as Artist, the longest piece, claims criticism is itself creative, and The Truth of Masks defends costume and paradox in Shakespeare. Wilde's epigrams here became the doctrine of the aesthetic movement, argued with a learning that keeps surprising readers who expected only wit.
jan-of-the-windmill-a-story-of-the-plain:
Jan of the Windmill, a story of the plains by Juliana Horatia Ewing, follows a baby left with a miller's family and raised beside the sails. Ewing's tale appears here in a fifth edition from London, dated 1890, with eleven illustrations by Helen Paterson Allingham. The contents promise a windmiller's wife, strangers at the mill, and a payment of ten shillings a week for the little Jan.

Chapter headings trace the boy's growing up in plain village terms. He works as a nurse boy, minds pigs, and learns beside Abel, the miller's man, who plays schoolmaster over a spelling column. A pocket book and a family Bible carry a five pound reward and a buried question about his birth. Visitors bring a tiny lady with a grand name and a cure for whooping cough. Kindness, class, and a foundling's secret carry the story.
jimmie-higgins:
Jimmie Higgins is a novel by Upton Sinclair, the American writer known for exposing social wrongs. Its contents page alone maps Jimmie's whole path in twenty chapter titles. He meets a candidate, hears a speech, and debates the issue. Then he strikes it rich, helps the Kaiser, and goes to jail.

Later chapters send Jimmie back to nature, face to face with an owner, and into open war. He meets a patriot, dodges trouble, and takes the road. The titles then turn sharp: Jimmie turns Bolshevik, meets a tempter, and wrestles with him. At last he takes the plunge and puts on khaki. Sinclair builds a working man's political education into a story.
journals-of-australian-explorations:
Journals of Australian Explorations gathers the expedition journals of Augustus Charles Gregory and his brother Francis Thomas Gregory. Both men were fellows of the Royal Geographical Society and gold medalists of it. The Brisbane government printer issued the volume in 1884. Its preface explains that readers kept asking for journals long out of print.

Earlier, the journals had appeared only in fragments. This volume collects them whole, for reference and for the permanent record. It leaves the brothers' first impressions unchanged, even where later knowledge corrected them. The first journal covers the 1846 expedition east and north of Swan River. A settlers' expedition under A. C. Gregory in 1848 follows. Together they trace early attempts to open Australia's unknown interior.
judith-of-the-plains:
Judith of the Plains is a novel by Marie Manning, published by Harper and Brothers in 1903. Twenty chapters carry the story, opening simply with Town. Judith works as postmistress, as one chapter title announces. Leander and his lady, the Rodneys at home, and Mrs. Yellett and her 'government' fill the early cast.

The plot moves onto the horse-thief trail and into a cabin in the valley. A round-up, a wolf hunt, and the land of the red silence follow. Mary spends her first day in camp, and Judith adjusts the situation. Cloudburst, hanging threats, and a final ball close the contents. Manning writes a Western of ranch life with a capable heroine at its center.
keith-of-the-border-a-tale-of-the-plains:
Keith of the Border: A Tale of the Plains is a Western novel by Randall Parrish. Thirty-six chapters carry it from The Plainsman to The End. Early chapters stage a sudden arrest and a desperate escape. A ride through sand and desert leads to a wilderness cabin and the girl there.

Keith crosses the ford of the Arkansas and reaches the marshal of Sheridan. Christie Maclaire enters as one who believes in him, and a message from the dead complicates his case. An Indian raid, a duel in the desert, and a single shot raise the stakes. The final chapters bring forgiveness and a last interview. Parrish writes fast frontier adventure around a wronged plainsman clearing his name.
life-of-charles-dickens:
Frank T. Marzials wrote this Dickens life for the Great Writers series. Walter Scott published it in London in 1887. Marzials acknowledges a heavy debt to Forster's life of Dickens. He also used the letters edited by Dickens's family.

Charles Dickens was born on February 7, 1812. Happy Chatham days gave way to family troubles and London hardship. His father entered the Marshalsea, and Charles worked in a blacking business. Marzials compares the boy's isolation with David Copperfield's story. Kitton's Dickensiana lightened Marzials's labor considerably, he acknowledges. Young Charles felt isolation keenly during the blacking warehouse months.
lives-of-the-three-mrs-judsons:
Arabella M. Willson wrote these lives of three missionary wives. Ann, Sarah, and Emily Judson each married the same missionary. All three served as missionaries to Burmah in turn. Lee and Shepard published the book in Boston.

Congress copyright records date its entry to 1855. Portraits of Ann and Emily Judson illustrate the volume. A verse epigraph praises their self-denying band of workers. They counted life cheap to fulfil their ministry, it says. Miller, Orton and Mulligan first entered the copyright in 1855. Charles Dillingham later sold the New York edition.
love-among-the-chickens:
Love Among the Chickens is an early comic novel by P. G. Wodehouse. In his dedication, Wodehouse thanks his friend W. Townend for giving him the stuff. Sixteen years before, he says, they were sprightly lads at school together. The stuff Townend gave him became a chicken farm by the sea.

A young writer joins his friend's hopeless chicken venture on the coast. Hens, eggs, and farm chaos fill the days there. Amid the squawking, the young man falls in love. Wodehouse keeps the tone light, bright, and full of jokes. The book shows his high spirits long before his fame peaked. It is vintage early Wodehouse, warm and very funny.
men-like-gods-dover-thrift-editions:
H. G. Wells published this utopian novel in 1923. Its hero, Mr. Barnstaple, is a tired journalist who takes a holiday drive in 1921. He and several other motorists are suddenly swept three thousand years into the future. This Dover edition reprints the original Macmillan text.

The travelers land in a world remade along Barnstaple's own ideals. Crime, poverty, war, disease, and bigotry have all vanished there. Wells uses the visit to test his hopes for science and social planning. The novel asks whether ordinary modern people could bear such a perfected world, or would spoil it.
missionary-work-among-the-ojebway-indian:
The Reverend Edward F. Wilson tells here how he came to work among the Ojibway of Canada. His contents trace the journey: first experiences, arrival at Sarnia, and work at Kettle Point. He records Indian names given to the missionaries and a Christmas spent on the reserve. The bishop's visit and a first trip to Garden River follow.

Later chapters describe baptisms of pagan Indians and the Red River expedition. Wilson meets Chief Little Pine and winters in Algoma. His account preserves detail about Ojibway life, language, and customs in his era. Mission memoirs like his remain sources, read critically, for nineteenth-century Indigenous history around the Great Lakes.
modern-italian-poets-essays-and-versions:
William Dean Howells wrote these essays on Italy's modern poets, adding his own English versions of their verse. The contents begin with the Arcadian shepherds of the eighteenth century. Giuseppe Parini, Vittorio Alfieri, and Vincenzo Monti follow. Ugo Foscolo and Alessandro Manzoni anchor the Romantic generation.

Howells gives Giacomo Leopardi a place among the later names. Giuseppe Giusti, Giovanni Prati, and Aleardo Aleardi continue the line to his own century. Silvio Pellico, famous for his prison memoir, appears as a poet here. Howells, America's leading novelist-critic of his day, introduced English readers to Italian poetry he had loved since his consulate at Venice.
more-toasts-jokes-stories-and-quotations:
Marion Dix Mosher, a Rochester public librarian, compiled this handbook in 1922. The H. W. Wilson Company published it at New York. At 552 pages it promises jokes, stories, and quotations for speakers. The contents open with an essay on the importance of humor.

That essay, reprinted from the Nineteenth Century, calls humor a divine gift. It deals, the essay says, with a mystery pleasantly woven into daily life. Toasts fill the body of the book, with an index for finding them fast. Banquet speakers and toastmasters of the 1920s kept such compilations at hand, and librarians like Mosher built them for reference shelves.
mother-carey-s-chickens:
Kate Douglas Wiggin opens this family story with the petrels called Mother Carey's chickens. The birds flit from wave to wave like swallows over the sea. Mother Carey herself heads the first chapter, and her chickens the second. A chapter called The Common Denominator introduces the family's shared life.

Then comes The Broken Circle, and the Careys' flitting, or move, to Beulah. Cousin Ann, a service on the threshold, and a housewarming mark the new home. Nancy's idea and Nancy's coming out carry the eldest girl forward. Wiggin, author of Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, writes of a widowed mother holding her brood together with cheer.
my-literary-passions:
William Dean Howells maps his reading life in this 1895 book. The contents begin with the bookcase at home. Goldsmith, Cervantes, and Irving mark his early loves. First fiction and drama follow, then Scott and Pope.

Uncle Tom's Cabin, Ossian, and Shakespeare each get a chapter. Dickens, Thackeray, Dante, and Tolstoy mark later stages. He ends with new names like Zola, Hardy, and Galdos. Howells tells how each book formed his taste and craft. The memoir is a reader's autobiography, warm and exact, showing how one boy's shelf became an American man of letters.
nasa-tm-19650015349-1964-publications:
Compiled by the Materials Division at Marshall and dated January 30, 1965, this volume lists NASA publications from 1964. The entries are technical notes from across the agency's programs. Subjects run from materials and propulsion to spacecraft and engineering development work of many kinds.

A yearly list like this one served as a finding aid. Researchers could scan one volume to see what the agency had released. They could then order the notes that mattered to their own work. As a record, it also freezes one busy year in place. The range of titles shows how wide NASA's technical work had become by 1964.
nasa-tm-19660020445-an-approximate-solut:
Peter Ralph Kurzhals submitted this work in May 1966 as a doctoral thesis at Virginia Polytechnic Institute. His subject is the motion of a rotating spacecraft of any shape. Real spacecraft tumble or spin in complex ways, pushed by small uneven forces. Kurzhals offers an approximate analytic solution for that motion, with disturbance effects that can vary over time.

Exact solutions exist only for simple, tidy shapes. Flight vehicles are neither simple nor tidy. An approximate solution that handles arbitrary shapes fills a real gap. Disturbance functions stand for the small torques that slowly change a spin in flight. Thesis work of this depth, done inside the space program, fed directly into attitude control practice.
nasa-tm-19680013932-biosatellite-2-opera:
John W. Dyer of NASA's Ames Research Center presented this account of Biosatellite II operations in February 1968. The spacecraft carried living specimens into orbit so scientists could study how space flight affects life. Dyer explains how the mission was planned, flown, and recovered using services that already existed.

The craft weighed about 950 pounds and rode a two-stage Delta launch vehicle. About half its weight sat in the reentry vehicle that returned the specimens to Earth. Batteries supplied power, since the smooth craft carried no solar panels. Gas jets and gyroscopes held rotation very slow, keeping forces on the specimens small during the flight.
nasa-tm-19680016151-morphological-studie:
Webb Haymaker of NASA's Ames Research Center reviews studies of laminar lesions in the brain in this essay, prepared in 1967. The cerebral cortex has six thin layers, or laminae. Researchers asked whether one layer could be destroyed while the others stayed intact.

If one layer alone could be removed, its role in cortical electrical activity could be tested. An early study used proton radiation on cats to damage a narrow zone of cortex. That work, reported ten years earlier, showed selective damage was feasible. Haymaker surveys the morphology, or physical form, of such lesions. Dose and tissue volume factors shape how the damage develops in the cortex.
nasa-tm-19700009336-low-frequency-cosmic:
Four Goddard Space Flight Center researchers, J. K. Alexander, L. W. Brown, T. A. Clark, and R. G. Stone, wrote this preprint on low frequency cosmic noise. Cosmic noise is the steady radio hiss arriving from our own galaxy. Their question is what that hiss reveals about the local system of stars and gas near Earth.

Working from galaxy-wide radio measurements, the team estimates how thermal electrons are spread through nearby space. They also estimate the glow from fast electrons spiraling in magnetic fields, plus the flow of low energy cosmic ray electrons. Their radio figures run far above direct measurements, by about a hundredfold. They suggest strong solar effects or an uneven cosmic ray spread could explain the gap.
nasa-tm-19710023966-the-degeneration-of-:
H. Volland and H. G. Mayr of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in August 1971, numbered X-621-71-331. It concerns Hough functions, the mathematical shapes that describe atmospheric tides in the lower atmosphere. The authors ask what happens to those shapes high in the thermosphere, where dissipation takes hold.

Heat conduction, viscosity, and drag between neutral air and ions all modify the Hough functions as height increases. The paper shows they ultimately degenerate into spherical harmonics above about two hundred kilometers. That degeneration changes the latitude structure of the tidal modes and how waves travel upward. In particular, the twice-daily tidal mode becomes nearly trapped above about one hundred sixty kilometers, explaining its apparent absence in upper thermosphere dynamics.
nasa-tm-19720007680-review-of-magnetic-f:
Norman F. Ness of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this review in November 1971, numbered X-690-71-465, on magnetic field observations in the magnetosphere. By then satellites were routinely mapping Earth's magnetic bubble and its boundaries. Ness gathered the recent observations into one account of what they showed.

The review describes improved pictures of the magnetosphere, magnetosheath, plasma sheet, and bow shock, and how storms distort them. Observations of the polar cusp region support the idea that particles reach the plasma sheet through the polar neutral points. Distortions there suggest currents flowing along field lines far from Earth. The plasma sheet's field reversal region proved more complex than simple single neutral line models. No clear solar cycle change in magnetosphere structure was detected.
navy-boys-behind-the-big-guns:
Halsey Davidson wrote Navy Boys Behind the Big Guns as a sea adventure for boys. Its subtitle is Sinking the German U-Boats, which places it in the First World War. George Sully and Company published it in New York, with pictures. Davidson had written other Navy Boys books before this one.

A front picture shows gunners stripped for action, alert as panthers, by their guns. The series list names Navy Boys After the Submarines and Navy Boys Chasing a Sea Raider. Sea fights, convoys, and prizes fill those titles. Young readers of the war years got their navy's fight told as fast, brave action close to the guns.
new-tabernacle-sermons:
T. De Witt Talmage preached the sermons in New Tabernacle Sermons at the Brooklyn Tabernacle. George Munro published volume one in New York in 1886. Talmage had already issued Crumbs Swept Up and The Abominations of Modern Society. A portrait of the preacher fronts the book.

Sermon titles range from Brawn and Muscle to The Pleiades and Orion. The Queen's Visit, Vicarious Suffering, and The Lord's Razor follow. Windows Toward Jerusalem, The Great Assize, and The Road to the City keep the biblical frame. One late sermon takes up capital and labor. Talmage spoke to city crowds on faith, duty, and the day they lived in.
options:
O. Henry gathered sixteen short stories in Options, one of his late collections of tales built on surprise endings and city-and-country contrasts. The table of contents names pieces such as The Third Ingredient, The Hiding of Black Bill, Supply and Demand, Buried Treasure, The Higher Pragmatism, Best-Seller, and Rus in Urbe.

The opening story, The Rose of Dixie, starts in Toombs City, Georgia, where a stock company has raised a hundred thousand dollars to found a magazine. A committee calls on Colonel Aquila Telfair, a man of learning, family, and Southern tradition, to beg him to edit it. O. Henry sets the scene in the colonel's inherited library of ten thousand volumes, and the comedy of old South meeting new publishing begins.
osage-traditions:
James Owen Dorsey was a missionary-linguist for the Smithsonian's Bureau of Ethnology. He recorded Osage Traditions in Indian Territory in January 1883. A secret society of seven degrees guarded the people's traditions, he learned. His short stay allowed only fragments. Initiated Osage men gave him parts of two traditions.

Red Corn, of the Tsiu washtake gens, dictated the first tradition. He had it from Sadekihe. Red Corn's own story fills much of the introduction. A white man adopted him. He studied at a Jesuit college in Missouri. Later he practiced as an Indian doctor, known to whites as Bill Nix. The pamphlet preserves sacred tradition and the tale of its telling.
our-churches-and-chapels-their-parsons-p:
A. Hewitson, writing as Atticus in the Preston Chronicle, surveyed every place of worship in Preston. Churches, chapels, parsons, priests, and congregations all came under his eye. He reprinted the sketches as a book in 1869. His preface warns readers that a lively spirit runs through the descriptions, which may offend the phlegmatic, the sad-faced, and the puritanical.

Hewitson promises the solemn their facts, the facetious their humour, and the analytical their criticism. The work embodies a fuller history of each Preston place of worship than any yet published, he claims. The town's Anglican, Catholic, and Dissenting clergy helped generously. Genial humour, he insists, only makes the dry enumeration palatable.
out-with-gun-and-camera-or-the-boy-hunte:
Edward Stratemeyer, writing as Captain Ralph Bonehill, sent his boy hunters into the mountains in Out with Gun and Camera, the fourth volume of the Boy Hunters Series. Its thirty chapters promise adventures with rod, rifle, shotgun, and camera. A lesson in photography comes early. Then the circus, the river rapids, and a cabin in the woods. A fight with two wildcats waits later, and a bear and a lion.

In his preface, addressed my dear lads, Stratemeyer says the series aims to acquaint boys with field, forest, river, and lake in winter and summer. The stories are complete in themselves. The hunting is half sporting manual. Game is photographed as well as shot. The Spink crowd returns as the standing enemy.
over-there-with-the-australians:
Captain R. Hugh Knyvett, an ANZAC scout and intelligence officer of the Fifteenth Australian Infantry, published Over There with the Australians with Scribner's in April 1918. He would not survive the year. The book opens not with his prose but with a poem, Bill-Jim's Christmas — Bill-Jim being Australia's name for her soldier.

Bill-Jim sits mucked up with Flanders mud. Pests he will not name to polite ears eat at him. Still he insists he is glad to be there. A man must fight for freedom and his blood. He must not growl while doing it. Then the homesickness breaks through: God, give me Christmas Day in Sydney town, and the flowers in Martin Place. Knyvett's memoir carries that double note — endurance and longing — through the Australian war.
peter-pan-in-kensington-gardens:
Barrie's Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens tells of Peter before Neverland. If you ask your grandmother about Peter, the narrator says, she knew him, but he had no goat in her day. Peter is ever so old, yet always one week of age, and he has never had a birthday.

At seven days old he escaped by the window and flew back to the Kensington Gardens, remembering that babies were birds before they were human. The short contents promise the thrush's nest, the little house, and lock-out time. It is a gentler, stranger Peter Pan book, full of fairies and the lore of birds.
plays-and-puritans:
Charles Kingsley's Plays and Puritans comes from his book of historical essays, in the Macmillan edition of 1890. Kingsley was a clergyman, novelist, and historian. The essay asks why the English stage and the arts around it seemed weak in his own day.

Kingsley argues that most Britons of his time cared little for art, however much the word was praised. He traces that cool temper back to the old Puritans, softened and widened over time. The middle classes, he says, liked art only when it meant nothing and stayed in its place.
podcast-joerogan-DBO5VRwGYns:
Satirist Seth Dillon joins Joe Rogan to react to the FBI raid on Donald Trump's home. Dillon runs the Babylon Bee, a joke news site. Trump had shared Bee posts many times, to Dillon's delight.

Dillon argues the raid poured fuel on Trump's support and fundraising. Rogan asks what agents found and what charges might follow. They weigh legal risk against political gain in plain terms. The episode mixes comedy-shop talk with a live read on a raid that reshaped a campaign before either man knew the full facts. It stays lively throughout.
podcast-joerogan-Ru7BIqXQZns:
Dr. Mary Talley Bowden joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2335. Bowden is a Texas doctor who clashed with hospitals and boards over her COVID treatment views, and her fight made her a hero to skeptics of the official line. Rogan hosts her to state that case.

She tells Rogan what she prescribed, what it cost her, and why she would not back down. Rogan asks about the patients she says recovered and the data fights behind the headlines. The episode preserves a dissenting doctor's full account, the kind of testimony his audience seeks out and his critics dispute.
podcast-joerogan-c6JdeL90ans:
Jeremie and Edouard Harris return to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2156, an earlier visit from the Gladstone AI brothers. The twins had already begun warning officials about advanced AI risks. This talk updates their case as the machines' march speeds up.

The brothers explain the gap between what labs can build and what governments understand. They share scenarios where control slips away step by reasonable step. Rogan asks how close the danger is and who is minding the store. Tech-wary and thoughtful listeners get a warning that has only grown louder since.
podcast-joerogan-mNPM0yUiyNs:
Michio Kaku returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1828. Kaku, the string-theory physicist and tireless explainer, uses his return to look ahead: the future, the cosmos, and the next big leaps for science and for our species. He is in fine form, as Rogan fans expect.

He sketches the coming century as he sees it, from fusion and space travel to contact with other minds. Rogan asks which leaps he will live to see. The episode is a bold, cheerful forecast from a man who has spent his life telling the public that the impossible is usually just early.
poems-and-songs-of-robert-burns:
Robert Burns, Scotland's national poet, fills this gathering of his poems and songs, arranged by the years of his writing. The order itself tells a life story: the contents begin with songs from 1771 to 1779. When Burns was a young farmer in Ayrshire, and move year by year through the work of his short career. Early pieces such as Handsome Nell and Mary Morison stand near the front.

Alongside the love songs come dirges, prayers, and paraphrases of psalms from 1781. Then the famous John Barleycorn ballad and the two elegies for Poor Mailie, his pet sheep, from the years just after. Burns wrote in Scots and English with equal ease, and the year-by-year arrangement lets readers watch a ploughman poet turn into a national voice within a single decade.
poor-relations:
Honoré de Balzac called two of his darkest novels Poor Relations, and this volume opens the pair with Cousin Betty, translated by James Waring in George Saintsbury's edition of Balzac. Balzac dedicates the work to Don Michele Angelo Cajetani, Prince of Teano. Not as prince but as the learned commentator who unlocked Dante for him, turning the Divine Comedy from an enigma into a framework of ideas. The dedication wanders, characteristically, into an attack on professors who live off other nations' learning.

Cousin Betty herself is Balzac's great study of envy: a plain, aging country cousin lodged in a rich Paris family. Repaying years of slight with methodical revenge, using the family's lusts as her weapons. Paired with Cousin Pons, the novel closes the Human Comedy's account of money and kinship. Saintsbury's Balzac gave English readers the master whole, and few parts of him cut deeper than this one.
precipitations:
Evelyn Scott published her first book of poems, Precipitations, in 1920, and the acknowledgments page reads like a directory of modernist little magazines. The Poetry Journal, Others, the Egoist in London, Poetry in Chicago, the Dial, the Liberator, and the Nation all printed pieces gathered here. Scott, a young southerner who had renamed herself and run to art, arranged the book in weather systems, as her title promises: things falling out of a charged sky.

Sections named Manhattan, Crowds, and Vanities organize the fall. Poems take up Brooklyn Bridge at midnight, autumn dusk in Central Park, winter streets, a snow dance. Potter's field, riots, and the city at night, all in the jagged free verse the magazines were fighting over. Scott later became a notable novelist of the South and Brazil. This debut preserves her first climate: New York seen by a runaway romantic with a modernist ear.
principal-cairns:
John Cairns wrote a life of his namesake for the Famous Scots Series, following a Berwickshire farm boy from Ayton Hill to the head of a Scottish college. John Cairns was born at Ayton Hill in the parish of Ayton on August 23, 1818, on a farm that later vanished.

Chapters trace his schooldays at Dunglass, his college years, his training in theology, and his work as minister, professor, and principal. One chapter calls him an apostle of union for his church work. Readers get a full Victorian life of study, preaching, and teaching in Scotland.
probable-sons:
Amy Le Feuvre wrote a story for young readers in 1896, taking her motto from the words that a little child shall lead them. A man who calls children a nuisance inherits an unwelcome charge, and the tale grows from that cold start.

Chapter titles retell the parable of the prodigal son in a home setting: a prodigal, a promise kept, a cross-examination, and a return to the father. Sorrow in the Maxwell household and a broken statue mark the early pages. Children and parents alike get a gentle lesson in love, pride, and forgiveness.
red-pepper-burns:
Grace S. Richmond wrote this novel of a doctor whose nickname gives the book its title, and every chapter is named for what he does. He vows a vow, creates a circus, assumes a duty, and prescribes for himself. He saws wood, suffers a defeat, proves himself a host, and defies superstition before the close.

The story opens with his car, the Green Imp, tearing past a porch on five cylinders. Neighbors know Red by the sound; he is in too much of a hurry, as usual, to stop and fix the car. Richmond builds her tale from his practice, his friends, and a temper as warm as his hair.
rose-in-bloom-a-sequel-to-eight-cousins:
Louisa May Alcott wrote Rose in Bloom as a sequel to Eight Cousins, and she signed the preface in September 1876. In that preface she says plainly that there is no moral to the story. Rose, she adds, is not meant as a model girl. The sequel was written to keep a promise, in hope of giving some fun and, here and there, a helpful hint to other young women about to bloom.

Chapter titles trace Rose coming home, meeting old friends with new faces, and facing thorns, small trials, and a sad and sober stretch. Later chapters turn to good works, a ball, and Phebe, and they end with how Phebe earned her welcome. The plan Alcott sets out keeps the tone light and kind, with growth shown through daily choices rather than through lessons forced on the reader.
round-about-the-carpathians: Andrew F. Crosse, a fellow of the Chemical Society, wrote Round About the Carpathians, issued at Edinburgh and London in 1878. The contents give full chapter outlines. Chapter I runs down the Danube from Buda-Pest, through amusements on board the steamer, Basiash, a drive to Oravicza, gipsy music, and the czardas dance.
seven-little-australians:
Ethel Turner wrote this tale of seven children in an Australian home, and dedicated the book to her mother. Contents promise chapters on fowl for dinner, a general who sees active service, and the sweetness of sweet sixteen. Turner warns readers at the start not to expect model children.

Better books exist for perfect youngsters, she jokes, naming Sandford and Merton as the place to find them. Her seven are lively, flawed, and fond of mischief. Trips to the bush at Yarrahappini and a picnic at Krangi-Bahtoo widen the tale. Young readers meet a warm, funny family story with real sorrow near its close.
sintram-and-his-companions:
Friedrich de la Motte Fouque wrote this winter tale, here with a foreword by Charlotte M. Yonge. An opening essay links Fouque's tales to the four seasons: stern Sintram to winter, Undine to spring, The Two Captains to summer, and Aslauga's Knight to autumn. Two of the four stand in this volume.

Fouque, born at Brandenburg on February 12, 1777, came of French Huguenot stock and took his name from his godfather, Frederick the Great. He served in Prussia's army through disaster and success. His realm of spiritual chivalry, the essay holds, stands kin to Arthur's knights and Spenser's Red Cross.
sixes-and-sevens:
O. Henry gathered twenty-five tales in this set, opening with The Last of the Troubadours. Contents range from Holding Up a Train and Witches' Loaves to The Duplicity of Hargraves and October and June. Shamrock Jolnes, a comic detective, appears among the later pieces.

Sam Galloway saddles his pony to leave Rancho Altito after three months, driven off at last by bad biscuits. Nick Napoleon, the ranch cook, never could make good ones, the narrator laments. O. Henry's twist endings and warm slang fill the set, with New York and the West sharing his stage in turn.
somerville-recollections:
Mary Somerville published her Personal Recollections in 1873, a year after her death, through her daughter's care. Somerville had been called the queen of science for her books on astronomy and physics. She wrote science clearly when few women could publish at all.

She recalls a Scottish girlhood with almost no schooling, then a late, self-driven turn to math. London drawing rooms brought her Herschel, Laplace's circle, and the whole Victorian scientific world. Her memory for people and places stayed keen into her nineties. The recollections show how one determined woman joined the highest ranks of science.
songs-of-two-nations:
Algernon Charles Swinburne joins A Song of Italy and an Ode on the Proclamation of the French Republic in Songs of Two Nations, with the Dirae. The first lines show a double-faced statue, Memnon or Janus, half veiled with night and bound with iron. Half stands crowned with light, holding all men's future in his hand, while the old westward face of time is writ with cursing and marked for death.

A Song of Italy is given with all devotion to Joseph Mazzini and dated 1867. On a windy night of falling stars, the poet sees one form shine against his sight, more fair and fearful and godlike than the glories that mete out night and day. Within his eyes the formless folded skies take shape around that worthier object of worship.
spanish-doubloons:
Camilla Kenyon wrote Spanish Doubloons, dated 1919, with a front picture by Louis Rogers, and gives the book to L. T., in thanks for her faith. The contents promise an errant aunt, an isle of fortune, a captain's legacy, and a cave with two mouths. Later heads name a rabbit's foot, what Crusoe and the teller found, secret dealings, and the Bishop's chest.

Chapter I, An Aunt Errant, opens in a fair hour. Life had never seemed more fair and smiling than at the moment when Aunt Jane's letter fell on the teller like a bolt from the blue. The teller, an orphan meant to live under Aunt Jane's wing, was in fact taking a holiday from Aunt Jane when the letter came.
speaking-of-operations:
Irvin S. Cobb gives Speaking of Operations to two classes of folk. One class has been operated on. The other has not yet been operated on. The last late bill is now paid and receipted. The stitch marks have faded from red to pink. So Cobb sits down to treat a small matter. That matter is his own: that operation.

Cobb notes a habit of those who come through surgery. They like to talk of it after, he says. Of all handy topics, an operation beats most. It beats the tariff, Roosevelt, or Bryan for men. A whale serves mixed company best of all. No one knows more of whales than you do. You may claim near anything about them. Blubber and tears alike pass without a check.
stones-of-venice-introductions:
John Ruskin issued The Stones of Venice: Introductory Chapters and Local Indices as a separate volume for travellers staying in Venice and Verona. His preface, dated from Brantwood on 3rd May 1879, explains that the book begins a series meant to give his earlier works a more handy and lasting form.

Ruskin planned to gather the most useful parts of his past writing into one steady body of teaching, with plates sold in separate parts. The opening chapter, The Quarry, starts the study of how Venice was built and what its stones can teach. Travellers could carry the volume on the spot and read the city through Ruskin's eyes.
stories-from-the-greek-tragedians:
The Rev. Alfred J. Church wrote Stories from Homer and Stories from Virgil. He then retold tales from the Greek tragedians. Dodd, Mead and Company printed the volume at New York. It carries twenty illustrations from designs by Flaxman and others. His preface is dated at Retford on October 11, 1879.

Church explains his method plainly. He added the single combat of Eteocles and Polynices from the Phoenissae of Euripides. He altered the story of Ion to suit the book. He used cutting and shortening freely throughout. He asks pardon of readers who know the great originals, calling his versions pale copies meant to lead the young toward them.
stories-of-great-americans-for-little-am:
Edward Eggleston's Stories of Great Americans for Little Americans, dated 1895, is a first reader built from tales of the nation's leading figures. Eggleston says his chief aim is to give the little learner reading matter that excites attention and gives pleasure, easing the hard task of learning to read.

He chose words that are short and familiar, with brief sentences and frequent breathing places, like rests on a steep hill. The stories teach by personal anecdote, and some, such as Putnam and the Wolf, are tales every American child was expected to know as a kind of national folklore. History here arrives as story first.
story-lives-of-great-musicians:
Francis Jameson Rowbotham wrote Story-Lives of Great Musicians, printed at New York by Frederick A. Stokes Company, with Beethoven as frontispiece. Rowbotham had already written Story-Lives of Great Authors and Tales from Plutarch, and he dedicated this volume to the memory of Frederick Westlake of the Royal Academy of Music.

The book tells composers' lives as stories for general and younger readers, stressing the human path behind the music: early gifts, hard study, setbacks, and fame. Musical signs in the text are kept simple, and pictures carry the eye. It belongs to a line of biography that taught music history through lives rather than through scores and dates.
successful-recitations:
Alfred H. Miles edited Successful Recitations, printed at London in 1901 under a motto from Hamlet urging the speaker to deliver the speech trippingly on the tongue. The book is an anthology of pieces chosen for reading aloud and platform performance.

Miles's preface argues that a clear aim comes first. Simple style comes with it. Fine subtleties are lost in all but the best platform work. The picturesque and the dramatic are what carry a room. Pieces that recite themselves succeed easily, he warns, but are soon done to death once everyone knows them. He aims instead for pieces with lasting quality, things of beauty that stay fresh after the novelty wears off.
susy-a-story-of-the-plains:
Bret Harte's Susy, A Story of the Plains, appears in Volume 7 of the Argonaut Edition of his works, printed at New York by P. F. Collier and Son. Chapter I leaves the settled coast and follows the San Leandro turnpike along a hot, dusty California valley.

Harte describes wild oats stretching without limit on either side. The horizon seems ever farther off. Then the road slips between scrub oaks. Centuries of western trade winds have bent them. The road climbs into a fair wood of live oak. Coolness, unseen brooks, moss, and clover replace the baked adobe as the traveller enters primeval forest. Into this changing country Harte brings his plains story, with the landscape itself marking the passage from plain to foothill life.
sybil-or-the-two-nations:
Benjamin Disraeli's Sybil, or The Two Nations, dated 1845 in the edition at hand, is a novel about the condition of the people in industrial England. A dedication inscribes the volumes to a wife whose noble spirit and gentle nature ever prompt her to sympathize with the suffering.

Disraeli's advertisement warns readers not to suspect exaggeration in his scenes. He states his belief plainly. There is not a trait in the work without authority behind it. The authority is his own observation. Or it is the evidence received by royal commissions and parliamentary committees. At the same time he confesses to suppressing much that is genuine, since the whole truth about the state of the country would seem improbable and might deter readers. The two nations of the subtitle are the rich and the poor.
tales-of-the-five-towns: Arnold Bennett's Tales of the Five Towns was first published in January 1905. Bennett gave the book to Marcel Schwob, named as his guide in France. The contents split the tales in two groups. At Home holds eight tales, and Abroad holds five. Titles include His Worship the Goosedriver, The Elixir of Youth, and Mary with the High Hand. The Abroad group adds The Hungarian Rhapsody and A Letter Home.
tanakh-jps-1917-lamentations:
Lamentations is a book of grief verse in the Hebrew Bible, here in the Masoretic-based English of the Jewish Publication Society, 1917. Five poems mourn Jerusalem after its fall, told in the voice of the city itself.

The city sits alone, once full of people, now like a widow with tears on her cheeks at night. No friend stays to comfort her, and her children have gone into exile before the foe. Zion's roads mourn and her gates stand bare. Readers get some of the Bible's most raw lines of loss, where blame, pain, and a thin thread of hope sit side by side in strict verse form.
ten-boys-from-dickens:
Kate Dickinson Sweetser made Ten Boys from Dickens in 1901, with art by George Alfred Williams, retelling Dickens through his boy figures. The ten are Tiny Tim, Oliver Twist, Tommy Traddles, Deputy, the boys of Dotheboys Hall, David Copperfield, Kit Nubbles, Jo, Paul Dombey, and Pip.

Sweetser starts with Tiny Tim, whom she calls less boy than spirit, with a fair oval face and deep grey eyes. She stresses his sunny, patient smile and the firm lines of his mouth as signs of a sweet nature. Readers meet Dickens by way of his most loved lads, in short prose portraits pitched for young readers new to the great novels.
ten-girls-from-dickens: Kate Dickinson Sweetser wrote Ten Girls from Dickens. George Alfred Williams drew the plates. Sweetser also wrote Ten Boys from Dickens. A front plate shows Little Nell and her grandfather. The ten girls start with the Marchioness and Morleena Kenwigs. Little Nell, the Infant Phenomenon, and Jenny Wren follow. Sissy Jupe, Florence Dombey, and Charley come next. Tilly Slowboy and Agnes Wickfield close the set.
the-acharnians:
Aristophanes wrote The Acharnians, a comedy here in an English rendering whose translator goes unnamed, with notes kept to gloss Greek names, rites, and puns. A long opening essay places the play in its war and in the set of peace plays.

The essay calls it first of three comedies, with Peace and Lysistrata, staged in the sixth, tenth, and twenty-first years of the Peloponnesian War. Each pressed on Athens the harms of war, above all to farms and trade. It was staged at the Lenaean Festival in January 426 B.C. and took first prize, with Cratinus second. Cleon raged at its attacks. Readers get the first full play Aristophanes put out in his own name.
the-adventure-of-the-bruce-partington-pl:
The Adventure of the Bruce-Partington Plans is a Sherlock Holmes tale told by Dr. Watson. Late November 1895 brings London a thick yellow fog that lasts for days on end.

From Monday to Thursday, Watson says, they could not see the houses across Baker Street from their windows. Holmes spends one day cross-indexing his great book of references, then two on the music of the Middle Ages, his new hobby. By the fourth day of greasy fog he paces the room, bites his nails, and chafes at the lack of crime worth his mind. Readers then get a case of stolen navy plans and a body on the rails.
the-albert-n-yanza-great-basin-of-the-ni: Sir Samuel White Baker wrote The Albert N'Yanza, Great Basin of the Nile. This copy opens with Project Gutenberg front matter alone. The front pages name the book and its author. They file it as etext 3668. A release date of January 2003 is given. First posting was in July 2001. Garry Gill is credited with the file's making. A proofreading team helped him. No page of Baker's Nile narrative itself stands here.
the-bandolero-or-a-marriage-among-the-mo:
Captain Mayne Reid set his Mexican tale, dated 1900 in the heading, in La Puebla de los Angeles. His narrator calls the city odd even for modern Mexico, with priests, poor folk, and pickpockets filling its streets. Church houses marked with saints' names line the doors.

Reid says the Church owns much of the city and the plain around it, by deed or mortgage. Yet Puebla lies in a rich plain ringed by grand mountains, near Cholula and Tlascala, with snow on Popocatepetl. The narrator entered as one of three thousand invaders, tired from marches and a skirmish with Santa Anna's lancers.
the-belgian-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote a story for young readers about Belgian twins, placed at grade six in a geographic series. Other twin books in the list cover Dutch, Eskimo, Japanese, Swiss, Irish, Italian, Scotch, Mexican, and French children. A historical series adds cave, Spartan, and Puritan twins.

In a preface Perkins speaks of homes broken up and hearts burdened in a sad hour of world history. Her tale of two small Belgian refugees, she says, rests on the real experience of two Belgian children, and an incident of a locket is true. The eel-woman and the twins' mother also draw on real people.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-25-lam:
Lamentations , read in the King James Version, begins with a city sitting solitary. Jerusalem, once full of people and great among nations, has become like a widow and tributary.

She weeps sore in the night, with tears on her cheeks, and finds no comfort among lovers turned enemies. Judah has gone into captivity under affliction and servitude, finding no rest among the heathen. Roads to Zion mourn because none come to the feasts; gates are desolate, priests sigh, and virgins are afflicted. The opening lays loss on the city's many transgressions, as an adversary prospers over her.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-45-rom:
Romans in King James wording, begins with Paul calling himself a servant of Christ, called to be an apostle and separated to God's gospel. That gospel, he says, was promised before by prophets in holy scriptures.

It concerns God's Son, made of David's seed in the flesh and declared Son of God with power by resurrection from the dead. Through him Paul received grace and apostleship, for obedience to faith among all nations. The letter greets all in Rome, beloved of God and called to be saints, with grace and peace. Paul first gives thanks for their faith.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-46-1-c:
First Corinthians in the King James text, starts with Paul, called an apostle through God's will, and Sosthenes our brother. The greeting is to God's church at Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ and called to be saints.

Grace and peace are wished from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Paul gives thanks always for grace given them in Christ, saying they are enriched in utterance and knowledge. The testimony of Christ was confirmed in them, and they lack no gift while waiting for Christ's coming. He will confirm them to the end, Paul adds.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-47-2-c:
Second Corinthians in the King James rendering, begins with Paul and Timothy writing to God's church at Corinth, with all the saints in Achaia. Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ follow.

Paul blesses God as a Father of mercies and God of all comfort. He comforts us in tribulation, Paul says, so we can comfort others in trouble with the same comfort. Sufferings of Christ abound in us, and consolation also abounds by Christ. Affliction, he argues, works for the readers' consolation and salvation when endured as the apostles endure it.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-48-gal:
Galatians , given here in King James English, opens with Paul stressing his call. His apostleship is not from men or by man, he says. It is by Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead.

With all the brethren with him, he writes to the churches of Galatia, wishing grace and peace. Christ gave himself for our sins, he says, to deliver us from this present evil world, by God's will. Then tone shifts fast: Paul marvels that they are so soon removed to another gospel. Some trouble them and would pervert Christ's gospel, he warns, even if an angel preached it.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-49-eph:
Ephesians in the authorised King James wording, opens with Paul, an apostle by God's will, writing to saints at Ephesus and the faithful in Christ. Grace and peace from God and Christ follow the address.

God is blessed for blessing them with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ. He chose them before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in love, the verses say. They were predestined to adoption as children through Christ, by God's good pleasure. Acceptance in the beloved and redemption through his blood are named next. Blessing piles on blessing in the first lines.
the-british-barbarians:
Grant Allen opens The British Barbarians, dated 1895, with an introduction every reader is asked to read first. He calls the book a Hill-top Novel. Of late, he says, the land has been flooded with tales of evil bent. A Hill-top Novel raises a protest in favor of purity. Why had no novelist raised the protest sooner? Bread, Allen answers: a writer must earn his living and find a publisher.

Most novels must first run as serials in magazines or newspapers. Their editors, he says, are timid past belief. One scene is unfit for the young person, the next would drive off the British matron. Allen doubts the fear has real ground. A first-class journal, he holds, would not suffer if a few formalists dropped it for six weeks in a pet, then took it back.
the-burial-of-the-guns:
Thomas Nelson Page wrote The Burial of the Guns, in an edition from New York dated 1894. A head note marks Page as a Virginian author, 1853 to 1922, and the book is given to his wife. Its contents hold six tales: My Cousin Fanny, the title tale, and The Gray Jacket of No. 4. Miss Dangerlie's Roses, How the Captain Made Christmas, and Little Darby complete the set.

My Cousin Fanny opens the book with Christmas in old Hanover. Christmas always brings his cousin Fanny to mind, for she was foolish about it. Fanny was an old maid of the old maids, proud as Lucifer, and no one who saw her could doubt it. She lived at Woodside, a place in the family since before the Revolution.
the-card-a-story-of-adventure-in-the-fiv: The opening pages under this title give no part of the story itself, only a list of works by Arnold Bennett. His novels are headed by Anna of the Five Towns, The Old Wives' Tale, Clayhanger, and The Card itself, with further lists for his fantasias and his short stories. The list stands as the publisher's catalogue of the author's shelf; no chapter, title page, or date is shown.
the-chouans:
Honore de Balzac wrote this novel of the Breton rising, translated here by Katharine Prescott Wormeley. He dedicates it to Monsieur Theodore Dablin, a merchant, calling Dablin his first friend and the book his first work. Part I, headed An Ambuscade, opens early in the year VIII of the French calendar.

The date works out to late September 1799. A hundred or so peasants, with many citizens, leave Fougeres in the morning on the road to Mayenne. They climb the little mountain of La Pelerine, halfway to Ernee, where travelers on that road rest. The company splits into groups of varied size. Balzac pauses to describe their fantastic costumes and mixed callings, town by town and trade by trade. That local color, he notes, gives the history its vivid ground, even if some critics say it dulls the feelings shown.
the-collegians:
Gerald Griffin wrote this Irish novel, headed with the year 1829. A brewer's son from Limerick, born in 1803, Griffin worked first as a reporter and then turned to fiction. In 1838 he joined the Christian Brothers in Dublin, entering that teaching order.

The volume appears in a Crime Classics series beside Dickens, Sapper, Hornung, Chesterton, Braddon, Poe, Childers, and Le Fanu. Its contents are told in a string of how-titles. How Garryowen rose and how it fell comes first, then how Eily O'Connor puzzled all the inhabitants of Garryowen. A third chapter shows Mr. Daly the middleman sitting down to breakfast. That Garryowen is Griffin's name for his native Limerick world gives the tale its local ground: a rising town, a puzzling heroine, and the middleman class between landlords and tenants.
the-count-s-millions: Emile Gaboriau's The Count's Millions is called a novel in two parts on its title page, with the second part placed in a companion volume, Baron Trigault's Vengeance. A heading, Pascal and Marguerite, stands over a contents list of numbered chapters running at least to XV. Only the title page, that note, and the contents list are present here, so the story itself does not appear.
the-cromptons: A publisher's catalogue page for the popular novels of Mrs. Mary J. Holmes names The Cromptons as a new title among her works, listed beside Tempest and Sunshine, English Orphans, Hugh Worthington, Lena Rivers, Rose Mather, and many more. Each volume is offered handsomely bound in cloth at one dollar, sent free by mail. A quoted notice praises Holmes as a pleasant writer who holds her readers with deep interest. Only this catalogue page is present here; the novel's own title page and text do not appear.
the-daisy-chain-or-aspirations: Charlotte Yonge's The Daisy Chain, or Aspirations, dated 1856, is shown here only through its contents. A preface is listed, then Part 1 of the tale with a run of numbered chapters reaching at least XV, none of them titled. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. A companion record in this set carries the preface and the opening chapter.
the-dutch-twins: Lucy Fitch Perkins's The Dutch Twins is present here as a title page, a list of her Twins books for schools, and a contents list. Six chapters tell of Kit and Kat, Dutch twins. They go fishing, ride to market with Father, and drive the milk cart. Last, they get their skates. Perkins drew the pictures herself. No story text appears in these pages.
the-eskimo-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins's The Eskimo Twins tells the true story, as she puts it, of Menie and Monnie, five-year-old twins of the far North, and their dogs Nip and Tup. Dressed alike, the boy and girl baffle even their mother at a small distance. Chapters take them coasting, fishing, and to the snow house, with Koolee dividing the meat.

Later heads name the reindeer hunt, a trip in the woman-boats, and a summer day. Perkins drew on her Twins series plan: one land, one pair of children, daily life made plain. Teacher notes close the book.
the-esperanto-teacher-a-simple-course-fo:
Helen Fryer's The Esperanto Teacher, a simple course for non-grammarians, reached a tenth edition from the British Esperanto Association. Its front note says no one gains more from Esperanto than the non-grammarian. A small cost in time and cash buys a clear grip on grammar. It buys word sense too. In a few months it buys talk with folk across the world. E. A. Millidge revised the book, on Dr. Zamenhof's drills.

Short lessons, word lists, and practice talks build skill step by step. All sale profits feed the cause. The book is a neat relic of the Esperanto push.
the-europeans:
Henry James's The Europeans opens on a May day in Boston, more than thirty years back from its telling. From the best hotel's window, a lady has stood half an hour watching a small graveyard in the city's heart, its mouldy stones and dark trees ill-refreshed by wet snow. Spring is six weeks old by the calendar, yet the scene holds no cheer.

The lady is the Baroness Eugenia Münster, come with her brother Felix to call on stiff Yankee kin. Old World ease meets New England conscience. James makes a light, keen comedy of manners from the clash.
the-french-twins:
Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote The French Twins as a tale for children of the Great War in France, giving the book to all friends of the brave children of France. Rheims and its great church stand at the start.

The tale opens on a September day with sun on the towers of Rheims Cathedral and organ music in its aisles. Chapters bring the coming of the Germans, the burning of the cathedral, flights from home, and the Foreign Legion. Perkins, famed for her twins books, shows war through the eyes of a French boy and girl who keep their courage as their town falls under shell fire.
the-girl-at-the-halfway-house-a-story-of: Emerson Hough wrote The Girl at the Halfway House. Its subtitle is A Story of the Plains. Grosset and Dunlap printed it in New York, dated 1900. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page, a dedication, and the start of the contents. It honors Edward Kemeys, soldier, hunter, and sculptor of the West. The contents split the book in two. Book I is The Day of War. Book II is The Day of the Buffalo. It brings in Edward Franklin, a lawyer.
the-gospel-of-the-pentateuch-a-set-of-pa:
The Gospel of the Pentateuch is a set of parish sermons. No author is named in what is present here. It opens at Sermon I, God in Christ. The sermon was preached for Septuagesima Sunday. Its text is Genesis chapter one, verse one. In the beginning, it says, God created the heaven and the earth.

The preacher urges the flock to hear Genesis with respect and awe. It is the oldest part of the Bible. It is the oldest of all known works, the earliest human thought handed down. Men might have chosen to record first how to be rich, strong, or happy. Instead the first lesson is that God made heaven and earth. That comes first, he argues, for a reason. The first question that marks a man from a brute is this: Where am I? How did I get into this world?
the-great-stone-face-and-other-tales-of-:
Nathaniel Hawthorne wrote The Great Stone Face and Other Tales of the White Mountains. The book is dated 1882. Its contents name four pieces. They are The Great Stone Face, The Ambitious Guest, and The Great Carbuncle. Sketches From Memory closes the book. The introduction says the first three are stories of New Hampshire's White Hills. It prints a note Hawthorne wrote in 1840. That note foreshadows the title tale.

The note pictures a human face shaped on a mountainside by a freak of nature, wondered at for centuries. Then a boy is born whose own features slowly grow into the face's likeness. At one great turn of his life, the match is found complete. The introduction also gives the source of The Ambitious Guest: the Willey family, destroyed in August 1826. A landslide swept past their house on either side. They rushed out, and were lost.
the-grim-smile-of-the-five-towns:
Arnold Bennett wrote The Grim Smile of the Five Towns. A contents list names thirteen tales. They run from The Lion's Share and Baby's Bath to The Death of Simon Fuge and In a New Bottle. The book is dedicated to Joseph Dawson, a student of the human nature of the Five Towns.

The Lion's Share opens with a warning. In the Five Towns the tale is told as one of the best jokes ever heard there. Now that the narrator writes it down, it strikes him as a pretty grim tragedy. It began in the little house of Mrs. Carpole, at Bleakridge, between Bursley and Hanbridge. Mrs. Carpole is a widow, the second wife. Her stepson Horace is nineteen, a model youth. He studies the chemistry of pottery in his evenings.
the-headsman-or-the-abbaye-des-vignerons:
J. Fenimore Cooper wrote The Headsman; or, The Abbaye des Vignerons, a tale shown in an edition dated 1860 and marked complete in one volume. The introduction begins early in October 1832, when a traveling carriage stops above the lake of Geneva near Vevey in Switzerland. The postilion chains a wheel, and an American family takes in the view of the lake and the Alps.

Four years earlier the same family had stopped at the same spot on the way to Italy. Charmed this time, they take a house within hours and settle in Vevey. The head of the family soon hires a boat from Jean Descloux, and a casual meeting grows into friendly contact on the lake.
the-heavenly-twins:
Madame Sarah Grand wrote The Heavenly Twins, and she is named on the title page as the author of Ideala. A short exchange at the front gives the title its sense: the twins are called signs of the times, not signs of the zodiac. A poem by Oliver Wendell Holmes follows, about new truth born amid birth pangs and scorned at first.

The proem opens with Mendelssohn's Elijah heard from a high cathedral tower. Bells ring out by day and night over a great city, flat country, small townships, and farmsteads, said to carry as far as the sea twenty miles away. Grand frames the tale with music, bells, and a sense of an age in labor.
the-history-of-england-from-the-first-in: John Lingard and Hilaire Belloc are named for The History of England. The work runs from the first invasion by the Romans. It ends at the accession of King George the Fifth. The set holds eleven volumes and is dated 1912. James Cardinal Gibbons wrote an introduction. The pages present give the contents of the eighth volume. Its first chapter continues Charles I. It covers the Battle of Edge Hill and Marston Moor. It also covers the trial of Archbishop Laud. Only the title page and volume contents are present here.
the-japanese-twins: Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote this children's book. The pages present here hold only an old etext header. None of the story itself appears. The header names the title and the author. Release came in July 2002, as etext 3496. License and donation boilerplate fills the rest. No chapter of Taro and Take's adventures can be read here. The record carries the wrapper and not the work. The twins' Japan stays behind that wrapper.
the-kentons:
William Dean Howells opens this novel in a Midwestern county town. The Kentons have mellowed in their great square brick house. Four acres and trees of their own planting surround it. They are richer than the average, but not rich. Kenton keeps his library for his law business. At night he joins his wife in her room. Parlors and piazzas fall to their girls then. Young fellows come to call there.

Howells draws the marriage in small habits. She sews while he reads his paper. Her silence satisfies him. They play checkers, and she will not let him win. Defeat threatens her men too often. Both were teachers before his war service and law practice. Five children were born to them. One son was lost in infancy. Their eldest has taken over the practice. The father's election to the bench freed him. Drama grows inside this contentment.
the-letters-of-robert-burns: J. Logie Robertson selected and arranged Robert Burns letters and supplied an introduction for this edition. Only the title page and a list of recipients are present here, showing early letters to Ellison Begbie, to his father, to Sir John Whitefoord, and to his schoolmaster John Murdoch. Two Burns sayings on the title page praise writing whatever comes first and compare his life to a ruined temple. The letters themselves are not included in this record.
the-life-of-buddha-and-its-lessons:
H. S. Olcott wrote his lecture on the Buddha for the Adyar Pamphlets series, first issued in May 1912 and again in September 1919. He opens with a claim about religious history. People, he says, tend to turn any man who rises above common weakness into a god.

Olcott calls that habit mean and ignorant, born of selfishness and superstition. Persecuted teachers win worship after death, and legend then pads their true lives with fancy incidents. His lesson asks readers to honor the Buddha as a man who raised his own nature, not as a heaven sent being.
the-literature-of-the-ancient-egyptians: E. A. Wallis Budge, Keeper of Egyptian and Assyrian Antiquities in the British Museum, wrote The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, published in London in 1914. A title page and contents are all that is present; the chapters themselves are absent. The contents open with Thoth as author of Egyptian literature and a chapter on writing materials, then turn to the Pyramid Texts, the Book of Opening the Mouth, funerary offerings, and hymns. A frontispiece shows the Elysian Fields from the Papyrus of Ani.
the-little-pilgrim-further-experiences-s:
Margaret Oliphant's The Little Pilgrim: Further Experiences, dated 1888, continues the story of a soul newly arrived in heaven.
