The little Pilgrim, whose earlier story was told elsewhere, has known the first rapture of arrival and the blessed work given her there. Yet her heart stays full of pity for those still suffering on earth, and questions keep returning to her in the midst of happiness.

She longs to be sent back with a message of light and brightness, telling those in darkness how soon all pain would be over. Her companions in heaven are touched by her questions. Oliphant writes gentle, reflective fiction about the afterlife, focused less on judgment than on comfort for people still struggling through mortal life.
the-little-white-bird-or-adventures-in-k:
J. M. Barrie's The Little White Bird, or Adventures in Kensington Gardens, mixes a grown narrator's friendship with a small boy named David. The contents promise chapters on David's mother, a runaway perambulator, the grand tour of the Gardens, and, at chapter fourteen, Peter Pan. The opening chapter shows the odd terms of the friendship: David calls the narrator father, and relays his mother's invitations, which the narrator always declines.

David urges him to come because it is her birthday and she is twenty-six, an age so great to the boy that he fears she cannot last much longer. Barrie's gentle humor and the Kensington Gardens setting frame the earliest appearance of Peter Pan in Barrie's work, tucked inside a story for and about a child.
the-loss-of-the-s-s-titanic-its-story-an:
Lawrence Beesley, a Cambridge scholar and one of the survivors, wrote The Loss of the S. S. Titanic: Its Story and Its Lessons. His preface explains that, five weeks after the survivors landed in New York, he told the story at a Boston luncheon. Robert Lincoln O'Brien, editor of the Boston Herald, urged him to write a correct history of the disaster as a matter of public interest.

Beesley says rival publications were already being prepared by people who had not been present, pieced together from newspaper accounts. He feared they would be erroneous and full of highly coloured details. Houghton Mifflin at first doubted whether the sinking should be recorded at all, then agreed with him that a history written as correctly as possible was the wiser course.
the-magnificent-ambersons: Booth Tarkington wrote The Magnificent Ambersons. Only the title line and a bare contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The contents show numbered chapters with no titles given, running at least to chapter twenty-one in what is listed. Nothing further is printed in what is present: no date, no publisher, and no opening lines. The family's story cannot be described from this record beyond its title and its author's name.
the-monikins:
J. Fenimore Cooper's The Monikins is present here only through its contents, which run past Chapter XXII, so none of the satire itself appears. The contents promise an introduction followed by chapters whose long titles mix family history, money, and philosophy. The author's pedigree, and his father's, open the list, followed by a chapter touching the author himself and ten thousand pounds.

Later headings grow stranger. A social-stake system, an amphibious animal, and wonders vouched as truth appear by Chapter IX. Human shrewdness is shamed in negotiation, and courts, courtiers, brides, tails, and diplomacy fill the middle chapters. Law with very little justice, and heads and tails each in their proper place, show the comic-philosophical bent of the missing text.
the-mountains:
Stewart Edward White's The Mountains opens with a preface explaining its central character. White, author of The Blazed Trail and Silent Places, says he followed a true sequence of events in nearly all particulars, except for the Tenderfoot. That figure is both fictitious and real: no single man, yet a combination of many tenderfeet, meaning greenhorn travellers, whose doings White had all witnessed at some time.

A contents list of twenty-two chapters maps the trip and the teaching mixed into it. Chapters on equipment, horses, camp cookery, and seeing deer sit between narrative stages: the Ridge Trail, the Coast Ranges, the Inferno, the Canon, the Giant Forest, and the Golden Trout. The Lure of the Trail closes the list.
the-naturalist-on-the-river-amazons:
Henry Walter Bates's The Naturalist on the River Amazons, in the Everyman's Library edition from J. M. Dent and Sons in London and E. P. Dutton in New York, is present here only in title pages and a contents list with chapter summaries, so Bates's narrative does not appear. The edition, edited by Ernest Rhys and first issued in 1910 and reprinted in 1914, promises an appreciation by Darwin on its illustrated title page.

Chapter summaries are generous. Para opens the book with arrival, the river, a first walk in the suburbs, and the leaf-carrying ant. Further chapters cover swampy forests, a Portuguese landed proprietor, life under the equator, religious holidays, marmoset monkeys, and the Tocantins River journey to Cammeta.
the-new-heavens:
George Ellery Hale's The New Heavens was published in New York in 1922. Charles Scribner's Sons issued it. Only a photograph caption, title page, dedication, and contents are present here, so the astronomy itself does not appear. Hale directed the Mount Wilson Observatory of the Carnegie Institution of Washington, and he dedicates the book to his wife. Only three chapters are listed: The New Heavens, Giant Stars, and Cosmic Crucibles.

The opening figure, credited to Hubble, shows the constellation Orion photographed through a small camera lens. Its three bright central stars form Orion's belt, and a small white patch in the sword handle is the great nebula, shown larger in the second figure. A 100-inch Hooker telescope appears among the illustrations.
the-pagans: Arlo Bates wrote the novel The Pagans, dedicated to those who would be pagans if any such group existed. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The contents list chapters with titles drawn from Shakespeare, among them Some Speech of Marriage, The Bitter Past, The Assay of Art, and Upon a Church-Bench. A line from All's Well That Ends Well stands at the front: the web of our life is a mingled yarn.
the-plant-hunters-adventures-among-the-h:
Captain Mayne Reid's The Plant Hunters, adventures among the Himalaya Mountains, opens by asking what a plant-hunter is. Reid answers that he is no truffle-digger serving the palate of the gourmand. A plant-hunter devotes his life to collecting rare plants and flowers. He does with his hands what the closet botanist only classifies.

England's gardens, Reid argues, owe the plant-hunter their dahlias, peonies, camellias, azaleas, and rhododendrons. They also owe him many fruits and vegetables at table. Early collectors such as the Tradescants, the Bartrams, and Catesby brought back tulip trees, magnolias, maples, and robinias from America. Hundreds of hunters now work in the Rockies, the Andes, the Amazon forests, Siberia, and the glacier valleys of the Himalaya. Hunger, thirst, wild beasts, and rough country are the ordinary price of their trade. Reid clearly admires them for paying it.
the-poems-of-emma-lazarus-volume-2-jewis: Volume II of The Poems of Emma Lazarus holds Jewish poems and translations. Here only the title page and contents appear; the poems themselves are absent. A transcriber's note explains that the biographical sketch from Volume I is reprinted here for convenience. Poems listed include The New Year, In Exile, The Banner of the Jew, Bar Kochba, and 1492. Two pieces treat Raschi, in Prague and at his death. A closing group, By the Waters of Babylon, offers prose poems: The Exodus, Treasures, and The Sower.
the-puritan-twins: Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote and illustrated a children's history story graded for the sixth and seventh school years, issued by Houghton Mifflin as part of her Twins series. Companion volumes pair Dutch, Eskimo, Filipino, Japanese, Swiss, Irish, Italian, Scotch, Mexican, Belgian, and French twins, while a historical line adds cave, Spartan, and Puritan pairs. Only the publisher's series lists and title information are present here, so the twins' own story does not appear.
the-puritans: Arlo Bates frames his novel with lines from Shakespeare and a Persian hymn, then lays out twenty-eight chapters whose headings are themselves Shakespearean phrases. Early headings move from confusion and marriage talk toward sharp discourse, duty, and accident. Only the title pages and the full chapter list are present here, so the narrative itself does not appear.
the-reconciliation-of-races-and-religion:
Thomas Kelly Cheyne held a fellowship of the British Academy. He argues that the religions are really one religion. Their union, he says, must come before any union of races. His preface calls the crisis alarming. The crisis is both political and religious. He offers the book for universal peace.

Cheyne reprints a manifesto of the Society of Friends. Britain's war declaration of August 4, 1914, called it forth. He also praises the Bahai ideal of peace. That ideal reaches back to the time of the Bab. A dedication to his wife praises her poems. It praises their faith and their charity. Readers meet a scholar pleading across creeds in wartime.
the-religions-of-india-handbooks-on-the-: Edward Washburn Hopkins taught Sanskrit at Bryn Mawr College. He opens a handbook series on religions here. Morris Jastrow, Junior, edited the series. Edward Arnold published the volume at London in 1896. Copyright dates from the year before. A motto from the Mahabharata stands on the title page. It declares that nothing is nobler than humanity. Hopkins dedicated the book to William Dwight Whitney. Whitney's memory receives the honor. Only the series pages and title pages are present here. The dedication appears with them. The survey itself does not appear.
the-rivet-in-grandfather-s-neck-a-comedy: James Branch Cabell published his comedy of limitations in 1915. He dedicated it to Priscilla Bradley Cabell. Sonnets on stars fill the dedication pages. Falling stars struggle briefly in those verses. Polaris gleams steadfast and unchanged above them all. A motto addresses a new South in the book. That South builds daily on its valued past. Contents divide the novel into six parts. Propinquity, renascence, and appreciation name three of them. Souvenir and byways close the division list. Only the title pages and dedication verses are present here.
the-satyricon-volume-03-encolpius-and-hi:
Volume three of W. C. Firebaugh's unexpurgated Satyricon translation bears the title Further Adventures of Encolpius and His Companions. It opens at chapter the seventy-ninth. The same bracket code used in volume two marks the text. Forgeries of Nodot and Marchena are flagged, as are additions of De Salas.

Encolpius and Giton wander drunk in midnight silence, with no torch to light them. The district is unfamiliar, and their bleeding feet drag over flints and broken tile. Giton's cleverness rescues them at last. The prudent youngster had marked pillars and columns with chalk the day before. The white marks point out their way through the pitchy night. At their lodging, Trimalchio's courier smashes in the door for them.
the-scotch-twins: Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote and illustrated The Scotch Twins. Houghton Mifflin Company published it, and the copyright is dated 1919. The title pages place it in a geographical series of twins books. The Scotch volume is marked for grades five and six. The pages shown give the series lists and the start of the contents only. The first chapters are the little gray house on the brae, the rabbit and the gamekeeper, and the Sabbath.
the-sewerage-of-sea-coast-towns:
Henry C. Adams wrote The Sewerage of Sea Coast Towns for engineers. His contents list fifteen chapters. They begin with the formation of tides and currents. Observations of tides, current observations, and choosing an outfall site follow. The volume of sewage and gauging flow in sewers come next. Rainfall and storm water also appear.

Later chapters treat wind and windmills, the design of sea outfalls, and the action of sea water on cement. Diving and the discharge of sea outfall sewers follow. Trigonometrical and hydrographical surveying close the list. Adams's preface says the notes are meant primarily for engineers with a general knowledge of sewerage. Such men may be called on to prepare a scheme for a sea coast town, he writes.
the-shame-of-motley-being-the-memoir-of-:
Rafael Sabatini's The Shame of Motley presents the memoir of Lazzaro Biancomonte. Lazzaro was sometime fool of the court of Pesaro. Part one is called Flower of the Quince. Part two is The Ogre of Cesena. The contents promise a cardinal of Valencia, poison, and a fall of Pesaro. Ave Caesar closes the list.

Chapter one finds Lazzaro cooling his heels about the Vatican for three days. Suspense vexes him, he says. He had discharged the mission that brought him from Pesaro. Madonna Lucrezia had promised him honourable employment as his reward. The Cardinal of Valencia would grant it for his service to the House of Borgia, she said. Lazzaro wonders how long the cardinal will keep him waiting.
the-siouan-indians: W. J. McGee wrote The Siouan Indians as a preliminary sketch for the fifteenth annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology. The report covers 1893 to 1894. The Government Printing Office at Washington issued it in 1897, at pages 153 to 204. The pages shown give a detailed contents list and a section heading only. The list treats the Siouan stock, its definition, extent, and tribal names. Phonetic and graphic arts, institutions, and beliefs follow. Dakota-Asiniboin, Winnebago, Mandan, and Hidatsa are each named. No sketch text beyond the heading Definition appears.
the-spartan-twins: Lucy Fitch Perkins published this children's story in 1918, in seven chapters that take twin children from their farm to Athens and home again. The pages present here give the contents and a list of characters. Melas is a Spartan overseer on Pericles' farm on Salamis. His wife Lydia, their twins Dion and Daphne, and the slave girl Chloe join him. The philosopher Anaxagoras and Pericles himself also appear. The setting is the fifth century B.C., around its middle, so the story itself does not appear.
the-story-of-my-life-recollections-and-r: Ellen Terry, the celebrated actress, published her recollections and reflections with Doubleday, Page and Company in New York in 1909, dedicating the book to Edy. Only the title pages and the start of a contents list are present here. The list opens with a child of the stage from 1848 to 1856. Training in Shakespeare under the Charles Keans follows. Life on the road in a stock company comes next. Terry's memoir itself does not appear.
the-story-of-the-invention-of-steel-pens:
Henry Bore traces the invention of steel pens and describes the manufacturing process by which they are produced, in a London volume of 1890. Although steel pens are now familiar to nearly everyone, Bore observes, scarcely a dozen people could say when, where, or by whom they were first made by presses and tools.

One fact survives on record from Sir Josiah Mason: his friend and patron Samuel Harrison made a steel pen about 1780 for Dr. Priestley. The balance of testimony, Bore argues, credits mechanical manufacture by screw press to the third decade of the nineteenth century, through John Mitchell, Joseph Gillott, and Mason himself. He also gathers the Bible's early references to pens, most of them to the iron stylus, before the metallic pens of Greece and Rome.
the-story-of-the-living-machine-a-review:
H. W. Conn, professor of biology at Wesleyan University, reviews the conclusions of modern biology on the mechanism controlling living activity, in a work copyrighted in 1899 and issued by D. Appleton and Company in 1903 with fifty illustrations. His preface, signed from Middletown, Connecticut, in October 1898, begins with a saying often made without much thought: that the living body is a machine.

Conn distinguishes the strict comparison, which reduces living beings to simple mechanisms, from the loose use of the phrase with no sense of its significance. The machine idea of life carries great weight, he argues. Fifty years of study have brought the story far. A review of progress can now pay off. Unexplored realms and unanswered questions remain.
the-summons: A. E. W. Mason, author of The Four Feathers, published this novel with the George H. Doran Company under a 1920 copyright, dedicating it to those who served with him abroad through the four years of war. Only the title pages and the opening of a contents list appear in this record. The opening chapters cover the Olympic games. An anthem intervenes in one. Mario Escobar and the secret of Harry Luttrell follow. Hillyard's messenger closes the heads. The summons itself does not appear.
the-swiss-twins: Lucy Fitch Perkins wrote this children's story of Swiss twins. Only the Project Gutenberg etext header appears in this record. It names the title and author. It gives ebook number 3497, first posted in May 2001. The file was last updated in July 2007. Lynn Hill produced this eleventh edition. The archive's standard notices follow. They speak of copyright laws and keeping the file open for future readers. No page of Perkins's story itself is present here.
the-terrible-twins: Edgar Jepson's Terrible Twins, copyrighted in 1913 and published by Bobbs-Merrill of Indianapolis with illustrations by Hanson Booth, appears here as front matter and a contents list only. Fourteen chapters pair the twins with Captain Baster, guardian angels, a cats' home, a sacred bird, a landed proprietor, and the Muttle Deeping peaches. Picture captions show an archduke bellowing and Sir Maurice Falconer crying 'Cats for the cats' home!' The twins' mischief is fully advertised, though chapter one begins only as a heading in the pages present.
the-theory-of-social-revolutions:
Brooks Adams published The Theory of Social Revolutions in 1913, building it from an Atlantic Monthly chapter and new work on constitutional law. His prefatory note thanks Dr. M. M. Bigelow for criticizing the legal chapters. Adams insists he wrote for no political movement and no passing purpose. The book expresses convictions formed over two decades of study.

The contents announce his themes: the collapse of capitalistic government, limits of the judicial function, American courts acting as legislative chambers, and political courts. Adams, a historian of decline, turns on his own country's institutions here. Readers interested in early twentieth-century doubts about capitalism and the courts will find his case stated with unusual frankness from the first page.
the-tracer-of-lost-persons:
R. W. Chambers opens The Tracer of Lost Persons in 1906 with Mr. Gatewood, thirty-three, handsome, cultured, rich, and professionless at the Lenox Club. A man with a larger income than seems good for him and no work, he is a pessimist before breakfast. He has also concluded that the world's most attractive girls are vastly overrated, having seen them all. A club servant arrives with gilt buttons and a message from Mr. Kerns.

Kerns sends compliments and asks to have his coffee served at Gatewood's table. Gatewood twists his tie viciously, inserts a pearl scarf pin, and grants the favour with gloomy politeness. Chambers sets a bored bachelor, an insistent friend, and an epigraph from Heraclitus about harmony made of discords. The tracer of lost persons waits in the wings of this polished, melancholy opening.
the-two-captains:
Friedrich de La Motte-Fouqué's Two Captains opens on a mild summer evening on the shores of Malaga, where guitars wake among the ships, houses, and garden villas. Troops waiting to embark at dawn for Charles V's siege of Tunis forget sleep, singing military songs and drinking Xeres wine to the Emperor's long life. Only two companies are Spaniards; the third is pure German, and earlier banter over language has melted in the fellowship of approaching peril. Each side tries the other's tongue and helps the other through mistakes.

Apart from the merriment, young German captain Heimbert of Waldhausen reclines under a cork-tree, gazing at the stars in a mood unlike his usual cheer. The austere Spanish captain, Don Fadrique Mendez, approaches to beg a knightly service before sunrise. Fouqué, the author of Undine, sets a tale of brotherhood and sacrifice between two captains of opposed nations.
the-virginian-a-horseman-of-the-plains:
Owen Wister dedicates The Virginian to Theodore Roosevelt, noting that one page stands rewritten because Roosevelt blamed it. A letter to the reader then defends the novel as historical. Wyoming between 1874 and 1890, Wister argues, was a colony as wild as Virginia a century earlier, with scantier people and the same primitive joys and dangers.

Any faithful picture of a day and generation, he claims, is historical, whether its figures are real or imagined. The world pictured here has vanished: travellers can reach Cheyenne quickly, yet find no buffalo, no antelope herds, no horseman with pasturing thousands. The sage-brush looks unchanged, and a visitor waits for a rider who will never come again.
the-virginians: William Makepeace Thackeray inscribes The Virginians to Sir Henry Madison, chief justice of Madras, as an affectionate old friend, dating the inscription at London in September 1859. The subtitle calls the work a tale of the last century. Only the inscription and a partial contents list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. Early chapters bring one Virginian home to England and introduce the Esmonds in Virginia. Later headings promise family jars, preparations for war, and a Sunday at Castlewood. The list stops at chapter thirty-three.
the-water-of-life-and-other-sermons: Charles Kingsley's Water of Life and Other Sermons appears in an 1890 Macmillan edition. Its printing history reaches back to a first edition of 1867, with new editions through the seventies and eighties. The pages present here give the title pages and contents, so the sermons themselves do not appear. Eight sermons are listed with their scripture texts. The title sermon takes Revelation's invitation to the water of life, and a physician's calling follows from Matthew. Later sermons treat the wages of sin, the battle of life, and free grace.
the-women-of-the-french-salons:
Amelia Gere Mason's The Women of the French Salons begins with a modest preface. French writers such as Cousin and Sainte-Beuve had worked the field before her. Mason admits little wholly new remains to say. Old facts, she argues, can still be grouped afresh. Past life can also be measured by modern standards.

Her sources were memoirs, chronicles, letters, and manuscripts. She was struck by the mental vigor of salon women. Their influence reached far beyond their drawing rooms. Society life, she notes, has frivolities but also real power. Readers get a portrait of two centuries when French women shaped taste and thought.
the-world-english-bible-web-1-corinthian:
Paul's first letter to the Corinthians appears here as book forty-six of the World English Bible. Paul introduces himself as an apostle called through God's will. Sosthenes, a fellow believer, is named beside him. The letter addresses God's assembly at Corinth. Its greeting wishes grace and peace from God the Father.

Paul thanks God for gifts of speech and knowledge among them. He says the testimony of Christ was confirmed in that church. No gift, he assures them, is lacking there. A footnote explains that the word rendered brothers can include sisters. Readers get practical counsel for a gifted but troubled early church.
the-world-english-bible-web-2-corinthian:
Book forty-seven of the World English Bible carries Paul's second letter to Corinth. Timothy joins Paul in the greeting this time. The letter praises God as the Father of mercies. He comforts believers in all their affliction. That comfort, Paul explains, equips them to comfort others. Christ's sufferings overflow to his people, and so does his comfort.

Affliction and comfort both serve the church's salvation, Paul argues. Endurance grows from shared suffering. His hope for the Corinthians stands steadfast, he says. A footnote again notes that brothers can mean siblings. The letter blends deep feeling with defense of Paul's ministry.
the-world-english-bible-web-ephesians:
Paul's letter to the Ephesians forms book forty-nine of the World English Bible. It greets saints and faithful believers in Ephesus. Paul blesses God for every spiritual blessing in heavenly places. Believers were chosen before the world's foundation, he writes. Adoption through Jesus Christ was planned in love. Redemption comes through his blood, forgiving trespasses.

Grace, Paul says, overflowed toward them with wisdom and understanding. The letter moves from cosmic blessing to daily conduct. Church unity and household life both get attention later. Its first chapter soars in one long sentence of praise. Readers often treat Ephesians as a summary of Paul's deepest themes.
the-world-english-bible-web-galatians:
Galatians, book forty-eight of the World English Bible, opens with Paul defending his calling. His apostleship came through Jesus Christ, not through men. God the Father, who raised Christ from the dead, sent him. The Galatian assemblies receive grace and peace. Paul praises Christ, who gave himself for their sins. Deliverance from the present evil age is his aim.

Paul then marvels at their quick desertion. Some troublemakers, he says, are perverting the good news. No other gospel exists, he insists. Even an angel preaching otherwise would be cursed. A footnote clarifies that brothers may mean siblings. The letter burns with urgency over freedom and law.
the-world-english-bible-web-lamentations:
Lamentations stands as book twenty-five in the World English Bible, mourning a fallen city. Jerusalem sits solitary, once full of people. She has become like a widow, great among nations no more. At night she weeps with tears on her cheeks. None of her lovers comfort her now. Friends have turned treacherous and become enemies.

Judah has gone into captivity under affliction. She finds no rest among the nations. Zion's roads mourn because festival crowds no longer come. Her gates stand desolate and her priests sigh. Enemies prosper while she sits in bitterness. Five poems of grief follow this opening. Readers witness scripture lamenting catastrophe without easy consolation.
the-world-english-bible-web-romans:
Book forty-five in the World English Bible is Paul's letter to Rome. Paul calls himself a servant set apart for God's good news. That message was promised through prophets in scripture. It concerns God's Son, descended from David in the flesh. The resurrection declared him Son of God with power. Through him Paul received grace and apostleship.

The letter addresses all in Rome who are beloved of God. Their faith, Paul says, is proclaimed worldwide. Obedience of faith among all nations is his mission's aim. Systematic teaching on sin, grace, and Israel follows. Romans became Paul's most influential letter for later theology.
the-world-s-best-poetry-volume-10-poetic:
Volume ten of The World's Best Poetry, Poetical Quotations, opens with an essay by its managing editor. John Raymond Howard asks, after all, what poetry is. He begins by noting how much poetry gets written and lost. Bliss Carman served as editor-in-chief of the 1904 set. Four associate editors helped him sort poems by theme.

Earlier volumes covered love, nature, sorrow, and national spirit. This final volume gathers quotable lines and passages. Howard's essay defends poetry's value before the quotations begin. Readers who hunt for apt lines will find the volume handy. The anthology closes its ten-volume survey with poetry in its most portable form.
those-extraordinary-twins:
Mark Twain introduced Those Extraordinary Twins by confessing how hard novel writing is without a born gift for it. Contents promise chapters on the twins as they really were, Ma Cooper's confusion, a supernatural clock, an amazing duel, and Luigi's hanging. Twain says a tale tells itself as he listens.

He explains that Pudd'nhead Wilson began as farce, turned tragedy, and proved to be two tangled stories obstructing each other. He carried the manuscript across the Atlantic repeatedly before seeing the problem. Readers get Twain's comic workshop confession alongside the separated twin story itself.
thoughts-on-educational-topics-and-insti: George S. Boutwell wrote a book on schools and how they should be run, printed at Boston in 1859. He gave the book to the teachers of his state. In his gift page he praises their hard work and says they have helped learning grow. Only the title page and that gift page are on these pages, so his views on schools themselves do not appear.
three-prayers-and-sermons:
Jonathan Swift's Three Prayers and Sermons was transcribed from an 1889 Routledge edition of his works. Contents list prayers used by the Dean for Stella, plus sermons on mutual subjection, sleeping in church, and the wisdom of this world. The prayers date from Stella's last sickness in 1727.

Swift begs God to teach the languishing woman hope, repentance, and a sound mind. He asks that her good deeds to the naked, hungry, sick, and fatherless be remembered. Readers get intimate devotional prose from a famous satirist, written beside a deathbed rather than for public controversy.
timon-of-athens: Editorial notes by Michael S. Hart open this record, explaining why old spelling survives in Shakespeare texts. Printers packed type into cliches and ran short of letters, swapping u for v and using double v for w. Hart argues Shakespeare probably did not write in as many odd spellings as printers produced, despite signing his own name several ways. No scene from the play itself follows in what is present. Readers get the editor's defence of preserving canon errors, while the drama itself does not appear here.
toaster-s-handbook-jokes-stories-and-quo:
Peggy Edmund and Harold Workman Williams compiled a handbook of jokes, stories, and quotations for toastmasters, published in 1916 with introductions by Mary Katharine Reely. An opening essay considers the possession of a sense of humour. It quotes Hazlitt calling man the only animal that laughs and weeps.

Both responses, the essay argues, spring from seeing how far things fall short of what they should be. Thinkers laugh at life's incongruities while feelers weep, following Horace Walpole's line about comedy and tragedy. Readers get a practical speaker's treasury framed by a serious theory of humour.
town-and-country-sermons:
Sermon one in this collection, preached before the Queen, explains how to keep Passion Week from Philippians chapter two. The text says Christ, being in the form of God, emptied himself, took a servant's form, and became obedient to death on the cross. The preacher calls this Passion Week's keynote.

Christ's glory, he argues, came by the opposite means men use to show their own. False gods sat aloft enjoying themselves, careless of mankind, while Christ saved others and not himself. No author is named in what is present. Readers get Victorian preaching on obedience, unselfishness, and exaltation through humility.
twenty-five-village-sermons: Charles Kingsley, rector of Eversley and canon of Middleham, published Twenty-Five Village Sermons at London in 1849. The contents give each sermon a title and a scripture text. Sermon one, God's World, takes Psalm 104 and its praise of a rich earth. Sermon two, Religion Not Godliness, works from the same psalm's watering hills and grass for cattle. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here, so the sermons themselves do not appear.
twenty-two-goblins: Arthur William Ryder translated Twenty-Two Goblins from the Sanskrit, and the contents pose each tale as a riddle. Three lovers revive a dead girl, and the question is whose wife she should be. A girl transposes the heads of her husband and brother, and the riddle asks which joined body is her husband. Other tales ask who is to blame when poison from a hawk's claw kills a Brahman. Only the contents are present here, so the goblin tales themselves do not appear.
two-christmas-celebrations:
Theodore Parker, minister of the 28th Congregational Society of Boston, wrote The Two Christmas Celebrations as a Christmas story for 1856. It pairs the year one with 1855. The first celebration begins with Augustus Caesar's tax decree sending Joseph and Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem.

Parker tells the nativity plainly: a stable lodging, a child laid in the cattle's crib, and no certain day, month, or year. He follows Jesus home to Nazareth, where brothers James, Joses, Simon, and Judas grew up. The boy learned his father's trade of yokes and ploughs. Parker also counts the three languages of Judea, Syro-Chaldaic, Greek, and old Hebrew, and argues that Jesus understood all three.
un-ga-res-john-f-kennedy-s-address-befor:
Delegates of the eighteenth General Assembly heard John F. Kennedy on September 20, 1963, in what became the last major foreign address of his presidency. The Limited Test Ban Treaty had been signed that summer by the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union. Kennedy came to New York to build on that step.

The address hails the test ban and urges further curbs on nuclear arms. It proposes joint work in space, even a shared voyage to the Moon. It also speaks to new nations and the poor. Two months later Kennedy was killed, which lends the speech its lasting glow.
un-un-res-ahmadinejad-s-2005-address-to-:
Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, the new president of Iran, addressed the United Nations in 2005, weeks after taking office. Western states were pressing Iran over its nuclear program at the time. His speech gave Tehran's answer on the world stage, in firm and defiant terms.

Ahmadinejad defended Iran's right to develop nuclear energy for peaceful use. He accused the big powers of hoarding nuclear know-how while denying it to others. He also called for reform of the Security Council. The address set the tone for years of standoff between Iran and the West.
un-un-res-constitution-of-the-food-and-a:
Feeding a hungry world was written into the founding charter of the Food and Agriculture Organization, adopted in 1945. The FAO was the first specialized agency of the new United Nations. Its constitution set the agency's aims, members, and rules of work at the close of the Second World War.

The text pledges states to raise nutrition, improve farm output, and better the lives of rural people. It creates the conference, council, and director-general who run the agency. Every FAO program since rests on this charter, which makes it a root document of world food policy.
un-un-res-report-of-the-secretary-genera:
Paying for the first United Nations Emergency Force is the subject of this 1956 report of the Secretary-General, document A/3383. The force had been created in haste during the Suez Crisis, and no budget line existed for it. How to fund it fairly among member states was a hard, new question.

The report sets out the force's expected costs and options for sharing them. It deals with pay, supply, transport, and claims for harm or loss. The funding model worked out here shaped how later peacekeeping forces were paid for, a fight that still flares at the UN.
unconscious-comedians:
Honore de Balzac's Unconscious Comedians, translated by Katharine Prescott Wormeley, is dedicated to the Comte Jules de Castellane. The tale opens on Leon de Lora, a celebrated landscape painter. His Roussillon family, Spanish in origin and noble, has endured a century of proverbial hidalgo poverty.

Leon reached Paris with eleven francs in his pocket and starved as a rapin, a studio apprentice, before fame came. Readers of A Start in Life will remember him as Mistigris, Schinner's pupil. Now he owns a house in the rue de Berlin, belongs to the Institute, and sells pictures for their weight in gold. A provincial cousin's letter sets the comedy of unrecognized relations moving.
verses-and-translations: Verses and Translations, by a writer who signs only C. S. C., came out in a second edition at Cambridge in 1862. Deighton, Bell, and Company published it. Pages shown here hold the title page and contents only, so the poems themselves are not shown. The contents list light and grave pieces side by side. They name Visions, Gemini and Virgo, and a dirge. One ode treats a distant prospect of making a fortune. Charades, proverbial philosophy, and pieces named Beer and Ode to Tobacco add the light side.
weymouth-new-testament-in-modern-speech-:
R. F. Weymouth rendered First Corinthians in modern speech for the third edition of his New Testament, dated 1913. The book is number 46 in his set. Paul writes to the church at Corinth with Sosthenes named beside him. The letter thanks God for gifts of speech and knowledge in that church.

Paul soon turns to a hard problem, since word from Chloe's household reports sharp splits among the members. Each group, he says, has picked a side and a name to follow. Weymouth puts the Greek into clear, plain English of his own day. Readers can follow the letter's plea for unity verse by verse, with each verse numbered.

Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians comes in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech version, third edition, 1913. It is book 52 in the set. Paul, Silas, and Timothy send the letter together. They thank God for the church's work of faith and its labor of love.

The writers recall how the good news came with power, not words alone. Local believers then became a pattern for churches across Macedonia and Greece. News of their faith spread so far that no report was needed. Weymouth turns each verse into plain modern lines. Readers see a young church praised for hope that held firm under attack.

R. F. Weymouth gave Second Corinthians, book 47, in his modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Paul writes with Timothy to the church at Corinth and to God's people across Greece. The letter opens with praise for a God full of pity and comfort. Such comfort, Paul says, fits people to help others in pain.

Paul then speaks of deep trouble in Asia that left the team with no hope of life. That low point taught them to trust God, not themselves. God had saved them from death once, and Paul trusts he will do so again. Weymouth's clear prose lets the letter's raw feeling come through.

R. F. Weymouth placed Second Thessalonians as book 53 in his modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Paul, Silas, and Timothy write again to the church at Thessalonica. They give thanks that faith there grows fast and love keeps spreading. The church holds up well under harsh attacks.

That patience, the writers say, shows God's fair judgment at work. Those who cause pain will face pain in return. Rest will come when the Lord appears with his mighty angels. Weymouth sets the strong words in clear modern lines. Readers meet a church urged to stand firm while it waits.

Colossians is book 51 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Paul writes with Timothy to the believers at Colossae. He thanks God for their faith in Christ and their love for all God's people. That love rests on a hope stored in heaven.

The good news, Paul notes, bears fruit across the whole world, as it did among them. Epaphras, their teacher, brought word of their love back to Paul. Prayer follows, asking that they gain clear sight of God's will. Weymouth's smooth lines carry the letter well. Readers find warmth, thanks, and a call to grow in knowledge.

R. F. Weymouth made Ephesians book 49 in his modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Paul writes to God's people in Ephesus who trust in Christ. He blesses God for giving every spiritual gift in the heavenly realms. In love, he says, God chose them before the world began.

The plan was to adopt them as sons through Jesus Christ. Through his blood comes release and pardon for wrongs. God has also shared the secret of his will. All things in heaven and earth will find one head in Christ. Weymouth writes in rich but clear terms. Readers get a grand view of grace in a short space.

Galatians is book 48 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Paul writes to the churches of Galatia with heat. He says his call came from Christ and God, not from men. Christ gave himself for sins to free people from a wicked age.

Paul is shocked that the Galatians turn so fast to a changed message. No other good news exists, he insists, and those who twist it stand cursed. He denies that he seeks praise from men. His message came by a direct reveal from Christ, not by lessons from men. Weymouth's sharp, plain lines match the letter's urgent tone.

Philippians is book 50 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Paul and Timothy write to God's people at Philippi, with the church leaders named too. Paul thanks God each time he thinks of them. Their help with the good news has lasted from the first day.

He trusts that God, who began a good work in them, will finish it. Prison has not dimmed his warm bond with this church. His prayer asks that their love grow with clear sight and keen sense. Fruit of right living should fill their lives. Weymouth's fond, plain tone suits this most joyful of Paul's letters.

Romans is book 45 in R. F. Weymouth's modern speech New Testament, third edition, 1913. Paul calls himself a servant set apart to tell God's good news. That news, promised through the prophets, concerns God's Son. By birth the Son came from David's line, and by his rising he was shown to be God's Son in power.

Paul writes to God's loved ones in Rome, a city he longs to visit. News of their faith has spread through the whole world. He prays for a clear path to come and share some gift with them. Both sides, he hopes, will gain strength. Weymouth's dignified plain style fits the weight of the letter.
what-peace-means:
Henry van Dyke published What Peace Means in 1919, just after the Great War. He gave the book to his son Tertius, named as both son in faith and brother in work. The contents list three parts: peace in the soul, peace on earth through right living, and the power of an endless life.

Van Dyke opens with words of Christ from John's Gospel. Peace, he says, runs through both testaments like a golden thread. It rests at the heart of God's own nature. Prophets foretold it and psalm writers sang of it. Readers get a short, warm call to ground world peace in the soul first.
where-the-blue-begins:
Christopher Morley wrote Where the Blue Begins, a whimsical tale set in the Canine Estates. Gissing lives alone in a small country house with his Japanese butler, Fuji. A modest income from his family lets him live with cheer and no display. He has no car, no duties, and simple tastes.

At the country club he laughs to see married members slip home in the rain while he stays by the fire. Yet odd adventures find this settled bachelor all the same. A verse before the tale speaks of a leash turned to a tightrope. Morley gives readers a gentle fable of freedom, told with dogs in human roles.
xenophon-agesilaus-dakyns:
Xenophon campaigned under Sparta's King Agesilaus II and admired him deeply. His short Agesilaus praises the king as a model ruler, and H. G. Dakyns translated it into English. It ranks among the earliest royal biographies ever written.

Xenophon praises Agesilaus for bravery, plain habits, loyalty, and decency toward enemies. Campaigns in Asia and Greece show the king sharing hardship with his soldiers. The praise is one-sided, since Xenophon wrote as a devoted follower. Still, the portrait set a pattern later biographers copied for centuries. Dakyns's clear English carries the Greek across without fuss.
xenophon-anabasis-dakyns:
Xenophon's Anabasis recounts the march of the Ten Thousand through Persia around 370 BCE. H. G. Dakyns translated the famous narrative into English. Xenophon marched with the army and became one of its leaders.

Ten thousand Greek mercenaries found themselves stranded deep inside the Persian Empire. Their employer dead, they elected new generals and marched for home. Mountains, snow, and hostile tribes blocked the road to the sea. The shout of 'The sea, the sea' became literature's great homecoming moment. Xenophon's account doubles as a firsthand window onto the ancient Near East. Dakyns keeps the march at a soldier's pace throughout.
xenophon-apology-dakyns:
Xenophon wrote his Apology to record how Socrates defended himself at trial in Athens. H. G. Dakyns translated the short work into English. Athens had charged Socrates with corrupting the young and impiety.

Socrates refuses to beg the court for mercy or pity. He argues that death now spares him the decay of extreme old age. His calm before the hemlock impressed followers as proof of his teaching. Xenophon's version is shorter and plainer than Plato's famous Apology. Together they give two ancient voices on philosophy's most famous trial. Dakyns keeps the soldierly plainness of Xenophon's style.
xenophon-cavalry-general-dakyns:
Xenophon wrote The Cavalry General for the officer taking command of Athens' horsemen. H. G. Dakyns translated the brisk manual into English. Xenophon had led cavalry in real campaigns across Greece and Asia.

He covers choosing officers, training riders, and keeping horses fit and calm. Chapters treat scouting, orderly retreats, and keeping up the men's spirits. Religious duties and festival processions also belong to the commander's job. The advice stays practical throughout, with nothing merely theoretical. Dakyns's translation keeps the no-nonsense tone of a soldier instructing soldiers. Modern officers still recognize the leadership problems Xenophon names.
xenophon-cyropaedia-dakyns:
Xenophon's Cyropaedia imagines the education and rise of Cyrus the Great of Persia. H. G. Dakyns translated the long work into English. Part adventure tale and part handbook for rulers, it shaped political writing for centuries.

The young Cyrus learns justice, endurance, and command among Persian boys. As king he wins loyalty through fairness and shared hardship rather than fear. Xenophon uses Persia to ask how good rulers are made. Ancient kings studied the book, and Machiavelli read it closely later. It is less history than a mirror for princes. Dakyns's old-fashioned English suits its heroic glow.
xenophon-economist-dakyns:
Xenophon's Economist, or Oeconomicus, stages Socrates discussing how to run a household well. H. G. Dakyns translated the dialogue into English. In ancient Greek, economics meant managing a home and estate.

Socrates questions a young landowner about training servants and storing grain. Keeping accounts and ordering work receive careful, practical attention. The landowner's wife appears as a true partner in managing the estate. That partnership struck readers as unusual for ancient Greece. The dialogue ranks among the earliest works of economic writing anywhere. Dakyns's version reads like easy, good-humored conversation. The talk stays plain and warm from start to end.
xenophon-hellenica-dakyns:
Xenophon's Hellenica continues Greek history where Thucydides' famous account breaks off unfinished. H. G. Dakyns translated the seven books into English. The narrative covers nearly fifty years, down to 362 BCE.

Readers follow the end of the Peloponnesian War and Athens' surrender. Sparta rises to dominance, overreaches, and falls to Thebes at Leuctra. Xenophon writes as a soldier who knew many of the actors personally. His Spartan sympathies show, and some major events receive puzzling silence. Even so, no other continuous account survives for these years. Dakyns keeps the narrative moving briskly.
xenophon-hiero-dakyns:
Xenophon's Hiero stages a conversation between a Sicilian tyrant and the poet Simonides. H. G. Dakyns translated the dialogue into English. Hiero of Syracuse explains why absolute power has made him miserable.

The tyrant describes fear, flattery, and loneliness instead of expected pleasures. He cannot trust friends, enjoy travel, or sleep without guards. Simonides answers that a ruler serving his people might earn genuine love. He sketches reforms in policing, prizes, and public works. The dialogue stands among antiquity's frankest examinations of unchecked power. Dakyns's translation keeps the exchange sharp and readable. It is brief, blunt, and hard to put down.
xenophon-memorabilia-dakyns:
Xenophon's Memorabilia collects his recollections of Socrates in conversation over four books. H. G. Dakyns translated the work into English. Xenophon knew Socrates personally and wrote partly to defend his memory.

Athens had executed Socrates for corrupting the young and denying the gods. Xenophon answers by showing Socrates advising generals, craftsmen, and know-it-alls helpfully. His Socrates teaches clear thinking, self-control, and decent conduct in practical terms. This Socrates feels less lofty than Plato's, more like a man one might meet. Dakyns lets that down-to-earth voice come through plainly for modern readers.
xenophon-on-horsemanship-dakyns:
Xenophon wrote On Horsemanship from a cavalryman's lifetime of experience with horses. H. G. Dakyns translated the treatise into English. It is the first complete guide to riding and horse care that survives.

He explains how to judge a young horse before buying it. Fitting the bridle, training gently, and keeping a mount calm follow in order. Xenophon also treats stable management, grooming, and common injuries of war horses. His rule against anger in training still sounds modern and humane. Horse people quote his advice after more than two thousand years. Dakyns preserves the plain, expert voice throughout.
xenophon-on-revenues-dakyns:
Xenophon's On Revenues proposes how Athens could fill its treasury without new citizen taxes. H. G. Dakyns translated the short pamphlet into English. Athens faced money troubles after years of war and lost empire.

He urges working the silver mines at Laurium more intensively with public slaves. Better harbor facilities and honors would draw foreign traders to Piraeus. Public buildings and a merchant fleet could earn steady income for citizens. The plan reads like an ancient policy memo, hopeful and detailed. Some proposals were tried, others ignored by the assembly. Dakyns keeps the businesslike tone of the original pamphlet.
xenophon-polity-athenians-lacedaemonians:
Two short studies of Greek government stand side by side in Dakyns's translation. One sketch describes the constitution of Athens, the other that of Sparta. Tradition assigns both to Xenophon, though scholars debate the Athenian piece.

The Athenian sketch coolly explains why democracy served Athens' sea empire well. It sounds grudging, as if written by a critic admitting democracy works. The Spartan sketch admires the laws and training behind Sparta's soldiers. Lycurgus's discipline, common meals, and austere education receive warm praise. Together the pair gives priceless snapshots of rival constitutions. Few short texts teach Greek politics so efficiently.
xenophon-sportsman-dakyns:
Xenophon's Sportsman, or Cynegeticus, teaches hunting with hounds to young Greek gentlemen. H. G. Dakyns translated the treatise into English. For Xenophon, hunting trained men for war and for life itself.

He covers picking hounds, training them, and reading the tracks of game. Setting nets and standing firm before a charging boar receive detailed instruction. Reflections on courage, discipline, and honoring the hunt's gods interrupt the practical tips. Xenophon defends hunting against critics who called it a waste of time. Dakyns's translation carries the outdoorsman's enthusiasm of the original Greek throughout.
xenophon-symposium-dakyns:
Xenophon's Symposium places Socrates at a rich young man's dinner party in Athens. H. G. Dakyns translated the dialogue into English. Wine, dancing girls, and a comic strongman entertain the guests between speeches.

Socrates steers the talk toward love, beauty, and what makes a life worthwhile. Guests praise their own talents, and Socrates jokes about his looks and dancing. The tone stays lighter and livelier than Plato's famous Symposium. Xenophon's version feels like an actual evening among friends. Dakyns keeps the banter sparkling in translation. Readers get Socrates laughing, not only lecturing, for once.
